The loves and emotions of the mind in general.—The love of understanding and of being wise.—The love of knowing secrets; wonder.—The love of knowing the future.—The love of good and of evil.—The affirmative and the negative.—Conscience.—The highest good and the highest truth.—The love of virtues and of vices.—Honesty.—Decorum <note>proper behavior and etiquette</note>.

That the rational mind is what properly defines a human being.

### **CHAPTER XVIII.—FREE WILL, OR THE CHOICE OF MORAL GOOD AND EVIL (numbers 351-377),..................................................................*page* 219**

What liberty consists of.—The first liberty is the ability to withdraw the mind from bodily things.—The second liberty is the ability to learn from sacred and other writings, and from reflection, that there is a spiritual and divine reality above us, and thus to acquire an intellectual faith.—The third liberty consists in using established means, namely, the sacred rites of religion.—The fourth liberty consists in knowing what is the highest good and in choosing what is best.—Seven reasons why freedom is granted to the human will, even though it causes so much unhappiness to the human race.

### **CHAPTER XIX.—THE WILL AND ITS LIBERTY: AND THE NATURE OF THE INTELLECT (numbers 378-400), .......................................*page* 244**

The intellect, viewed in itself, has Truth as its object.—The analytic and synthetic methods <note>approaches to reasoning from parts to whole, or whole to parts</note>.—Rational logic.—The "will" generally refers to the mind, but specifically refers to a particular mental state or a focused love.—The mind thinks when it considers means to an end; it judges when it arranges those means in their proper order; finally, it concludes or desires, and this conclusion is called the "Will."—The liberty of the mind consists only in this: that it can choose to obey or not obey the intellect.—All will aims for an effect which contains a goal, and is therefore a future event.

<meta>This page begins the Translator's Preface, detailing Emanuel Swedenborg's lifelong scientific and philosophical quest to discover the nature of the soul. It outlines the specific "doctrines" he developed as tools for this search and traces how this specific volume fits into his larger series of published works.</meta>

<page-num>vii</page-num>
<header>TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.</header>

# TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.

From the author’s statement in his preface to the treatise on the Soul, as well as from the general character of his scientific and philosophical writings, it is unmistakably clear that the search for the soul was the real goal and inspiring motive of all his labors.

The passion with which he sought this precious knowledge is shown by the frequent early drafts and preliminary essays scattered through his writings. In these, he records his partial glimpses of the subject and pursues, as it were, the fleeting vision of a sublime figure that always seemed to elude his grasp.

For example, in his prologue to the work titled *The Animal Kingdom* <note>original: *Regnum Animale*; Swedenborg's anatomical study of the "kingdom" of the soul, the body</note>, the author publishes a "Summary of his intended work." In this outline, after a series of anatomical studies, he places an "Introduction to Rational Psychology." He remarks that this section consists of "new doctrines through which we may be led from the material organism of the body to a knowledge of the soul, which is immaterial." These are: the doctrine of Forms, the doctrine of Order and Degrees, the doctrine of Series and Society, the doctrine of Inflow <note>original: "Influx"; the way spiritual forces act upon the physical</note>, the doctrine of Correspondence and Representation, and lastly, the doctrine of Modification.

The author had actually already provided this "Introduction to Rational Psychology" in the first part (chapter 8) of the *Economy of the Animal Kingdom* <note>original: *Oeconomia Regni Animalis*</note>, published several years earlier. In the proposed summary, the introduction was to be followed immediately by the *Rational Psychology* itself. This work was meant to cover "the subjects of Action, of the external and internal senses, of Imagination and Memory; also of the emotions <note>original: "affections"</note> of the lower mind <note>original: "animus"; the seat of worldly passions and sensory perception</note>, of the intellect (that is, of thought and will), and of the emotions of the rational mind, as well as instinct. Finally, it would cover the Soul—its state in the body, its interactions, emotions, and immortality—and its state when the body dies. The work was to conclude with a Comparison <note>original: "Concordance"</note> of Systems."

In the series as it was actually published, however, we find the "Introduction to Rational Psychology" followed by chapters 1 and 2 of the second part of the *Economy*. These chapters treat the motion of the brain and its cortical substance <note>the gray matter or outer layer of the brain</note>. These are then abruptly followed by a chapter on the human soul. At the start of that chapter, the author refers to his previous effort "to explain a doctrine of Series and Degrees as a way of introducing a knowledge of the—"

<summary>The translator explains that Swedenborg's entire scientific career was driven by a search for the soul, utilizing a specific set of philosophical "doctrines" to bridge the gap between anatomy and psychology.</summary>
<keywords>Emanuel Swedenborg, Rational Psychology, The Animal Kingdom, Economy of the Animal Kingdom, Soul, Influx, Correspondence, Animus, Cortical Substance</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the Translator's Preface, quoting Emanuel Swedenborg on his struggle to understand the soul through pure philosophy versus physical anatomy. It introduces his belief that a new "universal science" combined with empirical evidence is necessary to bridge the gap between the visible world of effects and the invisible world of causes.</meta>

<page-num>viii</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

soul." "I could not help but think," he says, "along with humanity in general, that all our knowledge of the soul was to be sought through pure philosophical reasoning, or more directly through the anatomy of the human body. But upon making the attempt, I found myself as far from my goal as ever. No sooner did I seem to have mastered the subject than I found it eluding my grasp again, though it never absolutely disappeared from my view. Thus, my hopes were not destroyed, but only delayed."

Speaking of the doctrine of Series and Degrees as only teaching "the distinction and relation between things superior and inferior, or prior and posterior," and as being unable "to express in its own suitable terms those things which go beyond the realm of familiar objects," he declares the necessity of our having recourse to a Mathematical Philosophy of Universals. He describes this as a kind of universal science to which all other sciences and arts are subject, and one which "advances through their innermost mysteries as it proceeds from its own principles to causes, and from causes to effects, by its own natural order." 

"But even if we assume," he continues, "that the doctrine of Order and the science of Universals were brought to the height of perfection by the human mind, it does not follow that we would, by these means alone, gain knowledge of everything that can be known. For these sciences are only supporting tools, serving as a concise method with mathematical certainty to lead us—through constant abstraction and higher levels of thought—from the lower to the higher realm; or from the visible world of effects to the invisible world of causes and principles. 

Therefore, for these sciences to be useful, we must turn to experiments and the evidence of the senses. Without these, they would remain mere theories and simple potentials to help us. . . . . . . . For these reasons, I am strongly convinced that the essence and nature of the soul, its inflow <note>original: "influx"; the way spiritual forces act upon the physical</note> into the body, and the body's reaction back upon it, can never be proven without these doctrines [of Series, Order, and Universals], combined with a knowledge of anatomy, pathology, and psychology. It even requires a knowledge of physics, especially regarding the natural atmospheres <note>original: "auras of the world"; Swedenborg's term for the subtle physical forces or ethers</note>. Unless our work follows this path and rises up from observable facts, we will have to build new systems in every new age, which will in turn collapse without any possibility of being rebuilt. . . . . This, and no other, is the reason that I have investigated the anatomy of the body—especially the human body, as far as it is known from experience—with diligent study and intense focus. I have followed the anatomy of all its parts in the same way I have investigated the gray matter <note>original: "cortical substance"</note> here. 

In doing this, I may have gone beyond the usual limits of inquiry, so that only a few of my readers may be able to understand me clearly. But I felt obligated to venture this far, for I have resolved, whatever the cost, to discover the nature of the human soul." He

<summary>Swedenborg argues that discovering the soul requires more than just philosophy or anatomy; it demands a "Mathematical Philosophy of Universals" combined with empirical scientific observation. He explains that without grounding universal doctrines in physical experience, scientific systems will continually collapse and fail.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Translator's Preface, concluding a quote from Swedenborg regarding the necessity of using the right means to reach a desired end. It discusses his realization that his early attempt to define the soul was premature and outlines his systematic plan to study the entire human body—the "Animal Kingdom"—as a way to eventually understand the soul.</meta>

<page-num>ix</page-num>
<header>TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.</header>

"...therefore, anyone who desires the end goal must also desire the means to reach it." He then proceeds to arrange into chapters what he calls "the first fruits of my psychological labors."*

The reverence and cautious modesty that consistently balance the author’s passion for his sublime goal are evident in his comments four years later. In his work *The Animal Kingdom* <note>original: *Regnum Animale*. In Swedenborg's usage, this refers to the "Kingdom of the Soul" (*anima*), specifically the human body as the soul's domain, rather than the modern biological category of animals.</note>, he mentions this same "Introduction <note>original: "Prodromus"</note> on the Human Soul." He writes:

> "Not long ago, I published *The Economy of the Animal Kingdom* <note>original: *Oeconomia Regni Animalis*. "Economy" here refers to the functional organization and management of the body's systems.</note>, a work divided into distinct treatises. However, it dealt only with the blood, the arteries, the heart, and the movement of the brain and its outer layers <note>original: "cortical substance"</note>. Before exploring the entire field in detail, I made a quick transition to the soul and published an introductory work regarding it. But upon deeper reflection, I realized that I had headed toward that goal both too hurriedly and too soon, having only explored the blood and its specific organs. I took that step driven by an intense desire for knowledge. However, because the soul operates in the highest and most internal things, and does not reveal herself until all her protective layers <note>original: "swathings"</note> have been unfolded one by one, I am determined to allow myself no rest until I have traveled through the entire 'animal kingdom' to reach the soul. In this way, I hope that by continually moving inward, I shall open all the doors that lead to her, and finally contemplate the soul herself, by Divine permission" (Prologue to *The Animal Kingdom*, no. 19).

Accordingly, in the work *The Animal Kingdom*, the author proceeds to examine the various parts of the human body in detail, omitting those already covered in the *Economy*—namely, the heart, the vessels, and the blood (Prologue to Part III, *An. King.*, no. 469). Part I deals with the organs of taste and digestion, the glands, the gall bladder, the kidneys, and so on. Part II deals with the internal organs of the chest <note>original: "Viscera of the Thorax"</note>, or the organs of the upper region. Part III covers the skin, the senses of touch and taste, and organic forms in general. It is worth noting that the brain is neither mentioned by the author as having been "fully treated" in the *Economy*, nor is it included in the three parts of *The Animal Kingdom* as they were translated and published in the volumes under that name. The treatises on the brain, which hold such a prominent place in the author's planned summary of his works, were intended by him to form the next section, or Part IV of *The Animal Kingdom*. This is clear from his statement at the end of section 468 in the Prologue to Part III. The extensive manuscripts left by the author covering this major division of his work have been partially brought to light through the translations of Dr. J. J. G. Wilkinson.

...and are currently in the process of being translated and published in their entirety under the editorship of Dr. Rudolph L. Tafel.*

At the close of the Prologue mentioned here, the author once again suggests his intention “to rise by degrees to the highest level, from which we may logically derive the principles of things, and where we may speak of the soul with relative certainty and clarity.” He does this so that, from the higher knowledge gained, he may more intelligently address a subject that—according to his original plan—would belong here: the subject of reproduction <note>original: "generation"</note> and “the organs through which new forms are conceived in the image of the form that preceded them.” 

He carried out this intention in his work on *The Brain*, where he states the “soul resides in its principles” <note>original: "principia"</note> within the brain's outer gray matter <note>original: "cortical or cineritious substance"</note> (*The Animal Kingdom*, no. 468). He also addressed this in the treatises edited in Latin by Dr. Immanuel Tafel (Tubingen, 1848). These were also titled “Part IV of *The Animal Kingdom*,” which covers the carotid arteries, the senses of smell, hearing, and sight, sensation and emotion <note>original: "affection"</note> in general, and the intellect and its operations. We have added an abstract of these treatises, which were previously untranslated, to the present work as Appendix II. This includes the author’s *Final Summary on the Senses* <note>original: "Epilogue on the Senses"</note>, or sensation in general; his *General Explanation regarding Sensation and Emotion*; his *Rules of Harmony and Music*; and his *Conclusion regarding the Intellect and its Operation*.

Returning now from these first principles back to the body, as he had promised, the author discusses the following in the subsequent parts of *The Animal Kingdom*: the membrane covering the bones and the breasts <note>original: *De Periosteo et de Mammis*; edited by Tafel, Tubingen, 1849</note>; and reproduction and its organs <note>original: *De Generatione, de Partibus Genitalibus utriusque sexus, et de Formatione Foetus in Utero* (On Generation, the Genital Parts of Both Sexes, and the Formation of the Fetus in the Womb); edited by Tafel, Tubingen, 1849. Translated by Wilkinson, London, 1852</note>. 

Finally, after surveying the entire field of human anatomy and physiology, he arrives at the treatise now offered to the reader: the long-awaited *Rational Psychology* itself. According to his plan in the Prologue to *The Animal Kingdom*, this work was meant to conclude the entire series. It was intended to “comprise the subjects of Action; of the external and internal senses; of imagination and memory; also of the emotions of the lower mind <note>original: "affections of the animus"; in Swedenborg's philosophy, the "animus" refers to the lower, sensory mind, while the "mens" refers to the higher rational mind</note>; of the intellect (that is, of thought) and of the will; of the emotions of the rational mind; also of instinct; and lastly of the soul—its state in the body, its interactions, its emotions, and its immortality, and its state after the body dies.” 

All of the subjects named here are addressed under their proper headings in this current work, with the exception of “Action.” A separate treatise on that subject, along with other short papers, was published in both Latin and an English translation in—

<meta>This page continues the Translator's Preface, providing a bibliography of Emanuel Swedenborg’s shorter psychological works and his own explanation for why his research was published in separate installments rather than a single volume.</meta>

<page-num>xi</page-num>
<header>TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.</header>

This was published in London, 1847, by Dr. J. J. G. Wilkinson under the title *Posthumous Tracts*. Besides the treatise on *Action* and another on *Sensation, or the Passive State of the Body* <note>original: "Passion of the Body"; here "passion" refers to the body's capacity to be acted upon by external stimuli</note>, this volume contains three brief essays <note>original: "transactions"</note>, all directly related to the subject before us. These were evidently written at different times and before the date of the present work. These three include: a brief essay titled *The Way to a Knowledge of the Soul*; a paper in four chapters on *The Origin and Propagation of the Soul*; and a significantly long treatise called a *Fragment on the Soul*.

Even as early as 1734, in the work titled *Outlines on the Infinite*—which immediately followed his major work, the *Principia*—the author devotes the second part of the treatise to a *Philosophical Argument on the Mechanism of the Interaction <note>original: "Intercourse"</note> between the Soul and the Body.*\*

Finally, among these preliminary looks at the great subject he aimed to address, we should mention two chapters on *The Soul* and *The Chain and Bond of Uses*. The latter treats the cerebrum <note>the main part of the brain</note> as the medium of interaction between the soul and the body. These are found in Codex 58 of the Manuscripts (*Photolithographed MSS.*, vol. vi., pp. 81-92) and were inserted by Dr. Rudolph L. Tafel in volume I of the work on *The Brain* mentioned above (see page 13).

An explanation for these frequent, scattered, and unfinished essays on the soul is found in the author's address to the reader, which introduces the *Fragment on the Soul* mentioned above. He says:

> "I was for some time in doubt whether to include all my long meditations on the soul and the body—and their mutual action and reaction <note>original: "passion"</note>—in a single volume, or whether it would be better to divide the work into sections and publish it sequentially <note>original: "seriatim"</note>, in the manner of scholarly reports <note>original: "transactions"</note>. My goal is to declare the nature of the soul, to show its state, to demonstrate the mutual interaction and actions existing between it and the body, and the connection of each with each in the bonds of harmony. In other words, I intend to display—philosophically, analytically, geometrically, and anatomically—the entire kingdom of the soul <note>original: "animal kingdom"; from the Latin *anima*, meaning soul</note> and its parts, along with the functions and duties of each. This is a labor of several years and must extend over several volumes... I have thought it most prudent to divide the labor and to take up my pen at short intervals, allowing myself an occasional rest to catch my breath and attend to my other duties. For the mind is just like a pen: too much use blunts its point and wears away its precision. This, gentle reader, is the reason I will return to my self-prescribed task at frequent intervals and appear before you often—probably no less than five or six times a year—with my publications, which may properly be called *Psychological Transactions*. By this means I hope, after a few years, to reach my goal and be in a position to explain the state of the soul when its connection with the body is ended by death and it is left to its own disposal."

That the work now before us, *On the Soul* <note>original: "De Anima"</note>, is the author's long-delayed *Rational Psychology* and the final summary of all his studies—

***

\* *Outlines of a Philosophical Argument on the Infinite, etc., by Emanuel Swedenborg. Translated from the Latin by James John Garth Wilkinson; London, 1847.*

<meta>This page continues the Translator's Preface, specifically arguing that the present work is the intended conclusion to Swedenborg’s anatomical and philosophical series, the *Animal Kingdom*.</meta>

<page-num>xii</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

It seems clearly evident that this work is the conclusion and peak of the great series titled the *Animal Kingdom* <note>original: *Regnum Animale*; Swedenborg used this term to mean "The Kingdom of the Soul," referring to the human body as the soul's domain</note>. This is apparent from how the contents align with the subjects mentioned in the final sections of the author’s planned outline for his work. It is also shown by the nearly constant references in his shorter works to a more complete and final volume yet to come, and by the clear statement in the author’s own preface to this book. In that preface, he explains that only after finishing his study of human anatomy does he now feel capable of truly moving forward and uncovering the previously hidden knowledge of the soul itself. He refers to his preliminary studies, including the *Introduction to a Rational Psychology*, as being complete; and "so now, at last," he writes, "we may treat of the soul from principles, or synthetically" <note>A "synthetic" approach in philosophy involves starting from established principles to explain specific facts, rather than working backward from observations (the "analytic" method)</note>. Finally, whereas he previously warned both himself and his readers against daring to enter the sacred boundaries of this supreme knowledge too early, he now boldly invites them to enter. He believes that his readers, if they have chosen to follow him this far, "will perceive what the soul is, what its state is in the body, and what its state is after the life of the body."

It seems remarkable that a work representing the peak and conclusion of Swedenborg’s entire series of scientific and philosophical writings remained hidden in manuscript form for a hundred years before being discovered and published in the Latin edition by Dr. J. F. Immanuel Tafel. It is hardly less surprising that nearly half a century has passed before an English translation was provided. The immense importance of this work is plain to see from the evidence we have presented—whether we judge it by the high value the author himself placed on the subject matter, or by the diligence and passion with which he pursued the exhausting studies necessary to produce it.

We wish to add a few thoughts on its value, viewed in terms of how this work relates to the history of philosophy in general, and specifically to the later theological portion of the author’s writings.

As we remarked at the start, the single desire and goal driving the entire series of Swedenborg’s scientific and philosophical writings was his "search for the soul." This single aim provides the key to understanding Swedenborg’s mission in the worlds of science, philosophy, and theology.

The twofold goal of his search was to know the nature of spirit and its relation to matter—or, as the author frequently phrases it, "a knowledge of the soul and of its interaction <note>original: "intercourse"; meaning the communication or connection between the spiritual and the physical</note> with the body." If we view the body as the "larger body" (the natural world) and the soul as the "larger soul" (the spiritual world), the knowledge of the soul and its interaction with the body becomes the same as the knowledge of the spiritual world and its relation to the natural world. This is primarily the subject of the descriptive parts of the author’s theological writings.

<summary>The translator argues that this work is the intended climax of Swedenborg's scientific career, finally transitioning from anatomical study to a "synthetic" philosophical explanation of the soul's nature and its relationship with the physical body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Translator's Preface, detailing Swedenborg's methodology for studying the soul through anatomy and introducing his central philosophical concept, the Doctrine of Correspondence.</meta>

<page-num>xiii</page-num>
<header>TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.</header>

Where did he seek this knowledge of the soul? 

In its own realm: in the living (rather than the dead) human body; in the "kingdom of uses," as shown in the beautiful order, harmony, and activities of human anatomy and physiology.

To Swedenborg, the "Animal Kingdom" <note>original: *Regnum Animale*; Swedenborg used this title to mean the "Kingdom of the Soul," derived from the Latin *anima*, meaning soul or breath of life</note> meant the kingdom of the *soul*—the realm over which the soul presides as queen.

The relationship of this soul to her body (her own kingdom and world) was what he first sought to understand; through that, he hoped to know the nature of the soul herself. While the knowledge he gained through these labors was not everything he aimed for, it nonetheless prepared his mind in a unique and superior way to receive a greater understanding of the true nature of spirit and the relationship between the spiritual and natural worlds.

The doctrine of <term>Correspondence</term> <note>The concept that every physical thing has a spiritual counterpart or cause to which it responds</note> was revealed to Swedenborg as a science through natural means, not supernatural ones. It was a conclusion reached through his own reasoning and a part of his own philosophy, much like his doctrines of Order, Series, Degrees, and Modification, upon which it is based. This is clearly shown by his own statements* and by his frequent use of and references to these doctrines throughout his scientific writings.

The doctrine of Correspondence became clear to Swedenborg while he was searching for the way the soul interacts with the body. It was here, within the province of the human soul, that our author found the key that would solve the mystery of the ages. This key would open the human mind to a truly heavenly knowledge of the relationship between the spiritual and natural worlds, spirit and matter, earth and heaven, the written Word <note>The Bible</note> and eternal truth, and between humanity and God.

To Swedenborg, "Correspondence" meant, in its first sense, the way the body fits its physical environment; then, it meant the way the soul within fits its physical environment—its nerves and senses.

The history of this doctrine of Correspondence takes us back to the beginnings of Greek philosophy and highlights the relationship between Swedenborg and Aristotle. Swedenborg himself outlined the historical background of the doctrine of <term>Influx</term> <note>The flow of life or influence from the soul into the body</note>, or the interaction of the soul and body, in several of his theological works. He did so most notably in his brief but wonderful treatise *On the Intercourse of the Soul and the Body* <note>original: *De Commercio Animae et Corporis*</note>.

Swedenborg deserves the title of the *Aristotle of modern philosophy* more than any other writer. Just as Aristotle, with his scientific method of drawing conclusions from observation, succeeded the abstract idealism of Plato, Swedenborg followed the theoretical and abstract systems of Descartes in France and Leibniz and Wolff in Germany. Swedenborg arrived with his strictly practical...

<meta>This page continues the Translator's Preface, comparing Swedenborg’s scientific and philosophical methods with those of Aristotle. It explores how both thinkers used observation and experience to study the soul, while also introducing the different historical theories on how the mind and body interact.</meta>

<page-num>xiv</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

method, his reasoning from experience, climbing the ladder of knowledge from observation <note>original: *a posteriori*; reasoning from observed effects to discover their causes</note> up to the higher and internal principles. From those principles, he could then descend back into a true philosophy of nature and of humanity. The overlap between the research of Aristotle and Swedenborg regarding the soul is striking to any historian. This is seen not necessarily in the similarity of their findings—though there are remarkable instances of this—but in their similar methods and ways of approaching the deeply hidden object of their search. Both used the experimental method, and this led them into very similar paths of investigation. 

As evidence of this, consider the contents of the series of Aristotle's writings in which his work *On the Soul* <note>original: περὶ ψυχῆς (*peri psyches*)</note> occurs. They are as follows: four books on the *Parts of Animals*; five books on the *Generation of Animals*; to which are added treatises on the *Walking of Animals*, on the *Motion of Animals*, and on the *Spirit*. There are also three books on the *Soul*; to which are added treatises on *Sense and the Sensitive*; on *Memory*; on *Sleep and Dreams*; on *Length and Shortness of Life*; on *Youth and Old Age*; on *Life and Death*; and on *Respiration*. 

So that our reader may compare at a glance the methods of discussion as well as the thoughts advanced by these two great psychologists of inductive reasoning <note>Inductive reasoning starts with specific observations to reach broad conclusions</note>—the leaders of ancient and modern learning respectively—I have thought it appropriate to include as an appendix to this work a series of random extracts from Taylor’s translation of Aristotle’s *On the Soul* <note>original: *De Anima*</note>, etc. (see Appendix III).

Swedenborg’s admiration for his illustrious master and predecessor in inductive research was great. He assigned Aristotle the highest place among the world’s great teachers, as shown by the titles he often and endearingly used when referring to him, such as the “Chief Philosopher of the Gentiles” and “Our Philosopher.”* Yet, Swedenborg was no blind follower of even so revered a teacher, nor did he hesitate to differ from him on the important question of how the body and soul interact.

Historically, three doctrines had prevailed in the learned world regarding the interaction of mind and matter. The first, which Swedenborg called **Physical Influx**, was taught by Aristotle and later by the Schoolmen <note>Medieval theologians and philosophers who taught in European universities</note> during the early period of Christian learning. After this came the doctrine of **Spiritual or Occasional Influx**, as taught by Descartes and his followers. Finally, Leibnitz introduced his doctrine of **Pre-established Harmony**†, which he believed was the only way to reconcile the two. Swedenborg, agreeing fully with none of them, sought to reconcile all three by extracting and combining the truth within each. The resulting theory he named the **Doctrine of Correspondence**, a doctrine which rests upon equally philosophical...

<meta>This page continues the Translator's Preface, specifically discussing how Swedenborg’s scientific doctrines of Series, Degrees, and Correspondence form the logical foundation for his later theological and spiritual works.</meta>

<page-num>xv</page-num>
<header>TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.</header>

and scientific doctrines of Series, Orders, Degrees, and Modifications. Correspondence, as seen from the perspective of nature alone—and it was only on this level that Swedenborg had discovered it up to this time—consists of a mutual adaptation of inner and outer, higher and lower, coarser and more refined spheres or bodies. This adaptation allows for the reception, communication, and transfer of motions and affections from one to the other. It is, therefore, the name we give to that kind of interaction <note>original: "intercourse"</note> which is not a physical flowing in <note>original: "bodily influx"; a philosophical term for the way one substance influences another</note>, or to a union that exists not by a blending or merging of substances, but by being side-by-side <note>original: "contiguity"</note> and by the changing of states. It is the relationship of the flowing waves of ether to the eye; of the eye to the sensory fiber; of the fiber to the cortical gland <note>Swedenborg used "cortical glands" to refer to the individual units of the brain's gray matter, which he believed were the primary seats of sensation and action</note>; of the gland to the common sensory <term>common sensory</term><note>The *sensorium commune*, or the part of the brain where all sensory input was thought to be integrated</note>; of the sensory to the imagination; of the imagination to the intellect; of the intellect to the soul; and of the soul to God. Through correspondence, the outer affects the inner without becoming one with it; through correspondence, things totally different in degree and in substance are nevertheless so adapted that motions or trembling vibrations in one may be continued through the other, or converted into some change in the other's state. In this way, the soul corresponds in general and in every specific detail to its body.

This doctrine of Correspondence, which Swedenborg learned from studying the human body and its relationship to the soul, was afterward applied by him to all things material and spiritual, and thus to both the natural and spiritual worlds.

<margin>*</margin> <note>This description of the doctrine of Correspondence is limited to how it appears in nature or through natural observation. For a full explanation of the doctrine's real significance and its universal application, the reader should refer to the author's works *Divine Love and Wisdom*, the *Doctrine of Sacred Scripture*, etc.</note>

Does it therefore follow that what Swedenborg presented in his theological writings as divinely revealed is, after all, reducible to purely natural and scientific knowledge? Swedenborg made no claims to any supernatural insight <note>original: "illumination"</note> while developing these doctrines of Correspondence, Degrees, and Series in his scientific works; and yet, the entire system of spiritual metaphysics found in his theological works rests logically on these very doctrines. The answer to this question is a matter of great importance, as it involves the whole nature of the insight Swedenborg claimed to have, and the relationship between his philosophical and his theological (or "inspired") writings.

We believe a brief answer may be stated this way: It is not the *concept* of Correspondence that is revealed or discovered supernaturally, but *the knowledge of the specific things that correspond to one another*.

Like the sciences of arithmetic, algebra, and logic, the science of Correspondence is a product of human reasoning. Indeed, Correspondence may truly be called the very logic of the universe, or of creation itself. But as mere logic or mere mathematics, it would be completely barren of results if there were no field of...

<meta>This page concludes the translator's discussion on how Swedenborg transitioned from using his scientific doctrines (like Correspondence and Degrees) to analyze the natural world to using them to understand the spiritual world. It highlights that while the "essence" of the soul remained a mystery to him, its practical operations became clear.</meta>

<page-num>xvi</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...experimental knowledge to which to apply it. This experimental knowledge is found in two areas <note>original: "planes"</note> of experience—the physical and the spiritual. Spiritual experience—the knowledge gained from things heard and seen in the spiritual world—was granted to Swedenborg by Divine permission. This provided the true, highest, and final field for applying those great sciences he had developed through years of intense study in the schools of nature. No one is more clear or emphatic than Swedenborg himself in defining the difference between a "doctrine" as a method and the actual knowledge to which that doctrine is applied.* We should not be surprised that when these doctrines (originally scientific formulas) were later filled with living knowledge—clothed in the facts of the spiritual world and the lives of its inhabitants—all his former knowledge seemed insignificant to him. Even the doctrines themselves, when illustrated only by nature, seemed like empty shadows. The senses whose phenomena were to be the field of exploration for the doctrines of <term>Correspondence</term> and <term>Discrete Degrees</term> were the senses of the spiritual body. Through this experience, the nature of the soul was truly learned in the spiritual world; it was never discovered by Swedenborg in this natural world, or by the deductions of logic alone. Once the soul was seen and known in its true nature there for the first time, the way it interacts <note>original: "mode of intercourse"</note> with the world of matter was detected at a glance by using his existing knowledge of <term>Influx</term>, Degrees, and Correspondence.

What, then, is the real gain achieved in the present work? The author virtually confesses in a remarkable statement in section 524 of this book that, even after all his laborious efforts, he has not attained a satisfactory knowledge of the essence of the soul itself, and that what he proposes is merely a series of guesses based on logic:

> "But these things are among the secrets; they are nothing but conjectures. Who has seen these things? Reason alone suggests them. When we live as souls, we will perhaps laugh at ourselves for having guessed so childishly." <note>original Latin: "Sed haec in secretis sunt ; non nisi quam conjecturae sunt ; quis haec vidit, ratio haec solum suadet. Quando animae vivimus, nos ipsos fortassis ridebimus, quod tam infantiliter divinaverimus."</note>

But while the substance of the soul still remains a secret, its way of interacting with the body—particularly in the outward levels of its life—is presented here with incredible depth. He also explains the soul's manifestations in the conscious acts of the imagination, the intellect, and the will with a clarity that has rarely, if ever, been matched by psychological writers of any age. The physiological basis of psychology is presented here with the exactness of a mathematical proof. The subjects of Innate Ideas, Instinct, the Freedom of the Will, and the Higher and Lower Minds are all explained through an argument that is both logical and beautiful, making the study of these difficult themes a delight.

But even these features are of secondary importance when compared—

<page-num>xvii</page-num>
<header>TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.</header>

...knowledge, achieving a great primary gain: the author’s clear understanding of the doctrine of <term>Correspondence</term> <note>The belief that everything in the natural world has a corresponding spiritual cause or meaning.</note>, along with its related doctrines of Series, <term>Degrees</term> <note>Distinct levels of existence, such as the relationship between an end (purpose), its cause, and the final effect.</note>, Orders, Uses, and Society. In these grand logical structures, we find the foundations of a truly spiritual science—a theology that makes the knowledge of God a <term>positive knowledge</term> <note>Knowledge based on certain facts rather than abstract speculation.</note>. This is achieved not by dragging the Divine down to a material level, but by illuminating the material and natural world with a heavenly light and showing it to be driven by a Divine presence.

While we argue that it is the knowledge of the things that correspond that is supernatural in Swedenborg’s disclosures, and not the science of Correspondence itself, we feel it is worth distinguishing more carefully than readers usually do between "revelation" in its highest sense and "knowledge." Revelation, in its strictest sense, refers to the opening of the spiritual meaning of the Bible. Knowledge of the spiritual world comes from "things heard and seen." While these experiences are truly supernatural, they cannot be called *revealed* in the *same sense*.

It has been common to treat the author’s accounts of "things heard and seen" in the spiritual world and his explanation of the internal meaning of the Scriptures both as "revelation." But according to the author himself, there is a clear distinction between these two types of truth. Strictly speaking, the only things that should be called "revelation" are those doctrines which the author declares he received "not from any angel but from the Lord alone while reading the Word." In these instances, truth is taught <term>synthetically and a priori</term> <note>original: "synthetically and a priori"; reasoning from general principles or causes to specific facts or effects.</note> in the fullest and most sublime sense. On the other hand, the knowledge the author shares from his own experience—from being consciously admitted into the spiritual world—is knowledge gained by a purely experimental method. Therefore, it is just as <term>inductive and analytic</term> <note>original: "strictly inductive and analytic"; reasoning from specific observations to reach general conclusions.</note> as the knowledge gained in any branch of natural science. This fact distinguishes Swedenborg’s theology from all previous theological writing; it gives his work not only a strictly scientific form but a factual content that is absolutely free from speculative theories.

This twofold character of his writing is shown in the titles of his various works. For example, the title of the *Heavenly Secrets* <note>original Latin: *Arcana Coelestia*</note> reads as follows: "*Heavenly Secrets which are in the Holy Scripture or Word of the Lord, uncovered; here first those which are in Genesis. Together with the Wonders which were seen in the World of Spirits and in the Heaven of Angels.*" <note>original: "Arcana Coelestia quae in Scripturae Sacra seu Verbo Domini sunt, detecta ; hic primum quae in Genesi. Una cum Mirabilibus quae visa sunt in Mundo Spirituum et in Coelo Angelorum."</note> The inner truths of the Word are "uncovered" (*detecta*), while the things of the spiritual world are "seen" (*visa*). In the same way, his explanation of the Book of Revelation in the New Testament is called *The Apocalypse Revealed*: "*The Apocalypse Revealed, in which the Secrets are uncovered which were predicted there and which until now have lain hidden.*" <note>original: "Apocalypsis Revelata, in qua deteguntur Arcana quae ibi praedicta sunt et hactenus recondita latuerunt."</note> Here again, mysteries are "uncovered" in the fullest sense of revelation, and these uncov—

<page-num>xviii</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

[The] revealed things of the Word <note>original: "Word"; refers to the Bible.</note> are the primary source of that doctrine which the writer gave to the churches as truly "descending from God out of heaven." Therefore, in his tract entitled *The New Jerusalem and its Heavenly Doctrine, from things heard from heaven* <note>original: "ex auditis e Caelo"</note>, he gives this explanation in the introduction regarding the doctrine to follow: "This also is from heaven, being from the spiritual sense of the Word, which is the same as the doctrine that is in heaven" (no. 7). And in the *Brief Exposition of the Doctrine of the New Church, signified by the "New Jerusalem" in the Revelation*, he says in the opening paragraph that, "The Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> having been revealed," he is prepared to lay before the world "a complete view of the doctrine" of the Lord’s new church.

In calling attention to this distinction in the contents of Swedenborg’s spiritual writing, it is not our intention to detract in the least from the validity of one class as compared with the other. Rather, we mean to maintain, even in this higher realm of his labors, the same distinction between the analytic and the synthetic, and between the experimental and the *a priori* <term>a priori</term> <note>Knowledge that comes from theoretical deduction or "absolute truth" rather than from observation.</note>, which characterizes his researches and his teaching everywhere. The ladder planted on earth seems to lose itself in the dazzling heights of heaven, but it remains a ladder of twofold passage—of both ascent and descent. 

Just as we have climbed from the body to the soul and its substantial world, so from that world—as a new basis of actual experimental knowledge—we climb to those principles of essential truth, love, and life which constitute that "internal sense of the Word which is in heaven." From there, only one further vision remains for the adoring soul: the one that reaches up to Him who is the eternal Word, who in the beginning "was with God and was God, and by whom all things were made." 

And yet, his writings acquire their synthetic unity, their *a priori* authority, and their power as revelation solely because this truth was constantly descending into the author’s mind—truth which he "received from the Lord alone, while reading the Word," and from no angel or spirit. We behold the eye seeing the face of its own Creator in the light. In all this splendid accumulation of scientific and philosophic knowledge, and in this laboriously acquired method and these secondary sciences, we see the most perfect instrument capable of being constructed out of the elements of human reason. It is the divinely prepared organ and the living, responsive human agent by which a true *science of God* was to be made possible for humanity, and things previously concealed were to be made known. 

Even in the world beyond, there will still remain axioms, necessary assumptions, and *a priori* truths. The realm of revealed knowledge will remain as entirely distinct from experimental knowledge there as it is here. But just as certainly, there will be a world of actual sensory life where knowledge will be acquired by observation, and reason will find a higher and nobler field of exercise than it has ever found in all the heights and depths of nature. Even in the spiritual world, what is revealed remains forever distinct...

<page-num>xix</page-num>
<header>TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE.</header>

...from what is "heard and seen." It would be possible for any person, if God permitted, to have conscious knowledge of the spiritual world by the opening of their spiritual senses, as was the case with the prophets and evangelists, with Paul, and with Swedenborg. What they might communicate about things heard and seen in that world might indeed seem to us—and could worthily be called—a supernatural or miraculous kind of knowledge. Yet, it would consist of things entirely within the scope of human observation and discovery, even if of an extraordinary kind. 

Revealed truth, however, is different; it can come from only one source—the Word <note>The Bible</note>, where God speaks through it to a mind that is worthy and capable of receiving such a revelation. Therefore, the relationship between Swedenborg's scientific (or inductive) writings and his theological writings is explained by a similar, more subtle relationship: the connection between his descriptive experiences and his formal religious doctrines. In the former, we find truths presented in an inductive or "ascending" order; in the latter, they are in a deductive order, descending from universal principles to practical application and proof.

After all, ultimate knowledge and ultimate discovery exist only in God and come only from God. Just as all life comes from God alone, so does all truth and all knowledge; therefore, in one sense, all knowledge is revelation. However, we are allowed to acquire some knowledge from external sources "as if by ourselves" so that we can enjoy the individuality and personality necessary for us to have any moral or rational character. Meanwhile, there are other kinds of knowledge that can only be given to us through that revelation where God clearly speaks, while human senses and human reason listen and obey. In this way, we are kept mindful of God and our own limitations, preventing us from desiring to "become like gods, knowing good and evil." Thus, a horizon is always opening above us, inviting us to endless aspiration, longing, hope, and worship.

It is true that Swedenborg fell short in his quest to find the actual quality and substance of the soul within nature; however, this is a fact for which both he and the world have reason to be grateful. If he had reached that goal too soon, his career would have ended there. While the soul remained hidden like an undiscovered continent, he was busy constructing a "great ship" within this massive series of works. This ship would eventually carry the bold navigator across unknown waters to his destination. Using this ship—the sublime <term>doctrine of Correspondence</term> <note>Swedenborg's system of symbolism teaching that every natural object corresponds to a spiritual reality.</note>—and guided by the favoring winds of heaven, he was carried to the great world of spiritual substance and spiritual life. From there, using that same wonderfully built vehicle, he brought back a clear account of this new and fascinating realm. He enabled people to read the deep <term>arcana</term> <note>original: "arcana"; hidden mysteries or secret knowledge.</note>, which had been hidden but are now revealed, and which exist equally in the natural world and in the Word of God.

Finally, does the science of today have anything to learn from the lesson of Swedenborg's heroic labors and their results? Is it the lesson of...

<meta>This page concludes Frank Sewall's preface, reflecting on whether Swedenborg’s scientific search for the soul was a failure or a necessary step toward a higher spiritual understanding.</meta>

<page-num>xx</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...a sublime tragedy, of a vast hope crushed, of a magnificent structure that fell because it reached too close to the skies? In other words, should we regard the stupendous scientific and philosophical achievements of Swedenborg as worthless, seeing that they failed to bring him to his desired goal—a true knowledge of the soul? 

We interpret the lesson of these pages very differently. The message they give is one of cheer and hope. They speak to the science of today just as they did to the science of a century ago, offering the glorious promise of a reward even greater than the one sought. They speak of a goal that was blindly pursued through the "ascending ladders" of knowledge; when that goal is finally reached, it fills and lights up all lower forms of science with a light, warmth, and beauty that was previously inconceivable. 

For all truth is one. Human science on every level is simply a container for higher and more divine forms of truth, wrapped in those which are lower and easier for man’s varying intelligence to grasp. Every scientific fact and every true philosophical conclusion is a stone laid and a scaffold raised for the building of that great temple in which humanity will one day worship its Creator and its God. Into this natural knowledge—which the Bible describes as *“all kinds of precious stones”* <note>A reference to Revelation 21:19, suggesting that natural truths are the foundation for spiritual ones.</note>—the light of Divine revealed truth shall flow. In this way, the glory of God shall illuminate the entire realm of the human intellect. 

The scientists of today, with their careful study of the facts of physical knowledge, are building more wisely than they know. Their own specific aims and the particular theories they try to prove are of secondary importance—they are like toys <note>original: "baubles"</note> placed before a child to encourage it to learn to walk. Even the selfish motives of pride and glory are useful for stimulating minds that might otherwise be idle or lazy to achieve great things. How much more powerful, then, is the sincere love of truth for its own sake, and the desire to truly advance humanity, which inspires the minds of many of our greatest thinkers and workers! 

As in the case of Swedenborg, Divine wisdom knows how to use the results of human research and study for its own ends, which are the ultimate elevation and blessing of mankind. Not only is the earth made new by these efforts, but "new heavens" are also created where righteousness shall live. In that society and kingdom of useful service <note>original: "kingdom of uses"</note>, humanity shall realize the purpose of its creation and the true glory of God.

->**FRANK SEWALL.**<-

->**URBANA, OHIO, Oct. 22, 1886.**<-

<header>LATIN EDITOR'S PREFACE.</header>

## PREFACE OF THE EDITOR OF THE LATIN EDITION.

The original manuscript of this work, published after the author's death, was one of **three** I was able to borrow in 1848 through the generosity of the Royal Academy at Stockholm. The learned librarian of that institution described the manuscript as follows:

> “This book, written in Swedenborg’s own handwriting, contains 130 leaves in a large folio format <note>original Latin: *fol. max.*, short for *folio maximo*, indicating the largest standard size of paper.</note>. On the spine, it bears the title (printed by the binder) ‘*Physiology and Metaphysics*’ <note>original: *Physiologica et Metaphysica*</note>, and it carries the same title in our library's old manuscript catalog. Folio 110 is missing, which makes it uncertain whether this *Dissertation on the State of the Soul*, etc., is complete or not. For the same reason, the heading and beginning of the next dissertation, found on folios 111 and 112 (page iv), are also missing. . . . . . The rest of this book, from folios 118 to 127 (page xx), is taken up by a dissertation titled ‘*Ontology*’ <note>original: *Ontologia*</note> at the top of folio 118. From the start of this dissertation, certain subjects are discussed generally and then treated individually under various headings. . . . . . Regarding the style of treatment, the opinions of Christian Wolff <note>original: "Wolf"; referring to the influential German Enlightenment philosopher Christian Wolff (1679–1754).</note>, Baron, and others are usually stated first, followed by the author’s own opinion or a hint of it. However, like many other works in Swedenborg’s manuscripts, this Ontology is incomplete; it is only a draft that the author intended to expand later. The entire book is written in a tight, and in some places cramped, handwriting, making it difficult to read and translate.”

In accordance with the decision of our Society (the Swedenborg Association, founded in 1845), which sponsored these three publications, we have omitted the attached folios 118–127, titled *Ontology*, from the present treatise. The chapters of that omitted dissertation are: (I.) Form, Formal Cause; (II.) Figure; (III.) Organ, Structure; (IV.) State, Changes of State; (V.) Substance; (VI.) Matter, Material; (VII.) Extent, Extension, Continuous, Neighboring, Part; (VIII.) Body, Corporeal; (IX.) Essence, Essentials; (X.) Attribute; (XI.) Predicate; (XII.) Subject; (XIII.) Affection; (XIV.) Accidents; (XV.) Contingencies; (XVI.) Modes, Modification.*

---

\* This valuable dissertation is now available to English readers. It was translated and published in 1880 in a volume titled “*Ontology*; by Emanuel Swedenborg. From a Photolithographic copy of the Original Latin Manuscript still preserved in the Library of the Academy of Science at Stockholm. Translated by Philip B. Cabell, A.M., Professor of Ancient Languages in Urbana University. Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1880.”

<page-num>xxiii</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTORY ESSAY.</header>

## AN INTRODUCTORY ESSAY ON SCIENCE AND THEOLOGY IN THE WRITINGS OF SWEDENBORG.

The single desire and goal evident throughout all of Swedenborg’s scientific and philosophical writings can be briefly described as his "Search for the Soul."

This is indicated in the fragmentary treatises *On the Soul* <note>original: *De Anima*</note> that frequently appear throughout his series of works. It is also manifest in the plan for his projects outlined in his prologue to the *Animal Kingdom* <note>original: *Regnum Animale*; Swedenborg used this Latin term to mean the "Kingdom of the Soul," focusing on the anatomy of the living body.</note>. In that plan, the soul forms the final part of the great series. The subject is to be approached slowly, through difficult steps—reverently and in awe of its majesty, yet with an eager and tireless desire.

This desire was fulfilled, to the extent that the scientific and philosophical resources of human knowledge allowed, in *On the Soul* <note>original: *De Anima*</note>, or *Rational Psychology*. This was the work on the soul with which Swedenborg concluded his distinguished career as a scientist, summarizing the results of his labors in the fields of natural, physiological, and psychological science.

In this search for the soul, we find what we might call the key to the developmental origin <note>original: "genetic development"; referring here to the way the system grew and evolved from its starting principles.</note> of Swedenborg's entire system. I use the word "development" because it implies a unity between what comes before and what follows, and suggests that final results are shaped by certain inner goals, even if those goals are pursued unconsciously. The process is like that of nature which, though unconscious itself, hides a most profound, definite, and unerring purpose.

To understand the nature of spirit and its relationship to matter—but especially through first gaining "a knowledge of the soul and of its interaction <note>original: "intercourse"; referring to the communication or reciprocal relationship between the soul and the physical body.</note> with the body"—was the double goal of our author's constant search.

If we now view the "body" in terms of a larger body—the natural world—and the "soul" as a larger soul—the spiritual world—then "the knowledge of the soul and its interaction with the body" becomes identical with the knowledge of the spiritual world and its relationship to the natural world. This topic occupies a prominent place in his later theological writings.

Where did Swedenborg seek this knowledge of the soul? He sought it in the soul’s own realm—the Soul-Kingdom <note>original: *Regnum Animale*</note>; in the living human body, rather than a dead one; and in the "kingdom of uses" as shown in the beautiful order, harmony, and activities of human anatomy and physiology.

<summary>This introductory essay identifies the "Search for the Soul" as the unifying theme of Swedenborg's scientific works, culminating in his "Rational Psychology" and bridging the gap between his physiological studies and later theology.</summary>
<keywords>Search for the Soul, De Anima, Regnum Animale, Rational Psychology, soul-body interaction, spiritual world, physiology, Emanuel Swedenborg</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory essay, exploring how Swedenborg’s scientific studies of the human body and the "animal kingdom" (meaning the kingdom of the soul) laid the groundwork for his later spiritual philosophy and his influence on modern psychology.</meta>

<page-num>xxiv</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

To Swedenborg, the "animal kingdom" actually meant the "kingdom of the soul" <note>original: *anima*</note>—the realm over which the soul presides like a queen. What he sought to understand was the relationship between this soul and its body, or its own kingdom and world. The knowledge he gained pre-eminently prepared his mind to receive a deeper understanding of the true nature of spirit and the relationship between the spiritual and natural worlds. 

By influencing his contemporary, Immanuel Kant (see *Kant's Inaugural Dissertation*; *On the Sensible and Intelligible World* <note>original: *De Mundo Sensibili et Mundo Intelligibili*</note>; also Professor Vaihinger’s *Commentary on Kant*, vol. ii.; *Archive for the History of Philosophy* <note>original: *Archiv fur Geschichte der Philosophie*</note>, Berlin, 1895; and Professor Heinze’s *Observations on Kant's Lectures on Metaphysics* in the *Transactions of the Saxon Society of Sciences* <note>original: *Abhandl. Sachs. Gesellsch. der Wissenschaften*</note> Leipzig, 1894, etc.), Swedenborg's doctrine of the "Two Worlds" can be said to have formed the foundation for modern transcendental psychology. This is the branch of modern idealism that grants the spiritual and supernatural a substantial, causal existence that is distinct from physical matter.

When we consider the massive role this doctrine of the human body and soul plays in his later teachings—specifically regarding the "Divine Humanity," the nature of heaven, and the order that prevails there—we begin to see the providential importance of these scientific works. We see how these sciences serve as the basic foundation for his entire system of spiritual doctrine. Because the body can only be studied within its own environment—as a part of that great "extended body" which is the entire physical universe—Swedenborg’s exhaustive survey of this physical foundation is evident in his massive system, as seen in his works on *Chemistry* (1721) and the *Principia* (1734).

Swedenborg first derived his "Doctrine of Correspondence" <note>the idea that every natural thing has a spiritual counterpart or cause</note> naturally—that is, as a science. It was a logical deduction of his own reasoning regarding how the different elements of the universe relate to one another. It was a core part of his own philosophy, just like the doctrines of Order, Series, Degrees, and Modifications <note>terms Swedenborg used to describe how life and energy flow from higher spiritual levels down into lower physical levels</note> upon which it rests (see *Animal Kingdom* <note>original: *An. King.*</note> ii., 50, 51, 250).

This is clearly visible from his own statements and from the way he repeatedly applied and referenced these sciences in his *Animal Kingdom* and elsewhere—especially in his *Introduction to Rational Psychology* and in the work itself.

The Doctrine of Correspondence became clear to Swedenborg while he was searching for the way the soul communicates with the body. It was right here, in the province of the human soul—in the relationship between our souls and our bodies—that Swedenborg found the key to solve the "problem of the ages." This key opens our minds to a truly heavenly knowledge of how the spiritual world relates to the natural world: how spirit relates to matter, earth to heaven, the written Bible to eternal truth, and humanity to God.

In its first and most basic sense, "Correspondence" meant to Swedenborg the way the body corresponds to the physical environments surrounding it, and subsequently, how the soul within corresponds to the surrounding body.

<summary>This page explains that Swedenborg’s study of the soul and body (the "Animal Kingdom") provided the scientific framework for his later theological doctrines and influenced modern transcendental psychology, particularly through the concept of "Correspondence."</summary>

<page-num>XXV</page-num>
## INTRODUCTORY ESSAY

The history of the doctrine of Correspondence leads us back to the origins of philosophy among the Greeks and highlights the relationship between Swedenborg and Aristotle. Swedenborg himself outlined the historical precedents of the doctrine of Influx—the interaction between the soul and the body—in several of his theological works, especially in his brief but remarkable book *On Intercourse, etc.* <note>original: *De Commercio*</note>, or the *Intercourse of Soul and Body*.

Swedenborg, perhaps more than any other writer, deserves the proud title of the "Aristotle of modern philosophy." Even though he assigned Aristotle the highest place among all the great teachers—calling him the "prince of philosophers" and using the almost endearing title "our philosopher"—he did not hesitate to disagree with him on the vital question of the interaction between mind and matter. He did so first on philosophical grounds, and later from the perspective of revealed spiritual knowledge. The three systems of psychology that had dominated the learned world before his time were represented by three philosophers whom Swedenborg described meeting in the spiritual world (as recounted in the work *On Intercourse*): Aristotle, Descartes, and Leibniz. These three systems sought to explain the relationship between mind and matter—the central problem Swedenborg set out to solve and to which his entire series of philosophical works is devoted. These three systems are known as:

->**I: Physical Influx**<-
->**II: Occasional or Spiritual Influx**<-
->**III: Pre-established Harmony**<-

Swedenborg sought to reconcile these three views by extracting and combining the core truth found in each. The resulting doctrine he named the "Doctrine of Correspondence." This doctrine rests upon the equally philosophical and scientific principles of **Series, Orders, Degrees, and Modifications**. 

Correspondence, as seen on the level of nature, is the mutual adaptation of the internal and external, the higher and lower, and the more gross or more subtle spheres or bodies. It allows for the reception, communication, and transfer of motion without the different bodies mixing together or becoming confused. It is, therefore, the name we give to the kind of interaction that can exist between things that are necessarily and perpetually distinct <note>original: discrete</note>. This interaction is not a "material influx" (where matter itself flows in), but rather a pathway for the influx of force. It is interaction by contact <note>original: contiguity</note> rather than by a continuous merging <note>original: continuity</note> or confusion of substances.

Examples of such correspondence in nature include:
1. The relationship of the ether wave and its spiral motion to the eye as the organ of vision;
2. Then the eye to the sensory fiber within;
3. Then the sensory fiber to the cortical gland <note>Swedenborg viewed these small "glands" in the gray matter of the brain as the primary units of nervous activity</note>;
4. Then the cortical gland to the inner common sensory of the imagination;
5. Then the imagination to the **intellectory** <term>intellectory: Swedenborg's term for the "pure intellect" or the seat of rational thought, acting as a bridge between the imagination and the soul</term>;
6. Then the intellectory to the soul; 
7. And finally, the soul to God. 

*By correspondence, the internal may affect the external without mixing with it or becoming one with it.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the doctrine of Correspondence, exploring how Swedenborg transitioned from a scientific understanding of the human body to a theological system involving spiritual and natural worlds.</meta>

<page-num>xxvi</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

*with it.* By correspondence, things that are completely different in degree or substance are still so well-matched that vibrations in one can be carried through the other. In this way, cause and effect are possible through physical contact <note>original: "contiguity"</note>, because the extension of an effect (or its movement backward within its own level) never actually turns it into its own cause.

Swedenborg first learned this doctrine of correspondence by studying the human body and its relationship to the soul. He later applied it to everything—both material and spiritual—and thus to the natural and spiritual worlds.

If this is true, then what exactly is "revealed" in Swedenborg's writings? Is there anything that is not, after all, simply the result of human logic and philosophy? Does it follow that the "divinely-revealed science" in his theological works can actually be reduced to purely natural scientific knowledge? After all, in his philosophical works, Swedenborg claimed no supernatural inspiration <note>original: "illumination"</note> for his doctrines of Degrees and Correspondence—yet these doctrines form the entire foundation for the spiritual metaphysics <term>metaphysics: the branch of philosophy dealing with the fundamental nature of reality, including the relationship between mind and matter</term> found in his theological works. The answer to this question is extremely important, as it involves the entire relationship between Swedenborg's scientific and philosophical writings and his theological ones.

We believe it is possible to phrase the answer this way: It is not the *concept* of Correspondence itself that is supernatural or revealed, but the knowledge of *which specific things* correspond to one another. Likewise, it is not the *concept* of Discrete Degrees <term>discrete degrees: distinct levels of existence (like end, cause, and effect) that do not blend into one another but act together</term> that is supernatural or revealed, but the knowledge of the specific things that make up those degrees. (Regarding the fact that the knowledge of Degrees was originally a philosophical discovery, see *Animal Kingdom*, volume 1, numbers 10, 11, 133; volume 2, number 333.)

Swedenborg spoke about Correspondence in this way after his spiritual awakening. In *Arcana Coelestia* <note>original: *A.C.* (Heavenly Secrets)</note>, number 1523, he states that:

> "The ear corresponds to the air and to sound; the eye is formed to correspond to the movements <note>original: "modifications"</note> of the ether and light; and all the organs and internal parts <note>original: "viscera"</note> correspond to things found in nature."

In *Arcana Coelestia*, number 5131:

> "There is a correspondence between sensory things and natural things; between material things and spiritual things; between spiritual things and celestial <note>original: "celestial" refers to the highest level of heaven or the heart's love</term> things; and between celestial things and the Lord. There is a sequence of correspondence from the Divine down to the lowest level of Nature. It is known from philosophy* that the 'end' <term>end: the purpose or goal (Latin: *finis*)</term> is the first part of the cause, and the cause is the first part of the effect.
> "The effect must correspond to the cause, and the cause must correspond to the end. Because they correspond, the end can exist within the cause and act—"

<note>* The author is likely referring to the doctrine taught by Aristotle in his *Metaphysics* concerning the four elements involved in a thing's existence: the first cause or end (purpose); the instrumental cause; the form; and the matter. All of these are united to become one in the final effect. (Aristotle's *Physics* <note>original: *Physicorum*</note>, book 2, chapter 7).</note>

<summary>This page explains that while Swedenborg discovered the logical framework of "Correspondence" and "Degrees" through scientific study of the body, his later theological works revealed the specific spiritual realities that fit into those frameworks. It distinguishes between the philosophical structure of reality and the revealed contents of the spiritual world.</summary>
<keywords>Correspondence, Discrete Degrees, Swedenborg, Aristotle, Metaphysics, Arcana Coelestia, cause and effect, spiritual metaphysics</keywords>

<page-num>xxvii</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTORY ESSAY.</header>

...and the cause can be within the effect and set it in motion; consequently, through the cause, the effect can activate itself. Everything in man and nature follows a sequence, like cause and effect, and when they correspond to each other in this way, they act as one."

Compare this doctrine with the scientific statements regarding the "Intercourse of the Soul with the Body," found in the work *The Soul*, chapter 12.

At the close of Swedenborg’s philosophical period of writing, the soul—like an undiscovered continent—remained hidden from his view. However, the great ship that was to carry the bold navigator there was already built. It was constructed with supreme human skill by his marvelous mind, secretly guided by the Divine hand. On that ship—the sublime science of Correspondence—and fueled by the favoring winds of heaven, he was carried to the great new world of spiritual substance and spiritual life. From that vantage point, using the same vehicle, he has made this new and interesting country understandable to us. He has enabled us to read the deep mysteries <note>original: "arcana"</note>, previously hidden but now revealed, which lie equally in all things of nature and in all things of the Word of God.

The fact that the relationship between his scientific and theological systems is one of natural development <note>original: "genetic"</note>—an orderly growth and evolution—is perhaps the most wonderful aspect of Swedenborg’s teachings. It is the most perfect illustration and support of his wonderful doctrine of Discrete Degrees <term>Discrete Degrees: Swedenborg’s concept that reality is organized into distinct levels (like end, cause, and effect) that do not shade into one another but act together by correspondence</term>. His science is not theological, and his theology is not scientific; yet they are related by a perfect correspondence. He was so opposed to any *a priori* <term>a priori: reasoning based on theoretical deduction rather than observation or experience</term> system of science—that is, a science constructed to fit a preconceived theory—that he would not even trust his own experiments in natural science. Instead, he used those of other accepted authorities of his time. His conclusions were his own; he pursued his search "following the intellect as leader, or the thread of reason" <note>original Latin: "secundum ducem Intellectum seu pilum rationis"</note>, and he reverently avoided claiming divine revelation for any of these results of his own investigations.

His science was not built with the conscious intention of providing a foundation for his theology. In fact, in some specific details, his early science actually conflicts with his later teachings from revelation. This is evident in those areas where he moved beyond nature and attempted to construct a system of spiritual science. For example, in this work, *The Soul*, he teaches certain things about the soul after death that he later corrected: *he suggests that the soul has no particular form but may assume any form, or that it may take wings and fly like a bird, or take any other shape suited to its sovereign desire, being free from all limitations of nature or natural heredity* (see *The Soul, or Rational Psychology*, numbers 521, 522). Notice also what he says in this work about the final destruction of the world and the "purging fires" which would finally sever the soul from the last entanglements of the body. These are instances where his science attempted to be prophetic. Swedenborg himself eventually regarded these predictions as being outside the realm of pure science...

<summary>This page explores how Swedenborg's early scientific studies in "Correspondence" served as a "ship" leading to his later spiritual revelations, while noting that his early philosophical theories on the soul's form after death sometimes contradicted his later theological teachings.</summary>
