<meta>This page continues the argument that Swedenborg’s scientific works were distinct from his later theological revelations, showing that he did not try to force his spiritual visions to match his earlier scientific theories.</meta>

<page-num>xxviii</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

It is clear that his earlier theories formed *no part of his own system as a science*. This is evident from his remark in section 524 of that same work, where he says "that we shall probably laugh in the next world at the guesses we have indulged in here about the future state of the soul." If he had been a typical natural philosopher, he would have insisted on making his later theological system harmonize with these earlier predictions. But this was not the case for a true seer. When the curtain fell, revealing the real spiritual world to his vision—the world which is the inner or spiritual dimension of our own human world—he saw the soul in its truly human aspects. It was entirely stripped of those "garments" <note>original: "habiliments"</note> it had inherited from pagan philosophers and medieval scholars <note>original: "schoolmen"</note>.

" *After death, a person is a spirit in a perfect human form*," he says, "just as they were in this world." He now tells us, speaking as the inspired interpreter of the Holy Word, that the "end of the world" is actually the completion of an era of human experience, serving as an introduction to a new spiritual age for mankind. This direct contradiction of his own earlier statements, written within a space of about five years, is convincing proof that whatever relationship exists between his scientific and theological writings, it is a strictly natural and organic one, not something forced or planned. Swedenborg neither constructed a science with the intention of building a theology on top of it, nor did he twist his theology to fit a previously constructed science. Each system stands on its own level; the agreement between them is one of "correspondence"—that is, the harmony of truth as it appears on different levels of divine order. Science rests on its basis of reason and experiment, while theology rests on its basis of revelation in the Word of God. The two do not agree by merging into one, but rather through the correspondence that exists between the distinct levels <term>discrete degrees: distinct layers of reality that do not blend into one another but act together in harmony, like the relationship between a thought and the word spoken</term> of things in their divine order.

The result of this agreement is that the warfare between science and religious faith is at an end. This could never have happened without this truly wonderful and providential reconciliation. In the natural course of events, theology had become so out of touch with science that people who loved natural truth and sought a deeper knowledge of the wonders of nature were almost driven to reject revealed religion. The only option for theology was to lose itself in politics, sociology, or occultism. In these forms, under the disguise of purely natural science, it tried to keep people's attention, even while it was losing their reverence and respect. At the same time, science might have posed as the "sacred priestess" <note>original: "sacred vestal," referring to the Vestal Virgins of Rome who guarded the sacred fire</note> in the temple of truth, claiming to be the only object of real worship left to humanity. In Swedenborg’s work, the normal order and the complete three-fold structure <note>original: "trine"</note> of mental life is restored: Science, Philosophy, and Theology. These represent the study of effects, of causes, and of ultimate purposes <note>original: "ends"</note>. Each of these fields finds itself free from the restrictions of any human system, while simultaneously being placed in a harmonious relationship with the other two. The secret of univers—

### AUTHOR'S PREFACE.

It has been my purpose to carefully investigate the nature of the soul and the body and their relationship <note>original: "intercourse"</note>; and also the state of the soul within the body and its state after the life of the body. But in order to reach this end, the means must also be sought. While I was meditating on how I might proceed, where I should look, and how I must direct my course toward that goal, I at length became aware that there is no other field of exploration than the anatomy of the soul's organic body. For it is within this body that the soul expresses herself and runs her course; and to understand what she is in her own field, she must be sought within her own domain.

For this reason, I have treated first of all the blood and the heart, and finally the particular organs and internal organs <note>original: "viscera"</note> of the body; then the cerebrum <note>the largest part of the brain, responsible for higher functions</note>, the cerebellum <note>the part of the brain at the back of the skull that coordinates muscular activity</note>, the medulla oblongata <note>the base of the brainstem</note>, and the spinal cord <note>original: "medulla spinalis"</note>.

Supported by these investigations, I may now make further progress. I have pursued this study of anatomy solely for the purpose of discovering the soul. If I have provided anything of use to the anatomical or medical world it will be gratifying, but it will be even more so if I have shed any light upon the discovery of the soul. For the body itself—and especially the human body and all its organs and members—is so wonderfully harmonized that nature has here brought together and infused all her art and science and whatever is most deeply concealed. Consequently, if one desires to investigate nature here in her supreme and innermost recesses, he must explore these details; and the longer he lingers, the more wonders and mysteries are revealed...

<summary>Swedenborg introduces his methodology for finding the soul, arguing that one must master the anatomy of the physical body—nature's masterpiece—to understand the spiritual essence that inhabits it.</summary>

...to light; and even if someone lived three times as long as Nestor <note>Nestor: A legendary King of Pylos in Greek mythology known for his great wisdom and long life.</note>, these things would still not be exhausted. It is like an abyss, and in the end, only wonder remains. Therefore, to explore the soul, I must unroll these many layers <note>original: "manifold coverings"</note> that hide her from our view—even though she lives in their very center. I must proceed by the analytic way <note>The method of logic that moves from observed effects back to their causes.</note>, going from experience to causes, and through causes to principles; that is, moving from later effects to their preceding origins <note>original: "from posterior to prior"</note>. This is the only way granted to us to achieve knowledge of this higher level. As soon as we have arrived at genuine principles through this method, only then can we proceed by the synthetic way <note>The method of logic that moves from established principles to their consequences or effects.</note>—moving from origins to effects—which is the way the soul herself acts within her own body. This is the angelic way, for angels see all later effects as subject to themselves by looking from the perspective of first principles. 

Therefore, before I treat the soul synthetically—*from the beginning* <note>original: "a priori"; reasoning from theoretical deduction rather than from observation</note>, or from first principles—I must first gain experience and observe effects through this human, analytic way. I must climb the ladder of resulting effects that leads us up to those principles and to that heaven. Thus, climbing to the soul is only possible through the very organs by which she descends into the body—which means through the study of the anatomy of her body. 

However, it was not possible to cross over from the organic, natural body to the soul—or to the spiritual and immaterial essence—unless I first established a path to lead me there. Therefore, I have been forced to develop certain new doctrines, such as the doctrine of forms, the doctrine of order and degrees, the doctrine of correspondences and representatives, and finally the doctrine of modifications. These doctrines were previously unknown; they are the guides without which we would attempt this journey in vain. I have written about these in the Fifth Treatise, or in my *Introduction to a Rational Psychology*.

And so now, at last, we may discuss the soul based on principles, or synthetically. The learned world, from the...

->From the<- earliest ages up to the present time—when that which has been so long conceived is now to be brought forth and born—humanity has labored constantly to attain these first principles <note>First principles: The fundamental, primary truths or causes from which everything else follows.</note>. Every science, both philosophical and physical, has existed for this purpose; every experiment that might provide clarification has been attempted for this end. This is the ultimate goal of the world of learning. We desire to speak from genuine first principles and treat subsequent things <note>original: "posterior things"; effects or results that follow a cause</note> synthetically <note>Synthetic method: Reasoning from a known cause to its effects.</note>. Such a perspective belongs to angelic perfection, heavenly science, and the highest natural science; it is, therefore, the innate ambition of us all. 

Alternatively, we may wish to emulate the integrity of our first parent <note>Referring to Adam in the biblical tradition, whom Swedenborg viewed as having a perfect, intuitive understanding of nature before the Fall.</note>, who determined all subsequent things from preceding causes. From this, it is clear how much effort is involved in attaining true principles. This can only be achieved if they are learned by the "posterior" way—that is, the path of the senses and of the human sciences and arts. These, however, do not belong to the soul itself, even though they are all grounded in the soul and flow from it.

But the way from experience—traveling through physical and philosophical sciences toward original causes and principles—is not only an arduous path but an extremely long one. It requires exploring many fields, not just one. One would need to live even longer than Nestor <note>Nestor: A legendary Greek king known for his great wisdom and for living through three generations of men.</note>; for things will constantly arise that confuse the mind and persuade it to believe only what the senses perceive. The mind then believes it has grasped a subject accurately because it operates according to the testimony of the senses, yet such reasoning is full of hypotheses and errors. In fact, the higher nature of things is hidden from us more deeply the more we rely on our senses. For the senses darken the mind the more their "rays" are concentrated upon it. The senses themselves are like shadows, so that it seems as if the light of our very sight and of...

# Part First.
## THE SENSES.

### I.
### THE SIMPLE FIBER, AND ITS CELESTIAL NATURE.

(1.) **The successive formation of the blood vessels from the simple fiber.** <note>This chapter outlines Swedenborg's theories on the "Simple Fiber," the most fundamental unit of biological structure, which he believed originated from a spiritual or "celestial" source.</note>

The simplest fiber is the "form of forms," or the primary structure that forms all other fibers following in order.

By winding around itself, the simplest fiber forms a certain perpetually spiral surface or membrane. This becomes the second type of fiber—the medullary <note>original: medullary; referring to the marrow-like white matter of the brain and spinal cord</note> or nervous fiber of the body. This is essentially a small channel constructed from the simplest fiber, which, together with the fluid that flows through it, constitutes a complete fiber.

Because this fiber originates from the prior one—being nothing more than that primary fiber coiled up—it flows in a spiral or continuously circular movement <note>original: flux</note>.

When this fiber enters the various regions <note>original: provinces</note> of the body, it again forms a kind of tiny gland, not unlike the cortical glands <note>original: cortical; the "gray matter" of the brain where Swedenborg believed the soul's activity began</note>. From this gland, the bodily fiber emerges, which in turn forms the small membrane <note>original: tunic</note> that encloses the arterial vessels.

The fiber descends further into the larger arteries, where it also forms glands that once again send out fibers—

---

<note>original: * This chapter gives in outline the results of the author's elaborate discussion of the Fiber in the *Economy of the Animal Kingdom* and elsewhere in his works. Concerning the production of the Simple Fiber, its relation to the spirituous fluid and to the soul, see volume 2, page 280, and following. [Translator]</note>

<summary>This page describes Swedenborg’s anatomical theory that the "simple fiber" is the fundamental building block of the body, coiling to create nervous fibers and eventually forming the structures of the blood vessels.</summary>
<keywords>simple fiber, medullary fiber, nervous fiber, cortical gland, arterial vessels, anatomy, Swedenborg, biological formation</keywords>

--- Page 44 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the formation of physiological structures from the "simple fiber," concluding the section on blood vessels and establishing the simple fiber as the fundamental building block of the entire body.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...from these glands, and from these fibers, the muscular tunic <note>tunic: a layer or membrane of tissue</note> is produced.

Thus, the nervous, glandular, tendinous, and muscular tunics—along with the membranous layer—constitute the arteries and veins. Each and every one of these is formed from fibers.

Therefore, blood vessels are produced from the simple fiber through a series of successive developments.

Accordingly, the arterial vessel can be called the "third fiber," the medullary <note>medullary: relating to the white matter of the brain or the internal marrow of the nerves</note> fiber the "second," and the simple fiber the "first."

In this sense, the first fiber may also be called the "first vessel," followed by the "second vessel," and finally the "vessel properly so-called," which is the blood vessel.

This hierarchy also applies to the fluids that flow through them: the first vital essence is the "supereminent blood" <note>supereminent blood: Swedenborg’s term for the highest, most spiritual fluid in the body, which he associated with the soul; see *Economy of the Animal Kingdom*, vol. 2, sections 49, 217-221</note>, or blood of the supreme degree. The fluid within the second fibers is the middle or "purer" blood. Finally, the fluid within the arteries is the blood properly so-called—the red blood.

Therefore, the simple fiber is the true animating essence <note>original: animal essence; here referring to the soul or life-force (from the Latin *anima*), the psychic essence that gives life to the body</note>, the "form of forms."

### (2.) *Nothing else in the body is continuous; its entire form is composed of the simple fiber alone.*

Everything in the body that is continuous or essentially structured <note>original: determined; here meaning having a fixed form or direction; see *Economy of the Animal Kingdom*, vol. 2, section 248</note>—that is, everything that is formed—is the simple fiber.

For there is nothing in the medullary fiber except the simple fiber.

There is nothing in the blood vessel except the medullary fiber.

There is nothing in the entire body that is not woven together from vessels and fibers.

<summary>Swedenborg argues that all physical structures—nerves, muscles, and blood vessels—are ultimately composed of the "simple fiber," and that bodily fluids follow a similar hierarchy from spiritual essence to red blood.</summary>
<keywords>simple fiber, medullary fiber, anatomy, blood vessels, vital essence, supereminent blood, animal essence, physiological structure, Economy of the Animal Kingdom</keywords>

--- Page 45 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that the "simple fiber" is the fundamental building block of all physiological structures, including those that appear solid, and defines the fiber's nature as celestial and primary.</meta>

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>THE SIMPLE FIBER.</header>

Even parts that do not appear to be so—such as the tendons, cartilages, and bones—are shown by experience to have been originally woven from vessels and fibers.

Thus, there is nothing in the entire body except the simple fiber, which constitutes its entire form.

Nor does anything continuous or coherent enter into the body except for the simple fiber, which is the only continuous substance <note>original: "substantial"; referring to the underlying material essence of the body</note>.*

To argue further: if the simple fiber is a living <note>original: "animate"</note> product of its first essence, it follows that nothing else forms the entire animal <note>original: "animal"; here meaning "living" or "animate," from the Latin *anima* (soul)</note> structure but this essence itself.

Various kinds of fluids found in the medullary <note>medullary: relating to the white matter of the brain or the internal marrow of the nerves</note> fibers and blood vessels—such as serous <note>serous: thin, watery fluids like lymph or blood serum</note> fluids—do not make up the structure itself, since structures are composed of fibers. Instead, these fluids flow within the fibers and vessels.

->(3.) If that essence is the soul, it follows that this<-
->alone is what constitutes the form.<-

*(4.) The Simple Fiber is of a celestial nature. What the Body is.*

This form is ruled by spiritual‡ forms alone.

Because this form is superior to other forms, it cannot be touched by them at all, much less can it be harmed; it is

is most secure from all injury. How can a complex structure <note>original: "compound"</note> act upon the simple, fundamental units <term>simples</term> <note>original: "simples"; in early modern philosophy, "simples" are the most basic, indivisible elements of reality</note> from which it is composed? It is far removed from them, nor are they dependent upon it.

(5.) Therefore, this fiber is not made of earthly matter <note>original: "terrestrial"</note>, as Aristotle teaches, but is of a celestial nature, essence, and form.

(6.) Consequently, it is immortal and cannot perish, because it is beyond the reach of physical impact.

(7.) What is earthly and physical is not the fiber itself, but rather that part of the red blood and the intermediate blood <note>original: "middle blood"</note> within the globule <note>original: "globule"; here referring to a blood cell or particle</note> which serves as an instrumental cause. This allows the primary essence of the blood to descend through a series of successive derivations and exist in the midst of the outermost world; in short, it allows it to form the various types of blood, within which that celestial form nevertheless governs.

(8.) The material from which the physical blood is made is merely corporeal; it contributes nothing to the form of the body except that it flows through these fibers and adapts them so they may take on specific shapes.

(9.) This physical part is mortal and returns to the earth when the blood globules are dissolved; but this is not the case for the fiber, which departs of its own accord while the body remains behind as a corpse.

## II.

### THE SENSES.

(15.) *The external sensory organs, such as the ear and the eye, are instruments for the vibrations <note>original: "modifications"; in Swedenborg’s physics, this refers to the patterns of motion in a medium</note> of the air and of the ether. These vibrations are the primary causes to which sensations exactly correspond, acting through the organs as intermediaries.*

Regarding the ear, it is the instrument that receives the vibrations of the air; for it receives and adapts itself to every form and pattern of the forces flowing toward it. The same is true of the eye in relation to the ether <note>In 18th-century science, "ether" was the theoretical medium thought to fill all space and transmit light, much like air transmits sound.</note>. In this respect, the ear differs from a musical or acoustic instrument because it does not merely receive sounds, but also transmits and further extends them. The eye differs from optical instruments in the same way. The eye is indeed like a *dark chamber* <note>original: "camera obscura"; an early optical device that projects an image of its surroundings onto a screen</note>, which reproduces the images transmitted from the object in front of it with great precision, without changing their forms or colors. 

However, in the eye, these vibrations do not simply pass onto the retina. The eye's functions stimulate the essential structures to act in kind, even down to the smallest parts of the retina. From there, the same visual information is carried through the optic nerve to the common sensory <note>original: "common sensory" or "sensorium commune"; the part of the brain where all sensory input was believed to be processed and integrated</note>. Thus, sensations correspond exactly to the vibrations within the organs. The same applies to taste and smell: the external shape of particles—which are generally either rounded or sharp <note>original: "prickly"</note>—affects the <term>papillae</term> <note>small bumps on the surface of the tongue or inside the nose containing sensory receptors</note> of the tongue or nostrils. The organ is affected by these countless points of contact, and from this, a corresponding sensation results.

<vocab>senses, ear, eye, ether, sensations, air, optic nerve, retina, dark chamber <note>original: "camera obscura"</note>, taste, smell, papillae, tongue, nostrils</vocab>

<summary>This page explains how the ear and eye act as physical instruments that translate environmental vibrations—air for sound and ether for light—into sensory perceptions. It also notes that taste and smell function through physical contact between particles and the sensory papillae.</summary>
<keywords>sensory organs, acoustics, optics, ether theory, camera obscura, neurobiology, common sensory, physiology of taste and smell</keywords>

(16.) *The sensory fibres leading to the common sensory <note>original: "common sensory" or "sensorium commune"; the central part of the brain where all sensory information was thought to be integrated</note> are exactly adapted to the form of the vibrations <note>original: "modifications"; in Swedenborg’s physics, this refers to the patterns of motion in a medium like air or ether</note> flowing into and affecting them. Thus, sensations flow by a natural spontaneity from the surrounding world, through the fibres in the living world <note>original: "animated world"; the realm of living, ensouled beings</note>, even to the Soul.*

In the inquiry into the form of the vibrations of the air and of the ether <note>In 18th-century science, "ether" was the theoretical medium thought to fill all space and transmit light</note>, we are led to conclude from experience that there can be no other form of vibration than that of the form of the individual parts. Since the whole volume is composed of these parts, if the parts are capable of change, a similar condition must result in the entire volume that is set in motion as in the individual parts, which serve as signs of the collective motion. The form of the vibrations of the ether is spiral (or perpetually circular), and that of the vibrations of the air is simply circular; for these are the external forms of their particles, as may be demonstrated by countless proofs. 

If it is then asked what is the form of the flow <note>original: "fluxions"</note> within the fibres, it has been proven in the treatise *The Fibres* that the flow of each compound fibre is spiral, and that the flow of many fibres taken together is circular. Thus, one form corresponds exactly to the vibrations of the ether, and the other to the vibrations of the air. However, the form of the higher ether is vortical <note>swirling like a vortex</note>, and this corresponds to the physical form of the spiral gland <note>original: "spiral glandule"; likely referring to the cortical glands of the brain</note>. Thus, when the vibrations of the atmospheres <note>original: "auras"</note> flow into the miniature world—that is, the animal system <note>the human body seen as a microcosm of the universe</note>—they continue their flow according to their own nature, and their essential characteristics are not changed.

(17.) *The sensations are carried from the external organs to the internal organs as if from a heavy to a lighter atmosphere, or from a lower to a higher region.*

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the physical structure of nerve fibres perfectly matches the geometric patterns of air and ether vibrations, allowing sensations to pass seamlessly from the environment to the soul. He describes these atmospheric patterns as circular, spiral, and vortical, corresponding to different levels of the nervous system.</summary>
<keywords>sensory fibres, common sensory, ether, air, geometry of motion, spiral form, cortical glands, microcosm, auras</keywords>

--- Page 50 ---
<meta>This page continues Swedenborg’s investigation into the physiology of the brain, moving from the geometric forms of vibrations to how these sensory inputs ascend into the cerebral cortex and how motor actions descend from it.</meta>

<page-num>10</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

Light bodies are raised from the center toward the surface and emerge, but those which are heavy fall toward the center and seek the bottom. In the same way, sensations strive from the outermost parts to the innermost, or from the lowest to the highest. Actions, however, fall from the innermost to the outermost, or from the highest to the lowest. Thus, sensations may be compared to lighter bodies and actions to heavier ones.

The cerebral cortex <note>original: "cortical brain"; the outer layer of gray matter in the brain, which Swedenborg identified as the seat of the soul's activity</note> holds the innermost and the highest position; for to climb toward it is to move upward, but to move from there toward the surface of the body is to move downward. That the cortex also occupies the highest region of the body can be seen from the nature of the fibers themselves. The most fluid and softest fibers are near the cortex, which is their primary source. Those fibers more remote from the cortex are harder and more stationary, as if they were more compressed. When a fiber rises toward a softer fiber, it rises to a more refined <note>original: "purer"</note> region, and vice versa. This is also why the nerves (or the sensory fibers) are soft, while the motor fibers are somewhat harder, and why this softness increases as the fibers ascend toward the brain.

> *(18.) Sensations do not arrive at any specific small glands <note>original: "glandules"; Swedenborg viewed the individual units of the cortex as tiny glands or "little hearts" that processed spirituous fluid</note> or clusters of glands in the brain, but at the entire cortex. Thus, there is not a single cortical gland in the whole brain that does not participate in every sensation and in its smallest movement, degree, and distinction.*

The anatomy of the brain shows this with sufficient clarity. Every nerve and every fiber, when it is immersed in the white matter <note>original: "medullary lake"; the inner volume of the brain composed of nerve fibers</note> of the brain, merges with all its neighbors so thoroughly that almost all distinctions disappear. One fold is continually connected with another, and a certain subtle membrane sits between every fiber and every vessel and the one next to it.

<vocab>soul, sensation, action, cortical brain, cortex, fibers, glandules, medullary lake, anatomy</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg argues that sensations move "upward" toward the refined cerebral cortex while actions move "downward" toward the body, and that sensory information is distributed across the entire cortex rather than localized in a single spot.</summary>
<keywords>neuroanatomy, cerebral cortex, sensory movement, motor action, medullary lake, cortical glandules, physiology of the soul</keywords>

<page-num>11</page-num>
<header>THE SENSES.</header>

This membrane joins and binds fiber to fiber and artery to artery. We call those intervening threads that are drawn out from the fiber the "emulating vessels" <note>original: "emulous vessels"; vessels that imitate or function similarly to others</note> of the fiber. Into these are inserted the most delicate threads drawn from the pia mater <note>original: "pia mater"; the delicate, innermost membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord</note>. 

Thus, it may clearly be seen that in the brain, in the cerebellum <note>the part of the brain at the back of the skull that coordinates muscular activity</note>, and in both types of medulla <note>referring to the medulla oblongata and the spinal cord</note>, there is nothing at all that is disconnected or disjoined. Sensation—which is a most subtle kind of trembling within a certain atmosphere—is not able to press solely upon a single fiber, or any specific fibers, as far as their origins. Instead, it is compelled to pursue its journey through everything that is continuous with that fiber; this is also true of the trembling and vibrations of harder bodies. 

The same is evident from a specific investigation of each sensory fiber. For instance, the optic nerve, as it spreads through the optic thalami <note>original: "beds of the optic nerves"; the thalamus was historically referred to as the "optic bed" because the optic nerves appear to rest upon it</note>, cannot help but spread across the entire circuit of the brain. Since the fibers drawn from this circuit and concentrated on a firmer base unite at the optic thalami, if the sensations follow their flow <note>original: "flux"</note>, they must inevitably end at the shared surface of the brain. 

The olfactory nerves <note>the nerves responsible for the sense of smell</note>, originating from the continuous pituitary membrane <note>the lining of the nasal cavity</note>, immerse themselves so deeply into the "oval center" <note>original: "centrum ovale"; the central white matter of the brain</note> or medullary globe of the brain that they seem to originate from everywhere; this is because the mammillary processes <note>small round bodies on the underside of the brain, part of the limbic system</note>, when inflated, expand the entire medulla of the brain. 

The acoustic or auditory nerves <note>hearing nerves</note>, emerging from the pons <note>original: "annular protuberance"; the pons Varolii, a part of the brainstem</note>, associate themselves with all the fibers which are sent out from the brain and from the cerebellum. And so it is in other instances. Therefore, the proportion <note>original: "ratio"</note> of the sensations is the same as that of their modifications: for having begun in the smallest center, they diffuse outward into the entire periphery. From these considerations, it follows that there is no part of the cerebral cortex <note>the outer layer of gray matter</note> which does not participate in and become conscious of the incoming sensation.

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the brain is a perfectly continuous system where sensory vibrations, such as sight and sound, diffuse from specific nerves to the entire cerebral cortex. He uses the anatomy of the optic, olfactory, and auditory nerves to demonstrate how sensations spread through the brain's interconnected fibers.</summary>

<keywords>neuroanatomy, optic nerve, olfactory nerves, auditory nerves, cerebral cortex, sensation, vibrations, medulla, cerebellum, pia mater</keywords>

(19.) ***The most distinct sensation is found in the cortex of the brain, especially the sensations of sight, perception, and understanding.***

Where the cortical tissues are most delicate and most spread out, the sensations should be more perfect and distinct. The reason the cerebrum <note>the largest part of the brain, responsible for higher-level functions</note> feels, perceives, and understands, while the cerebellum <note>the part of the brain at the back of the skull that coordinates muscular activity</note> does not, is because the cortical glands <note>original: "glandules"; Swedenborg’s term for the fundamental cellular units of the brain, which we now call neurons</note> act like many tiny sensory organs capable of perceiving patterns distinctly. 

In either protrusion, or the peak of the brain—that is, in its highest lobe—this cortex is clearly divided. A countless number of fissures and furrows <note>the sulci and gyri that create the folds of the brain</note> separate the masses, which allows the cortex to be expanded and pulled in any direction. Therefore, when this division is more perfect, the sensation is also more perfect. This is also the reason why all the folds and curves of the cortex concentrate themselves here or tend toward this area through a continuous flow and union. This is observed in both outward and inward perceptions; we even direct our deep thoughts toward this front "prow" of the brain. 

Furthermore, when this area is injured, the ability to see and perceive clearly changes according to the severity of the injury, as is evident from various diseases of the head. Thus, while sensation actually belongs to every cortical gland, it is more perfect in one part of the brain than in another. In one area, sensation is more specific and individual according to the divisions of the brain, while in another part it is more general. Consequently, the sensation there is more indistinct and obscure, as in the lowest layers of the brain and in the cerebellum.

*...cortical glands <note>original: "glandules"; Swedenborg’s term for the fundamental cellular units of the brain, now called neurons</note>. However, a certain variety exists among them, which is so harmonious that the only difference in the quality of any sensation is that it is perceived more perfectly in one gland than in another.*

It has been sufficiently demonstrated in the treatise concerning these glands that there are infinite changes of state—both essential and accidental—in the cortical glands, which serve as many internal sensory organs. There are larger and smaller glands, harder and softer ones, and those consisting of more or fewer fibers. Some are in a more constricted state and others more expanded; some associate with many others, and some with few. To list every difference, however, would be too tedious <note>original: "prolix"</note>. 

The cortical glands in the cerebrum are of one kind, while those of the cerebellum are another, and those in the medulla oblongata <note>the lower part of the brainstem</note> and the spinal cord <note>original: "medulla spinalis"</note> are yet another. They also vary within the brain itself: at its peak <note>original: "vertex"</note>, along its borders, on the outside near the pia mater <note>the delicate innermost membrane surrounding the brain</note>, and on the inside around the ventricles <note>the fluid-filled cavities of the brain</note>. All these cortical glands—which are the starting points of the nerve fibers and serve as tiny sensory and motor centers—are internal. 

For the brain to be free to receive all sensations and feel every subtle difference, there must be order among these sensory centers. This order must be completely harmonious. Even if one gland receives a more refined <note>original: "purer"</note> signal and another a coarser <note>original: "grosser"</note> signal <note>original: "mode"</note>, the sensation of each must be communicated to the others, like a part contributing to the whole. This is called "harmonious variety," a concept so inherent to the natural world that it deserves to be called the "nature of nature." Such variety exists in individual fibers, in individual muscles, and in the individual parts of the atmosphere. In a similar way, the lower layers of the atmosphere are more compressed than the higher ones, yet there remains a certain harmonious variety between them all. In this way, each individual part contributes its own share to the common and public state.

<summary>Swedenborg describes the "harmonious variety" of the brain's cortical glands, explaining how their diverse structures and locations allow them to function as a unified sensory system. He argues that this diversity is a fundamental principle of nature, where individual parts contribute to a collective whole.</summary>

(21.) *The sensations spread throughout the whole brain should be understood as winding themselves in a spiral manner, following the circular path of the brain's circuitry and the cortical substances <note>the gray matter of the brain</note>. These more refined sensations revolve like a vortex through the cortical glands <note>original: "glandule"; Swedenborg's term for the individual units of the brain, now known as neurons</note>; thus, they follow the very structure of the sensory organ itself.*

The folds of the cortical glands in the brain follow the path of a perfect spiral. Because sensations reach every point, every fiber, and every part of the brain's cortex, we must imagine a similar winding and whirling motion for the sensations themselves. This allows for an easy flow <note>original: "fluxion"</note> and spread of these sensations from a single part into the whole. This same process occurs within each individual cortical gland, which is shaped like a continuous spiral or vortex. Any active force acting upon an organic substance moves and is directed exactly according to that substance's shape. To move in any other way would go against the natural stream and current of its nature, or against the rotation of its axis.

The sensation also circles <note>original: "circumgyrates"</note> in a similar way as it travels along its nerve fiber, and likewise when it exits that fiber. Thus, the patterns of a flow and those of its surrounding medium <note>original: "atmosphere"</note> or its changes <note>original: "modifications"</note> are similar. In this way, the universe <note>original: "macrocosm"</note> and the human body <note>original: "microcosm"</note> correspond to one another, exerting the same patterns upon each other. This kind of whirling motion is clearly visible in the external organs as well, such as when the mind is intoxicated <note>original: "inebriated"</note> or the brain is affected by a similar illness or delirium. From these points, we can see the intricate windings and revolutions through which our deepest sensations or our understanding are processed. The form of this movement is celestial <note>in Swedenborg’s philosophy, the "celestial" form is the highest and most perfect degree of geometry and order</note>; and so forth.

<summary>Swedenborg argues that sensations move through the brain in spiral and vortical patterns, matching the physical geometry of the cortical glands (neurons). He suggests that the microcosm of the human body reflects the macrocosm of the universe through these shared geometric laws of motion.</summary>

### (22.) *We may naturally perceive for ourselves the harmony and the disharmony of sensations.*

That the soul naturally understands <note>original: "apprehends"</note> and is aware of every harmonious or discordant thing that occurs in any of the senses is clear from how each sense functions. A harmony of touch on the outermost skin tickles and triggers laughter. A harmony of taste and smell pleases and satisfies the organs in such a way that it creates pleasure, sweetness, and appetite. A harmony of hearing so pleases the ear that a person smiles at what they hear. The same is true for a harmony of sight, which is the source of beauty, elegance, and delight. 

But disharmony produces the opposite effect; these discords sadden the soul and the mind, inducing a certain horror or even pain, and leading to aversions. Even within the imagination and thought, a similar agreement <note>original: "concord"</note> of truths—which are themselves various forms of harmony—is likewise produced by nature itself, without the need for formal science to guide it or artistic skill to act as a mistress. 

Because of this, those with healthy minds who possess some degree of knowledge can grasp natural truths immediately and give them their approval. However, if these same truths are opposed, it is the result of a disordered <note>original: "vicious," meaning faulty or corrupted</note> state of their mind. That the soul perceives the harmony or disharmony of images and ideas at first glance is clear enough in animals <note>original: "brute animals"</note>. For instance, birds naturally know how to cleverly construct their nests, choose the food best suited for them, and avoid what is harmful. The spider weaves its web with perfect geometric precision—to say nothing of other examples which are the results of a natural perception of harmony. 

Even the sensory organs themselves are not only soothed by harmonies and pleasant things but are also restored by them; conversely, they are injured by things that are disharmonious. The reason for this is that the soul is pure intelligence, representing the order and truth of its own microcosm <note>original: "microcosm"; the human body viewed as a "small world" that mirrors the universe</note>. Therefore, the recognition <note>original: "cognition"</note> of order and truth is a faculty born within us, and

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the soul has an innate ability to recognize harmony and disharmony, which manifests as pleasure or pain in the senses and as truth or error in the mind. He points to animal instincts and the restorative nature of beauty as evidence that the soul is the "pure intelligence" and governing order of the human body.</summary>

<keywords>soul, harmony, disharmony, sensation, microcosm, intelligence, instinct, natural truth, order</keywords>

--- Page 56 ---
<meta>This page continues Swedenborg’s discussion of how the soul and mind process sensory information, moving from the natural perception of harmony to the physical mechanism in the brain where sensation turns into action.</meta>

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...is a skill that is rarely learned. Furthermore, the senses cannot exist in any other way; for sensation to occur, harmony must be mixed with disharmony. Sensation arises from the differences between these, their connections, and their positions. In the same way, reasoning <note>original: "ratiocination"</note>, thoughts, speech, controversy, and opinions arise from a mixture of truths, fallacies, and falsehoods. Without these, there would be very little speech, and neither schools nor sciences; even the shelves of libraries would remain empty.

->*(23.) The end of sensations and the beginning of actions meet in the same inmost sensory organ.*<-

The cortical glandule <note>original: "glandule"; Swedenborg refers to the small cellular structures or "glands" in the cerebral cortex as the primary units of brain function</note> is the final boundary where sensations end and the first "prison-house" from which actions break out. This is because both sensory and motor <note>original: "motory"</note> fibers begin and end in these small glands.

Sensations travel from the outermost parts to the innermost; however, actions run from the innermost to the outermost. Thus, the cortical gland serves as both a small internal sensory organ and a motor organ. It is both active and passive, just like all highly developed organic substances. For natural bodies, to "suffer" <note>original: "passion"; in this philosophical context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or to receive an external impression, rather than an emotion</note> as well as to act is a mark of perfection; this is the source of elasticity and the resulting forces and powers. Higher forms receive every incoming force and return one similar to it. If we compare this to the sensory organs described here, sensation itself is the "passion" (the receiving) to which a corresponding action responds. The purpose of the action may be to turn what is felt into a physical act, or to represent the perceived idea through that act; for action is the physical expression <note>original: "representation"</note> of the mind's idea. This explains why a perceived idea turns into action so quickly, as seen in speech. This would not be possible if both action and "passion" did not meet in the very same organ.

<summary>Swedenborg explains that sensation requires a contrast between harmony and disharmony and identifies the brain's cortical glands as the vital junction where sensory input is received and motor action begins.</summary>

## III.

# THE INTELLECT AND ACTION.

<margin>(24.)</margin> *Intellection <note>original: "Intellection"; the act of understanding or the highest level of sensory processing</note>, which is the final stage of sensations, does not immediately turn itself into will—which is the first stage of actions. Instead, a certain thought and judgment intervene; thus, there are intermediate operations of the mind that connect the last part of sensation with the first part of action.*

There is a certain progressive sequence or cycle <note>original: "gyre"</note> as intellection passes over into will. Undoubtedly, "thought" intervenes, which is the final sorting <note>original: "involution"</note> of things perceived and understood, as well as the calling forth of similar things from the depths of the memory. "Judging," or judgment, is the shaping of those thoughts into a rational form, where things that have nothing to do with the matter at hand are cast out. At length comes the "conclusion," and from that, the "will."

Intellection itself is the first part of the operations of the intellect; thought is the second part; judging is the third; and the conclusion is the fourth. All of these taken together are designated by the single word "intellect." However, this cycle is often completed with such mental focus and speed that it hardly appears as if there are so many intermediate steps between the first rational perception and the beginning of an action. It is sometimes run through in a single moment. I do not doubt that there is a similar series of operations in physical substances gifted with perfect elasticity to which this might be compared. It may be that the elastic power <note>original: "elatery"; a 17th- and 18th-century term for the inherent force of a spring or the expansive power of a gas</note> of nature, when it is subjected to a force or impact <note>original: "impetus"</note>, resolves and restores itself...

<summary>Swedenborg describes the four-step process of the intellect: understanding (intellection), thinking, judging, and concluding, which bridges the gap between sensation and physical action.</summary>
<keywords>intellection, will, judgment, psychology, cognition, elatery, cortical glands, decision making</keywords>

<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...through similar intermediate operations toward a similar act, even though it may seem to be instantaneous. However, we cannot expand further on the subject here.

->**(25.) There is such a connection between rational perception (the intellect) and the will (the beginning of actions)—that is, between passion <note>original: "passion"; in this philosophical context, passion refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving sensory input, the opposite of "action."</note> and action in a single mind—that the state of one determines the state of the other. In other words, a mind deprived of perception is also deprived of will.**<-

The mind's perception can be compared to "passion" (reception), while the will can be compared to action. Therefore, a perfect mind can be compared to a perfect **elatery** <term>elatery: an archaic term for elasticity or the inherent power in a physical body to spring back or exert force</term> in nature. 

It is a property of elasticity that its force increases as the body is more compressed; that this elasticity is equal to the compressing force; and that the power of an elastic body is determined by the actions of the body compressing it. Furthermore, elasticity, once freed from that compression, is immediately restored to its former state. A body with perfect elasticity, no matter how much it is compressed, loses none of its own force. It always restores itself and exerts as much force as it received, so that a similar force and momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> are spread into its immediate surroundings, then into the nearby area, and finally everywhere. 

When elastic bodies strike each other, the center of gravity—both before and after the collision—moves with the same speed (if it moves at all), so that the state of the center of gravity is preserved during the encounter. Many other principles could be compared to this organic substance and its rational operation; these could be explained through **correspondences** <note>original: "correspondences"; Swedenborg’s signature theory that physical laws and structures reflect spiritual or mental realities</note> for the understanding of those who are knowledgeable.

In the meantime, it is clear from observable phenomena that the will is shaped by the intellect or perception...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the intellect and the will are inextricably linked, comparing the mind's reactivity to the physical laws of elasticity (elatery).</summary>
<keywords>intellect, will, perception, elatery, elasticity, physics of the mind, correspondences, passion and action</keywords>

<page-num>19</page-num>
<header>THE INTELLECT AND ACTION</header>

or the affections of the mind, of the **animus** <term>animus: in Swedenborg's philosophy, the "animus" is the lower or intermediate mind associated with emotions, desires, and sensory awareness, distinct from the higher rational mind</term>, or of the brain. For the will increases along with perception itself in both youths and adults. When one fails, the other fails, for they meet in the same organ. When the brain is injured, compressed by foreign matter, or disturbed in its order, not only does sensation become unsteady according to the degree of injury, but action also suffers—as seen in loss of memory, catalepsy, lethargy, sleep, and other conditions. The reason for this is that nothing can enter the will that does not originate in perception; for the will is the conclusion of thoughts, and it possesses the power to act in accordance with the ideas formed by those thoughts.

->**(26.) The initial perception cannot be immediately converted into thought, and even less into the will, unless some force is added that stimulates and promotes it; without this exciting and promoting force, perception would be extinguished at once, and thought along with it, as the two go hand in hand.**<-

That the initial perception is a simple internal sensation or a mere **passion** <note>original: "passion"; in this context, the state of being acted upon or receiving external stimuli, as opposed to taking active initiative.</note> is evident from both observation and reflection. Whenever our eyes are open, we experience visual images passing through the eye and the fibers of the optic nerve to a **common sensory** <term>common sensory: the "sensorium commune," a conceptual part of the brain where all the different senses (sight, sound, etc.) are unified into a single conscious experience</term> or a certain internal sensation. It is the same with sound and its modulations in the air, with taste on the tongue, smell in the nostrils, and touch in the body. However, for this perception to become an even deeper internal sensation, and for the rational sensation called **intellection** <term>intellection: the act or process of the intellect; rational understanding</term> to move into thought and then into the will—this cannot happen without some additional and stimulating force. I will now proceed to explain what these forces are.

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the will depends entirely on sensory perception and that the brain must be physically healthy for both to function. He explains that sensory input is a passive reception that requires an additional "stimulating force" to be transformed into rational thought and intentional action.</summary>

<keywords>animus, brain injury, will, perception, sensation, intellection, common sensory, cognitive mechanics</keywords>

*(27.) The first force is harmony itself and the pleasure and sweetness proceeding from it. This is perceived in the external and internal sensory organs at the very first impression of an object. It so affects the **animus** <term>animus: the lower or sensory mind, which deals with emotions and desires, as distinguished from the "mens" or higher rational mind</term> and the mind, and gives such life to the perception, that the process inevitably continues until it reaches the will.*

These facts are clear in themselves. Anything beautiful and elegant immediately affects the eye or internal sight with a certain hidden pleasure. At the harmony of similar sounds, as well as the sweetness of taste and smell, and even the charms of touch, the mind is immediately pleased. Therefore, its perception does not remain still; it is activated at that moment and calls forth similar ideas from the depths of the memory, which gives rise to thought; and this is followed by the will.

*(28.) Another force is the love of self-preservation, or self-love, which ignites the internal sensations. From the first perception to the last, this force drives these sensations toward the beginning of action; without the addition of such a force, our intellect would be deprived of its life and would waste away.*

If we examine the natural harmonies themselves that are first perceived in the sensory organs of the body, it will appear that these are forces that preserve the body. Not only do they provide charms to the senses, but they also restore whatever is defective in them, as can be shown by many phenomena. For harmonies revive the soul; the

The spring greenness and the various colors of the meadows restore one's sight because they gladden the **animus** <term>animus: the lower or sensory mind, which deals with emotions, passions, and the "animal" spirit, as distinguished from the higher rational mind</term>. Likewise, symmetrical patterns affect our hearing. However, opposite things cause offense and injury; consequently, the body suffers and the animus grieves. It follows from this that natural harmonies contain a certain driving and active force because they contribute to the body’s preservation. Self-love is the primary love of the soul, the chief desire of the mind, and the fundamental craving <note>original: "cupidity"</note> of the body. All desires for specific goals <note>original: "ends"</note> flow from there as if from a source. There are also other loves that branch out like streams from this source, which are triggered by specific perceptions. These are undoubtedly so many forces, vitalities, or "heats" that give life to the mind's operations and drive them toward action. This is the reason why every person finds strength in their own loves and desires, and every person lives according to their own vital spirit. Those who are deprived of such loves and desires are also dull in temperament, senseless, and as lifeless as dry wood <note>original: "dry stocks"</note>, possessing a spirit and blood that are equally cold and sluggish.

### (29.) *From these loves are born the desires for particular goals, and these desires are the actual forces present in the intellect and the will.*

There is no intellect or rational perception—and therefore no thought or judgment, and even less a will that accompanies perception—without the intuition and desire for a certain goal <note>original: "end"</note>. Without this goal, the will is never moved to action. Therefore, for a will to exist, the mind must contemplate a specific goal. However, there are higher and lower goals. Higher goals belong only to the human mind; they do not look solely toward the preservation of the body or the self. Instead, they regard the preservation of the society to which the mind belongs,

He introduces the idea that the "will" requires a specific goal (end) to function, distinguishing between self-preservation and higher social goals.</summary>

...and many other things besides. In place of these rational goals <note>original: "ends"</note>, animals possess physical goals <note>original: "corporeal ends"</note>, the desires for which are called lusts and pleasures. These goals exist solely for the sake of self-preservation, or perhaps simply for the preservation of the body. Because such a goal does not originate from a specific source or principle of reason, it prioritizes the preservation of the self over the preservation of society as a whole. However, we shall discuss these goals hereafter, when we treat the **animus** <term>animus: the lower or sensory mind, which deals with emotions, passions, and the "animal" spirit, as distinguished from the higher rational mind</term> and the mind.

### (30.) *Nothing is innate in the human mind except for a perception of order, of harmonies, and of truths within forms, substances, forces, and modes. The rational mind is affected by these to the extent that they concern self-preservation. However, other things—including the forms, substances, forces, modes, and truths themselves—must be learned through the help of the senses; from this learning come discipline and the arts. It is different for brute animals.*

It has been shown above that harmonies themselves are innate within us, meaning that we perceive them without a teacher. Examples include the sweetness of taste and smell, the symmetry of sound, and the excellence and beauty of nature; in a word, the very order of things or the harmony of modes, forces, substances, and forms. From this, we may also perceive the actual truths of things, for these correspond to the order found in nature itself; this is why order is called "transcendental truth."* We clearly perceive this in our intellect, for we grasp truths as soon as they are stated, without needing any demonstration. Therefore, some people are said to have the "seeds" of virtue and beauty innate within them. However, the form itself and the perfection of that form are—

...different things. Through our senses and through learning <note>original: "discipline"</note>, we must acquire for ourselves—using scientific and experimental methods—the specific information <note>original: "form"</note>, but we do not need to acquire the underlying harmony or the order of how things are arranged within that form. This harmony and order are natural because they align with the physical structure of our sensory organs and the way we experience sensations and perceptions. Because they align, they attract the senses so that they may soothe, stimulate, and pleasantly affect them; however, the actual knowledge <note>original: "form"</note> that results from this is something that must be learned.

This is the reason for the debate among scholars about whether ideas are innate (born within us) or entirely acquired through experience. This is also proven by reflecting on our own thoughts, imagination, and speech. For thought and speech to occur, an infinite number of things related to order are required. This order is followed so precisely by children that the entire Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: referring to the school of Aristotle, known for a systematic and logical approach to nature</term> and Pythagorean <term>Pythagorean: referring to the followers of Pythagoras, who sought the mathematical and harmonic laws of the universe</term> schools of philosophy could not, in ten years, define as formal rules what a young boy produces naturally and spontaneously in an instant.

We also agree with certain truths immediately, without needing any proof from experience <note>original: *a posteriori*</note>, the very first time we hear them, as long as they possess a natural harmony that pleases the mind. In addition to these harmonies, this order, and these naturally implanted truths, there are also various types of love. These all originate from self-love, though only through formal study <note>original: "doctrine"</note> can we understand where these loves come from and what their true nature is.

However, the situation is different for brute animals. They possess even more innate qualities, whether these are specific ideas, forms, behaviors <note>original: "modifications"</note>, and so on. They are born with their sensations, perceptions, and instincts <note>original: "wills"</note> already intact; they can stand alone as soon as they emerge from the womb or the egg.

*(31.) The external senses are very dull <note>original: "obtuse"</note>, crude <note>original: "gross"</note>, and weak. Consequently, they are often misleading, deceiving even our internal senses with countless phenomena that we mistake for truth. This happens because the internal senses look deeper into the causes and fundamental laws <note>original: "principles"</note> of things. Therefore, knowledge based solely on the senses is purely animalistic; the knowledge that is truly rational and human is of a different nature.*

There is no other way for us to know or understand except through sensation and experience—that is, the "posterior" way <note>original: "posterior," referring to the *a posteriori* method of reasoning from effects back to causes</note>, also called the analytical method. Our physical sensations develop first, followed by our internal perceptions, and finally our intellect. Good judgment, or the understanding of ultimate purposes <note>original: "knowledges of the true end"</note>, does not arrive until later in adult life. Since this is the natural path available to us, we must depend on observing and gathering experiments and natural phenomena. 

For example, the science of optics is intimately familiar with the structure <note>original: "organism"</note> of the eye, yet it still knows no rules except those discovered through experimental science. The same is true for the acoustics of the ear. Even the deep truths, causes, and principles of nature—and even of morality—must be learned in this same way. We may be delighted when objects appear before us, but we do not actually understand their inner nature any better than we understand the intrinsic beauty of a flower that is striking for its lovely blend of colors and symmetrical parts. When we look at a blooming rose, we perceive nothing but its beauty, order, and truth; however, we cannot explore its specific form, its color, or the relationship and position of its parts without the information provided by the senses. The soul itself, which is the only thing that truly understands the objects presented to the senses, is the embodiment of order, law, and truth. Consequently, the soul is pleased by whatever aligns with its own logic <note>original: "reason"</note>, while it avoids and rejects everything else.

<summary>Swedenborg argues that human knowledge must begin with sensory experience (the analytical or "a posteriori" way), even though the senses are often misleading compared to the soul's innate understanding of order.</summary>

However, there are countless things that appear to the senses to be something they are not, as we can see clearly from many examples. For instance, it is a sensory appearance that the sun, stars, and planets are tiny specks <note>original: "molecules"</note> instead of being worlds as large as our own. It appears as if we are completely stationary, even though our Earth <note>original: "terrestrial globe"</note> rotates and revolves around the sun. This is just like being on a ship where we seem to be at rest, even though within an hour we may be carried miles away from the port under full sail.

It appears as if people on the other side of the world <note>original: "antipodes"</note> could not possibly stand on their feet; as if our blood were not circulating; as if the brain <note>original: "cerebrum"</note> were not active <note>original: "animate"</note>; and as if the stomach <note>original: "ventricle"</note> lacked its rhythmic, digestive motion <note>original: "peristaltic motion"</note>. The senses do not perceive that a specific fluid flows very quickly through the smallest fibers, or that the atmosphere is made of individual particles, since the air seems like water—either a continuous whole or nothing at all.

To our senses, it also seems as if there were such things as attraction, a vacuum, or only a single atmosphere, and as if a ray of light were a single particle <note>original: "atom"</note>. It can seem as if there is no underlying substance, or as if a very fast-moving object were a continuous solid. It can seem as if divine providence, fate, and fortune are just random accidents. It can appear as if insanity is wisdom, falsehood is truth, and as if what is appropriate <note>original: "becoming"</note> is the same as what is inappropriate. It might seem like vice is virtue, that reckless behavior <note>original: "license"</note> is free will, and that the pleasures and temptations of the senses are the highest happiness and the greatest good.

It appears as if art is more clever than nature, and as if philosophers have more common sense than ordinary people <note>original: "the plebeian world"</note>. It seems as if the wise are those who speak elegantly, know many languages, and offer sharp criticisms—or, conversely, those who stay silent or speak in riddles <note>original: "express only half the meaning"</note>. We often judge people based on the opinions of others whom we consider to be of good judgment. Countless more examples exist when it comes to distinguishing <note>original: "discriminations"</note> between truth and falsehood, good and evil, and beauty and appropriateness. Because these distinctions are not visible to the senses, we tend to believe they do not exist as long as they remain hidden.

> (32.) *The soul acts in harmony <note>original: "concurs"</note> with every sensation, perception, and thought process <note>original: "intellection"</note>. The senses provide information to the mind so that the rational part of us can "hear" <note>Swedenborg uses the metaphor of "hearing" to describe the mind processing information from the senses</note>; without sensory experience, we could understand nothing. The soul can be compared to the light surrounding the eye: without light, there would be no way to distinguish between brightness and shadow, or the differences in objects that create colors and forms. In the same way, the soul provides a kind of light so that truths <note>original: "verities"</note> can be recognized as truths. However, more perfect forms—such as circles and spheres, which are higher in perfection than angular forms—and those even more perfect, naturally please us because they are soothing; examples include sweet and sugary substances. 

The forms that affect our hearing are mainly circular, as these are the shapes of the vibrations <note>original: "modifications or of the fluxions"</note> of air particles. To the extent that these vibrations approach a circular form, they become more harmonious and pleasing <note>original: "grateful"</note>. They become even more delightful as they approach a "perpetually circular" or spiral form, such as the vibrations of the ether <note>A substance once theoretically believed to fill the upper regions of space and transmit light.</note> or of sight itself. But as they move away from these harmonies or approach angular shapes—becoming sharp, prickly, or, in a word, unrounded—they become disagreeable to that same degree. 

It is the same with sight: as its forms or images become more perfectly spiral in their composition, mixing light and shade, they are more pleasing. Indeed, they are most pleasing as they approach the forms of the higher or internal senses—specifically, the "perpetually spiral" or vortical <note>original: "vortical"; relating to a vortex or whirling motion.</note> form. Above these are the superior forms, such as the celestial and spiritual, where every part is seemingly eternal <note>original: "perpetual"</note> and every angular or sharp edge is removed. In this way, every organ has its own specific form, which looks toward a higher form and relates to a lower one. Every form undergoes infinite changes of state, and from these changes come the infinite varieties of sensation.

<vocab>intellect, action, sensation, circular, spherical, angular, spiral, vortical, fluxions, ether</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg explains that the soul perceives pleasure through "perfect" geometric forms (circular, spiral, and vortical) and displeasure through "imperfect" angular forms. He argues that sensory organs are structured to respond to these geometric hierarchies, ranging from physical air vibrations to spiritual forms.</summary>

## IV.

### THE SENSE OF TOUCH.

(35.) *Touch is the lowest and most purely physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> sense. Its countless organic structures are spread over the entire outer skin <note>original: "cuticle"</note> and surface of the body; together, these structures constitute the organ of touch.*

Under the skin, tucked within minute folds as if in their own beds, lie hidden tiny sensory bumps <note>original: "molecular papillae"</note> of a pyramidal shape, which are protected by the epidermis. They exist in such great numbers that they are scattered throughout the entire skin covering the body. There is not a single point on the surface that these do not partially occupy. When they prepare to receive a sensation, they essentially fill that point, for they are able to contract and expand. By drawing themselves in or out, they make the entire skin sensitive along with themselves. 

Thus, the organ of touch is not a single continuous surface, but is "concrete"—meaning it is a composite made up of an infinite number of distinct parts. Anything that is perfectly continuous <note>meaning a single, undivided mass without internal structure</note> is contrary to nature. Nature reaches higher degrees of perfection when her products and compositions are more distinct and individual. In the smallest particulars, nature lies hidden and thrives as if left to herself; she does not thrive in those composite things where her order, form, and harmony are lost.

---

* The organ of touch is a composite structure, yet it preserves the order and harmony of its individual parts. <note>Translator's note.</note>

(36.) *The perfection of the sense of touch depends on the quantity, quality, placement, and connection of its organs—that is, on the specific form of each part and the general form of the whole. It also depends on a certain variety, since no single organ is exactly like another. This is similar to the perfection of the cortical glands <note>the "grey matter" or clusters of nerve cells in the brain</note>, to which these bodily structures correspond.*

The papillae <note>tiny, nipple-like sensory bumps on the skin</note>, which are the organic structures of touch, are very soft and adapt to every tactile force. They withdraw into themselves as soon as they are touched by anything that injures or irritates them, but they extend themselves when they are stimulated and pleased by rounded forms. Consequently, they become erect or relaxed exactly according to the nature of the impact they receive. 

Regarding quantity, the greater their number, the more precise their discriminations and the more subtle the distinctions they recognize. Regarding quality, the softer they are, the more they can adapt to every tactile force, and therefore the more sensitive they are. Their perfection, therefore, lies in their ability to change their states and to apply themselves to the shapes of the objects with which they come in contact. 

For this reason, they are moist and supplied with a constant, very slight fluid <note>original: "humour"</note> of a marrow-like <note>original: "medullous"</note> nature. There are also glands from which bodily <note>original: "corporeal"</note> fibers emerge, continually absorbing and transmitting this fluid from the surrounding air. Regarding their location and connection (or their specific and general form), the more perfect they are in themselves, the more powerful they are at producing or capturing sensation. However, the raw power of individual parts cannot produce these effects unless all parts possessing similar power work together <note>original: "conspire"</note> toward the same result. To ensure they work together, a definite and mutual connection is required; from this connection arises an order and a concern for the whole system, so that, for instance, one part may treat the other as its partner...

(38.) *The soul perceives every specific change occurring throughout the entire body. It reacts, both specifically and generally, to anything that harms the body's organic forms. However, we are only conscious of changes that specifically affect the cortex of the brain.*

Whatever strikes a fiber travels to the fiber’s origin, essentially announcing the change that has occurred. Every sensation rises—moving, as it were, from heavier to lighter substances <note>Swedenborg refers to the transition from physical matter to more refined substances like "animal spirits"</note>—as it is elevated to its source. Thus, a starting point or "beginning" is present in every minute part of its fiber; because of this, each part is made aware of any change. Every organic structure in the body is constructed from fibers and vessels; the fiber itself is the producer and the formative substance of the vessel. Therefore, no change can occur in any part of the body—which is made of fibers—without the cortical gland (and thus the soul) being made aware of it. 

However, the cortical glands in the spinal cord and brainstem perceive things differently than those in the brain, and the glands in the cerebellum perceive differently than those in the <term>cerebrum</term> <note>the large, upper part of the brain responsible for voluntary activity</note>. The former perceive in a general and vague way, while the latter perceive specifically and distinctly. From this arises a type of sensation that does not reach the conscious awareness of our intellectual mind. For a sensation to be consciously perceived, it must specifically reach the cortex of the cerebrum...

### V.

## THE SENSE OF TASTE.

(39.) *Taste is a superior sense of touch; it distinguishes those shaped particles or angular forms that are simpler and which flow within a liquid.*

The tongue contains <term>papillae</term> <note>the tiny bumps on the tongue that contain taste buds</note> almost identical to those described previously in the pores of the skin, though there are three main differences. They lie hidden beneath the skin of the tongue and a specific nervous membrane, but they extend and reach out when the appetite is stimulated and the mind desires to perceive the quality of food and drink. This explains why these papillae are retracted and hidden in a corpse. 

The outermost layer is like a net—permeable and full of tiny holes—so that the particles pressed and rolled against the tongue can immediately use their sharp points and corners to contact the membranes and the tiny extended tips of the papillae. This process could not happen unless the specific particles to be tasted were dissolved and flowing in a liquid. This is why the tongue and the surrounding glands—such as those in the mouth, jaws, and palate—secrete saliva. A dry tongue has only a dull and weak sense of taste, very similar to basic touch alone. 

The fact that taste is a superior form of touch is evident because the sense of touch cannot be refined enough to perceive the <term>effluvia</term> <note>original: "effluvia"; microscopic particles or vapors given off by substances</note> floating in moist environments, nor can it detect their sharp points—much less the order and arrangement of the angles among...

## VI.

### THE SENSE OF SMELL.

(43.) *The sense of smell is an even more refined form of touch. It perceives those shaped particles or external angular forms that are even simpler than those perceived by taste, and which float and are carried through the air.*

The organs responsible for the sense of smell are spread throughout the entire <term>pituitary membrane</term> <note>the mucous membrane of the nose</note>, which lines not only the nasal cavities but also covers the walls of many small air cells or <term>cellules</term>. In addition to the nasal cavities, there are the <term>frontal sinuses</term>, which are hollowed out between the layers of the frontal bone, as well as the <term>antra of Highmore</term> <note>the maxillary sinuses located in the cheekbones</note> in the upper jaw. There are also the small cells of the <term>cuneiform bone</term> <note>now known as the sphenoid bone at the base of the skull</note>, as well as caverns and spongy, maze-like spaces; all of these connect with the nostrils and are covered with a shared membrane and <term>periosteum</term> <note>the connective tissue covering the surface of bones</note>.

Countless tiny vessels and numerous interwoven glandular and round bodies creep through this membrane across the head and these wide spaces. There are six sinus cavities and four small cells of the <term>spongious bones</term> <note>referring to the ethmoid bone</note> which connect with each other and are equipped and filled with similar organs or glands. This entire expansive structure originates from the <term>olfactory nerves</term>. These nerves—formerly called the <term>mammillary processes</term> <note>original: "processus mammillares"; so-called because of their breast-like shape</note>—are attached to the front part of the brain. They become thinner around the <term>ethmoidal crest</term> <note>the crista galli, a bony ridge in the skull</note> and are passed through a perforated layer of bone called the <term>cribriform plate</term> <note>from the Latin "cribrum," meaning sieve; a bone with many small holes for nerve fibers</note>. This structure follows these nerve fibers outward, even extending beyond the <term>meninx</term> <note>the protective membranes or meninges covering the brain</note>,
