Based on the description of how this organ expands and connects, it is clear that it possesses a sense even more refined—perceiving even simpler components—than the sense of taste. The particles floating in the air are lighter and more volatile than those found in water or other liquids that affect taste.

For the sense of taste to distinguish the shape of particles, the substances must first be dissolved. However, for smell to perceive these shapes, dissolution is not required. Instead, the very <term>effluvia</term> <note>original: "effluvia"; the microscopic vapors or particles given off by a substance</note> released by animal or vegetable bodies, as well as those exhaled from minerals, are detected by this sense. From these sources, particles that do not stay attached to the main body are released, separating spontaneously to drift through the air.

The emissions of the animal kingdom are so abundant that dogs, using only their sense of smell, can distinguish their masters from other people and can track and hunt animals. Even more abundant and noticeable are the emissions from the vegetable kingdom, such as the scents from gardens and fields. In the mineral kingdom, although many objects have no scent, there are still many that trigger this sense when they are in liquid form. Thus, smell seems to distinguish simpler components than those detected by taste. Nevertheless, these forms remain angular, naturally heavy, inert, hard, shaped, and entirely physical and material.

->*external forms, but not internal forms, as do the*<-

However, their internal quality or "internal forms" are not perceived; this is because only the parts on the surface affect the <term>papillae</term> <note>the small sensory receptors on the tongue or skin</note>. And because these are inert...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that smell is a more refined sense than taste because it detects volatile particles (effluvia) in the air without needing them to be dissolved, though it still only perceives the external, material shape of these particles.</summary>

Therefore, the laws governing hearing and sight are entirely different from those governing smell, taste, and touch.

These roots do not seem to be as widely scattered in human brains as they are in the brains of <term>irrational animals</term> <note>non-human animals</note>. This is perhaps to prevent odors from constantly disrupting the reasoning and judgment of the human mind by causing frequent internal changes. Because the sense of smell extends through the entire brain, it follows that the mind is repelled by anything that harms the harmony of its parts and substances—

## VII.

### THE SENSE OF HEARING.

*(49.) The ear is the organ of Hearing, exactly adapted to receiving the modifications of the air <note>original: "modifications of the air"; Swedenborg uses this phrase to refer to what we now call sound waves or vibrations</note>.*

We can learn enough about the nature of sound waves by studying the structure of the ear, just as we can understand the formation of the ear by studying the nature of sound waves. For the vibrating air is the **principal cause** <note>the primary force or active agent</note> and the ear is the **instrumental cause** <note>the physical tool or mechanism that receives the action</note>; they are so perfectly designed for one another that every detail of the sound is reflected in the structure of the ear. However, it takes a sharp mind, well-equipped with scientific knowledge, to uncover the nature of one by examining the other.

The outer ear—the **auricle** <note>the visible part of the ear outside the head</note>—with its **pinna** (lobe), its **helix** and **antihelix** (the curved rims of the ear), **tragus** and **antitragus** (the small fleshy bumps), **scapha** (the hollow between the rims), **concha** (the deepest part of the outer ear), as well as its ligaments, cartilages, **follicles** or small glands, and muscles, is spread out and spirally twisted. It is designed to catch the very first impulse of sound or vibration so that not even the smallest "ray" of sound escapes. Instead, every vibration is funneled perfectly into the auditory canal. 

This passage itself, with its winding path, its structure made of bone and cartilage, its lining, **ceruminous glands** <note>original: "cerumanous glandules"; the glands that produce earwax</note>, network of tissues, and hairs, is perfectly adapted to guide the approaching, concentrated sound toward the **tympanum** <term>the eardrum</term>. At the same time, this structure regulates the sound to prevent any damage to the membrane. The eardrum itself is concave, oval-shaped, positioned at an angle, and composed of three distinct layers, the outermost one being...

...it may enter into a union <note>original: "marriage union"; Swedenborg often uses this term to describe the harmonious joining of two different substances or forces</note> with the blood, even from the brain itself, through its sinuses into the jugular veins, and from the jugular veins into the heart. Because of this, it contributes something to the animal life <note>original: "animal life"; here meaning the vital biological functions and movements of a living creature, derived from the Latin *anima*</note>. For speech and its sound are a kind of vibration <note>original: "trembling"</note> that pervades both liquids and solids. This is why the ear is formed within the petrous bone <note>the dense, "stony" part of the temporal bone at the base of the skull that protects the inner ear</note>, and why its nerve passes over that part of the skull where the sinuses meet, and why the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>a subtle, invisible fluid believed by early anatomists to flow through the nerves to transmit sensation and motion</note> itself passes through the pores of the skull.

(66.) Differences in sound can neither exist nor be distinguished unless there is a certain "common sound"—a general, undifferentiated background resonance—within which and under which specific details can be discerned. This is no different from the case of sight, which also cannot exist without a "common light," through which all things are perceived as being more or less luminous. Such a background sound is provided by the entire skull, which is why the ear is embedded in the stony and most porous bone. It is also for this reason that musical instruments are more distinct, perfect, and resonant when their strings are attached to a soundboard or surface made of a more vibrating substance; this surface provides a common sound of its own. However, this common sound, much like light itself, is not consciously perceived when one is focused on the specific sounds.

(67.) The sense of hearing communicates immediately with the cerebrum <note>the large, front part of the brain associated with conscious thought</note> via the "softer nerve" of the seventh pair <note>in older anatomical systems, the seventh pair of cranial nerves included both the facial nerve and the auditory nerve (now called the eighth pair). The "softer" portion is the auditory nerve</note>, which likely arises from the medulla of the brain. However, its "harder portion" <note>the facial nerve</note> communicates with the medulla of the cerebellum <note>the part of the brain at the back of the skull, which Swedenborg associates with involuntary or natural functions</note>, from which it seems to originate. From this, it follows that the ear is adapted for receiving physical sound by the harder nerve, but for grasping the meaning of that sound by the softer nerve. Each of these nerves is distributed throughout the sensitive membranes, cylinders, and spirals of the ear’s vestibule <note>the central part of the bony labyrinth in the inner ear</note>.

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the skull acts as a resonator for a "common sound" necessary for hearing, and distinguishes between the roles of the auditory and facial nerves in processing sound and meaning.</summary>

## VIII.

### THE SENSE OF SIGHT.

(68.) The organ of sight is the eye, situated in its own <term>orbit</term> <note>the bony socket of the skull</note>. It is globular in shape and can be black, brown, gray, bluish-gray, or blue in color. Aside from the eyelashes and eyelids, the eye itself is equipped with six muscles for movement. These are called the <term>attollens</term> <note>original Latin: "the lifter"; the superior rectus muscle</note> and the <term>deprimens</term> <note>original Latin: "the depressor"; the inferior rectus muscle</note>, the <term>abductor</term> <note>the muscle that moves the eye outward, away from the nose</note>, the <term>adductor</term> <note>the muscle that moves the eye inward, toward the nose</note>, and the <term>superior</term> and <term>inferior oblique</term> muscles. 

The eyeball itself is composed of <term>tunics</term> <note>the protective layers or membranes of the eye</note>, <term>humors</term> <note>the clear fluids within the eye</note>, and blood vessels. There are many tunics. The <term>albuginea</term>—which is also called the *adnata* or *conjunctiva*—is the white membrane that covers the front and connects the eye to the orbit. Next is the <term>cornea</term>, which is transparent and divided into layers. The third is the <term>sclerotic</term> <note>now commonly called the sclera</note>, which is tough and opaque. The fourth is the <term>choroid</term>, which is black in humans and consists of a double layer. The fifth is the <term>uvea</term>, which is the front part of the <term>choroid</term>; it is perforated and colored, visible through the cornea, and convex in shape. Within the uvea, one can see the <term>iris</term> in various colors. The <term>pupilla</term> [pupil] is the round opening located almost in the center of the iris. The back surface of the uvea is black. 

In addition to these, one can see the <term>sphincter pupillae</term> <note>the muscle responsible for constricting the pupil</note> for contracting the opening, the <term>ciliary fibers</term> for dilating it, and the <term>ciliary</term> or <term>annular ligament</term> <note>a ring-shaped ligament</note> for the movement of the <term>vitreous body</term> <note>the clear, gel-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina</note> and the <term>crystalline lens</term>. Notably, there is also the <term>arterial and venous circle</term> <note>the network of blood vessels</note> and the <term>black ducts</term> <note>original Latin: *ductus nigri*; likely referring to the pigmented ciliary processes</note>. 

Then there is the <term>retina</term>, a very delicate, glistening, and somewhat mucous membrane. It is an expansion of the <term>optic nerve</term> around the base of the eye and is the primary organ of vision. The <term>humors</term> [fluids] consist of the <term>aqueous</term> or <term>albugineous</term> <note>white-like or clear</note> fluid, which fills both chambers of the eye. The uvea floats freely in this fluid, which is continually replenished;

...the <term>vitreous humor</term> <note>the clear, gel-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina</note>, which likely consists of very delicate vessels or cells that fill the back part of the eye and touch the membrane of the <term>retina</term>. It hangs freely right behind the pupil and is moved by it; it is composed of many transparent layers, making it look like an onion. Next is the <term>arachnoid</term> <note>original: "arachnoid vascular tunic"; a spider-web-like layer of blood vessels</note> membrane, which surrounds both the crystalline lens and the vitreous body. Finally, the <term>optic nerve</term>, which forms the retina, enters the eye from the side near the nose. In addition to these, there are the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth pairs of cranial nerves.

(69.) The eye is an organ built to receive the vibrations <note>original: "modifications"</note> of the <term>ether</term> <note>in 18th-century science, the subtle substance believed to fill space and carry light waves</note>, just as the ear is designed to receive the vibrations of the air. Therefore, by studying the structure and form of the eye, we can learn about the nature of the ether, and vice versa. This is because they correspond to one another as an instrument <note>original: "instrumental cause"</note> corresponds to its primary purpose <note>original: "principal cause"</note>. This correspondence is so exact that the eye could not have been formed in any other way and still be able to receive every variation of the incoming light, adapt to them, and transmit them to the <term>common sensory</term> <note>original Latin: "sensorium commune," the part of the brain where the soul was thought to perceive all physical sensations</note>.

(70.) The soul intended to provide her body with sight so that she might observe every variety of the visible world that lies within her range of vision. Without this sense, these things would never be known to her. Only through sight could she care for the body and protect it from danger—which is the ultimate purpose of all the senses. Furthermore, the soul uses sight to refine the intellect or the rational mind through a <term>posterior</term> path <note>meaning through external experience and sensory data, rather than through innate reason</note>. Beyond these goals, there are many other specific purposes for sight.

(71.) However, even though the sense of sight is the highest and most perfect of all the external senses, it is still so limited that it can only perceive the final effects of nature—its outward shapes and forms; and

...infinite things still lie hidden from her <note>the soul</note> and escape her view, while only a very few are revealed—and indeed these very obscurely and indistinctly, as if they were of a continuous degree <note>original: "continuous degree"; in Swedenborg's philosophy, this refers to a gradual change in size or density, as opposed to "discrete degrees" which are distinct levels of existence</note>. This is the reason why interior things and the underlying causes of bodies and objects must be investigated through the experience of many centuries, and indeed with the help of those sciences by which the intellect is sharpened to penetrate more deeply into things.

(72.) By means of the optical arts, or microscopes, we have detected how many infinite things escape our physical vision. Even the smallest insects—whose shadows we can hardly perceive at all, or see only as the tiniest points—are revealed to be provided with nerves, vessels, blood, a heart, a brain, a spinal cord <note>original: "medulla"</note>, muscles, and organs for the senses, nutrition, and reproduction. We have also seen that a droplet of red blood, previously hardly visible, contains infinite parts; and so it is with many other examples. From these, we may conclude that even these parts, which are the final objects of microscopic vision, also contain within themselves innumerable smaller parts—even an entire system. Thus, nature in its smallest parts still lies hidden far beyond our optical experience. 

But we are gifted with a certain internal vision, or imagination, which penetrates still farther into the forms of things presented to us, while the inmost sight of all penetrates even farther. The same is true regarding distances: while our hearing extends to a moderate distance, our eyesight extends to an immense distance, even to the sun and the stars. The rational mind, through its own vision, reaches even beyond the stars, while the soul—which is intelligence itself and pure vision—is not limited in its knowledge <note>original: "cognition"</note> by anything narrower than the created universe. For if such a difference exists between the perfection of hearing and that of sight, how much greater must the difference be between physical sight and the insights of the soul when left to itself?

(74.) Because our mind can only judge objects through the eye, it judges their figure based on the variations of light and shadow, their magnitude and mass from their distance, and their form from their motion. It also judges harmony based on the pleasure felt by the sight or the <term>animus</term> <note>The *animus* refers to the lower or natural mind, which is the seat of the emotions, passions, and the immediate processing of sensory information.</note>. It follows that the mind, when judging by sight, is prone to being greatly deceived whenever the information from which it forms its judgments is obscure. For sight is the servant and messenger of the rational mind, informing it about the visible world and its diversity.

(75.) There are as many delicate pulsations and touches as there are rays of light. Although these seem like nothing when compared to the coarser sense of touch—as do the vibrations <note>original: "modifications"</note> of the air—nothing can be affected without some form of touch. The more luminous and intense a ray is, the stronger it is; the less light it has, the less power it has to act; and shadow itself has no force at all. The power contained within solar rays is evident from their effects, such as heat or the way they irritate the membrane of the nose to cause sneezing; it is also shown by the reflection of visible things from objects and figures into the eye, the phenomena of refraction, and countless other examples.

The ratio itself produces the color, but the form and harmony create its brilliance and beauty, while the harmony of the colors with one another produces the delight of vision.

(77.) No image can be presented to the eye without general light, which allows us to see what is more or less luminous and what is in shadow. Thus, in darkness, sight disappears; in twilight, it is weak; and at midday, it is clear.

(78.) Every vision, object, or image causes a change of state in its <term>sensory</term> <note>The sense organ or the neural pathway responsible for processing sensation.</note>. The eye automatically adapts itself to every quality of the object it sees; therefore, there is an active force or action in the eye that corresponds to the passive sensation. This is evident from the structure of the eye itself and from our own observations whenever images enter the eye. Regarding its structure: the pupil is movable by means of the <term>crystalline humours</term> <note>The lens of the eye.</note>; to move precisely toward every variety of object, it is equipped with the sphincter, fibers, and ciliary ligaments. Even the crystalline lens itself is composed of many layers. The <term>uvea</term> <note>The pigmented middle layer of the eye, including the iris.</note> floats freely in the <term>aqueous humour</term> <note>The clear fluid filling the space in the front of the eyeball between the lens and the cornea.</note>, which is also called the <term>albugineous humour</term> and is constantly replenished. Thus, the eye adapts itself wonderfully to perceive every object through these changes in its state.

### THE SENSE OF SIGHT.

The eye adjusts itself based on the position of the object, which is accomplished by the six muscles of the eye. It also partially shields itself by dropping the eyelids or admits the full <term>influx</term> <note>The sensory input or "flowing in" of light and images.</note> of the object by raising them. In a specific adjustment, the position of the pupil changes. In even finer detail, all the smallest particles that make up the eye's <term>humors</term> <note>The fluids of the eye.</note>—the aqueous, the crystalline <note>The lens of the eye.</note>, and the vitreous body—also change. The vitreous body is thought to consist of extremely delicate vessels and cells. Furthermore, the retina itself distinctly receives all these incoming sensory forces.

(80.) Visual objects also cause a change of state in the individual fibers of the optic nerve, in the various fibers of the brain's <term>medulla</term> <note>In this context, the white matter or internal substance of the brain.</note>, and finally in the individual <term>cortical glands</term> <note>Swedenborg's term for the neurons or individual cells of the brain's cortex.</note>. The same force that is carried into the vitreous humor and the retina is also communicated through the fibers, extending to their very ends. However, the change of state caused by these visual forces is lighter and more delicate than the changes produced by the forces of sound or hearing.

(81.) Light rays do not merely try to reach specific cortical cells; they aim for the entire cortical covering, or all the cells universally. Thus, there is not a single cell in the brain that is not made conscious of, and aligned with, some specific light ray. This is also true for every fiber. After the optic nerve meets its counterpart in the larger <term>ventricles</term> <note>Fluid-filled cavities in the brain.</note> of the brain, it expands into two swellings called the thalami of the optic nerves, or the <term>posterior legs</term> <note>original: "posteriora crura"; anatomical stalks or supports.</note> of the <term>medulla oblongata</term> <note>The lower part of the brainstem.</note>. These thalami communicate with all the matter—both the white and the <term>gray</term> <note>original: "cineritious"; ashen-colored matter, now known as gray matter.</note>—of the entire brain. They are attached to and rest upon the brain's hindmost lobes and borders. Meanwhile, the fibers of the upper brain lobes, as well as those at the very top of the head, are concentrated into a sort of fixed cylinder of white matter called the <term>base of the fornix</term> <note>original: "basis fornicis"; an arch-like structure in the brain.</note>. From there, they mostly spread out over the thalami of the optic nerves. In this way, the entire brain, both its inner and outer substance, participates in the experience of sight.

(82.) There is no <term>cortical gland</term> <note>original: "cortical gland"; Swedenborg's term for the individual nerve cells or neurons of the brain's cerebral cortex.</note> that does not represent a kind of internal small eye—or a semblance of an eye—since the gland is located at the final endpoint of the fibers, and thus at the end of the patterns and rays of both sight and hearing.

(83.) The visual rays of the images of sight induce an internal and external change of state in every <term>cortical gland</term>, just as the vibrations of sound do in the whole brain. This is because the <term>cortical gland</term> is a brain in miniature; it receives the sensation of sight just as the entire brain receives the sensation of sound.

(84.) The visual rays and their shapes, forms, or images pass over the <term>cortical gland</term> and its surface. They bend themselves according to its most perfect or <term>vortical</term> <note>Spiral-like or whirlpool-shaped; in Swedenborg’s philosophy, this is considered the most efficient and perfect form of motion and organization.</note> form, and their bending and changing is communicated to all the fibers and vessels that compose the gland, and thus to the whole gland itself.

(85.) But since the <term>cortical gland</term> adapts itself even more perfectly than the eye to receive every variety of visual objects, it uses its own power to induce a change in itself, taking on another form that agrees with the incoming image. This change—which is the action of the mind itself or of the soul and corresponds to the sensation of sight as a passive experience—produces what is called the <term>idea of imagination</term>. This is a part of the memory, because it is reproduced as often as the gland again assumes that same state.

(86.) In this way, the images of sight produce and perfect the imagination, which is the internal sense of sight. This happens not because the visual image induces this change by itself—for the gland is only passive to the impact of the rays—but because the gland itself participates actively from its own interior power. Thus, a correspondence is established, where a specific change of state corresponds to a specific image. It follows that if the imagination is strong and intent upon one object, or if there is a thought in the mind from which an interior active power flows forth...

But the inharmonious disagrees; it forces, injures, and endeavors to destroy the <term>nexus</term> <note>original: "nexus"; the connections or bonds between parts of a system.</note>, position, order, and form—in a word, both the external and internal state of the whole gland. From this results aversion, horror, and whatever is unpleasant, cheerless, or even leads to sadness.

<header>PERCEPTION, IMAGINATION, MEMORY, ETC.</header>

## IX.

### PERCEPTION, IMAGINATION, MEMORY, AND THEIR IDEAS.

(91.) Words that are heard are seen almost instantly, as it were, for words represent many forms, quantities, qualities, movements, and <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidents"; in classical philosophy, these are the non-essential properties or characteristics of a thing (like its color or position) rather than its essential nature.</note> which are usually objects of sight. But whatever is seen is also taken in by a certain internal sight or imagination; that is, it is perceived. Moreover, whatever is perceived by the imagination is also understood by man. Thus, the patterns of sound or hearing transition into visual images; these move into ideas of the imagination, which are also called "material ideas"; and these, in turn, transition into rational ideas or logical concepts. From the analytical connection of these ideas, the intellect arises. Such is the progression of sensations from the external to the internal, and from this, we may distinguish their differences.

(92.) The imagination is, therefore, an internal sight that corresponds to external sight. The eye is merely the organ and instrument of vision; the true vision itself resides in the brain, or in the <term>common sensory</term> <note>original: "common sensory" (sensorium commune); a historical term for the part of the brain where all the senses were thought to meet and be processed into a unified experience.</note>. When this area is injured, disturbed, or obstructed, the eye no longer sees. On the other hand, an image that was present during the day is revived when the eyes are closed or during sleep, appearing as though it existed in the eye itself.

(93.) The components of external sight are called images, but the components of internal sight are called ideas—by some, indeed, they are called "material ideas." This is because they are represented much like visual images, except they are arranged in a different order and connection. The nature of this difference can be understood through observation and example alone.

(94.) External sight observes only the shapes of objects—for example, one wall of a palace after another, then the roof, the tiles, the foundations, the rooms, the paintings, the tapestries, the thrones, and the dukes and ministers who live there. But internal sight observes all these things at once, whereas the eye sees them only one after another over a period of time. In a city, external sight sees one house after another—the squares, streets, temples, monuments, the government, and the inhabitants—but internal sight sees all these various things instantly rather than in a sequence. External sight views the entire starry sky—with its sun, stars, planets, moons, meteors, clouds, and their various appearances—looking at one after the other. Meanwhile, the imagination grasps them all at the same time and sees the form of the whole heaven as perceived by the eye. This is true in all other instances as well. 

Thus, external sight takes in only one part of an object at a time, while internal vision takes them in simultaneously. In a single moment, internal vision can travel through a palace, a city, or the starry heavens, contemplating as one complex idea what was presented to the eye in small details. In this way, the total complexity of the internal vision differs infinitely from that of the external; it adds something almost infinite or perpetual, creating a superior form compared to the one immediately below it. Therefore, it follows that internal sight, or imagination, is proportionally higher, more fundamental, more internal, simpler, and more perfect than external sight.

(95.) We can also conclude from the physical organs themselves that imagination, or internal sight, is of a directly superior and more perfect level. The organ of sight is the eye, while the organ of internal sight is the <term>cortical gland</term> <note>original: "cortical gland"; Swedenborg's term for the individual nerve cells or clusters in the cerebral cortex, which he believed were the fundamental units of brain function.</note>, particularly in the brain. This cortical gland is like a miniature eye or brain, yet it is an organ of a higher level because its structure is <term>vortical</term> <note>original: "vortical"; Swedenborg used this term to describe a complex, spiral-like geometric form that he believed allowed for higher-order functioning than simple linear or circular forms.</note>, according to its physical description. Consequently, it is of a purer, more perfect, and simpler nature than the structure of the eye, whose rays and movements are...

> (96.) The balanced variety of these glands ensures that every detail of an object is grasped; what is seen clearly in one gland may be seen more obscurely in another. Just as having more eyes leads to clearer sight, having more cortical glands leads to a more distinct imagination. Furthermore, the overarching system perfects the individual parts so they all work together toward a shared result.

> (97.) The images from our sight travel up the fibers of the optic nerve to all the cortical glands in the brain. As a result, the entire gland becomes aware of the image and the visual phenomenon. The gland, serving as the organ for internal sight or imagination, immediately and perfectly adapts itself to receive its object—much more perfectly than the physical eye or the organ of external sight can. The gland undergoes a change of state that corresponds closely to the incoming image or object. It either contracts or expands, adopts a more perfect shape, or distorts itself into an imperfect one. This is because something harmonious refreshes and expands the sensory organ, while anything discordant constricts and distorts it—exactly as we see in the fibers and organs of touch. This very change, which the gland undergoes as it adapts to a visual image, is called an **idea**. It can no longer be called a mere image, because it possesses a superior and more perfect form and is infused with intelligence. (98.) From these things it appears that a certain natural correspondence <note>original: "correspondence"; a central term in Swedenborg’s philosophy meaning a functional relationship between different levels of reality, such as the physical and the spiritual</note> exists between the imagination and the vision of the eyes. This is because anything harmonious naturally expands the organ and restores it to its most perfect form, while anything inharmonious compresses and distorts it into a less perfect form. This happens in countless ways, according to every quality of the object and whether it possesses a perfect or imperfect form.

(99.) The object or the image is perceived as soon as it strikes upon these tiny sensory organs, or the brain's cortex <note>original: "cortical brain"</note>. This subtle vibration, trembling, and initial change in the aforementioned glands produces what is called the sensation of sight; for sight does not exist in the eye, but in the common sensory <note>original: "common sensory"; the *sensorium commune*, or the part of the brain where all sensory inputs are processed and united</note>. When this modification spreads through the gland itself—bringing it into its most perfect form—and simultaneously through the simple fibers (which are like the intellectual rays of the soul), it is inevitable that whatever touches and instantly crosses these various fibers should be felt. But this sight is only surface-level and cannot yet be called perception.

(100.) However, we must first learn what sight properly is, as well as the nature of perception, imagination, memory, image, and idea, and the differences between them. At the start, it must be observed that all of these are carried out in a single organ or sensory site: the cortical substance <note>original: "cortical substance"; the gray matter of the brain</note>.

(101.) Whenever those variations of the patterns <note>original: "modes"</note> or modifications of the ether—consisting of the differences between light and shade, or black and white, from which colors arise—strike upon a tiny sensory organ in the brain, sight then exists. These variations quiver over the surface and through the medullary <note>original: "medullary"; referring to the white matter or "marrow" of the brain</note>, fibrous, and vascular substances. They prepare the tiny sensory organ to receive a modification similar to their own. The sensory organ does not enter into other states but remains simply in the state that agrees with what flows into it.

Therefore, while the organ passes through other states, they all relate back to this first or common state, and they are all compared and adapted to it. Countless states are possible—universal, specific, and individual. Within every universal state, there are infinitely many unique ones; or, in one general state, there are infinite particular states that make up its individual parts. These parts inevitably contribute to a specific general form, since they exist within a general structure that they help to maintain.

(103.) The components of imagination are not called images, but ***ideas***; for taken together, they create a specific form that approaches being rational, even though it is not yet truly rational. Only things that are similar and in agreement enter the imagination, and these are all specific ideas. From these, a complex idea arises, which in turn acts as a component for an even more complex idea yet to be formed.

(104.) When the imagination is active, external or physical sight stops or moves into the background. At that point, the seen object remains only as a common foundation for other states. By turning this object over in the mind, related ideas are gathered and brought together. Thus, imagination is stronger when the eyes are closed or in the dark, and weaker in bright light.

(106.) ***Memory*** is everything produced by the imagination, or rather, it is the capacity for the sensory organ's state to change. By nature, the sensory organ <note>original: "sensory"; the *sensorium*, or the part of the brain—specifically the cortical glands—that processes sensation</note> only has the potential to change its state. It actually adopts various states because of sensations that act upon it, using a kind of force to cause these changes. Once a specific change <note>original: "mutation"</note> is acquired, it remains, and its quality is recognized through the images impressed upon it. Therefore, a specific change that exists as a potential is part of the memory, while a specific change that is currently active is part of the imagination. Thus, the ideas in the memory are identical to the ideas in the imagination, but they are only brought back to life through an actual change of state. In this sense, imagination can be called "active memory."

(107.) These changes of state are acquired through practice, education, and habit as sensations flow into the mind. In this way, the sensory organ becomes accustomed to and learns over time to undergo many different changes of state, thereby enriching its memory. Every change, once learned, remains stored as memory and returns to the present whenever the sensory organ returns to that same state.

(108.) From these observations, we can now conclude what imagination, memory, and ideas are. We can also see how sight transitions into imagination and the relationship between them.

(109.) Animals <note>original: "brute animals"</note>, however, are born not only with their natural memory but also with their imagination—that is, with the ability to change the state of their sensory organs from birth. They possess, right away, a perfect sensory awareness of their bodies and the power to act.

(111.) (112.) (113.) Pure imagination is nothing else than the power of comprehending and embracing all at once those things which are obvious to the senses and which reside in the memory. This, to a degree, belongs to animals <note>original: "brutes"</note>; it is also exercised by sleepwalkers <note>original: "somnambulists"</note> and by children whose imagination is not yet well directed or ordered by the pure intellect.

When the nerve fibers relax, the glands lose their tone, stick to those next to them, and become thickened as the flow of bodily fluids <note>original: "humours"</note> becomes sluggish.

This is not the case elsewhere in the cerebrum, and even less so in the cerebellum, where sensations are general <note>original: "common"</note> and consequently indistinct. A general whole that lacks the distinct power of its specific parts is obscure; imagination cannot be ascribed to such a vague process.

<header>THE PURE INTELLECT.</header>

## Part Second.
# THE INTELLECT.

---

### X.
### THE PURE INTELLECT.

**(123.)** Before we discuss the "mixed intellect"—that is, thought and our rational mind—it is necessary to discuss the pure intellect. This is because thought acts as a middle point between the pure intellect and the imagination, and in a certain way, it draws its essence from both. Therefore, we must investigate the preceding and following causes <note>original: "priors and posteriors"; in Swedenborg’s philosophy, these refer to the higher causes and the lower effects</note>, or the extremes that influence it from both sides, so that the nature of the intermediate or mixed outcome may be understood.

**(124.)** Within each cortical gland <note>original: "cortical gland"; Swedenborg's term for the microscopic units of the brain, similar to what we now call neurons</note>, there is a specific substance of the brain's cortex from which "simple fibers" originate. This is just as the medullary or composite fibers <term>medullary fibers</term> <note>term: medullary fibers; the nerve fibers that make up the white matter of the brain</note> arise from the cortical glands themselves. For the cortical gland, which we call the internal tiny sensory organ, is essentially the brain <note>original: "cerebrum"</note> in its smallest likeness.

**(125.)** This <term>simple cortex</term> <note>term: simple cortex; the most refined, fundamental substance within the brain’s individual nerve cells, believed by the author to be the seat of the highest natural intelligence</note>, or simple cortical substance, is the most distinguished organ of the pure intellect. It surpasses the perfection of the sensory organ used for imagination or perception (the cortical gland) as much as that gland surpasses the brain as a whole, or as much as sight surpasses hearing. Its very form is superior—indeed, it is the highest form in nature, that truly celestial form described previously. It recognizes no higher form except for what is spiritual. Since this substance is located at the highest peak of nature, it cannot be described using the same terms used...

<summary>This page introduces the "pure intellect" as a superior faculty residing in the "simple cortex" of the brain, positioned above human thought and imagination. It establishes a hierarchy of the mind, where rational thought is a mixture of this pure intellect and the lower faculty of imagination.</summary>
<keywords>pure intellect, mixed intellect, cortical gland, simple cortex, simple fibres, rational mind, brain physiology, celestial form</keywords>

--- Page 114 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "simple cortex," which Swedenborg identifies as the biological seat of the highest natural faculty of the mind, the "pure intellect."</meta>

<page-num>74</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...in describing lower-level substances, for these are too crude to be applied to it. Therefore, we can hardly call it the cortex, nor the cortical substance, nor even a substance that merely imitates the cortex. It is nothing less than the most superior organ. We may not even call it a sensory organ <note>original: "sensory"</note>, for it does not simply feel; it understands. Therefore, in what follows, I shall call this the **intellectory** <term>intellectory</term> <note>term: intellectory; a term coined by Swedenborg (intellectorium) to describe the highest mental organ that processes raw sensation into understanding</note>.

**(126.)** The sensory system depends upon this intellectory; that is, sensation depends upon the pure intellect. There can be no sensation or perception of a sensation unless there is some more internal or superior faculty that understands what is being perceived. The smallest differences found in every idea, and the differences between individual ideas, cannot be distinguished by feeling and perception alone. There must be an intellectory that judges and decides whether one idea harmonizes with another or is discordant with it, and whether it agrees with other related or similar ideas. This is necessary so that we may know what is harmonious, what is specifically appropriate, and what is pleasant, true, and good. Without the pure intellect, there would be no thought, and even less imagination or sensation.

Similarly, the very organization of the body depends upon its intellectory, or inmost sensory organ. There is no "composite cortex" <note>the visible outer layer of the brain</note> without the "simple cortex," such as that of the brain; for simple fibers <note>the most refined, fundamental nerve threads</note> arise from the simple cortex and organize the cortical gland itself through their own pathways. No brain <note>original: "cerebrum"</note> exists without these cortical glands; no sensory organ of sight, hearing, taste, smell, or touch exists without them, and therefore, no body exists without them. Consequently, all things look toward this intellectory or pure intellect as their beginning, and at the same time, as the ultimate sense to which every individual operation refers itself.

<header>THE PURE INTELLECT</header>

**(127.)** Above itself, this **intellectory** <term>intellectory</term> recognizes no form other than spiritual form—that is, the soul itself or the form of the soul. Consequently, the pure intellect recognizes nothing above itself except pure intelligence, which belongs to the soul because the soul is spirit. Therefore, we should not confuse the pure intellect with intelligence, or the intellectory with the soul. The intellectory—whose form is celestial and is the highest level of nature—cannot understand anything on its own power; it can only understand through its essence or spiritual form. This spiritual form alone understands, and it enables the level that follows next in order to understand as well. Thus, it is clear that our soul resides in a realm far above the possible perceptions of our rational mind. We often believe that thought is the highest and most characteristic power of the soul itself; however, above our ordinary thought (which is always impure or "mixed" with sensory data), there is a purer thought, and above that, spiritual intelligence itself. Still higher, above even this, there is a wisdom which is divine rather than human; for intelligence draws its wisdom from a divine spirit alone, and thus from God.

**(128.)** Thus, the intellectory is born from the soul itself; its form clearly arises from the soul’s essential qualities. However, it is not easy to express in words what this first form following the soul actually is, since the attributes and powers of this form lie beyond the reach of common language. Words only express those things that exist within nature and within the cycle <note>original: "gyre"</note> of nature, but they cannot describe the highest things that are closest to spiritual essence. This is why we must speak about the intellectory in terms that are so general and difficult to understand, and why what is said must be explained through indirect descriptions and complex ideas. By these means, we may obtain a faint idea of it—or perhaps even a relatively clear one for those with cultivated minds and profound judgment.

**(129.)** We cannot doubt that such an intellectory or pure intellect exists, for it clearly manifests itself in various parts of our thought and speech, to...

<summary>Swedenborg distinguishes the "intellectory" (the highest natural organ) from the spiritual soul and divine wisdom, noting that human language struggles to describe these elevated states of being.</summary>

<page-num>76</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

The pure intellect resides most closely within this realm, and it is here that it most intimately exists. We organize the ideas of our memory—much like we do with the things we see—in an instant. We put them into such an order, form, and harmony that a certain rational analysis results from them. This analysis is recognized as true or false through a kind of understanding found in our higher, purer thought. 

Our sensations do not provide anything other than the raw materials for our imagination. However, the ability to analytically organize those materials into forms—and thus to conceive and create new forms that belong to a more sublime level of thought—is a different matter. To observe truths, likely outcomes <note>original: "verisimilitudes"</note>, and probabilities based on their connection and order alone is not a function of our physical senses, but of the **pure intellect**. 

This is not even a process of "thought" itself, because thought is actually the *result* of being organized into such a form. Therefore, thought is an outcome of that higher intellect which exists beforehand and produces the intellectual or rational ideas used in thinking.*

Such an intellectual, analytical, philosophical, and even spiritual principle exists in every sentence and every speech, even those of a child. Indeed, a child speaks spontaneously in a manner that is more perfectly philosophical, logical, and grammatical than anything the Peripatetic <note>original: "Peripatetic"; refers to the followers of Aristotle</note> and Pythagorean schools could ever learn to do through artificial or scientific study. 

This is why we learn the philosophical sciences—such as logic and other theoretical branches of knowledge—from within ourselves and from the deepest examination of our own thoughts and speech. We do this in the same way that anatomists gain knowledge of the body by inspecting the internal organs <note>original: "viscera"</note>. Therefore, there must be an "inmost intellect" within us that dictates the rules and laws for these mental operations. These laws are just as hidden from us as the shapes of our brain, heart, and stomach are hidden from someone who has never studied anatomy. Consequently, the science of philosophy is itself a kind of "anatomy of the mind," for which we are also seeking a "medicine" or corrective.

From this, it follows that no thought can exist—and therefore no speech—without the influence of such an intellect.

(130.) The operation of this intellectory <note>original: "intellectory"; refers to the specific faculty or "organ" where the pure intellect resides</note>, or this intellect, must be pure, for its form is born from the essential activities <note>original: "determinations"</note> of the soul. These activities are like many spiritual rays <note>original: "radii"</note> or pure intelligences. Because this form flows only from these spiritual rays and is perfectly structured, it can only express what is purely intellectual. What this form actually is can be understood by comparing it with the structure of the internal sensory organ <note>the faculty of imagination and memory</note>, and then comparing that with the physical structure of the brain; nevertheless, it cannot be fully described. However, it is indicated through analysis by the simple elevation of perceptions from a lower to a higher level, and by adding the qualities of the perpetual and the infinite, according to the doctrines of order, degrees, and forms—the laws of which I have discussed above.

(131.) Therefore, to describe what the pure intellect is, we must resort to universal terms, as previously mentioned; for it represents the very nature of its own structure and is the inherent knowledge of the natural things that exist below it. When the pure intellect acts, it acts from itself—that is, from nature itself and from its own knowledge—since all things translate into action in harmony with its intuition. The pure intellect does not first inform itself <insert>from other sources</insert> how and in what manner it should act. Instead, from within itself and by its own nature, it knows those measurements, laws, rules, and truths which are found (though imperfectly) in our thought, imagination, physical sensation, action, and in our various organs. Hidden within all of these are the deepest and most complex principles of the sciences—such as metaphysics <note>original: "first philosophy"</note>, logic, anthropology, dialectics, physiology, physics, geometry, mathematics, mechanics, optics, acoustics, chemistry, medicine, law <note>original: "jurisprudence"</note>, ethics, grammar, and many others by whatever name they are called. We may clearly see an example and summary of these sciences within our entire organic system, in its various members and parts,

It operates intuitively and perfectly because it is derived directly from the soul's spiritual "rays."</summary>

...and operations, all of which must flow and exist—not from themselves—but from a specific efficient cause <note>original: "efficient cause"; the primary agent or force that produces an effect</note> in which such knowledge resides, or which is knowledge itself: the order, truth, harmony, and the "form of forms" <note>a philosophical term for the highest organizing principle or the soul itself</note>. These are all universal terms that apply to the pure intellect. Thus, deep within ourselves, we possess a most perfect knowledge of all natural things. Yet, we anxiously seek to learn even a small part of this science or of what lies within us, trying to draw this hidden knowledge out of the shadows and into the light. Therefore, this pure intellect can be called the "science of natural sciences." All individual sciences are merely parts of a universal science which we call the philosophy and mathematics <note>original: "mathesis"; refers to the formal, mathematical structure of the universe</note> of universals. From this foundation, the pure intellect can descend into specific details whenever it wishes. Thus, it appears that we cannot speak about this pure intellect except in abstract and obscure terms.

(132.) This pure intellect understands simultaneously what our thought or rational mind can only understand sequentially. For instance, it sees premises and antecedents at the same time as the conclusions, just as in a logical conclusion or an analytical equation. It grasps principles and causes alongside the things derived from them <note>original: "principiates"</note>, the things caused <note>original: "causates"</note>, and their effects. It views even the effect as already existing within its efficient cause. Thus, it sees everything to be formed as if it were already formed, and everything already formed as something still in the process of being formed. It does not hesitate when determining the means to an end, for it understands the entire complex system at once. Only a failure in the physical tools <note>original: "instrumental causes"; the bodily organs or external conditions needed to act</note> hinders its action. It contemplates all past events as if they were present, along with future events that naturally and logically follow the current order. 

Therefore, regarding the operations of this pure intellect, we can describe them using neither movement nor degrees. We cannot apply concepts of time, space, place, movement, speed <note>original: "celerity"</note>, or anything that implies sequence or distance. Its form is the primary state of nature; from this—as if from a beginning or from a level below it—all the chance occurrences and qualities of nature descend or arise. For the celestial form <note>original: "celestial form"; the highest and most perfect organizational structure in Swedenborg's hierarchy of forms</note> embraces and, as it were, contemplates...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the pure intellect possesses an innate, total knowledge of nature and functions outside the constraints of time and space, seeing causes and effects simultaneously.</summary>

-> # THE PURE INTELLECT. <-

...all following forms as if existing in itself, when it begins its operations.

(133.) The pure intellect sees nothing as merely likely or probable, but perceives things as either true or false—or exactly how far they are from truth or falsehood. Because of this, all its ideas are natural truths. From this position of truth, it clearly distinguishes falsehoods and fallacies, just as the eyes distinguish shadows from light. Therefore, its observations consist of many truths united together, from which a universal truth arises. 

This is why people who are more intelligent—those whose thinking or rational analysis comes closer to this pure intellect—can perceive and know many propositions to be true or false instantly. They do this without needing proof from experience <note>original: "a posteriori"; reasoning based on observed effects and experience</note>, formal logic, or academic sciences. Indeed, they are often frustrated that the rational mind wishes to prove things that are already clearer, more certain, and higher than any possible demonstration. They view such attempts at proof as dim shadows that obscure the truth rather than illustrate it. We will be like this when we become pure intelligences or souls; then, we shall laugh at our academic treatises as child's play, and we will regard the entire system of formal logical arguments <term>syllogistic logic</term> as nothing more than a simple game of chance.

(134.) The pure intellect, whose nature it is to know the universe and to perceive all the secrets <term>arcana</term> of nature from within itself, cannot be taught by the internal senses, and even less so by the external senses. For the pure intellect itself has formed all the senses—both internal and external—according to every idea of its own nature. It furnished these senses with organs to receive information even before they were ever used. 

Consequently, such an intellect—which exists before the senses—cannot be acquired, developed, or perfected by the senses. Instead, it remains exactly the same from the beginning of life to the end. It is as perfect in the embryo and the infant as it is in the adult and the old man. It is as perfect in a simple servant <note>original: "Davus"; a common name for a slave in Roman comedy, representing an uneducated or ordinary person</note> as in a genius <note>original: "Oedipus"; the Greek king who solved the Sphinx's riddle, representing a person of great insight</note>, and it is as perfect in a person who is insane or simple-minded as it is in an eminent philosopher.

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the pure intellect possesses an innate, perfect knowledge of truth that exists independently of sensory experience or formal education. This inner intelligence is equally perfect in every human being, regardless of their age, education, or mental health.</summary>

<page-num>80</page-num>

# THE SOUL.

The intellect that is capable of being taught and improved is positioned just below the pure intellect; it is called human reason, or the rational mind. Its operation is thought, which is never pure but always mixed—meaning it derives more from ignorance than from intelligence. This is the cause of the conflict that has arisen among scholars about whether ideas are innate <term>connate; born within the mind</term>, whether they are acquired through experience, or whether anything exists in the intellect that did not first come through the senses. Each position has its supporters. 

There are signs of a kind of intellect innate within us, and in a sense, all ideas are found to be innate. However, the organization and arrangement of these ideas into a logical analysis cannot be innate, for that is a purely intellectual task. At the same time, there would be no ideas to arrange in this way unless they were already innate. From this, it follows that either viewpoint may be true in a certain sense.*

(135.) From these points, it is also clear that the pure intellect is unable to express or organize its own ideas or universal truths through speech. This is because the parts of speech are themselves made of ideas, images, and forms that must be acquired through the senses, and these exist on a much lower level. Instead, the pure intellect represents its own simple and universal analyses through symbolic representations, such as those seen in dreams, or through parables and simili— <note>The text continues onto the next page.</note>

***

* > "There are no innate ideas or imprinted laws in the human mind, but only in the soul. Unless these ideas and laws were innate <note>original: "connate"</note> in the soul, there could be no memory of things perceived by the senses and no understanding; indeed, no animal could exist or survive as an organic being that shares in life." (*Economy of the Animal Kingdom*, part 2, no. 300.)

> "It appears, then, that both those who support the doctrine of innate ideas and those who oppose it may base their arguments on the same facts. This shows that the controversy is not about the truth itself, but only about the way the truth is explained. For if ideas are innate in the soul, and if ideas are obtained by the mind, then the two opinions agree. Their reconciliation comes from the same demonstration that shows the communication between the operations of the soul and the mind" (*ibid*, no. 294).

The practical value of Swedenborg's doctrine regarding the distinction between the mind <note>original: *mens*</note> and the soul <note>original: *anima*</note> appears nowhere more clearly than in the solution it offers to the difficult problem of innate ideas. See also numbers 308–311 in the work mentioned above. <note>Translator's note</note>

(136.) It is not easy for thought to perceive what the pure intellect is; its very existence is even questioned. This is because thought itself cannot comprehend what is above it or what is pure, since thought is not pure but mixed. However, the mind does comprehend that where there is a mixture, there must be something pure with which the impure is mixed. In our thought—where intelligence and ignorance, or light and darkness, reign together—something intellectual flows in from above. This illumines the sphere of thoughts and provides the faculty of thinking, since the sensations of the body cannot possibly achieve this.* Then, something that is not intellectual flows in from below, causing the mixture of intelligence and ignorance; this is our mixed intellect, or thought. But the pure intellect itself is the intermediary <note>original: "mediate"</note> between the soul's spiritual intelligence and the rational mind's thought. To understand what the pure intellect is, we must therefore examine what the soul is and what the rational mind is, as well as the influx <term>influx; the flow of influence or energy from a higher level of being to a lower one</term> of both. (137.) The soul is pure intelligence, a spiritual essence and form. Because of this, it is positioned directly above the pure intellect, whose essence and form represent the highest level of nature—the celestial realm. The "intellectorium" <term>intellectorium: a term Swedenborg used for the biological organ or spiritual center where the pure intellect resides</term> itself cannot be formed except from the essential characteristics <note>original: "determinations"</note> of the soul. Just as there are many characteristics, so there are many rays of spiritual light; for the soul’s intelligence is not natural but spiritual, and its knowledge is not philosophical but metaphysical, pneumatological <note>original: "pneumatical"; relating to the study of spirits or the soul</note>, and—as I might say—theological. From this it follows that the soul's first descendant is the pure intellect. It is the nature of the pure intellect to know immediately, from within itself, everything that is natural.

(138.) The ideas of the soul itself are *spiritual truths*; however, the ideas of the pure intellect are the *primary natural truths*. The ideas of our human intellect are called *reasons*, but the ideas of the memory or imagination are properly called *ideas*. The ideas of sight are *images* and *objects*; the ideas of hearing are *modes, modulations, and words*. This is the hierarchy <note>original: "subordination"</note> of ideas; therefore, every spiritual element within speech comes from the soul, every intellectual element comes from the pure intellect, and every rational element comes from thought, and so on.

(139.) But it may be asked: how does the pure intellect flow into the sphere of thought? Is it a direct influx <term>influx: the flow of influence or energy from a higher level of being to a lower one</term>, or is it a relationship of correspondence and harmony? We learn this specifically from the form of the internal sensory organ or "cortical gland." <note>cortical gland: Swedenborg’s term for the microscopic units of the brain's gray matter (neurons), which he believed were the primary seats of sensation and thought.</note> Inside this gland is the "simple cortex," which is called the intellectorium, just as the larger cortical substance is contained within the brain. This simple cortex is the origin of all the "simple fibers," just as the brain is the origin of all the medullary fibers <note>medullary fibers: the nerve fibers making up the white matter of the brain and the nerves of the body.</note> and the nerves of the body. The pure intellect, which resides in this aforementioned intellectorium or simple cortex, cannot flow into the sphere of thoughts except in the same way that images of sight or ideas of imagination relate to the modes of hearing or to speech. This is not a physical influx but a "correspondence" <term>correspondence: a relationship where a higher spiritual reality is expressed through a lower natural form without the two substances mixing</term>; for the modes of hearing, which are composed of many articulated vibrations...

<summary>Swedenborg defines the hierarchy of consciousness, placing the soul (spiritual truth) above the pure intellect (natural truth) and the rational mind. He argues that these levels interact through "correspondence"—a symbolic alignment—rather than physical mixing, using the anatomy of the brain's "cortical glands" as a biological model.</summary>

<header>THE SOUL.</header>

## XI.

# Intellect, Thought, Reasoning, and Judgment,

### or,

## The Human Intellect.

(140.) There is no thought without imagination, because no thought can exist without the ideas stored in memory. These ideas are as much a part of thought as they are of imagination, since we cannot think without memory. Consequently, it is very difficult to clearly distinguish between imagination and thought. However, that they are indeed distinct and can be separated is evident from several examples. 

First, consider the case of sleepwalkers <note>original: "somnambulists"</note>, who see with their eyes open and possess a kind of imagination—though often a distorted one—because there is no actual thought involved. Second, we see this in animals <note>original: "brute animals"</note>, which possess imagination even if they lack the capacity for thought. Third, it is visible in infants who are just beginning to babble <note>original: "prattle"</note> and say things they have imagined but not yet thought through. Even many adults are similar, varying in their individual capacities for genuine thought versus mere fancy. But because imagination is present in thought, and thought is present in imagination, we often mistakenly believe that thought is simply a more perfect and refined version of imagination. We assume they cannot be separated, as previously mentioned. Therefore, it is important to investigate more thoroughly what each one truly is.

(141.) Imagination is nothing more than a higher and internal form of sight. It is exercised when we reproduce individual objects in the same order in which they were originally seen—for instance, a palace or building with all its external and internal structure, along with its furnishings and even the people <note>original: "masters"</note> and...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that while thought and imagination are closely linked through memory, they are distinct faculties, using examples like sleepwalkers and animals to show that imagination can exist without rational thought.</summary>
<keywords>imagination, thought, memory, sleepwalkers, animal intelligence, human intellect, internal sight</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the distinction between imagination and thought. While the previous page defined imagination as internal sight, this page explores how thought acts upon those imaginative images to create new, abstract ideas through a process of mental "calculation."</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>THE HUMAN INTELLECT.</header>

...servants who inhabit it, maintaining the same connections and order that were observed through sight and hearing. The same applies to the cities, provinces, and kingdoms we have visited. The internal sight, or imagination, views these objects all at once <note>original: "collectively"</note>, whereas the eye observes them one after another <note>original: "successively"</note>. This also applies to the human body itself—its individual organs <note>original: "viscera"</note> and parts, their positions and connections, and ultimately their entire anatomy. It is the same with other fields, such as the various practical sciences—mechanics, experimental physics, and astronomy—as well as the theoretical sciences, so far as we have learned them and retained them in our memory. Therefore, imagination is the reproduction of memories of things seen and heard—a simultaneous viewing <note>original: "intuition"</note> of them without progressing into things that have not yet been perceived by the senses.

(142.) Thought, however, is not satisfied with merely reproducing ideas from memory or imagination, or with viewing objects simultaneously that were originally seen one after another. Instead, it goes further. From these and similar things that are reviewed and represented, thought grasps and produces a new idea never seen before. It achieves this through a specific type of analysis, similar to the calculus of infinites <note>original: "analysis of infinites"; Swedenborg is comparing the process of thought to the mathematical processing of complex variables</note>. For example, it uses the laws of natural philosophy and methods of reduction, transposition, and equation. 

This "equation" itself, formed by the mind alone, is called an **idea of thought**. Thus, an idea of the imagination is something introduced through the "doors" of the senses, whereas an idea of thought is something formed by the mind's own power using ideas of the imagination, much like numbers in a calculation. These ideas of thought—which are called rational, intellectual, and immaterial—once formed, are regarded as simple ideas, no matter how complex <note>original: "compounded"</note> they are. They are treated much like complete <note>original: "integral"</note> equations in algebra or established analogies...

<summary>Swedenborg distinguishes imagination as the simultaneous recall of sensory data, while thought is the active mental process that analyzes these images to create entirely new, abstract, and rational ideas.</summary>

...for unity in geometry and arithmetic. The mind organizes and divides its own ideas into a different order or rational structure, and from these, it derives a new analysis or "equation." From this process, an even more perfectly rational and intellectual idea emerges. In this way, thought is perfected; it becomes more refined and pure as it moves closer toward the pure intellect. It rises to a higher level as it takes the complex ideas it has gathered and treats them as if they were simple truths. By organizing these analytically, an even higher concept is drawn out. This is the only way we can be raised to a knowledge of the pure intellect <note>original: "intellectory"; refers to the faculty of pure understanding that exists above the level of spoken language</note>. It cannot be achieved through speech, the use of words, or imaginative ideas alone, because the truths of the intellect are more refined than words. They cannot be expressed or revealed except through language <note>original: "vocal forms"</note> that has been elevated and adapted to match them.

(143.) This, then, is the nature of thought. From this description, the difference between thought and imagination becomes clear. For example, the ideas used in thought are produced by the mind <term>mens</term> <note>The rational mind or intellect as distinguished from the lower soul or physical senses</note> itself, whereas the ideas of the imagination come only from the external senses. Furthermore, thought can be perfected and elevated as it approaches the pure intellect, but imagination is perfected only through sensory experience—either our own or that of others. Whatever symbols exist in the memory—whether learned through our own senses, from teachers, from books <note>original: "letters"</note>, or from writing tablets—these are all ideas of the imagination. This is because they belong to the memory alone and were originally gathered through the senses. However, they serve as the building blocks and tools <note>original: "instrumental causes"</note> that the rational mind uses to form its own intellectual ideas and analyses. It follows, then, that whatever we are capable of understanding, but do not yet understand, is stored in our memory. The *potential* for understanding resides in the memory, but this potential <note>original: "potency"</note> alone does not result in an act of understanding. Therefore, something else...

(144.) Thought, therefore, is a superior form of imagination; and just as there is a superior imagination, there is also a superior memory. The inferior memory is a memory of all particular things and of those ideas introduced through the senses, both of sight and of hearing. But the superior memory is a memory of general and universal things and of all those ideas that are formed and, as it were, created by the mind itself. These also impress themselves on our memory just as if they were impressed on the senses; for when we think, the thoughts themselves and the results of those thoughts remain equally fixed. This memory, however, contains rational, intellectual, and immaterial ideas, while on the other hand, the inferior memory holds only ideas of things that are purely natural and material. 

Therefore, there is a memory of universals <note>General concepts or principles that apply to many things</note> and a memory of singulars <note>Specific, individual instances or objects</note>; the former belongs to thought, while the latter belongs to imagination. These memories, if we observed them more internally, are distinct from each other. One can have a great memory for universals and a poor memory for singulars, or the reverse <note>original: "vice versa"</note>. This is because the memory of universals contains within it the singulars which, as supporting evidence <note>original: "symbols of confirmation"</note>, can easily be drawn out or present themselves to the mind. 

To ensure that specific details are properly retained in their order by the memory, it is necessary that we form an idea of all universal principles, which is called their reason. From this mental order, specific details may be drawn forth as if from a single general rule or a mathematical formula. Just as in arithmetic and algebra—and indeed in other theoretical sciences—we can derive an infinite number of specific and particular instances on our own. In this way, we are able to skim through an entire book containing nothing but specific examples in a moment and understand them all...

(145.) Imagination, therefore, only takes in the form and quality of an object (or objects) according to the order, placement, and connection of its parts or ideas. But thought does not extract the material <note>physical or tangible</note> form of the parts themselves; instead, from such a form—or from many similar forms gathered together—it obtains a certain meaning <note>original: "sense"</note> that is not found in the visible parts or their connections, but lies hidden within. For this reason, thought is said to *understand* and imagination to *perceive*. The idea produced by thought is called immaterial, while the idea produced by imagination is called material. An intellection <note>The act of the mind in understanding; original Latin: *intellectio*</note> is an inmost sensation.

(146.) Thought can neither exist nor survive—much less be perfected—without the pure intellect. The pure intellect appears as though it flows into the sphere of thought to illuminate it with a certain light of intelligence. However, there is no actual influx <note>A direct flowing-in of one thing into another</note>; rather, it is only a concurrence, a correspondence, or an established harmony. Indeed, there is a greater, better, and more perfect concurrence and correspondence to the degree that the thought is more elevated. But before plunging our thoughts deeper into these psychological mysteries, we ought to explain the meanings of the words themselves—what is meant by understanding, judgment, thought, meditation, fancy, genius, and other terms.

...perceive, we understand; from what we understand, we think; from what we think, we judge; from what we judge, we choose; from what we choose, we conclude; from what we conclude, we will; and at length, we act. This entire process is called the "common intellect," in which the senses of hearing and seeing play their own roles, but not the other senses like smell, taste, and touch. The human intellect—the intellect specific to humanity—consists of understanding, thinking, judging, choosing, concluding, willing, and acting accordingly. This entire sequence is, indeed, run through in order, but very often it happens so quickly that the individual stages and steps are not even noticed. This speed is called *presence of mind*, or according to others, the *presence of the animus* <note>original: "presence of the animus"; the "animus" refers to the conscious mind or the soul as the seat of feelings and thought</note>. However, where the process is slower, it is called *absence of mind* or *sluggishness*. 

It is possible to have "presence of imagination" without simultaneously having "presence of intellect," and *vice versa* <note>original: "vice versa"; Latin for "the other way around"</note>, for the one is distinct from the other, as was noted above. Someone who quickly perceives specific details <note>original: "singulars"; individual objects or instances as opposed to general concepts</note> or brings them into the imagination, while the "pure intellect" joins in quickly but only slightly, is called *ingenious*, and that faculty is called *genius*. But someone who quickly understands those things which he perceives while the pure intellect fully participates—that is, who thinks on a higher level and sees things in a way that is more harmonious with the ideas or truths of the pure intellect—is said to possess *judgment*, and that faculty is called *judgment*. 

Thus, *genius* is the perfection of the imagination, but *judgment* is the perfection of thought. Or, *genius* draws more from the imagination and the external senses, while *judgment* draws more from the pure intellect. Therefore, *genius* is the characteristic quality of the intellect of animals, but *judgment* is the characteristic quality of the human intellect. *Genius* is common to boys, youths, women <note>The author reflects the gender perspectives of the 18th century, associating "genius" with youthful creativity and "judgment" with male-coded maturity</note>, poets, and singers; but *judgment* is common to adults, the elderly, men, and philosophers; for with age, judgment matures and increases, whereas genius decreases. For the most perfect judgment, not only the pure intellect...

(148.) **Understanding** is a higher form of perception, and thus an innermost sensation. More intense and constant thought, deeply focused on one object, is called **meditation**; the state and habit of meditation is called **fantasy** <note>original: "phantasy"; here meaning a persistent or obsessive use of the imagination</note>.

(150.) When ideas or reasons are turned and considered in thought, they are at length brought into the form of an equation. The more perfect the form of the equation—and the more similar and harmonious the things found within it—the more perfect the judgment is. This operation has no proper name, unless it may be called **choice** <note>original: "election"; the act of selecting a course of action from various possibilities</note>, which, being free, coincides with **free will** or with the liberty of willing and acting. For this reason, I have not been able to treat the subject of the will until these loves and desires have been first considered.
