However, because the external state must harmonize with the internal state—or, because the state of the parts must naturally agree with their own internal nature—it follows that a change in the external state immediately signals that there is a change in the internal state and reveals what kind of change it is. Once the internal state becomes aware of this change, it immediately perceives its meaning. This happens exactly like the way words or speech heard by the ear are immediately turned into visual ideas. This occurs not by "influx" <note>original: "influx"; the direct flowing of one substance or state into another</note>, but by correspondence. For example, an idea can be expressed by different words or different spoken sounds, and yet the same idea will still occur. Whether we speak the same sentence in Greek, Latin, French, Italian, English, or Swedish, the same mental image is presented.

It is, therefore, the practice and cultivation of the mind that allows one idea to correspond to another. The same relationship exists between the ideas of memory, imagination, thought, and the pure intellect. An internal change of state in the sensory organ acts as an external change of state for the intellectory. Through use and experience, the intellectory perceives what this external change means; it immediately agrees and, through this agreement, produces a corresponding idea in the pure intellect. Consequently, the more universal, general, and common a change of state is, the more clearly it is perceived, because it more closely matches the essence and nature of the intellectory. For all ideas are universal truths, and they can be made even more abstract through the use of specific word endings <note>original: "verbal terminations"; referring to how suffixes can change a concrete noun into an abstract concept</note>.

Whether in an infant, a simple-minded person <note>original: "stupid"</note>, or an insane person, the *pure intellect* always remains the same. It cannot reveal itself until it recognizes the changes of state to which it must correspond; furthermore, the *sensory* <term>sensory</term> <note>The faculty of the mind that receives and processes physical sensations.</note> cannot change its own states unless it learns how to do so through the use and the inflow <term>influx</term> of *external sensations*, as previously noted. (156.) However, both experience and theory prove that the *human intellect itself* depends very little on its *pure intellect*. Instead, it relies on what is *imagined*. For this reason, our *intellect* is exceedingly *impure*—so much so that it should rather be called *false* <note>original: "spurious"</note> and *corrupted* <note>original: "adulterous"</note>. Nevertheless, it appears so beautiful and pure to us that we believe it to be the soul itself—which is not merely pure intellect, but actually spiritual intelligence. The error of this belief is obvious from the statement itself. Our intellect is often so far removed from the pure intellect that they conflict with each other; the former accepts worldly things as truths, while the latter knows them to be entirely lying <note>original: "mendacious"</note> and realizes that their deceptive ornaments only make them look like truths to win approval.

Without such variation, there would be no society on earth; no diversity of thought, manners, actions, or bodies; no affirmations or negations; no uncertain outcomes; no predictions <note>original: "auguries"</note>; and indeed, no desire for goals to be achieved, no earthly loves, and none of the other necessities that contribute to human society itself. ->THE INTERCOURSE OF SOUL AND BODY.<-

## XII.

### OF THE INTERCOURSE OF THE SOUL AND THE BODY.

(159.) It is useless to ask how the soul communicates with the body unless we first determine what the soul and body are. We must also understand the nature of sensation, imagination, thought, the pure intellect, and spiritual intelligence <note>original: "[intelligence*]"; the bracketed word was likely added or clarified by the original translator.</note>. We need to know what will and action are, the nature of the internal and external organs of both sense and movement, the physical connection of the organism, and a vast number of other points. As long as the nature of the soul, the body, and the bridge between them remains unknown, all cooperation and interaction between them will necessarily remain a mystery. We cannot derive knowledge from what is unknown; we can only speak out of ignorance about things whose basic principles we do not understand, no matter how long we keep talking. 

I must admit that I feel I have not yet arrived at even a single part of such a vast subject. If this concept consists of millions upon millions of parts, I have only managed to form a vague idea based on the premises I have already discussed. However, it is clearly visible that external sensations and actions communicate with internal and deepest sensations, even reaching the soul and its intelligence. For it is through the soul—which is the source of movement <note>original: "motive principle"</note>, the life, and the essence of our body—that we live, move, and exist <note>The author is paraphrasing Acts 17:28: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being."</note> within the physical body.

(160.) (161.) It is evident that spoken words, or sounds heard in the brain and the common sensorium <note>original: "common sensory"; the brain's internal processing center where all sensations meet.</note>, are transformed into ideas similar to visual images. For example, when we use words to describe a house, a palace, a city, meadows, fields, the sky, or other things, an image of these things immediately forms in our mind. Yet, this interaction cannot be defined as "influx" or "harmony"; rather, it is an *acquired correspondence.*

The sound of words is merely a vibration, which cannot on its own create a visual idea. Whether we speak of palaces, cities, and fields in French, English, Latin, or Greek, the same idea is awakened, even though the sound or the pronunciation of the words is entirely different. This correspondence is learned through use and education. We learn a language, discovering that a specific sound <note>original: "modulation"</note> represents a certain image, building, or picture. Every time that specific spoken sound returns, the same idea returns with it.

There is also a physical and anatomical reason for this. Sounds—whether complex spoken words or simple tones—cause the fibers, the cortex <note>the outer layer of the brain</note>, and the meninges <note>the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord</note> to vibrate. This trembling makes the physical substances of the brain vibrate, producing a localized movement of their parts. This vibration does not change the internal nature of these parts, but only their external state or the state of the brain itself. Nevertheless, because of how these parts are interconnected and organized—that is, their physical position and order—they immediately perceive not only that a change <note>original: "mutation"</note> has occurred, but also the specific nature of that change. Through experience, they learn what such a change means; consequently, the sensorium eventually links the physical sensation with its corresponding idea.

Such harmony, love, rational delight, and ends—existing within and among the ideas themselves—naturally affect the **pure intellectory**, whose ideas consist of pure natural truths and whose harmonies are pure natural goodness. There should be little doubt regarding this **natural correspondence**, since we can perceive through reflection alone that there is something interior in our thought which consents or dissents, affirms or denies. The intellectory itself is the primary form of nature, and is thus the first "natural" thing; however, the soul is spiritual and exists above the natural world, even though it works through the pure intellect to operate within the natural world.

<meta>This page continues Swedenborg’s discussion of the communication between the soul, the intellect, and the body. He is attempting to harmonize various philosophical theories regarding how immaterial spirits and physical bodies interact.</meta>

The interaction between the sensations of the body does not occur through any "influx" <note>original: "influx"; the idea of a spiritual or physical force flowing from one thing into another</note> whatsoever—and certainly not by a physical influx—unless we define "influx" as a natural correspondence. Even in that case, it would be an influx of the harmony itself rather than an influx of the physical things that create that harmony. The author of the theory of *Occasional Causes* seems to have understood that this kind of influx of harmony exists. 

Natural correspondence is essentially the same as "pre-established harmony," while "acquired correspondence" <note>correspondence learned through experience or habit</note> is the same as "co-established harmony." This is because even natural correspondence arises from co-established harmony. In the soul, this harmony is indeed pre-established (innate). However, between the soul and the intellect, and between the intellect and conscious thought, it is co-established (developed through their relationship). Nevertheless, because this harmony exists before other later correspondences are formed, it can still be described as pre-established, or established prior to those later harmonies. 

In this way, we can reconcile the various hypotheses regarding the interaction of the soul and the body: namely, the theories of those who argue for "occasional causes," those who claim a "physical influx" <note>original: *influxus physicus*; the theory that the soul and body physically influence one another</note>, and those who advocate for "pre-established harmony."* For the ways, modes, and differences of communication—

\* "Descartes viewed the body and spirit as a dualism of completely different entities, separated in nature by an absolute and unbridgeable gap. Therefore, the interaction between soul and body that he asserted was inconceivable, even though he supported it with the claim of divine assistance. Consequently, **Geulincx**, a follower of Descartes, developed the theory of Occasionalism. This is the doctrine that whenever a mental process occurs, God produces the corresponding motion in the body, and *vice versa*." — *Ueberweg, History of Philosophy*, ii. p. 42.

"It is not possible, says Leibniz, for the soul or any other true substance to receive anything from the outside, except through God's all-powerful nature. . . . There is no physical influx <note>original: *influxus physicus*</note> between any created substances; therefore, there is no such influx between the substance of the soul and the substances that make up its body. . . . Furthermore, the soul cannot, as Descartes supposed, influence or change the direction of bodily movements. . . . The doctrine of Occasionalism turns the most common events into miracles, since it depicts God as constantly interfering anew with the course of nature.

> "The relation of this theory of Pre-established Harmony to the two other possible explanations of the correspondence between soul and body is illustrated by Leibniz <note>original: "Leibnitz"; Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), a German philosopher and mathematician</note> through the following comparison: A constant agreement between two clocks can be achieved in one of three ways. The first corresponds with the doctrine of a *Physical Interaction* between body and soul; the second with the doctrine of *Occasionalism*; and the third with the system of *Pre-established Harmony*. Either both clocks may be so connected with each other through some sort of mechanism that the motion of the one shall exert a determining influence on the motion of the other; or someone may be charged constantly to set the one so that it may agree with the other; or both may have been constructed in the beginning with such perfect exactness that their permanent agreement can be relied upon without the interference of the correcting hand of the workman. Since Leibniz held that it was impossible for the soul to exert a physical influence on the body (or vice-versa), it only remained for him to choose between the last two theories. He decided in favor of the theory of 'pre-established agreement' <note>original French: *consentement préétabli*</note> because he considered this way of securing agreement more natural and more worthy of God than that of occasional interference."—*Ibid.*, p. 109.

Regarding the three theories of intercourse between body and soul named here—namely, Physical Influx, Occasional Influx, and Pre-established Harmony—Swedenborg evidently does not intend to add a fourth, but rather hopes to find a term that shall include the truth concealed in all three. This he finds in "Correspondence," when understood in its two senses: Natural and Acquired. Natural Correspondence arises from a pre-established harmony in the soul, which, however, acts as a "co-established harmony" or "occasional influx" in every specific instance of bodily action. In his later theological writings, Swedenborg emphatically declares for the theory of Occasional Influx, which he designates distinctly as "Spiritual Influx," or the flowing of "the soul into the body," as maintained by the "followers of Descartes." "This theory," he says, "originates in order and its laws. For the soul is a spiritual substance, and therefore purer, prior, and internal; but the body is material, and therefore coarser, subsequent, and external. It is according to the laws of order that the purer should flow into the coarser, the prior into the subsequent, and the internal into the external—thus, what is spiritual into what is material, and not the reverse. Consequently, the thinking mind flows into the sight according to the state produced in the eyes by the objects before them (a state which the mind also organizes at its pleasure), and likewise the perceiving mind flows into the hearing, according to the state produced in the ears by speech."

The other two theories—both that of Physical Influx <note>the theory that the body physically influences the soul</note>, which he attributes to Aristotle and the Schoolmen <note>medieval scholars who integrated logic and Christian theology</note>, and that of Pre-established Harmony, which he attributes to Leibniz—he rejects as arising from appearances and fallacies. He argues it is a "fallacy of the reasoning faculty to establish that which is simultaneous <note>happening at the same time</note> while excluding that which is successive <note>happening in a sequence</note>. For the mind in its operation acts as one and simultaneously with the body; but still, every operation is first successive and only afterwards simultaneous. Now, successive operation is Influx, and simultaneous operation is Harmony: as when the mind thinks and afterward speaks, or when it wills and afterward acts." See the tract *On the Intercourse of the Soul and the Body*, nos. 1–18. By "simultaneous operation" and "harmony," the author here apparently means the same thing he calls "natural correspondence" and "pre-established harmony" in the present section, while "successive operation" and "influx" coincide with "acquired correspondence" and "co-established harmony." [*Translator*.]

Even the passion or sensation itself performs a certain **cycle** <note>original: "gyre"; from the Latin *gyrus*, referring to a circular or spiral motion</note> and passes over into **action**. Thus, through **action**, it produces an effect that agrees with the desired and understood end. Such being the **cycle** which takes place before a sensation passes over into action, the question arises: what is the interaction between the actions of the body and the soul?

(169.) The cerebral cortex <note>original: "cortical brain"</note> is a common motor center as well as a common sensory center; from this depend the actions of the body which take place through the muscles. This common motor center, or the cortex of the brain, actually expands and contracts itself while it is determining any action; and this constriction and expansion is called **determination**. By this expansion and constriction—or by the **contraction and expansion** <note>original: "systole and diastole"; terms usually describing the heartbeat, here applied to the rhythmic motion of the brain</note>—it expels through the composite and simple fibers its <term>animal spirit</term> <note>A historical term for a subtle fluid once believed to flow through the nerves to transmit sensation and movement</note> and purer blood, which produce that action. From this, there is a real communication of operations by means of a fluid. 

Hence, in the sensory organ, there is the acting or determining force itself; but in the muscle, there is the action which takes place through the connection and flow of the fibers—and of the fluid within the fibers—into the motor-fibers of the muscle, according to the nature of the determining force and the form and organism of the muscles. To the intellectory belong the "simple fibers"—indeed, the very beginnings of the simple fibers—and unless they cooperate, no action whatsoever can be decided upon. 

For the "purer blood" <note>Also called "animal spirit" in the physiology of the time; a refined fluid thought to carry life and signals through the nerves.</note> to be directed through the medullary fibers of the brain and the nerves of the body into the motor fibers of the muscles, it is also necessary that the animal spirit be simultaneously directed through the simple fibers. Without the agreement of both, the "animal machine" (the body) would struggle, and the fibers would be torn apart. 

The sensory organ itself is given the power of changing its internal state, which in turn serves as the external state of the intellectory. Therefore, whether the intellectory wills it or not, it must still cooperate. Unless it supports the action by consent and cooperation, the external state of the intellectory itself, the internal state of the sensory, and the state of the brain (which is the external state of the sensory)—and consequently the state of the whole body—would run the risk of perishing and becoming extinct and void. 

Hence, the necessity of preserving health and integrity requires that the intellect shall descend into those parts and consent. We use the phrase "favor with consent" when loves and goals <note>original: "ends"</note> agree or correspond; otherwise, we say it simply "concurs" or cooperates. For in order for there to be action, there must be a principal cause, and so on.

(171.) But indeed, when no rational will precedes an action—as occurs in the cerebellum and in the brain itself during sleep—then every force begins immediately in the pure intellect. It allows <note>original: "suffers"</note> the sensory organ to act; otherwise, there would be no free choice between moral good and evil. As soon as the soul perceives—through the consent of the higher intellect <note>original: "intellectory"; Swedenborg’s term for the faculty between the soul and the sensory mind.</note>—that the sensory mind wishes to act, it allows and permits the "animal machine" (the physical body) below it to do so. This also happens within the higher intellect in the case of sleepwalkers <note>original: "night-walkers"</note>. Since the Fall of the first man <note>A reference to the biblical story of Adam and Eve, which Swedenborg often interprets as the moment human consciousness became divided and the soul lost direct control over the body's impulses.</note>, all of the soul's freedom to act through its own body has been taken away and given to the sensory mind. All that remains for the soul is to provide and maintain within each individual part <note>original: "singulis"</note> the faculty or power of acting and of being acted upon <note>original: "suffering"; in this philosophical context, it means the capacity to receive impressions or undergo change.</note>.

(173.) From these points, it will appear how the soul participates in the actions of her body—namely, by permitting them. Meanwhile, the pure intellect participates by consenting, but the sensory mind participates by active force or by acting. From this follows the movement of the muscle, which is required to act and obey exactly as the sensory mind commands; thus, the body participates by obeying.

<header>THE INTERCOURSE OF SOUL AND BODY.</header>

...communicate with the motor and sensory organs of her body so that she may provide them with the ability to act and feel, and sustain this ability? From what has been stated above, it is clearly evident that there is a soul which feels; that is to say, it sees, hears, tastes, perceives, thinks, understands, judges, and wills. In other words, the body derives its power of feeling and acting from the soul. 

However, this is not merely a communication or interaction <note>original: "intercourse"</note>; it is the very presence of the soul itself, which is actually in the whole and in every part of her body. For there is no external motor or sensory organ that does not consist of vessels and fibers. No vessel exists that is not constructed from fibers, and no such fiber exists that is not constructed from "simple fibers." Furthermore, no simple fiber exists that does not originate from the intellectory <note>Swedenborg’s term for the intermediate faculty or "organ" of the pure intellect, positioned between the soul and the sensory mind.</note>, which itself is derived from the substances of the soul. 

Consequently, there is no external motor or sensory organ that does not derive its essence from the soul. Thus, there is a real presence, or a kind of omnipresence, of the soul everywhere. The soul forms the organs so that they perceive in a specific way and no other; for every organ derives its character and function from its form. 

Furthermore, the soul guides the individual fibers—in which she entirely resides—from the organs to the brain. There, she has formed the common sensory <note>original: "common sensory" (Latin: *sensorium commune*); the part of the brain where all individual sensations are gathered and perceived as a whole.</note>, which distinctly perceives the things presented to it and understands them in its own way. For the sensory organ also derives its nature from its form. This allows specific details to communicate with one another through a certain correspondence <note>A key concept in Swedenborg’s work where physical structures mirror and respond to spiritual or mental functions.</note>, and at the same time with the person themselves, so that they may know the things that occur and happen in the world outside.

# Part Third.
## THE AFFECTIONS.
---
### XIII.
#### REGARDING HARMONIES, THE AFFECTIONS THAT ARISE FROM THEM, AND DESIRES IN GENERAL.

(175.) There is no entity or substance in the universe that lacks a *form*; the fact that something exists at all, and that it is what it is, is due entirely to its form. The *essential determinations* <note>original: "essential determinations"; the specific ways the components of a thing are arranged and defined to give it its unique character</note> constitute *form*. What these essences are (which are being defined) cannot be imagined without the concept of parts or substances, nor can this definition itself be understood without the idea of *flow* <note>original: "fluxion"; continuous movement, change, or the process of becoming</note> or *coexistence*. These substances are called the "determining factors," and that which is defined by these substances is a new, *composite substance* <note>A whole made up of several smaller parts</note> which possesses a *form*.

(176.) The substances that define themselves, or are defined by others, maintain a relationship with one another, and this is called *analogy* <note>In this context, a proportional or structural relationship between parts</note>. The *analogy* of all these definitions—whether they occur one after another or all at once—is called *Harmony* or *Discord*. Therefore, every form possesses either its own *harmony* or *discord*. The *quality* of a form is known by its *harmony* or *discord*.

(177.) Just as forms can be *perfect* or *imperfect*, so too are their *harmonies*. There are forms that are inherently and by their very nature most *perfect*, and those which are inherently and by their nature most *imperfect*; between these two extremes lie infinite degrees. The same is true for *harmonies*.

<vocab>The Soul, Affections, Harmonies, Desires, Entity, Substance, Form, Essential determinations, Flow, Co-existence, Analogy, Harmony, Discord</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg argues that every substance in the universe is defined by its "form," which is the specific arrangement of its parts. He explains that the quality of these forms is measured by their "harmony" or "discord," ranging from perfect to imperfect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Part Three, "The Affections," where Swedenborg explores the relationship between the geometric "form" of a substance and its "harmony." He establishes a hierarchy of perfection, moving from simple shapes like triangles and circles to complex spiritual forms.</meta>

<page-num>111</page-num>
<header>HARMONIES, AFFECTIONS, AND DESIRES.</header>

Forms and harmonies reach their highest perfection when their underlying nature is perfect. Conversely, forms and harmonies are imperfect when they arise from a nature that is itself imperfect. The closer these forms approach an ideal, perfect nature, the more harmonious they become, and the opposite is also true. <note>original: "vice versa"</note>

(178.) Forms that are simpler, more fundamental <note>original: "prior"</note>, and higher <note>original: "superior"</note> are naturally more perfect than those that are complex <note>original: "composite"</note>, derived <note>original: "posterior"</note>, or lower; the same is true of their harmonies. To illustrate this with examples: The most perfect "angular form" (a form defined by angles) is the equilateral triangle, which has three identical corners. More imperfect angular forms include the oblong, the parallelogram, the trapezium, and similar shapes. The spherical or circular form is naturally more perfect than any triangular form, but among spherical forms, the perfect circle is the highest; less perfect versions include ellipses, cycloids, parabolas, and others. The same hierarchy applies to higher forms, whether they are spiral, vortical <note>original: "vortical"; a vortex-like shape that Swedenborg considered higher than a simple circle</note>, celestial, or spiritual. The quality of a harmony is derived entirely from the quality of the form that produces it.

(179.) Every form possesses its own "state," which is the way the substances that make it up exist together. This state is called *harmonious* when those substances exist together or follow one another according to the perfect order of nature.

(180.) Every form—with the exception of angular forms—within the physical atmosphere and the animal and vegetable kingdoms is able to change its state. It can pass from a more perfect natural state into an imperfect one and then return to the more perfect state again. This power to change state is itself a mark of the perfection of a form. In higher forms, this capacity is so vast that the possible changes of state are beyond counting and should be considered infinite.

(181.) When a circular form shifts into an elliptical shape or other geometric curves, it is said to change its state. The same is true when a spiral form passes into spirals of another...

<vocab>angular form, equilateral triangle, parallelogram, trapezium, spherical, circular, triangular, ellipses, cycloids, parabolæ, spiral, vortical, celestial, spiritual, harmonies, state, substances</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg defines the hierarchy of perfection in forms, noting that simpler and higher forms (like circles and spirals) are more perfect than complex or angular ones. He introduces the concept of a "state" as the arrangement of a form's components and highlights the ability of perfect forms to change their states.</summary>

--- Page 152 ---
<meta>This page continues Swedenborg’s exploration of "forms" and "harmonies," moving from the static definition of a form's "state" to the dynamic ways forms change, expand, and interact to create complex new structures.</meta>

<page-num>112</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

When a form—whether it is a geometric or mathematical <note>original: "arithmetical"</note> type <note>original: "genus"</note>—undergoes a transformation, it is said to "change its state." This same principle applies to higher-level <note>original: "superior"</note> forms, though their specific variations cannot be mathematically demonstrated or even described in words. In any given level of reality, the most perfect form is unchangeable, while all other forms at that level are subject to change. For example, there is only one perfect circle, but there are infinite varieties of ellipses; the same rule applies to all other shapes.

(182.) However, the simple expansion or contraction of a form is not considered a true "change of state." This is because the form's defining characteristics <note>original: "essential determinations"</note>, proportions, and harmonies remain the same whether it is stretched or shrunk. These movements are instead called *modifications*, which are the means by which forms exert their power <note>original: "forces"</note>. Even so, the specific *way* a form exerts its power is varied by these expansions or contractions.

(183.) Forms that are capable of perfectly changing their states—expanding and compressing at the same time—actually produce harmonies through those changes, as well as through many diverse modifications. These very changes of state are themselves the defining factors <note>original: "essential determinations"</note> that result in a new form, which then possesses its own unique state and harmony. When many such similar forms exist, they give rise to even newer forms through their changes of state, and this process continues similarly with their harmonies.

(184.) All changes of state occur one after another <note>original: "successively"</note>. However, when these changes result in the production of a new form, all those previous successive changes exist within that new form all at once <note>original: "simultaneously"</note>. Thus, there are forms, states, and harmonies that can be classified as common or particular, universal or singular, or general, special, and individual. This demonstrates the infinite diversity found among forms, states, and harmonies.

(185.) Furthermore, modifications—which are variations in size, or the expansion and contraction of the substance to which a form belongs—produce harmony through a specific mutual relationship. We see this in the harmonies of sounds, the objects of our vision, and the relationship of colors within and among themselves.

<summary>Swedenborg distinguishes between "changes of state" (which create new forms and harmonies) and "modifications" (simple expansions or contractions). He argues that complex forms contain the history of their changes simultaneously, leading to infinite variety in nature and perception.</summary>
<keywords>change of state, modifications, geometric forms, harmony, expansion and contraction, successive vs simultaneous, spiritual psychology</keywords>

### HARMONIES, AFFECTIONS, AND DESIRES.

From this, it follows that there are also forms of "modes," which are simply called **modifications**. <note>original: "modifications" — In 18th-century science, this refers to the patterns of motion, vibrations, or disturbances in a substance like air or water.</note>

(186.) Harmonies in the atmospheric world <note>The physical environment composed of air, water, and the "ether."</note> are created by modifications alone, and not by "changes of state." The physical forces are contained within these modifications themselves. However, the harmonies of the animal kingdom <note>original: "animal kingdom" — Referring to the *Regnum Animale*, or the kingdom of living beings possessed of a soul (*anima*), including humans.</note> are produced both by modifications—which act as its many forces and actions—and by "changes of state," which are its many sensations.

(187.) The organs of the animal kingdom, both external and internal, are designed so that they may receive the modifications of the atmospheric world and transform them into sensations. In this way, the modifications of the air are turned into the sensation of hearing, and the modifications of the ether <note>A historical scientific term for the invisible medium thought to carry light and electromagnetic waves.</note> are turned into the sensation of sight. Furthermore, the organs mentioned—especially the internal ones—are affected not by the raw modifications themselves, but by the **harmonies** (the patterns and ratios) of those modifications. They change their internal states to match these harmonies, which results in "perceptions." Thus, sight is transformed into imagination, and imagination into ideas. This process is said to occur through **natural correspondence**. <note>The philosophical idea that physical movements in the world have a direct, symbolic, and functional relationship with spiritual or mental states.</note>

(188.) The external and internal organs of all individuals are not affected in the same way by the same harmonies. Instead, they are affected according to the specific quality of their own organs, for that is how they "correspond" to the world. The variety in how these harmonies are received—or the diversity of **affections** <note>The internal emotional or mental response to a stimulus.</note>—is as vast as the diversity of individual brains or people.

(189.) Affections are changes of state that correspond to the harmonies flowing into the sensory organs. Specifically:
* The whole brain, or the "common sensory," <note>The faculty of the mind that coordinates and organizes the data from the five physical senses.</note> is affected by the harmonies of sound and hearing.
* The inner sensory <note>The imagination.</note> is affected by the harmonies of the objects of sight.
* The **pure intellect** is affected by the harmonies of the ideas of the imagination, and especially of thought.
* The **soul** is affected by the harmony of the natural truths recognized by the pure intellect.

It establishes a hierarchy of perception moving from physical sound and light up to the intellectual perception of truth in the soul.</summary>

(191.) All harmonies affect the sensory organs—both external (like the ears and eyes) and internal (like the imagination)—either pleasantly and delightfully or unpleasantly and distressingly. This is because delightful harmonies soothe the sensory organs by refreshing and bringing life to them, whereas disharmonies grate against them because they are destructive and deadening to the senses.

(192.) However, all harmonies are relative to the state of the sensory organ being affected. Perfect harmonies may seem unpleasant to a sensory organ that is itself in a state of disharmony. Furthermore, the more perfect a harmony is, the more unpleasant it will feel to such a corrupted sense; therefore, to that sensory organ, disharmonies actually feel like "harmonies." But because harmonies and forms possess their own inherent perfection or imperfection—based on their very nature and essence—we must judge the actual state of a sensory organ by the way it is affected. To judge truly, it is necessary that the state of the person's sensory organ be perfectly harmonious itself.

(193.) Therefore, the state of the whole brain determines how it is affected by the harmonies of sound in hearing. (194.) We seek and desire what affects our senses in a pleasant and delightful way; we recoil from whatever affects us in the opposite manner. # XIV.

## CONCERNING THE LOWER MIND [ANIMUS] AND ITS SPECIFIC AFFECTIONS.

(197.) Sensations—such as sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch—are attributed to the brain. Because of this, the brain is called the Common Sensory <note>original: *sensorium commune*, the faculty believed to integrate all sensory input into a single perception.</note>. Its organs and instruments are located in and belong to the body, such as the eye, ear, nostrils, tongue, and skin. These organs do not actually feel; instead, they distinguish, receive, and transmit the various forms of touch to the brain. This is why the senses—which appear as if they exist within the organs themselves—become weak <note>original: "languid"</note> when the brain is diseased.

(198.) However, sensations are not attributed to the lower mind <term>animus</term> <note>The *animus* is the lower, "natural" mind that deals with emotions and sensory images, distinguishing it from the *mens*, the higher rational mind.</note>. Instead, we attribute to it those feelings <note>original: "affections"</note> which are also called its passions <note>In historical psychology, "passions" are the ways the mind is "acted upon" by external stimuli, encompassing emotions like joy, anger, or fear.</note>. While the brain perceives sensations, it is affected by those sensations according to its own form. *Therefore, the lower mind is the form taken by the ideas of the common or external sensory faculty, and it is the active and living principle behind all the changes in the body.* As the lower mind is affected, so it desires; and as the desire of the lower mind is, such is the pleasure of the body. This is because the lower mind is essentially the form of the sensory faculty; thus, we may judge the mind by the sensory faculty, and judge the sensory faculty by the mind.

(199.) In general, the affections of the lower mind either agree or disagree with the common sensory faculty. Those which agree are pleasant, and those which disagree are unpleasant. Pleasant affections expand the brain and spread <note>original: "diffuse"</note> the lower mind; unpleasant affections compress the brain and restrict the lower mind. The blood flows more freely through both larger and smaller vessels, and runs through its own glands and fibers. This is why we are able to judge the emotional state <note>original: *affection*</note> of the cerebrum or the internal sensory faculty by looking at the body—and especially the face, upon which the mind’s state is written. 

In excessive joy, not only are the "muscles" of the cortex, the nerve fiber layers <term>medullary strata</term>, and the fibrous and vascular channels of the brain and body opened, but even the pores of the skull and bones. Additionally, passages such as the fluid-carrying <term>chyliferous</term>, lymphatic, and salivary ducts pour out liquids necessary for the body's health, as do the sweat pores of the skin. Thus, through joy, all ways of communication are opened. 

In a state of joy, a pleasant and agreeable vibration <note>original: *tremor*</note>, as well as vital heat, light, and the very presence of the lower mind, spreads through both the external and internal senses. This lively vibration and light in the face is clearly revealed by the eyes, by speech, and by every action. Because of this, the brain is cleared, restored, and revitalized; in that moment, it returns, as it were, to the state of its original youth and innocence. In a state of joy, the mind is inclined toward every kind of waving and back-and-forth motion—such as beating time to music, leaping, and tossing the limbs—as well as vibration and actual physical response <note>original: *reciprocation*</note>, because all things are loosened and set free. The first degree of joy is to be content with one’s lot; the second is hilarity; the third is joy; and the fourth, which is the final effect, is laughter and a flinging of the body.

### *Sadness.*

(202.) Sadness, however—which is also termed sorrow and distress of mind—is the general unpleasant emotional state, for all unpleasant emotions cause sadness. The causes are all forms of discord, in general and in particular, which disagree with or are not suited to our sensory organs—especially to the internal sensory organ when it perceives or suspects misfortune, unhappiness, the loss of life, or the destruction of the body. Sadness compresses the brain and torments the lower mind <term>animus</term> <note>original: *animus*; the seat of emotions and sensory perception, distinct from the higher rational mind.</note>, casting it as if into fetters and chains and depriving it of its liberty. This constriction of the brain and anxiety of the mind appear in the face and its sensory organs, which are likewise compressed so that tears are forced out; it also appears in the whole body, which, though previously expanded, is now clearly contracted. Through this general constriction of the brain—the muscles of the gray matter <term>cortical substance</term> <note>Swedenborg viewed the brain's outer layer (cortex) as a collection of tiny active units that expand and contract like muscles to drive the body's functions.</note> being closed—every internal sensory faculty is restrained and loses its freedom of action. In this state, one part compresses the other; consequently, the brain becomes heavy and sluggish <note>original: *torpid*</note>, and the blood flow is impeded, nor does...

...[In a state of joy, the blood] flows freely through the larger and smaller vessels. In the deepest sadness, not only are the cortical regions <note>The outer layer of the brain's gray matter.</note> and the medullary layers <note>The inner white matter of the brain and spinal cord.</note> of the cerebrum, the cerebellum, the brainstem <note>original: *oblong medulla*</note>, and the spinal cord constricted, but so too are the fibrous and vascular channels of both the brain and the body. Even the pores of the skull and the bones, and the passages—such as the chyliferous <note>Vessels that carry chyle, a milky fluid containing fats, from the intestines.</note>, the lymphatic, and others that distribute liquids essential for the biological system <term>animal economy</term> <note>A term for the organized structure and functioning of a living organism.</note>—are tightened. If these are compressed, they cannot fulfill their purposes in the "kingdom" of the body. Thus, through sadness, all the ways of communication are partially closed. 

In a state of sadness, an unpleasant numbness <note>original: *torpor*</note> and stupor, coldness, darkness, and an absence of mind and of the emotional spirit <term>animus</term> <note>In Swedenborg’s psychology, the *animus* is the lower, emotional mind closely tied to the body and senses.</note> occupy both the physical brain <note>original: *common sensory*</note> and the internal mental faculty <note>original: *internal sensory*</note>. This numbness and darkness appear clearly in a person's countenance, eyes, and speech; consequently, the brain is, as it were, clouded and obscured, twisted, troubled, and deteriorating, while the mind is extinguished or falls into a kind of premature old age. 

In sadness, because the brain suffers and its individual ducts are compressed yet struggle to expand, an effect arises that is the opposite of laughter: namely, weeping and mourning. Sadness itself is an emotional state <note>original: *affection*</note> of the internal mental faculty, but weeping belongs to the external senses or the brain. Weeping cannot exist without the deepest sadness of the internal mind and without a reflection upon an unhappy condition or misfortune, whether present or future. This is why weeping does not occur in any creature except humans; it can only arise from a "mixed intellect," which does not know what the future holds. 

The first degree of sadness is being dissatisfied with one's lot; the second is a certain hidden anxiety; the third is sadness itself and grief of mind; the fourth and last, which is the physical effect, is weeping, mourning, and the total inaction of the body's muscles.

### *Loves in General.*

(203.) There are many types of emotional affections <term>animus</term> <note>The *animus* refers to the lower mind, the seat of emotions, passions, and sensory desires, as opposed to the higher rational mind.</note> that are called "loves," such as sexual love <term>venereal love</term> <note>Named for Venus, the goddess of love; in this context, it refers specifically to physical or sexual attraction.</note>, marriage love <term>conjugal love</term>, the love of parents toward their children (or *storge* <note>original Greek: *storge*; the natural, instinctual affection of parents for their offspring.</note>), and friendships. These various loves are, in a sense, so many unions, bonds, and associations of parts with a whole. To live without love is like being a part separated from the whole; for every part, in order to live, draws its share in life from the collective body, or from participating with many others. Society is the very form of living for these individual parts; the quality of an individual member's life flows from the structure of the community or society. Thus, a single life without this connection is effectively nothing. To ensure we are something, loves are granted to us, by which we are connected and through which we regard our friends as ourselves—viewing them as united to us rather than separate. Thus, there are loves of the body (sexual loves), loves of the emotional mind (marriage love and the love of friends), and there are loves of the higher mind, loves of the intellectual faculty <term>intellectory</term> <note>In the author's philosophical system, this is an intermediate faculty that bridges the pure soul and the rational mind.</note>, and loves of the soul. From these things, it can be seen that love is properly the vital heat itself and the very force of life; for without love, the individual members would become sluggish and die out.

This is why animals act from the same drive and toward the same goal. Their soul is equivalent to our pure intellect, meaning they desire only natural ends rather than spiritual ones; they do not seek a heavenly community <term>celestial society</term> as human souls do.

### ***Sexual Hatred and Aversion.***

(206.) There are people who, by nature, and those who, by principle or reason, have an aversion to sexual activity <note>original: "venery"</note>. Those who naturally—or from a purely intellectual standpoint—hate human society and its procreation are characterized by pride and an excessive love of self. Those whose rational minds and lower minds <term>animus</term> are unaffected by any charms are almost always sad and gloomy. Those whose blood is thicker and colder, and whose vital energy <term>animal spirit</term> is too scarce to fulfill its proper function, become old before their time; additionally, those whose reproductive organs are diseased are impotent. 

However, those who hate all sexual activity based on moral principle regard it as base and something that should not be surrendered to; they see its practice as an injury to the spirit and to a higher way of life. Thus, the principles behind this aversion are either spiritual or natural. This restraint is called chastity and is considered the highest virtue.

### ***Marital Love.***

(207.) "Love" is a spiritual term, while "harmony" is a natural term. These two correspond to one another, for both love and harmony create a union. This is because things that are in harmonious agreement are naturally joined together. Genuine marital love <note>original: "conjugial love." Swedenborg uses this specific term to describe a spiritualized form of marriage union.</note> not only brings about the union of two bodies and two lower minds <term>animus</term>, but also the union of two rational minds <term>mens</term>. 

The causes of love between a married couple are many, and indeed they all work together as far as nature allows. First, there is the union of the body, which is confirmed and strengthened by mutual delights. Second, there is a similarity in their lower minds <term>animus</term>, which gives rise to a shared desire for those pleasures. Third, there is the likeness of their rational minds <term>mens</term>, which are united more closely through living together. Because the affections of the mind are changeable, and the very structure of our rational ideas is acquired through experience and education, the rational mind is shaped over time. These minds—

If both partners also desire a spiritual goal, their souls are intimately united in their operation. From this comes a heavenly life on earth, and it is right to believe that the souls of both will be united in the heavens. Such marriages and loves are not formed or perfected by chance, but by the special providence of God.

### *Marital Hatred.*

(208.) Hatred is the opposite of love. What love truly is cannot be understood on its own, but only by looking at its opposite, just as musical harmonies are not recognized except by hearing discords. This is the reason why discords are introduced—so that the mind may be more pleasantly affected by the harmonies. However, it is the task of both science and art to ensure they are properly balanced, so that the quarrels of lovers do not give birth to hatred. 

True marital <note>original: "conjugial." Swedenborg uses this term to describe a spiritual, eternal union of minds rather than just a legal or physical bond.</note> hatred does not immediately separate physical bodies and lower minds <note>original: *animus*, the seat of emotions and passions</note>. Instead, it gradually pulls apart the rational minds <note>original: *mens*</note>, which are prone to change. From that starting point, the lower minds <note>original: *animus*</note> become divided, followed by the physical bodies; then the desires themselves disappear along with the pleasures they once brought. 

The causes of hatred and separation are many. The primary cause is a suspicion of unfaithfulness, which is called jealousy. When this takes hold, the love is no longer believed to be mutual. On the husband's part, he no longer believes the children are their common offspring; therefore, the love of children fails to unite their higher and lower minds. Other causes include disagreements over the various goals that are loved and desired by one or the other. This dislike is increased if, contrary to the natural order, neither person is willing to yield, but both insist on ruling. 

Because the mind and will of one is no longer in harmony with the other, and both are deprived of that freedom which is the mind's greatest delight, that freedom is replaced by either servitude, contempt, or hatred. These and many other factors drive minds apart, to such a degree that when sexual <note>original: "venereal"</note> love or love of the body ends, a deep aversion arises. Over time, these conflicts also affect the "pure mind" or <term>intellectory</term> <note>The most subtle part of the mind that serves as the interface between the soul and rational thought.</note> of each person. From this arises an undying and murderous hatred that defies description. This is a hell on earth; and it is right to believe that the souls of each, like two vengeful spirits <note>original: *furies* or *erinnyes*; in Greek mythology, the Erinyes were goddesses of vengeance who punished those who violated natural or social laws</note>, are destined to be tortured in hell. ### *The Love of Parents toward their Children, or Storge.*
<note>Storge: A Greek word for natural or familial affection, particularly the love of parents for their offspring.</note>

(209.) The love of parents for their children is completely distinct from other types of love in both its origin and its essence. Our rational mind and intellect are entirely unaware of where this love comes from; therefore, it is also called instinct, as it exists in the mind naturally and of itself. This love is shared by both animals and humans, and in animals, it is often more intense—so powerful that it overcomes self-love and gives courage to the timid. 

This is a kind of sympathy. Whether the child is one's biological offspring or someone else's child believed to be one's own, the passion is the same in both beasts and humans. Yet, this love is not reciprocated in the same way by the children; thus, this love is said to descend rather than ascend. It is natural in the parent but acquired <note>meaning learned or developed over time</note> in the child. 

Other forms of love, like marital love or friendship, enter the lower mind <note>original: *animus*, the seat of emotions and passions</note> through the senses, and from there move into the rational mind <note>original: *mens*</note>. But parental love is introduced by way of the pure intellect, flowing from the soul into the rational mind <note>original: *mens*</note>. Consequently, its origin and the path it takes are unknown, because whatever flows down from the pure mind into the rational mind is not revealed to our internal sensory <note>The "internal sensory" refers to the part of the mind that perceives conscious thoughts and images.</note>. The pure mind is unable to explain itself through the structure of words. 

This is the reason why the love is the same whether the child is our own biological offspring (as mentioned above) or another’s, as long as our rational mind is convinced the child belongs to us. From the effect of this love, it is clearly seen that in us the ra- <note>The text continues on the next page.</note>

The rational mind is something superior and purer that observes and, at the same time, desires more universal goals—those toward which all of nature works. These goals, which are purely natural and shared by both animals and humans, are primarily the propagation of the species and the extension of life on earth through others in whom that life is reborn. For the mind strives to form a colony from itself and pour its entire spirit into a new body; this is clearly demonstrated by sexual love <note>original: "venereal love." In this historical context, Swedenborg uses this term to refer to the biological drive for reproduction and the physical attraction between the sexes.</note>, as described earlier. 

This pure or superior mind knows quite clearly that the soul of the child is taken from the soul of the parent; thus, one soul is transcribed into many bodies. Our conscious rational mind is actually unaware of this; yet, it still understands through the intense effects of this love and desire that it wants to live in the closest possible union with its own children. It is even frustrated that it cannot be physically reunited with them, which it tries to achieve through tight embraces, holding them close, and kisses. Therefore, in this love is concentrated the love of oneself, the love of continuing one's life, and the love of society—of which this love is the first and foundational part. 

In humans, as much as this love comes from the pure intellect, it focuses on self-love, the continuation of life, and society. However, as much as it comes from the soul—the mind <note>original: "mens"</note> of which is spiritual—the love of eternity and the love of heavenly society are added to it; our earthly society is meant to be a part of that heavenly society. From these facts, as living and existing proofs, it is clear that the human soul is superior in its essence and form, and that the soul of animals <note>original: "brutes"</note> is equivalent to our pure intellect. 

This parental love toward children decreases over time—more slowly in humans and more rapidly in various kinds of animals. This happens because every child eventually adopts and acquires their own unique appearance, their own lower mind <note>original: "animus." This refers to the seat of the passions, emotions, and sensory perceptions, distinct from the higher rational mind.</note>, and their own rational mind, which are not identical to those of their parents. Thus, they are naturally separated as soon as the child's new brain develops a relationship to...

### *The Love of Society and of Country.*

(210.) There are smaller societies, larger societies, and the greatest societies. A small society is a home or family; a larger society is a province, a state, a kingdom, or an empire; the greatest is the whole world. Earthly society is called the world, just as heavenly society is called heaven. There are as many worlds as there are earthly societies, and there are as many heavens as there are heavenly societies. 

The love of society is both innate <note>original: "natural"</note> and acquired, for to live alone or to live without society is not truly living. One’s own identity and possessions are not truly known as one’s own except in relation to others. Our deepest delights are not truly enjoyable unless we are convinced of our own joy through the joy of others. Moreover, no desired goals <note>original: "ends"</note> can be achieved without the necessary means; thus, our goals cannot be reached without our friends and their assistance, nor can those of our friends be reached without the cooperation of that community of which we are all parts. 

Thus, nature herself creates and encourages this love and connection. When this love is purely animalistic, it is greatest for oneself and one's own family, less for friends, and least of all for society. But if this love descends directly from the mind <note>original: "mens"</note> of the pure intellect <note>original: "intellectory." In Swedenborg's system, this refers to the organic seat of the higher, intuitive intellect.</note>, it is then strongest for society, less for friends, and least for oneself. The logic is like that of the whole world compared to its individual parts. Indeed, if this love is spiritual, or belongs to the soul, then the love of heavenly society is prioritized above the love...

of all terrestrial societies or the whole world, and above that is God, who is love itself.

(211.) Our minds are rational—that is, they are both natural and spiritual. Natural minds, or purely animal minds, prioritize themselves over friends, prioritize friends over society, and prioritize the earth over heaven. Truly spiritual minds, however, put themselves in the lowest position; they treat and love their neighbors as equals; above all else, they place God; and they place others in their proper intermediate order. This subordination of the self is the true excellence of our minds; this is genuine magnanimity, wisdom, true honesty, virtue, happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>, and religion. These people are the heroes of their own age—the very essence, power, virtue, and stars of the world. A society made of such people is the City of God. By the wonders of this love, the Roman Empire flourished, where by a special providence of God, the entire universe was subjected to it. 

Such men are born even today, though they are regarded as wonders. Everyone recognizes this as an obvious truth. Who does not praise to the stars Quintus Mucius, Horatius Cocles, Scipio Africanus the elder, Cato, Octavius <note>These are legendary Roman figures celebrated for their self-sacrifice and devotion to the state.</note>, the Gustavi, and the Caroli <note>original: "the Gustavi, and Caroli"; these refer to the various Swedish kings named Gustavus and Charles, such as Gustavus Adolphus and Charles XII.</note>, and many others? Who does not admire that divine quality within them? Who does not exalt such a nature and pretend to it <note>original: "affect it"</note> in himself by placing himself last, or in no place at all, if he wishes to strive for the glory, favor, and applause of the whole of society? Thus, it is a matter of artifice for a man to feign—even for selfish reasons—magnanimity, wisdom, honesty, virtue, and religion, and to act as a man above other men, even at the very moment he is trying to put himself in the highest position.

(212.) There are as many forms of society as there are social groups. The entire human race, or the world, constitutes a universal form; empires and kingdoms are less universal forms; the dukedoms of empires and the provinces of kingdoms are even less universal; and families and households are the smallest. Every person is naturally bound by a love for the group to which they belong. Thus, a man loves his own country above others when they come into conflict, because in protecting its structure, he is protecting himself.

### *Love towards Friends, or Friendship.*

(213.) All love is natural, but all friendship is acquired love. The love between husbands and wives is natural, but friendship is something acquired through mutual association. The sentiment that exists in parents toward children—and in others toward blood relatives or relatives by marriage—is love; however, the sentiment toward others not related by blood is called friendship. Affection for one’s country and society is also called love, insofar as it is innate <note>original: "connate"</note>. Love exists between both equals and unequals, but friendship exists only between equals. The sentiment of inferiors toward superiors is not called friendship but veneration, which easily gives way to love, since the veneration of superiors is natural and is contained within every form of love. 

There are, however, many causes, natures, and degrees of friendship. It is a general rule that friendship is produced through a similarity of manners—that is, a similarity of the lower mind <term>original: "animus"; in Swedenborg’s philosophy, the "animus" refers to the lower, more sensory part of the mind, distinct from the higher rational "mens."</term> and the rational mind <term>original: "mens"; the higher, intellectual part of the soul.</term>. The lower mind, which is the external state of the rational mind and the brain alone, does not consider goals <note>original: "ends"</note> but only the pleasures of the body. It is only affected by similarities in condition, age, sex, fortune, physical appearance, or actions. Consequently, the friendship resulting from this is the type found among infants, boys, and youths, or even among adults who are controlled more by their lower impulses and pleasures than by their rational mind and the desire for reasonable goals. In these cases, there is frequently an initial attachment, for we tend to judge internal character based on external appearances. 

But friendship based on rational causes is gained through shared goals in which both people unite, for similarity is recognized through these goals. Thus, as far as we desire certain goals, we love those friends and companions who help advance them; for the ultimate goals and the means (or all intermediate goals) move forward together. Goals are either physical and purely natural, or they are rational, or they are spiritual. The pleasant affections themselves are goals; thus, they are virtuous goals among virtuous men, evil goals among evil men, and friendships among those related by blood, and so forth. But in...

<summary>This page distinguishes between innate "love" (such as family bonds) and acquired "friendship," explaining that true friendship arises from shared rational goals and similarities in character.</summary>

For friendship, it is necessary that one person should be the leader and the other the follower; if both attempt to lead, there will be a collision, as often happens among ill-tempered, envious, and greedy persons. Furthermore, the nature of friendship varies; there may be sincere friendship or deceitful friendship, and even friendship mixed with hatred. Very often we dislike a person’s lower mind <term>original: "animus"; the lower, more sensory part of the mind, distinct from the higher rational mind</term> and their manners, yet we love their higher mind <term>original: "mens"; the rational, intellectual part of the soul</term> and their will—that is, the person themselves—and vice versa. Sometimes we even prefer not to live with a loved one, but rather with someone we dislike <note>Swedenborg suggests that we may find someone's personality (animus) difficult to live with even if we love their essential character (mens).</note>. Our primary affection and ruling love is the measure of our friendship toward another. Thus, it can be seen how diverse the materials are from which friendship is composed. 

It ought to be a general rule that all people should be loved while their vices are hated; that is, even enemies should be embraced with love, though not necessarily with friendship. For love is natural and belongs to the pure mind and the soul itself, while friendship is acquired and belongs to the rational mind. The goals <note>original: "ends"</note> of the soul are spiritual, the first of which is eternal happiness. When several people agree on these goals, they are already regarded as friends whom love alone binds. In this way, there can be a love of souls however hostile their rational minds <note>original: "mens"</note> may be. Without this spiritual love, there is no divine love; for it is through this alone that souls are joined together, if they aspire toward this one goal.

### *Hatred*

(214.) Hatred is not merely an absence of love, but it is the love of evil and, consequently, the hatred of truth. Hatred is both natural and acquired. Natural hatred is the opposite of love, but acquired hatred is the opposite of friendship. Just as love is a pleasing affection that delights the senses, renewing the blood and the animal spirits <term>In historical physiology, "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid that transmitted sensation and motion through the nerves.</term> with new heat, light, and life, and restoring the individual parts of the body—

Thus, hatred is an unpleasant emotion <note>original: "affection"</note> that causes distress to the sensory organs <note>original: "sensories"</note> and disturbs the blood and animal spirits <term>animal spirits: In 18th-century physiology, these were thought to be a subtle fluid that transmitted signals through the nerves.</term>, depriving them of their vitality and destroying various parts of the body. The lower mind <term>original: "animus"; the sensory or emotional mind</term> is then in anguish and the brain feels compressed; it is cheered, made peaceful, and expanded only by the misfortunes of others. Just as love is a union of personalities <note>original: *animus*</note> and rational minds <note>original: *mens*</note>, hatred is their separation. As love is life and heaven, hatred is death and hell.

Disagreements, discord, and disharmony arise from hatred. The greatest joy of the most intense hatred would be achieved if heaven and earth were to collapse. However, there are many causes, types, and degrees of both natural and acquired hatred. The causes of natural hatred stem from the state of the pure intellect and the soul, as there are as many different states as there are souls and intellectories <term>intellectories: Swedenborg’s term for the organic or spiritual structures within the brain that facilitate thought.</term>. There are spiritual essences and forms that are more perfect or less perfect—the best and the worst. In the former, love and harmony dwell; in the latter, hatred and discord. Those souls in which love dwells are heavenly essences; according to their degree of love, they are closer to the supreme love, which is God, and are more pleasing and happy. But those in which hatred dwells are hellish essences; according to their degree of hatred, they are more distant from God, more ungrateful, and more unhappy. 

Acquired hatred is caused and increased by a lack of similarity in personalities and by a conflict or clash between minds, as well as by the desires and wishes revealed by one’s goals <note>original: "ends"</note>. All desired goals are pleasant to the mind; hatred is born from disagreement, difference, and opposition. For love to exist, one person must yield while the other acts; conversely, hatred arises when one opposes the other. Just as the love of a shared goal is the measure of friendship, so is the opposition of goals the measure of hatred. Other observations regarding hatred can be inferred from the description of the different types of love, since hatred is the opposite of **love.**

### *Self-love; Ambition; Haughtiness; Pride.*

(215.) Ambition is not love itself, but is something added to it—an accompaniment. If it were separated from love, love would be passive rather than active. We have seen that love is the life-force of both the rational mind <note>original: *mens*</note> and the lower mind <note>original: *animus*</note>, for neither exists without love. Ambition is essentially the driving force of this life, or the intensity with which the mind expresses its love. Thus, love is the passive principle and ambition is its active counterpart. From this, it follows that there are as many types of ambition as there are types of love. For instance, there is ambition in marriage love <note>original: "conjugial love," a term Swedenborg uses for the spiritual and eternal bond between spouses</note>, in the love parents have for their children, in the love of society, and in self-love. 

The reason ambition is frequently mistaken for love is because the two together constitute a person's rational mind <note>original: *mens*</note>, their lower mind <note>original: *animus*</note>, or their very life. Because ambition is joined to love like a husband to a wife—and because there are loves that are more or less perfect (some being virtues and others being vices)—there are also more or less perfect ambitions. Ambition derives its core essence and nature from the specific love to which it is bound or "wedded." Ambition is a vice, or is "spurious," when joined to self-love; however, it is a virtue, or is legitimate, when joined to a love for society.

(216.) Corrupted or illegitimate ambition, which is joined to self-love, craves the highest positions. The higher it climbs, the higher it aspires, and its desires increase as it advances. It especially hungers for status, supreme honors, and worldly wealth—even viewing heaven itself as something to be subjected to its will. In this way, the ambition of Adam <note>A reference to the biblical Fall of Man, where Adam sought to be like God</note> remains deeply rooted in the nature of his descendants. Every "child of the earth" desires in his mind to occupy all of heaven. He tries to mimic the omnipresence of God through his fame, God's providence through his own universal concerns, and God's omnipotence through his pursuit of absolute power. He even tries to mimic God's omniscience (all-knowingness), for he is so arrogant that he is unaware of anything he does not know, and so per- <meta>The text ends mid-word; "per-" likely continues as "perceives" or "persists" on the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page defines ambition as the active force that drives love, distinguishing between virtuous ambition (aimed at serving society) and vicious ambition (driven by self-love). Swedenborg argues that self-centered ambition is a corruption of the human spirit that seeks to mimic divine attributes like omnipotence and omniscience.</summary>

At the same time, it indicates a state of the internal sensory <note>the part of the mind that processes internal perceptions</note> that corresponds to the <term>intellectory</term>. This state is natural rather than acquired through learning; for even if it is learned through rules, it is rarely acquired in a way that remains constantly active unless the mind is continually stripped of its own natural passion <note>original: "ardour"</note> and thus made ready for the <term>influx</term> of the higher mind.

(218.) But the highest or spiritual ambition, which belongs to the soul, is that which is joined to the love of heavenly society. This sees its own glory and happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> not in itself, but in the love of God and in His kingdom, which it earnestly desires to promote. It is humble, a worshipper of the Divine <note>original: "Deity"</note>, and disregards its own importance; yet, to the degree that it is less in its own eyes, it is greater before God. For this purpose, this zeal is granted to souls, and ambition is granted to human minds.

### *Humility; Contempt; Lowliness of Mind [Lower Mind].*

(219.) There is a natural and an acquired humility, just as there is an internal humility of the rational mind and an external humility of the <term>lower mind</term> <note>original: "animus"; in Swedenborg's psychology, the "animus" is the lower, emotional mind, distinct from the higher rational mind or "mens."</note> and body. Natural humility arises from self-contempt—by which is meant an absence of ego—making it an emotion contrary to false ambition or self-love. It is entirely united to love toward others, which is why it deserves to be called "legitimate ambition." This is because the more we withdraw from the love of ourselves, the more we enter into a love toward others, viewing them as more excellent and higher than ourselves. 

Strictly speaking, humility is shown toward superiors, and is thus a form of veneration. Because love toward superiors is expressed through veneration, humility is essentially veneration itself. For this reason, humility is a virtue. If it is innate or natural, it is rooted in the pure intellect itself; if it resides in the soul itself, it is evidence of love toward God. In that state, it is a complete setting aside of the self <note>original: "annihilation of self"</note>, which results in the highest form of religion: adoration and the plea for grace. The quality and depth of this love can be known from the act of adoration itself, which is an act of humility. 

The reason humility proves our love toward others—whether they are truly superior and more perfect or simply perceived as such—is based on a natural principle: if we want the love and work of another to influence us, we must extinguish the heat of our own <term>lower mind</term> and rational mind, reducing them to a state of passivity. In this state, the love of the other person is what operates alongside our own love; it becomes the active principle that must exist in love for it to be the warmth of our life. 

Therefore, humility is what allows the minds of others to join with our own, and it is the very source of benevolence. Without this state of mind, Divine love could never work within us. Indeed, false ambition, through its own restless activity, rejects every <term>influx</term> <note>the flow of spiritual or higher energy into the lower parts of a person</note> and completely extinguishes it. No emotion approves of this virtue or praises it more than corrupt or false ambition does; for false ambition demands...

(220.) Humility which is acquired does not originate from our nature or natural inclination, nor from principles built into our pure intellect and soul. Instead, it comes from principles developed through the reflection of our mind, drawn from our own experience or from the experience of others who teach us. If we put faith in our teachers and acknowledge the truths they have examined, a principle arises from which either virtues or vices are acquired. 

Thus, if we are filled with truths—especially the truth that illegitimate ambition or self-love is a vice and a barrier to communicating with the love of another (particularly a superior)—then as self-love recedes, love toward others and the love of others toward us takes its place, leading to humility. Over time, as these principles are deeply implanted, they pass into the pure intellect and become as if they were natural. This state is even transferred to one's descendants as if it were a natural inclination; this is the origin of natural humility. This humility is called **internal**.

(221.) **External** humility belongs to the <term>lower mind</term> <note>original: "animus"</note> and body alone, and not to the rational mind. In a word, honesty and virtue can be faked. Vices can also be simulated, such as self-love and contempt of...

<page-num>140</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL</header>

...friends, and many other things. This type of humility is called external because it exists outside of the higher mind and is, in a sense, superficial. The higher mind is a superior or internal <term>lower mind</term> <note>original: "animus"; in Swedenborg’s philosophy, the "animus" refers to the sensory or lower mind, while the "mens" is the rational or higher mind</note>. The will is subject to this higher mind, because it is where intellect, judgment, and choice reside. The higher mind, which governs the will, is able to command the external or <term>lower mind</term>, and through it, the body. Indeed, it can do this with such skill that it can prevent any sign of the mind’s true state from showing in the face. 

For every emotion, there are certain corresponding expressions of the face, body, gestures, and actions. For example, the joyful expression of humility seen in the faces of two people in love is not necessarily their own natural state, but rather a reflection of the other person’s state. Reverence itself appears in the form of actions, in the tone of speech, and the style of language, as a kind of yielding and obedience. However, the deepest humility breaks out even into tears or a pitiful physical condition; we lie face down, we cry out that we are as nothing, and we beat upon our breasts. These are the natural physical effects of humility, and it spontaneously flows out in this manner when it is truly present. However, we are also taught how to fake all of these signs.

(222.) Lowliness of mind or spirit is a virtue as well as a vice. It is a virtue when humility is gained from sound principles, or when self-love and <term>false ambition</term> <note>original: "spurious ambition"</note> are driven out of our minds. When this happens, it is immediately replaced by an ambition to serve and obey others, or a willingness to be guided by others.

Both self-love and ambition (or this lower mind) are cast down by sickness, disease, misfortune, and anxieties; but these are tools of Divine Providence. On the other hand, lowliness of mind is an evil when it arises from a sudden loss of passion or the collapse of a false ambition while self-love remains—either without its usual intensity or without the possibility of acting. When this happens, great stress or harm is inflicted on the internal organs and, consequently, on the external ones and the rest of the body. This results in an outbreak of weeping, despair, frenzy, grief, disease, insanity, and madness.
