### *Hope and Despair*

(223.) When we strive for and desire what we love, yet find that obstacles prevent us from reaching our goal, we call this state of desire **hope**. It appears to exist within the will as a persistent effort that these obstacles are preventing from turning into action or movement. Therefore, hope is not merely an emotion of the <term>lower mind</term> <note>original: "animus"; Swedenborg uses this term for the sensory or emotional mind, as opposed to the "mens" or rational mind</note>, but a state of its **will**. 

The will always strives to act, but as long as it faces resistance, it cannot do so. In the meantime, it is influenced by a certain hope, which keeps it balanced between action and inaction. Consequently, hope does not belong to the <term>lower mind</term> but to the **rational mind**, because it belongs to the will; for this reason, hope is a human quality and does not belong to animals or irrational beings. 

Hope increases and grows exactly as far as impossibilities—that is, resistances—withdraw or are removed. Overcoming these obstacles is the work of wisdom and skill. However, the strength of hope itself is greater or less depending on the degree of love and desire one has for the goal. Therefore, hope focuses on desired outcomes and is connected to all the motivations that seek those ends. Because of this, hope is the continuation of life—that is, the continuation of our loves, our passion, and our <term>ambition</term> <note>original: "ambition"; in this context, the driving force or desire for excellence and purpose</note>. The greatest hope is that which we place in God, for whom nothing is impossible; this is why hope is one of the three spiritual virtues. <note>original: "1 Corinthians 13:13"—The three spiritual or "theological" virtues are faith, hope, and charity (love).</note>

(224.) **Despair** occurs when we lose all hope. At that point, love and ambition—which are the very life and passion of the mind—collapse and are, in a sense, extinguished. This leads to that "dejection of the lower mind" whose effects were described previously. The general results of despair are various types of insanity (which are diseases of the rational mind), different states of frenzy (which are diseases of the lower mind), and various physical illnesses of the body.

<summary>Swedenborg defines hope as a state of the rational will that persists despite obstacles, identifying it as a uniquely human and spiritual virtue. Conversely, despair is the extinction of this life-affirming hope, leading to mental, emotional, and physical illness.</summary>

<keywords>hope, despair, will, rational mind, animus, spiritual virtues, ambition, mental health, Swedenborgian psychology</keywords>

### *The Love of an Immortality of Fame after Death.*

(225.) The love for the immortality of fame—or what we usually call "making a name for oneself"—is natural to everyone, as shown by countless proofs. Who does not desire grand funerals and memorial services? Who does not provide for the building of a tomb to remain as a monument for the sake of his name after his body dies? Who is not pleased by the thought of people talking about him in the future, or moved by the flattery (though he cannot hear it yet) when it is said that "he has gained immortal fame and has earned the gratitude of <term>posterity</term>" <note>Posterity refers to all future generations of people.</note>? Indeed, a person would feel great pride, and the whole world would applaud him almost instinctively, if he could convince them that he did not work to serve himself, but rather to serve future generations; this is the source of a great man’s glory.

From these and many other proofs, it is clearly established that the love of our own immortality, fame, or name is innate—something we are born with. Therefore, it is one of those truths that reside within the <term>pure intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectory"; in Swedenborg’s philosophy, the "pure intellectory" is the highest part of the mind, which perceives universal truths instinctively without the need for sensory data.</note>. Unless the pure intellect and the soul were aware of this, such a love could never exist in a rational mind. Because it does exist, it follows that it is a truth that we are destined to live after the death of our bodies. 

However, our rational mind does not always recognize this on its own, because it is often ignorant of where this love truly comes from. Some even deny it exists—especially those minds that passionately chase only physical and worldly goals. Both natural and spiritual elements exist within our rational minds, and when one dominates, it suffocates the other. Nevertheless, this truth remains like a spark hidden under embers, becoming visible when even these people <insert>when they come to die</insert> desire grand funeral ceremonies.

(226.) This love, with its unique ambition, is of the highest importance and is either a virtue or a vice. It is a virtue when it seeks an immortal name through virtuous behavior, honesty, and praiseworthy deeds for the benefit of society and one’s country; and

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the universal human desire for a lasting reputation after death is innate proof that the soul is immortal. He explains that while worldly minds might deny this spiritual reality, the desire for a legacy remains a "spark" of the soul's internal knowledge.</summary>

This love is even greater when it is directed not only toward present societies but toward all future ones. If there is an innate love for our society and country, it follows that a love extending to all <term>posterity</term> <note>original: "posterity"; all future generations.</note> must be even greater. Such a love, or "virtuous ambition," is a pure love when it is joined with our self-love—provided that the individual does not desire for their own name to live on, but rather that their service and resulting public usefulness do. 

Such people are the true heroes of the world. They reject all personal glory for their deeds and merits; they are even repelled by such things. Instead, they rejoice from their deepest conscience that they were the means of their country’s happiness and safety. They find joy in the thought that God, heaven, and the eternal beings are aware of their deeds, and that they may draw near to these higher powers in a kind of spiritual likeness. 

Furthermore, once the body has perished in death, such souls are granted a certain heaven. This heaven exists not only within themselves but also outside of themselves, through other souls with whom they necessarily share an immediate connection of spiritual affection. Both faith and reason refuse to doubt these things, though we will discuss them elsewhere. Such "internal men" despise—and are even repulsed by—the kind of fame represented by monuments, palaces, buildings, statues, amphitheaters, inscribed titles, and similar things. They aspire to something higher, something with which these material things cannot be compared. 

However, this love becomes a vice when the true virtue behind it is dead, leaving nothing but a fake appearance. In such cases, a person tries to trick a gullible public into valuing their deeds by pretending to be sincere or truthful. This happens where self-love or <term>spurious ambition</term> <note>original: "spurious ambition"; a false or fake desire for status that is not based on actual merit or service.</note> is dominant. In these people, the love of fame naturally rules, but the ultimate goal is the fame of the self rather than the fame of their virtues. This is like the man who burned the Temple of Diana at Ephesus <note>This refers to Herostratus, who destroyed the famous temple in 356 BCE solely to ensure his name would be remembered throughout history.</note>. 

Yet, without this innate love, no one would love their own children, for they would not see their own immortality through them. Neither would anyone fight for their country out of love, nor seek death, nor willingly offer themselves as a sacrifice. True heroic virtue arises from this incentive, such as was exhibited...

### *Generosity; Magnanimity; The Nature of Worldly and Physical Desires.*

(227.) The *animus* <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; in Swedenborg’s system, the "lower mind" or the seat of emotions and passions, which bridges the physical senses and the higher rational mind.</note> is called generous and great to the extent that it is raised above what is worldly and physical, and thus closer to the heavenly and divine. By "animus" here, we mean the higher mind; for this reason, this mind is also called divine. This mind views physical and worldly things as nothing by comparison, because they are changeable, inconsistent, temporary, perishable, and lifeless. They are destined to become nothing—mere tools for living, which are valued only according to how well they serve a purpose. But heavenly things are seen as the only true essentials—the only things that truly exist—the eternal constants, and happiness itself.

(228.) In a strict sense, "worldly" <term>mundane</term> <note>original: "mundane"; from the Latin *mundanus*, meaning belonging to the world.</note> refers to the earth and the universe—with its planets, moons, sun, and stars—and especially everything within the earth’s three kingdoms <note>The animal, vegetable, and mineral kingdoms.</note>. Even human societies are called worlds, and every individual within a society is considered a "microcosm" <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "microcosm"; literally a "little world," representing the idea that the human being contains all the elements of the larger universe.</note>. Worldly things also include riches, possessions, and other earthly objects. In themselves, these are just clumps of dirt, but in society, they are treated as goods that serve the needs of life. 

Physical <term>corporeal</term> <note>original: "corporeal"; relating to the physical body.</note> things, however, are those that appeal only to the body and the lower mind, such as the senses of touch, taste, smell, hearing, and sight, or the pleasant feelings they produce. These also include titles and honors, which are disregarded when a person seeks only the pleasures of the body and the lower mind. These are called worldly loves, desires <term>cupidities</term> <note>original: "cupidities"; strong, often selfish, desires.</note> of the lower mind, and pleasures of the body, because they affect our blood and our physical senses. <summary>Swedenborg defines a "generous" mind as one that prioritizes eternal spiritual values over temporary physical and worldly desires. He explains that the rational mind serves as a balance between these two opposing forces.</summary>

From these traits, one can judge the character of the lower mind and the goals toward which its desires lean.

### *Small-mindedness and Folly.*

(232.) Small-mindedness <term>pusillanimity</term> <note>From the Latin "pusillus" (very small) and "animus" (soul); the opposite of being great-souled.</note> is the opposite of magnanimity, and it is named for this contrast. When contrasted with generosity, it is called folly. A small-minded person has no strength of their own, nor enough intellect to allow them to stand by their own mind. Instead, they are tossed inconsistently from one side to the other, wherever their lust, their overconfidence <note>original: "presumption"</note>, or the persuasion of others may lead them. Even if such a person should focus on higher things for a moment, they immediately fall back into lower concerns and remain submerged in a purely physical existence. 

Folly, however, completely rejects higher things. It embraces lower things with the entire heart and lower mind <term>animus</term>, considering physical matters to be the only reality—and even the very substance of reason. This is characteristic of a person who is purely animalistic and brutish.

Further conclusions on this subject can be drawn by comparing them to the descriptions of magnanimity and generosity provided above.

### *Avarice.*

(233.) Avarice <note>greed or the excessive desire for wealth</note> is the love of riches and earthly possessions, but its true nature can be recognized by its purpose <note>original: "end"</note>. It is natural to love wealth in the same way one loves the goals for which wealth is the tool <note>original: "means"</note>. Therefore, it is natural for animals <note>original: "brutes"</note>, and even insects, to collect and store away the necessities of life for the coming winter. Because money is the universal tool <note>original: "medium"</note> for promoting and achieving various goals, it is called the "sinew <note>original: "nerve"</note> of business." 

This drive is not greed, but rather prudence in providing for one's needs—a kind of human foresight <note>original: "providence"</note> granted by God—provided that the love of the money itself does not outweigh the love of the goal it serves. Often, however, it goes further. Worldly and physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> loves never stop growing; they expand in all directions, such as the love of status <note>original: "dignities"</note>, honors, and power; the love of vanity, display, and arrogance; and the love of pleasure. This includes the desire to provide for one's own family, not only during one's own life and that of one's children, but even for grandchildren. This is because parental love <term>storge</term> <note>From the Greek *storgē*, referring specifically to the natural, instinctive affection between parents and children.</note> inspires a sense of lasting legacy <note>original: "perpetual life"</note> that grows toward future generations. 

The love of riches—the tools meant to achieve this lasting legacy—increases to the same degree. There are also higher forms of love that wealth serves, such as the love of farming <note>original: "agriculture"</note>, of defending one's country, and of preserving society. This is why a ruler's greatest concern is to ensure his kingdom is wealthy. Wealth can also serve spiritual goals <note>original: "ends"</note>, such as performing works of charity, helping those in need, promoting and spreading religious worship, building temples, and many other things. Because money is the universal tool <note>original: "medium"</note> for so many—nearly all—purposes, and since every person has their own loves, desires, and goals, it follows that the love or valuation of money dominates the entire world.

(234.) However, if wealth is sought not for the sake of these goals, but merely for the sake of possessing it—that is, not as a tool...

<summary>Swedenborg defines avarice not as the simple possession of wealth, but as the love of money for its own sake rather than as a means to achieve productive or spiritual ends. He argues that while storing resources is a natural instinct shared by animals, humans must ensure their pursuit of wealth serves higher purposes like family, country, or charity.</summary>

But if wealth is regarded as the goal itself <note>original: "as the end itself"</note>, then this love is that greed <note>original: "avarice"</note> which is called sordid; it is pure folly and the mark of a lowly mind. It goes against nature itself and against the principles of all reason for wealth to be seen as the ultimate goal, for something that is in itself a tool <note>original: "means"</note> cannot be the end goal. This is why money is seen as the "possibility" of all goals—essentially, it represents all potential desires <note>original: "loves in potency"</note>. 

The mind takes more delight in thinking about its desires than the body does in actually carrying them out or experiencing their pleasures. This is because the mental view is more lasting and steady, while physical pleasure is inconsistent and ends with the act itself (as seen in sexual <note>original: "venereal"</note> love). For this reason, pleasures are often credited to the imagination, because the very life of the mind thrives on these kinds of mental desires. Furthermore, in greedy minds, all these potential desires remain active because of the "possibility of all things" which wealth promises. These desires stir up a universal idea that is more pleasing simply because it is so broad. This appears to be the underlying cause of greed. 

This is confirmed by the location of this feeling: it exists in the rational mind alone. It is not a feeling of the higher mind, as it is never natural; rather, it is acquired over time and increases in old age just as physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> desires fade away. It is also not a feeling of the lower mind <term>animus</term> <note>The *animus* in Swedenborg's psychology refers to the seat of emotions and lower drives connected to the body.</note>, because it does not originate in the body; the cravings <note>original: "cupidities"</note> of the lower mind and the pleasures of the body are inseparable.

(235.) The extent to which greed can become a mental disease—insanity, irrationality, and stinginess <note>original: "niggardliness"</note>—is fully evident from its effects. The more deeply it takes root, the more it blunts and wipes out <note>original: "extirpated"</note> all other loves. A mind occupied by this constant obsession is effectively suffocated; it is buried not just in the body, but in the earth itself. Consequently, it cannot be raised toward higher things, nor can spiritual influence flow into what is so crudely physical. Thus, the god whom the greedy man worships is like Pluto <note>The Roman god of the underworld and of wealth found underground.</note> himself, for the worshipper adores that...

He prays that he himself may be blessed—meaning, so that he might be given more riches. ### *Wastefulness; Generosity; Contempt of Wealth.*

(237.) Wastefulness <term>prodigality</term> <note>the excessive or reckless spending of money</note> arises from various causes. A wasteful person either desires their goals too intensely, or has no goals at all; they might focus only on the present and ignore the future, or deny that riches are simply a tool for reaching an end. Some believe wealth replenishes itself automatically, while others wish to show off a generous spirit or despise wealth as a source of evil. Thus, wastefulness is both a vice and a virtue. When it is a vice, it is properly called prodigality; but when it is a virtue, it is called liberality <note>the quality of being open-handed and generous</note>, which is a form of generosity and greatness of soul <term>magnanimity</term>. When this virtue reaches its highest level, it is called the "contempt of money." Wastefulness belongs to the lower mind <term>animus</term> <note>The *animus* refers to the lower, impulsive part of the mind driven by emotions and physical senses, as opposed to the higher rational mind.</note> but not to the natural mind; therefore, it differs completely from greed <note>original: "avarice"</note>.

<summary>This page describes how extreme greed (avarice) replaces religious and social values with the worship of money, then introduces the concept of prodigality, distinguishing between reckless wastefulness and virtuous generosity.</summary>

<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...even regarding its origin. That it belongs to the lower mind <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; in Swedenborg’s psychology, the "animus" is the lower, sensory mind—the seat of emotions and physical impulses—as distinct from the "mens" or higher rational mind.</note> and not to the higher rational mind is evident from the nature of the wasteful person <note>original: "prodigal"</note>. For such a person does not care for the future but only for the present; he lives only for the day, or he craves physical pleasures too much as ends in themselves. Thus, he indulges only his natural disposition, his lower mind, and his physical desires <term>cupidities</term> <note>original: "cupidities"; here referring to intense or irrational cravings for worldly things.</note>. 

Alternatively, if he is conscious of no strong motivation or goal, he is like a lifeless stump—weakened in his higher mind. Or, like a child growing up, he does not realize that wealth should be acquired with care as the general means to achieve higher goals. All these factors indicate that the lower mind is the source of wastefulness, not the higher rational mind. 

Generosity <note>original: "liberality"</note> is also either a vice or a virtue, for it is done for a specific goal, and the goal defines the value of the action. It is a vice if it is motivated by a love for the world and the body—that is, if it is done for ostentation or show. It is a virtue if it stems from superior loves, such as for the works of charity. In this case, people regard wealth as something received in trust and committed to their care, to be distributed and given back where needed. 

To hold money in contempt—provided this is not faked—is a supreme <note>original: "supereminent"</note> virtue. This is because the person who scorns money turns away from it as they would from the vices and evils for which money is a constant irritant and temptation. The possession of wealth can never be separated from the thought of those physical delights and pleasures for which it is a tool. 

The mind regards things that are possible or yet to come as if they were already present and real. Consequently, all loves of the world and the body exist in the imagination as worldly and physical realities, as if they were already being acted upon. In this way, the possession of wealth acts as a constant irritation and a universal lure. Thus, the mind descends and buries itself in all natural, worldly, and physical things, from which it is impossible for the mind to be raised toward higher, heavenly <note>original: "celestial"</note>, and divine things. If money is despised for this reason, such contempt is, as stated, a supreme virtue.

He concludes that genuine contempt for wealth is a supreme virtue because it prevents the mind from being buried in worldly and physical distractions.</summary>

<header>THE LOWER MIND AND ITS EMOTIONS <term>animus and its affections</term> <note>original: "The Animus and its Affections"; the "animus" in Swedenborg’s system refers to the lower, sensory mind—the seat of emotions and physical impulses—as distinct from the "mens" or higher rational mind.</note></header>

### *Pity and Charity.*

(238.) There are some who are compassionate by nature, some by habit <note>original: "use"</note>, some for purely moral reasons, and some based on principles of reason. *Compassion from nature*—or what is the same thing, from the pure mind and soul—flows out toward others from an innate love. In this sense, it is the same as love itself; it is the first effect of love, or another form of charity <note>In Swedenborg’s philosophy, "charity" is not merely giving to the poor, but the internal desire to act with justice, kindness, and love toward others.</note>. For love treats another person as itself, and so it pities others even if it might be deserving of pity itself. Love toward a spouse, children, and relatives—that is, toward one's own family—produces pity, and from that, charity, which extends as far as the love does. Love toward society and one's country, and the even more universal love for the human race—including the most universal love for humanity past and future—is a purer and more perfect love than the former. It produces a pity and charity toward all who, through this love, are spiritually called "neighbors." Naturally, these neighbors may be close or distant (since nature alone recognizes degrees of distance), but spiritually they are one. Thus, true pity and charity are not joined to self-love or false <note>original: "spurious"</note> ambition; because of this, they are the highest of virtues <note>original: "virtues of virtues"</note>. Such love always produces an effect; therefore, we can judge a person’s love—and thus the state of their mind and soul—by the charity and pity they show.

*Pity from habit* <note>original: "use"</note> mimics natural pity because, over time, it stains the mind with the principles of love. This is properly called a moral virtue because it is within the power of our will—not of its own accord, but through our own choices. We contribute to it as "instrumental causes" by applying ourselves to the flow <term>influx</term> <note>original: "influx"; the spiritual process where life and influence flow from the soul into the mind and body.</note> of the primary cause.

*Pity is also conceived from purely moral causes* and is acquired through habit. Once it is born in this way, it may stem from principles of virtue and piety; however, this type of pity assumes a faith that is not purely intellectual. Instead, it is introduced <note>original: "insinuated"</note> through obedience and habit, for faith is not something within our own power to create.

<vocab>Pity, Charity, Compassion, Moral virtue, Faith, Principles of reason, Animus</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg categorizes pity and charity into four types: natural, habitual, moral, and rational, explaining that true charity stems from an innate love that views the neighbor as oneself.</summary>

*Pity based on rational principles—whether stemming from a false <note>original: "spurious"</note> or a legitimate love—actually derives from a false love, namely, the love of self.* A person who loves only themselves is never truly compassionate, for they do not love others as they love themselves. Nor does someone who hates ever pity the person they hate; no one hates another person simply as another person unless they love themselves—that is, unless there are reasons that conflict with their own self-love. Nevertheless, outward acts of pity can spring from this same self-love, so that a person may appear kind, compassionate, and altruistic. They do this because they know these traits are seen as virtues, and their self-love motivates them to appear this way to gain status or distinction. It may also come from the idea that others might pity them if they were to become unfortunate. In such a case, they show charity toward the wealthy specifically so they might be rewarded, but this is done without any real pity or love.

*Pity based on principles of legitimate love* requires an intellectual faith—the conviction that pity is the natural result of pure heavenly <note>original: "celestial"</note> and spiritual love. These mental principles are regarded as rational truths, for everyone believes their own principles are true.

(239.) The effect of pity is experienced as anxiety in the mind, sadness in the <term>animus</term> <note>In Swedenborg’s system, the "animus" is the lower, sensory mind—the seat of emotions and physical impulses.</note>, and weeping in the body, accompanied by a sorrowful voice. The image of pity is also visible in one's facial expression. Thus, the effects of pity and sadness overlap, but in such a way that the person suffers as if the sadness were their own, because the person they pity is viewed as their "other self."

(240.) The objects of pity are countless. Generally, they include poverty and unhappiness. However, there are also people who pity the wealth <note>original: "opulence"</note> and fame of others, viewing these things as causes of misery and temptations toward vice. Everyone pities a greedy <note>original: "avaricious"</note> man. Poverty can exist in worldly, intellectual, and spiritual matters. Worldly poverty is well understood; intellectual poverty is ignorance or a delusion <note>original: "hallucination"</note> regarding one's core principles...

<summary>Swedenborg distinguishes between "false" pity, which stems from self-interest and a desire for status, and "legitimate" pity, which arises from spiritual love. He describes pity as a form of shared suffering where one views the other as an extension of oneself.</summary>

### *Fear and Dread.*

(241.) Nothing is more natural than to protect one's life and its essence, to desire to continue existing, and to preserve the structural connection that defines one's form. The soul—which is the living essence—is united to the body and provides it with sensory organs so that it may be aware of any attempt to destroy it. With every injury that harms it, and at every disturbance <note>original: "disharmony"</note>, the soul feels grief, sadness, and a sense of being altered or constrained. 

This change is called fear. In a state of fear, the nerve fibers <note>original: "fibre"</note> contract and withdraw into themselves; they become hard and resist as if they were numb. Blood is forced out of the arteries, causing the heart to race or palpitate. The <term>animal spirit</term> <note>In historical physiology, "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid or gas that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note> is driven out of the fibers, leaving the muscles without their moving force and the sensory organs without their ability to perceive. A coldness and paleness take over the face and limbs; they shiver and shake. The <term>animus</term> <note>In Swedenborg’s system, the "animus" is the lower, sensory mind—the seat of emotions and physical impulses.</note>, stripped of its desires <note>original: "cupidities"</note>, goes dormant; the mind is filled with the image of death. Thus, fear is a kind of death for the mind and the animus—a foreshadowing of the body's death, as its physical symptoms are clearly visible in the body.

(242.) Since the life of the animus and the life of the mind are fueled by pure loves—that is, by affections—it follows that we are apprehensive, fearful, or full of dread regarding anything that might harm...

<summary>Swedenborg defines spiritual and intellectual poverty as a lack of faith and truth, then analyzes fear as a physical and mental "anticipation of death" that causes the body to contract and the mind to lose its vital energy.</summary>

We also fear any love that serves as a means to, or assists in, such an injury; thus, we fear all things that we believe will bring any deadly harm. To the exact same degree that we love a goal, we fear being deprived of it and dread its total destruction. This same principle applies to the subject who holds that goal, for love cannot exist as a goal unless it resides within some conscious being.

(243.) Thus, all fear is a natural response; it is as intense and of the same character as the love or goal that we desire. There are loves that are innate <note>original: "natural"</note> and those that are learned <note>original: "acquired"</note>. However, whether a love is innate or learned, fear—and a departure from our natural state—accompanies it whenever the danger of its loss or destruction threatens. This "nature" resides in the rational mind, which is the seat of our loves, desires, and goals. Whatever the mind does not perceive, it does not fear; but when it does feel fear, the mind is no longer master of itself or capable of functioning correctly, instead undergoing a kind of paralysis or swoon.

(244.) There are as many types of fear as there are types of love. Everyone naturally fears for their own body, whether they love themselves more than others or others more than themselves. The drive to preserve the connection between the body and the soul is innate in everyone; wherever one thing depends upon another, love exists. 

A person who loves themselves more than others also fears more for their own safety than for the safety of others. On the other hand, someone who truly loves others more than themselves fears more for the safety of others than for their own. Therefore, we can recognize the quality and degree of a person's love by observing what they fear. A person who loves their country more than themselves considers it glorious to die for their nation, or at least for the sake of the fame that is a part of such illustrious glory. Someone who loves their wife and children more than themselves would rather suffer death than see those they love perish. This instinct is also found in animals <note>original: "brutes"</note>, such as does, stags, hens, and geese; for the female boldly...

Those who fear for their reputation for honesty and virtue are magnanimous <note>original: "magnanimous"; meaning great-souled or noble in spirit</note>. From this, it follows that the fear of losing a superior love makes one bold in defending an inferior love. A hero is someone who does not fear the loss of their physical life when their fame is endangered, because they fear the loss of that fame much more. Yet, that same hero—when his fame is not at risk—fears greatly for his own body, so that he may continue to live for the sake of his reputation and for society.

(245.) A person lacks reason if they prefer their physical life over their reputation, or over honesty, virtue, society, country, and the human race. Yet, even more contemptible is the miser who, like a servant to his gold, prefers wealth and similar things to himself and his own life. Though the miser is the most timid of all men, he remains a fearless <note>original: "intrepid"</note> defender of his treasure; the loss of that treasure often leads him to suicide. The most despicable and lowest of all mortals is the one who fears nothing for truth, sacred things, heaven, and God <note>original: "Deity"</note>, but fears only for their own life. 

In this way, our fears reveal the nature of our loves and which love is prioritized over another. The martyrs have testified to what love is and what it means to fear losing the love of God. Souls that are sublime and elevated above mortal things do not fear undergoing death for the sake of truth—especially truth that is celestial and divine—because they fear for the truth itself and dread its extinction. However, our own "truths" (except those that are divinely revealed) are merely principles of the rational mind. To face the danger of death or to die defending these personal beliefs certainly indicates a sublime mind, but it may also indicate an insane one. Historians relate such instances in the martyrdoms of heretics and others.

False bravery secretly conceals fear. Genuine bravery is present during the greatest dangers of life, both in the spirit and the mind, and it is the more present and prudent as the perils are greater. In those moments, a false bravery in the spirit either melts away or becomes a rage, and the person acts insanely like one who has lost his mind; he is beside himself and no longer his own master. Genuine bravery is never united to self-love, but is the inseparable companion of the supreme love of many and of society, with which love it increases. False bravery comes from an opposite principle; for an extreme love of self inspires a desire for the immortality of fame. (248.) Fearlessness <note>original: "Intrepidity"</note>, which is an attribute of fortitude, is not acquired but is inborn. For this reason, it belongs to the race and descends to distant descendants, for the brave beget the brave; it is often a trait belonging naturally to an entire people. For the fearless person does not truly fear the loss or the destruction of that love or goal by which he is led—whether it be for life, for fame, or for country—but he boldly defends these. His <term>animus</term> <note>the seat of emotions and lower passions</note> is roused and inflamed by any insults, and it is more passionate according to his natural bravery. At the same time, he acts more moderately as danger increases, because the fearlessness of true bravery is joined with a presence of mind and emotional stability. He carefully judges the nature of dangers and takes counsel in the heat of the moment, acting either with passion or with prudence, according to the situation and the level of risk. But fear, which is the opposite effect and likewise a natural trait, does not rouse or inflame the <term>animus</term> in the presence of danger, but instead disheartens and extinguishes it.

(249.) Since fear and fearlessness are both natural traits, they are written into the very blood itself, into the spirit of the blood, into the organs, and into the body. It follows that fearlessness shows itself in the face, in the eyes, in the sound of the voice, in the breathing, in the strength of the muscles, and in one's actions. It is especially visible in the arteries of the body and the fibers of the brain, which are stronger and more robust in the fearless than in the timid, since the strength of the whole body lies in the arterial blood and the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>original: "animal spirit"; in pre-modern physiology, these were subtle fluids thought to flow through the nerves to transmit sensation and motion</note>.

A unique divine providence <note>the protective care of God</note> guides such souls because there is something divine within them; it provides them with a life they do not even seek—one that is immortal even while they are among mortals.

(250.) Not all bravery and fearlessness is inborn; there is also a type that is acquired. We can see this in the examples of timid and fearful people who sometimes act bravely—not because of their natural character, but through artificial means, resulting from the state of their blood and changes in their spirits. For instance, intoxicating drinks, certain foods that stimulate the blood <note>original: "aliments of the blood"</note>, and even fevers, mania, or insanity often fill the <term>animus</term> with such energy, lifting the mind into a state of apparent bravery. 

However, this is not true bravery, but rather "courage"—a quality that exists only in the blood and the body, on the surface and in the outermost parts. Meanwhile, fear still lies hidden within, ready to return as soon as the heat of the blood cools. This type of courage actually reinforces our conviction that true bravery and fearlessness are natural gifts. This type of bravery is actually a greater moral virtue, because it does not come to the mind naturally or instinctively. Instead, it arises from a recognition of a truth that the person admires in others but finds impossible in themselves unless they take active steps to achieve it. For whatever the mind does through its own will is either a virtue or a vice; but whatever happens naturally, without the mind's intent, is neither a virtue nor a vice until the mind chooses to participate in the action. Yet, this acquired bravery never equals natural bravery, because it is as inconsistent as the mind itself, which is ruled by shifting principles.

In the discussion that followed, it was also proved that the intelligence or the reason of the mind corresponds to light. Terms such as light, clearness, shade, darkness, and other words applicable to light are therefore applied to the intellect. We have also observed above that ambition may be compared to heat, for love without ambition is like life without heat. 

Furthermore, zeal is to be likened to a kind of fire, for ambition without zeal is like heat without fire. When the zeal—the "fire" of the superior mind—passes over into the rational or inferior mind, it is commonly called ardor <note>original Latin: *excandescentia*, meaning a glowing heat or the beginning of anger</note>. However, when it passes into the animus and from there into the body, it becomes the bodily and impure fire called anger, while the flame itself is called fury. 

From this, it appears that the beginning of ardor, anger, and fury lies in the soul itself and the <term>pure intellectory</term> <note>Swedenborg's term for the highest faculty of the human mind, which perceives universal truths</note>. In other words, these emotions are conceived and born within these higher faculties. Thus, at its proper source, zeal (or "pure fire") is naturally mild and becomes active only when truths—whether natural or spiritual—must be guarded. But it becomes impure as it descends. When the mind grows warm, it defends its principles with a kind of zeal, carried away by the love of those principles as if they were absolute truths, and it attacks anything contrary to them; this is the source of disputes and philosophical contests. 

However, it is clear from the physical effects that this ardor of the mind breaks out into a specific fire or anger in the animus, and eventually into a flame that ignites the whole physical system—that is, into fury. This is manifest in the actual heat and fire felt by the person: the blood burns, the internal organs are heated even to the marrow, the membranes and extremities are inflamed, breathing becomes harsh, and the sound of the voice hardens (just as air reacts when heated). The arteries swell like the atmosphere does when heated, and both the internal and external senses are disturbed, as though some fire had shaken them from their natural equilibrium into a turmoil of motion. Also...

<summary>Swedenborg explains that anger and fury are physical degradations of a "pure fire" or zeal that originates in the soul to protect truth. He details the physiological transformation of this spiritual energy as it moves from the higher mind into the blood and organs.</summary>

By its grains or hard particles, the lighter and softer blood is excited into a similar rage, as if by external stimulants. In this way, not even the smallest part of the body is without its share of anger or heat.

(253.) Therefore, zeal is a natural emotion <note>original: "affection"</note> endowed to the superior mind—the soul—and the <term>pure intellectory</term> <note>Swedenborg’s term for the highest faculty of the human mind, which perceives universal truths naturally and perfectly</note>. It exists, it would appear, so that the soul may guard its spiritual truths and the intellectory its natural truths. It allows them to oppose the falsehoods that contradict these truths with increased heat, or even with fire. For when there is a conflict between truth and falsehood, or good and evil—and when both sides possess a force of acting or a life—it is necessary for there to be a zeal or heat that rises to the "fire" of action so that the enemies may be engaged. This is the reason why zeal is attributed to spiritual beings and even to the Deity <note>God</note> himself, who is described in scripture as being moved by wrath or anger. It is also why, when any person is heated and angered, they justify it as a legitimate zeal for the truth or for the defense of a just cause. There would be no such emotion unless there were an enemy; therefore, anger is the visible proof that in the spiritual and invisible world, there is some evil that must be fought.

(254.) But our rational mind, which views its own principles as if they were absolute truths, is also said to be ignited with a certain zeal. However, because the very principles of our human reason are rarely based on actual truths, this zeal is also rarely a pure one. The wrathful ignition originating in the rational mind is harsh and vehement, like glowing charcoal <note>original: "ignited carbon"</note> which is eventually consumed by its own fire. Whether this fire is pure or impure may be known from the underlying love and from the specific emotions and desires of the mind—especially from ambition, which is a form of heat that most immediately triggers this fire. As is the quality of the love or the ambition, so is the quality of the zeal or the ignition of the mind.

(256.) But indignation belongs only to the rational mind and is the first stage of angry heat. There are, nevertheless, many elements within indignation that moderate, temper, and restrain it, preventing it from breaking out; for there is either fear, or some love, or shame, or sadness, which act as reins and barriers to hold it in check.

### *Patience; Gentleness; Tranquility of Mind; Impatience.*

(257.) From anger, we may understand the nature and quality of patience, for where patience exists, anger does not. Indeed, just as anger may be compared to a certain fire and flame, patience may be compared to a kind of cold. As anger is compared to hardness (for its elements are hardened by fire as if they were bronze), so patience is compared to softness. As anger represents the highest degree of activity, so patience represents passivity—which is the source of the name itself <note>The word "patience" is derived from the Latin *pati*, meaning to suffer or endure.</note>. Therefore, patience is a tranquil, serene state of the mind, which is, as it were, free from the storms and commotions of the emotions <note>original: "affections of the animus"</note>.

(258.) Like anger, patience is also "written" in the body; a mild and patient quality shines forth from the face, from the very sound of the voice, and—as far as it relates to the mind—from conversation as well. The face is serene and smiling, even while others are burning with rage. The blood is softer, healthier, and warm but not burning; it is full of vital heat but not clotted <note>original: "concreted"</note> into fibers. The pulse is lighter and more steady, the bile is not dark but more yellow in color, the arteries are more flexible, the fibers are tender, and the...

(259.) Patience—insofar as it is the tranquil and serene state of the mind, free from disturbance by the emotions of the animus—is itself the most perfect state. In this state, the mind is left to itself and has time for its own operations. It considers its reasons more deeply and forms its judgments more honestly <note>original: "sincerely"</note>. Out of these, it selects what is truer, better, and more fitting, and passes them into its will, which is then not possessed by the chaos of natural desires. 

Thus enjoying an almost perfect liberty, the mind holds the animus subject to itself as if in chains, and does not permit it to wander beyond the limits of its own choice. In this way, it also commands the actions of its body and receives and contemplates its sensations more purely and intelligently. When the mind is thus left to itself, and neither physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> nor worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> things—nor the heat arising from them—disturb its ease, it enjoys the inmost fellowship with its pure intellectory <term>intellectory</term> <note>Swedenborg’s term for the soul’s immediate faculty of pure, wordless understanding.</note> or the soul, and allows natural and spiritual truths to flow in. Indeed, it is only the physical affections and desires of the animus which obscure and pervert the intellectual ideas of the mind. 

This is why the mind, in its state of patience or tranquility, is "cold" in its constitution compared with the heat of the animus and the body, yet it is very full of love—that is, of a more pure and perfect life. For a mind to exist at all, it must be warmed with a certain love; the purer this love is, the purer is the mind, because the life itself is better. From this state, the mind regards lower loves and those that are purely physical as child's play <note>original: "infantile sports"</note> or as insanity—and the more so when those lower loves are believed to be...

(261.) The nature of impatience may be inferred from this description of patience. Impatience belongs to the rational mind when it desires certain goals <note>original: "ends"</note>, but those goals are hindered or blocked by obstacles or the thought that they are impossible. These obstacles act as resistances that prevent the will from breaking out into action. Consequently, the desiring animus is tortured, the body is distressed, and the mind regards every single moment as a long delay. Thus, the more passionate <note>original: "ardent"</note> the animus is, the greater the impatience; the more tranquil the mind is, the less impatience there will be. Impatience is least present in those who entrust their fortunes to **Divine Providence.**

### *Shame.*

(262.) In shame, both the internal and external sensory organs <note>The "internal sensory" refers to the mind’s internal perception or imagination, while the "external sensory" refers to the five physical senses.</note>, as well as individual fibers and arteries, contract. This happens because the state of the fibers and arteries always mirrors the state of the sensory organs. Consequently, the animal spirit <note>original: "spirit"; in Swedenborg’s physiology, "animal spirit" is a highly refined fluid that flows through the nerves to transmit signals.</note> is driven from the nerve fibers into the motor fibers of the arteries, and blood is pushed from the larger arteries into the capillaries. This results in a redness and flushing of the face, a lowering of the eyes, a desire to hide, a numbing of the senses, and a cessation of breathing and of the acts of the will—essentially, a state of inaction. Because the sensory organ itself is compressed, it does not dare, so to speak, to assert itself; instead, it withdraws so that the mind may hide, not only from others but from itself. This is self-shame, occurring whenever the mind is conscious of anything improper, dishonest, or criminal. Therefore, when no one but the mind itself is aware of a fault, a person is rarely ashamed, unless they worry that someone else might find out. Accordingly, even without committing a crime, the mind may be overcome with shame simply by reflecting on the possibility of a fault occurring, or on something it alone has noticed. Shame affects both the bold and the fearful alike; in the bold, the face blushes, but in the fearful, it turns pale, because the fear of some injury or loss follows. Shame also causes the facial muscles to slacken, so that they are left without any directing force, like a pendulum that has stopped swinging.

(263.) There is another difference between fear and shame: fear causes the internal and external sensory systems to become lifeless and lose awareness of themselves, but shame—by its own choice and through an inherent force—contracts its sensory organ and takes away its ability to change its state. For this reason, in that moment before the mind recovers itself, all willpower ceases, and there follows a blank state or a forgetfulness of specific details.

This is because there are those who do not distinguish well between decorum and honor, and therefore are affected by the shame of both. But since honor expresses itself through decorum—as decorum is the external manifestation of honor—we are careful to observe the laws of both. 

Shame is greater in the presence of superiors than of equals, and there is none in the presence of inferiors unless the mind is a great lover of honor. Shame is also greater in the presence of those we love and revere; but when the love is mutual and pure love replaces reverence, there is, as it were, another self. In that case, shame is no different than what one feels when alone. A truly sublime mind feels shame even when no one else is present—proof that it is guided by reverence toward truth, honesty, justice, and the other virtues, and regards these virtues as its own superiors.

(265.) There is little or no shame in those who scorn and are averse to virtue itself, and who regard no one as their superior; the same is true for the foolish and the slow-witted. Therefore, the lowest of men—those without conscience and without a love of honor—are those who feel no shame. They possess the most criminal intentions, and even when faced with crimes they know they have committed or are about to commit, they stand with open and lifted eyes <note>Meaning they show no physical signs of remorse or the "downcast" look typically associated with shame.</note>, showing no spark of the higher mind within.

(266.) But because principles regarding honor and decorum vary somewhat, the sense of shame also varies; one person may not be affected by the same things as another, and thus these feelings of shame occur in different ways. We are even affected by the shame of people we do not know; this happens because their situation is reflected from them onto ourselves.

<summary>Swedenborg explores how shame stems from a love of honor and virtue, noting that it varies based on social hierarchy and is notably absent in those lacking conscience or intelligence. He also describes "vicarious shame," where we feel embarrassed for others through a process of reflection.</summary>

### *Envy.*

(267.) Envy is hatred mixed with anger, but the anger stays hidden like fire under ashes. Therefore, it is an internal, consuming heat that causes insanity when it erupts. Because of this, the blood is saturated and heavy with bile; it is thick, speckled, dark in color, and stagnant in the smallest pores, which causes a bluish tint in the face. This same fire also consumes and withers the body, leading to thinness <note>original: "leanness"; Swedenborg is referring to the physical wasting away often associated with chronic stress or bitter emotions.</note>. The gallbladder is crowded with black bile <note>In traditional medicine, "black bile" was one of the four humors, thought to cause melancholy and bitterness when in excess.</note> because it is constantly being produced and mixed into the blood. There is also a darkness in the face; hatred mixed with anger shines from the eyes, where there is no light of joy. Even in the voice and speech, a certain harshness is felt. The emotional soul <note>original: "animus"; Swedenborg uses this term to refer to the lower, sensory part of the mind where passions and worldly desires reside.</note> is always gloomy, and the mind is sad; it is rarely lightened or cheered, for it feels nothing of the sweetness of harmony. The very state of the mind is in discord; therefore, it perversely loves disharmony as if it were harmony. Because of this, the misfortunes, poverty, and miseries of others are what comfort and satisfy it. It does not even rejoice in its own good fortune or happiness unless there is some element of revenge hidden within it.

(268.) Specific envy <note>original: "Particular envy"</note> is common to everyone and is quite natural, as it is found even in small children and in wild animals and their offspring. For example, we envy in another person the very thing we ourselves love—such as a lover envying a rival's bride, or a competitor envying the honor of a rival. In these cases, envy never goes beyond the boundaries of what we specifically love and desire.

But a general envy arises from an extreme self-love. It envies all people, all things, and every individual object. It imagines the universe belongs to it alone, seeing itself as the whole rather than just a part. It envies others—

### *Revenge.*

(270.) Revenge flows from hatred and envy. Hatred is indeed the opposite of love, but it is not the total absence of love and, consequently, of life. Rather, it is a "contrary love"—specifically, a love of what is evil. Just as there is a love for what is good, there is a love for what is evil. One is the opposite of the other; therefore, one hates the other. Because of this, there is a kind of "life" within hatred, and where there is life, there is also heat and fire—though a kind that is coarser, more impure, and therefore natural and physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>. It resides in the <term>animus</term> <note>In Swedenborg’s philosophy, the "animus" refers to the lower, sensory soul—the seat of passions and worldly desires—as distinct from the higher, rational "mind."</note> rather than the rational mind, unless the mind is joined with the body's lower passions. This heat of hatred is called the "lust for revenge." If anger follows—such as the anger found in envy—it then becomes a fire and acts as vengeance. Thus, the lust for revenge is the actual fire, the driving force <note>original: "active principle"</note>, or the highest level of activity within hatred or the love of evil.

(271.) Just as envy can be specific or general, so too are revenge and the desire for it. Specific envy is natural to everyone and takes the form of a desire for revenge. Because of this, it is innate in young children before they reach the age of reason, and even in certain animals that are naturally equipped with weapons to defend themselves against harm. Since revenge is natural, it is also naturally satisfying, as it clears a sorrowful mind and a clouded <term>animus</term>. It refreshes and restores them to their natural state by dispersing hatred and extinguishing envy. The pleasure found in revenge is proportional to the intensity of the hatred and specific envy that existed before it. However, the desire for revenge is mostly accompanied by sadness, unless the mind sees the possibility of obtaining its...

(272.) The general desire for revenge is similar to general envy, for it arises from the same source, and thus both share similar qualities. Envy is always joined with a false <note>original: "spurious"</note> ambition or with the love of self. Such is the nature of divine vengeance: the greater the love, the greater the desire to avenge evil, since love encourages everything to be like itself and to be united with itself. Therefore, love hates and devours whatever separates it from or hinders its possession of the desired good, and it eagerly seeks to destroy it. This is often accompanied by anxiety, grief, and unhappiness in the person experiencing it.

### *Misanthropy; Love of Solitude.*

(273.) Misanthropy is strictly the hatred of the human race, or it stems from such a universal hatred. It rarely arises from envy or from hatred mixed with anger, since those emotions breathe a spirit of revenge, which assumes a life spent in society. Misanthropy is joined with contempt, or a loss of sensitivity to the pleasures of the body or the delights of the <term>animus</term>. There are misanthropes who do not appear to be so because they possess an <term>animus</term> that craves pleasures which can only be enjoyed in the company of others and in social or civic life. There are also those who, because they value their reputation, are unwilling to appear as misanthropes; however, once this desire and love of fame cease, they reveal themselves as such. For the most part, they are extremely devoted to self-love. This vice is very natural and innate, for it sometimes arises from the failure...

In society, the misanthrope is seen as a non-entity or as a wretched person <note>original: "an abject"</note>, a reputation he deserves because his hatred separates him from everyone. (274.) There are specific and particular types of misanthropes—namely, those who feel an aversion or hatred toward a specific race, nation, family, or certain individuals. If this comes from hatred and its causes, or from aversion (especially a natural aversion), it is called **antipathy**. If it is acquired, it stems from a perceived or real difference <note>original: "dissimilitude"</note> in principles and loves. This can also turn into an antipathy that persists in one's descendants <note>original: "posterity"</note>.

(275.) The love of solitude is commonly mistaken for misanthropy because the misanthrope enjoys being alone. However, the love of solitude can originate from many other causes. It arises naturally from melancholy, which is sometimes a curable disease; in that state, the person deeply desires to indulge their fantasies <note>original: "phantasies"; in this context, inward imaginings or delusions</note>, even extending them so far that they become absorbed in specific things—if not physically, then in thought. 

A person who is devoted to studies, especially theoretical ones, also loves to be alone. He chooses solitude so the mind will not be disturbed, loving his studies and his solitude equally. For the mind to be at rest, it must be separated, as it were, from those things that excite the <term>animus</term> <note>In Swedenborg’s system, the "animus" is the lower, sensory soul—the seat of emotions, passions, and worldly desires—as opposed to the higher, rational "mind."</note>, the sensations of the body, and the other affections <note>original: "loves"</note> of the mind. Someone who thinks everything is mere vanity—while believing himself alone not to be vain—is also typically solitary. Alternatively, he may desire to be safe from the world's vanities and therefore separates himself from society. ### *Cruelty.*

(276.) Cruelty, in general, is the desire to destroy <note>original: "extirpating"</note> the human race, finding its highest pleasure in people’s distress, grief, and pain. It arises from hatred, general misanthropy, and an extreme degree of self-love. For the person possessed by this love views himself alone as the center of the universe, and sees all those around him as obstacles because he cannot exist in isolation. This love also arises from an intense love of the world, or perhaps of status <note>original: "honours"</note>, or from an extreme love of material things—namely, riches—and thus from a general sense of envy. It is the direct opposite of pity. The nature of cruelty reveals itself in a person’s face; it shows whether the cruelty comes from self-love, love of the world, or love of material wealth, manifesting as hatred or envy toward those who possess what the cruel person desires for themselves alone. This is why cruelty is often hidden behind a very respectable <note>original: "honest"</note> face; however, if it is acted upon, it is likely to transform into the appearance of hatred and revenge, and ultimately end in madness.

(277.) In all revenge there is cruelty, for the person who seeks revenge wants the one he hates to be tortured in mind and body, in proportion to the intensity of his hatred. However, the "vengeance" that arises from moral passion <note>original: "zeal"</note> and righteous indignation seeks to cause pain only as a means of rooting out evil, while love for the person remains unchanged throughout. The cruelty is the same whether it flows from one's own

Therefore, as the vengeance is, so is the cruelty; as the hatred is, so is the vengeance; and as the anger and intensity <note>original: "zeal"</note> are in that vengeance, such is the pleasure derived from it.

(278.) There is a certain correspondence between sexual love <note>original: "venereal love"</note> and cruelty—that is, between the love of procreating and the love of destroying <note>original: "extirpating"</note> the human race. They are opposites in their essence, but they share similar observable effects. This happens because opposites often meet at a shared point <note>original: "third term"</note>; otherwise, the circular relationship between them could not exist. Both of these types of "love" stimulate the sensory organs, the nerves <note>original: "fibres"</note>, and the reproductive organs, and both produce the reproductive fluid <note>original: "generative substance"</note>, as is known from natural history. From this, it appears that the feeling of cruelty is as pleasurable to distorted minds as sexual love is to pure minds, for the one does not cancel out the other but rather excites it. Such a person would be like a Devil clothed in human form.

### *Clemency.*

(279.) Clemency is the queen and, so to speak, the goddess of virtues. Therefore, to be clement is to be not only regal but divine, as a king who shows mercy mirrors the Deity. For true clemency is free from hatred, self-love, envy, vengeance, anger, and cruelty; it is free from any naturally harmful emotion <note>original: "unpleasant affection"</note>. It is always joined with love toward those to whom the mercy is shown, and is thus united with a peaceful <term>animus</term> <note>Swedenborg uses "animus" to refer to the lower, sensitive soul or the seat of the emotions and passions, as opposed to the higher rational mind.</note>, happiness of mind, and pity. Love is always merciful. Through clemency, the quality of a person's love may be known, as well as to whom that love is extended. If it is the love of truth, then clemency is joined with justice; if it is the love of honor and virtue...

### *Intemperance and Luxury*

(281.) Generally speaking, intemperance refers to any excess in the desires of the rational mind, the lusts of the lower mind <term>animus: the lower, sensory soul that experiences emotions and passions.</term>, the delights and pleasures of the body, and the material goods of the earth. More specifically, however, intemperance refers to overindulgence in eating and drinking—what we call indulging one’s appetite, "sacrificing to Bacchus and Ceres" <note>original: "sacrificing to Bacchus and Ceres"; refers to the Roman gods of wine and grain, symbolizing drunkenness and gluttony.</note>, and living only for the belly. Every form of love and pleasure exists for a purpose: so that we may live a healthy life in a healthy body. Therefore, the earth provides an abundance of everything we need to enjoy these loves and pleasures, provided they are treated as means to an end and not as the ends themselves. When we view specific loves and pleasures as means, we enjoy each of them in a temperate way that helps us achieve our higher purpose. But when we view these as the ultimate goals rather than the means, we fall into excess; the more passionately we love the goal, the more intensely we overindulge.

(282.) Thus, intemperance signifies a distorted state of mind—one that is very limited and materialistic—which, in short, restricts its goals to very narrow limits. In contrast, a more elevated mind perceives that one thing exists for the sake of another, and that there is a chain of means leading toward a most universal...

(283.) There is nothing in our entire body which is not a means to some higher end. The final goal <note>original: "last end"</note> is the soul, for the sake of which the body exists. We do not stop at anything short of the very God <note>original: "Deity"</note> of the universe, who is the beginning and the end of all things.

(284.) Therefore, since there is nothing that is not an intermediate goal, it follows that intemperance can exist in any "means" that are wrongly treated as "ends" in themselves. Anyone can judge the lack or excess of these emotions based on their descriptions.

(285.) This alone needs to be said: all intemperance is contrary to nature, and whatever does violence to nature destroys either our rational mind, our lower mind, or our body. Thus, when these are ruled by the will, and the will is ruled by desire, and desire is ruled by self-serving loves—treating these as final goals rather than means—we rush into many causes of destruction, which leads to the death of the body.

(286.) But virtues, honesty, perfection, and spiritual happiness can never be desired or loved intemperately. In the body, we will never be able to reach perfection itself, as the infinite will always remain beyond us. However, "spiritual intemperance" would be to desire a perfection greater than one's own nature allows; for example, acting as if the mind could become like the soul, or the soul like God, instead of being perfect within its own level <note>original: "degree"</note> and thus serving as an image, type, and likeness of higher things.

### *Temperance; Parsimony; Frugality.*

(288.) We learn what temperance is from the description of intemperance: namely, that it is a moderate use of the delights and pleasures of the body so that these may serve as appropriate and proportionate means to higher ends. Thus, while intemperance properly signifies excess, it also involves a deficiency. A deficiency in one area does not exist without an excess in another; for example, a failure to nourish the body indicates an excessive stinginess <note>original: "economy"</note>. Furthermore, there is an excess of greed <note>original: "avarice"</note> or of abstinence which is equally injurious to the body. 

Therefore, moderation in all things is temperance itself, but it is known by other names depending on the subject. For instance, "temperance" specifically denotes moderation in eating and drinking; "parsimony" refers to moderation in spending wealth and earthly goods; while "frugality" relates to domestic management. This applies to other things as well. Meanwhile, because temperance is a natural middle ground <note>original: "mediocrity," referring to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean" rather than being "average."</note>, it is defined according to each person's nature; therefore, the temperance of one person might be the intemperance of another, and so on. Consequently, temperance is the standard and the balance of all the affections of the rational mind, the lower mind <term>animus</term>, and the body which we have discussed so far. It is the preserver of all things, ensuring a sound mind in a sound body <note>original: "mens sana in corpore sano"</note>.

*In a word, explore so that you may understand what is true and what is good; regard all things as intermediate ends <note>original: "mediate ends"</note> through which you may arrive at the ultimate goal by continually asking: "For what purpose?"*

<summary>Swedenborg defines temperance as the "natural middle ground" that maintains harmony between the mind and body, distinguishing it from parsimony and frugality while labeling all excess as vice.</summary>

## XV.

### CONCERNING THE LOWER MIND <term>animus: the lower, sensory soul or "animal spirit" that experiences emotions and passions.</term> AND THE RATIONAL MIND <term>mens: the higher, intellectual mind capable of reason.</term>.

(289.) **Nothing is more difficult in the science of rational psychology than to clearly understand—and, once understood, to clearly explain—what is properly the lower mind <note>original: "animus"</note> and what is properly the rational mind <note>original: "mens"</note>;** for the various things that act within our internal sensory organs appear like a small chaos. We cannot see even its surface clearly, let alone its individual parts, which are linked together like a chain. 

This may be compared in some measure to a microscopic organism <note>original: "animalcule"</note> which we can barely see even with the aid of a microscope. We know it is a living thing only by its motion, yet we do not doubt that its tiny internal organs <note>original: "viscera"</note> are distinctly formed and separate. We assume it possesses a brain, a spinal cord <note>original: "medulla spinalis"</note>, lungs, a stomach, intestines, muscles, and sensory organs, since the eye has detected these in similar microscopic creatures through the science of optics <note>original: "optic art"</note>. 

However, where our sight can barely graze the surface, it is very difficult to guess at the interior and more hidden things; such is the case with our internal sensory faculty. Through self-reflection, we are able to discover that we perceive, understand, think, choose, desire, and will, and that we are determined to act. We see that these are clusters of loves, cravings <note>original: "cupidities"</note>, desires, pleasures, and goals <note>original: "ends"</note>. Because these all belong to a single sensory organ and appear to be continuous and united, it is only with the greatest difficulty that they can be separately unfolded <note>original: "evolved"</note> so that the ideas of our own intellect may be clearly presented to the intellect of another. For who can see in the dark the intricate skill of the

He uses the analogy of a microscopic organism to illustrate how complex internal structures exist even when they appear as a single, chaotic whole to the observer.</summary>

However, the philosophers distinguished between the lower mind <note>original: *animus*</note> and the rational mind <note>original: *mens*</note>. But to discover what each one is, how they differ, and how they are joined, we must use tireless reflection and intellectual observation. We should examine their various functions <note>original: "operations"</note> one by one in their proper order. After completing this work, we must frequently revisit these parts to examine the "chain" that binds them together. The structure of our mind is no different from the internal form of the body: we can only understand what it is through its functions—by "anatomically" laying bare one part after another to explore and inspect it from within. Such an "anatomy of the mind" is required. In this way, we are taught what we are by looking at ourselves; the mind must be investigated by the mind itself. The mind acts so scientifically on its own that all the philosophical sciences combined have gathered barely a fraction of the knowledge concerning it. But let us move on and ask: What is the lower mind <note>original: *animus*</note>, and what is the rational mind <note>original: *mens*</note>?

Insofar as it is the <term>sensory</term> itself that is affected, that sensory center is, regarding its emotional state, the <term>animus</term>. Therefore, perception is a distinct thing from affection, and yet both belong to the brain.

(296.) Thus, it is the common <term>sensory</term> that is affected pleasantly or unpleasantly, delightfully or undelightfully. This results in the feelings—and thus the joy, the sadness, or any other <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passion"; here meaning an intense emotion or a state of being acted upon</note>—which are attributed to the <term>animus</term> alone. Properly speaking, it is the joy or the sadness itself, flowing from the grace, harmony, or disharmony of the patterns felt and perceived, which is called the "external affection" of the <term>animus</term>; however, there is also an "internal affection." 

The <term>animus</term> is also the principle or source of all the changes in the body. The affection of the <term>sensory</term> (or of a single part of the <term>cortical substance</term> <note>the gray matter of the brain</note>) is transmitted into the containing <term>fibers</term> <note>nerves</note>, and through them into the whole body, which is composed entirely of <term>fibers</term>. Thus, "passion"—that is, affection—is attributed to the mind, as is "action"—the beginning or source of physical movement.

(297.) But because one person's mind is not exactly like another's—and what affects one person pleasantly affects another unpleasantly, so that the same harmony of sound or visual form makes one person happy and another sad—it follows that the state of one person's <term>sensory</term> is different from that of another. This is because the affection depends on the state of the <term>sensory</term> organ. The same operation performed upon two different subjects varies according to the state of the recipient or the person being affected. Because the <term>animus</term> rejoices, saddens, desires, becomes angry, and decides to act—and thus has life within it—it must be that in the common <term>sensory</term> and in the individual tiny <term>sensories</term> there is...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the "animus" (emotional mind) is physically located in the brain's sensory centers, where it transforms raw data into emotional responses like joy or sadness. He also suggests that because everyone's physical brain state is unique, people react differently to the same sensory experiences.</summary>

...that which lives. Therefore, we must investigate where the <term>animus</term> <note>the seat of emotions and lower desires</note> derives its essence and its life.

(298.) To better understand what the *animus* is, let us use examples. In the sense of taste, something <term>flavorful</term> <note>original: "saporiferous"</note> is perceived by the common <term>sensory</term> <note>the physical center of the brain that integrates sensations</note> as sweet, bitter, or acidic. However, this perception does not go any further; even the physical pleasure felt is part of that same sense, acting as a kind of general taste. Yet, from this, an appetite is excited—specifically for things that suit the state of the body. We see this in animals, which use taste alone to seek out things that agree with their nature. This faculty of appetite is what belongs to the *animus*.

The same is true for the sense of smell. In the sounds we hear, this distinction is even more evident. The common sensory perceives the modulations of a song, the specific differences in sounds, and even harmony and grace themselves—all of which constitute a general sensation. But the <term>cheerfulness</term> <note>original: "hilarity"</note> and joy, and the <term>affections</term> <note>emotional states or being "moved" by an experience</note> of every kind of love that arise from them, belong to the *animus*. 

Likewise, regarding the objects of sight: the eye and the common sensory perceive pleasant gardens, specific flowers like roses, and orchards, as well as the beauty created by their orderly arrangement. However, the deep delights that arise from them—the love felt when viewing the beautiful, or the revenge, fear, and anger felt at the sight of an enemy, or the pity felt at the sight of the suffering—these belong to the *animus*. The *animus* is carried away into these various emotions, and from these into desires that are then communicated to the body.

From these examples, we see how difficult it is to clearly distinguish between what the *animus* is and what perception is, for each has its own distinct nature. There are as many different types of perception as there are sensations, which are innumerable. Similarly, there are as many types of *animus* states <note>original Latin: *animi*</note> as there are emotions, each of which...

(300.) It is just as difficult to understand what the mind is, even though the word is used constantly in everyday speech. The fact that we use this word so appropriately in conversation suggests that our rational mind knows exactly what it is, even if we are consciously ignorant of its nature.* We should investigate the mind just as we would ask an anatomist what is inside the heart and arteries when he knows from the pulse that there is a source for the heartbeat. If we do not define it as the "form of forms," it would be better to simply say "the mind is the mind," or that there is a certain quality even more hidden than the mind that we call "form." After all, "principle" is a general term like "force" or "cause," which can be applied to anything.
