...immaterial ideas, just as the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; the lower mind associated with emotions and physical urges</note> results from ideas that are not immaterial. By saying this, something is expressed that brings us closer to a knowledge of the mind. However, to truly perceive it, we must investigate the source itself. We must trace it from its "streams," and trace those streams from the things derived from them—things that either appear before our senses as effects or have some analogy with physical things.

(301.) Therefore, to explore what the mind or the higher animus is, we must proceed in the same way we did when exploring the lower animus and its physical substance; we must seek out that "internal sensory" where the mind resides. It is beyond any doubt that the mind is in the brain. The state of the mind is the state of the brain; they are so united that whenever one is injured, weakened, or seems about to die, the other is affected equally. 

It should be kept in mind that the external senses travel through their containing fibers all the way to their starting points: the <term>cortical glandules</term> <note>original: "cortical glandules"; the tiny functional units of the brain's gray matter</note>. The principle found in the senses must surely reside within these glands. It has been frequently shown above that this glandule is the brain in miniature. Within it, there is a <term>medullary</term> <note>inner "white matter" substance</note> and cortical substance similar and analogous to what is seen in the brain as a whole. Therefore, we have called this small body the "internal sensory," and we have observed that these little sensories taken together constitute the "common sensory" <note>the brain's overall center for processing sensory information</note>. 

Accordingly, if there is a similar analogous cortical substance in each of these little sensories, it follows that this substance, taken as a whole, is the internal sensory itself. Each of its smallest cortical parts is an <term>intellectory</term> <note>a term coined by the author for the organ of the intellect</note> in which, we will assume, the <term>pure intellect</term> <note>a level of understanding that operates above conscious reasoning</note> resides; we will discuss this further later on.

From this idea, through simple comparison and analogy, we can understand the nature and quality of the higher animus or the mind. Let us now establish that comparative analogy.

Sensations of sight can be particularly compared to the ideas found in imagination or thought, for they correspond to one another. Through practice and experience, visual images transition into similar ideas; thus, intellectual ideas take the place of visual images. We can proceed with these ideas in the same way we did with the sensations described previously—the ones we used to investigate the origin of the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; the lower mind, driven by emotions and physical senses</note>. By doing so, we will discover the mind itself.

(302.) A vast number of ideas—which we might call "immaterial images," to use a simple term—are impressed upon the internal <term>sensory</term> <note>original: "sensory"; the specialized organ or center in the brain that receives and processes sensations</note> itself. These ideas are the images of memory and imagination, which are formed and drawn out by the changes in the state of the sensory organ. These immaterial or rational ideas are perceived in the "pure intellect," or in that simplest <term>cortex</term> <note>original: "cortex"; here referring to the most refined parts of the brain's gray matter</note>, in the same way that visual images are perceived in the common or external sensory.

Consequently, these ideas are like internal sensations, each with its own unique characteristics. Ideas understood this way constitute the mind, but specifically its intellect or its thought. That good and lovable affection which results from the harmony of these ideas, or from thought itself, is what we say flows from the mind. Consequently, it is the mind that is affected; the mind is the very life within the animus, and it is the starting point or origin of all the animus's changes.

(303.) Even so, we are still uncertain as to what the mind actually is. When the mind is called "life" and a "principle," it is rationally conceived as a certain quality flowing from the form of its <term>intellectory</term> <note>original: "intellectory"; a term Swedenborg uses for the organic unit or physical-spiritual structure where rational thought occurs</note> when it is affected. [Conse]quently, it is the life of the mind itself. This life remains so deeply hidden or dwells so far within that it is separated from the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; the lower mind, driven by emotions and physical senses</note> by several degrees of perfection. By describing the soul, we come to understand this mind—its nature, its quality, its form, and its guiding principle.

(304.) There are, therefore, a superior mind and an inferior mind (the latter being the "mind properly so called"), which govern the living body and communicate their activities to one another. The "mind properly so called" is spiritual; in contrast, the *animus* is purely natural. The *animus* may even be called <term>corporeal</term> <note>original: "corporeal"; relating to the physical body</note> because it is directly affected by the harmonies of the physical senses and directly influences our facial expressions and our physical actions. This is why some ancient philosophers called the *animus* "immortal"—they actually meant the "mind," as can be seen when their language is correctly interpreted.

(305.) To allow the "mind properly so called" to communicate with the *animus*, and through the *animus* with the body, an intermediate mind intervenes called the **rational mind**. This is our distinctively human mind—the part of us that is affected by things, and which feels desires and wishes, and finally turns those desires into actions. 

Many people have believed that this rational mind is the superior—or even the supreme—mind within us, and they often confuse this supreme mind with thought itself. However, it is clear from the details we have already discussed (and from those that follow) that this is not the case. The rational mind cannot provide its own essence or life; instead, it develops through culture, knowledge, and the arts. In the course of time, it grows so much that it contains more within itself than all the sciences in the universe could ever fully explain. The rational mind does not get these qualities solely from culture and experience, nor can it create them on its own. There must be a superior mind that flows into it. This superior mind is pure and spiritual, possessing within itself all those qualities that we admire as superior in...

...that mind, and from which we draw forth only a few drops so that we may conceive and develop our theoretical and psychological sciences.

(306.) However, this mind which is called the **rational mind** is not properly "the mind" itself, for it is an intermediate between the [spiritual] mind and the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; the lower mind driven by emotions and physical sensations</note>. It participates in both and is thus born of both. A spiritual mind flows into it from above, and a natural mind (or the animus) flows into it from below. This is the reason why it is called "rational"; for in order to be rational, it must participate in both the natural and the spiritual realms. Thus, the more it communicates with the spiritual mind, the more excellently rational or the more spiritual this mind becomes. Conversely, the more it derives from the animus or natural mind, the less rational or more <term>corporeal</term> <note>original: "corporeal"; relating to the physical body and its material desires</note> it is. Accordingly, the superior mind and the animus meet and, conjoined in the <term>internal sensory</term> <note>original: "internal sensory"; the inner faculty of perception where the soul meets the senses</note>, they produce their shared offspring.

This is also apparent from various <term>affections</term> <note>original: "affections"; here meaning emotions, impulses, or states of mind</note>. While the rational mind is excited by the animus—through anger, revenge, forbidden love, and other impulses—it does not immediately descend to take part in them. Instead, it is held back by a certain higher and purer mind. Consequently, it is [reluctantly] led away by the animus into either commanding those things which are opposed to its higher nature or favoring them with its consent. 

This deliberation and pondering could never exist unless the rational mind were positioned in the middle, between two loves that sometimes oppose one another. It is, therefore, like the beam of a balance scale, turning whichever way the greater weight draws it. To this mind may be ascribed the <term>intellect</term>—that is, thought—as well as judgment, choice, and will. However, intellect cannot be attributed to the mind in any other way than the perception of sensations is attributed to the animus. It may be that the mind is the life itself of the intellect, or that thought could not exist and persist without its mind—that is, without the loves and desires which not only excite but also <term>vivify</term> <note>original: "vivify"; to give life to or animate</note> its intellect. *The mind is therefore the life of the thoughts, as the animus is the life of the sensations.*

## XVI.

### ON THE FORMATION AND THE AFFECTIONS OF THE RATIONAL MIND.

(307.) We have already discussed the <term>affections</term> <note>original: "affections"; in this context, the word refers to emotions, desires, or mental states that move a person to action</note> of the *animus*. Before we discuss the affections of the rational mind—which is, so to speak, the middle ground and the center where different forces meet—we ought to discuss the affections or "loves" of the pure or superior mind. However, to treat the loves of the supreme mind immediately would be to leap from the lowest level to the highest. It would take us from things perceived by the senses to things that are beyond our intellectual grasp and which cannot be described with adequate terms. On the other hand, the things found in the rational mind do fall within the reach of our intellect because they belong to us. Yet, even these would by no means be understood by our intellect if there were not a purer intellect or a more sublime mind flowing into it. It is from this higher mind that we are able to view the things in the rational mind as if looking down from above.

(308.) It cannot be described as anything other than the shared essence of the two, or a single nature composed of both. ...In what sense it can be called an essence of its own remains to be seen later. However, some preliminary consideration is necessary here.

(309.) Experience and reflection make it sufficiently clear that our rational mind possesses desires. Desires cannot exist without <term>affections</term> <note>original: "affections"; here meaning the emotional or spiritual states that draw the mind toward something</note> or loves; for we love what we desire, and we desire what we love in proportion to the intensity of that love. These desires in the rational mind are called <term>cupidities</term> <note>original: "cupidities"; the word refers to lower, bodily cravings or irrational passions</note> in the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; the lower, sensory-driven mind shared by humans and animals</note>, which cannot exist without bodily affections or loves. It is also clear that we are able to choose what is best and reject what is bad—in other words, that our rational mind is able to judge freely and act according to its own judgments. If these loves did not belong to the rational mind itself, but instead only flowed in from elsewhere and forced the mind to judge and act, then the mind would have no ownership of its actions, and nothing about it could be called "free." However, the very existence of free choice demonstrates that the rational mind sits in the middle, between the different loves that flow into it, and acts as an umpire in choosing the best path. It is also clear that there would be no "will" unless the mind possessed certain affections that allowed it to prefer one thing over another. Without this capacity, there would only be cupidity or instinct in the place of will, as there is in <term>brute animals</term> <note>original: "brute animals"; a common historical term for non-human animals, emphasizing their lack of human reasoning</note>. For everything arising from the *animus* is cupidity, and everything flowing down from the superior mind (the soul) is instinct.

(310.) These points clearly indicate that the loves introduced into the rational mind are united in such a way that they are distinct in essence and nature from the loves of the superior mind and from those of the *animus*. Thus, they constitute a certain distinct mind of its own. However, this mind is such that while it exists because of both the soul and the *animus*, it is also sustained by both and depends on both. It does not depend on them equally, but rather according to how it bends and inclines itself more toward one than toward the other. To these arguments, we may also add that we could never be...

...blamed for any fault or crime if there were no love existing in the mind that was truly its own or most emphatically our own. (311.) However, if we look at the matter more deeply and try to explore what actually belongs to the rational mind and what does not, we must make a distinction. Although what resides in the mind is said to "belong" to it, it is not truly its own in the same way sight belongs to the eye. Sight actually belongs to the <term>internal sensory</term> <note>original: "internal sensory"; the inner faculty of perception</note>, because this inner sense "sees" even without the physical eyes, while the eye cannot see without the internal sense. Strictly speaking, I see nothing that truly belongs to this whole internal sensory or human <term>intellectory</term> <note>original: "intellectory"; the seat of the intellect or the faculty of understanding</note> except for the mind's ability to bend or turn itself toward the higher mind—the soul—and allow its loves to flow in and be received (how this happens will be explained elsewhere). Alternatively, it can turn toward the lower mind or the mind of the body—the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; the lower, sensory-driven mind shared with animals</note>—and permit its loves to flow in and be received. Nothing else belongs to this faculty except what enters it through this flowing in. For the rational mind acts like the beam of a scale that holds the balance. In the human body, there is nothing except the soul and the body—the spiritual and the natural. Everything else in between participates in both, and to the degree they participate, they depend on both, just like the pans of a scale. Therefore, to ensure that each side is held in equilibrium, the rational mind is provided...

It is widely accepted as a truth—because everyday experience teaches it to everyone—that as long as our rational mind allows in desires <note>original: "loves"</note> that flow from the body and its blood, or from the world through the gates of the senses, and devotes itself to them, giving and surrendering itself to them, it is distanced from the desires of the higher mind or spiritual desires. 

Conversely, the more the rational mind detaches itself from the desires of the body and the attractions of the world, the more it opens itself to the desires of the higher or spiritual mind. The spiritual is, in a sense, suffocated by the natural, and the natural is driven out by the spiritual. Thus, it appears that there is an **internal man** who fights against a certain **external man**, and the mind itself perceives this battle, eventually either surrendering in defeat or emerging victorious.

(313.) Therefore, since the desires of the higher mind and the desires of the *animus* <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; in Swedenborg’s system, this refers to the lower or natural mind, the seat of emotions and sensory appetites</note> flow into the rational mind freely and of their own accord, and since it is the role of the rational mind only to steer itself toward one or the other, we can see how everything else within the rational (or specifically human) mind originates from that choice. 

Thus, these things can be said to truly "belong" to the mind. Whatever originates from what is personal—or from the will as an essential component—is also considered personal and derives its character and power from its source. But let us proceed in an orderly fashion using examples.

(i.) The first love, will, and desire, so to speak, of the pure mind or soul is to associate itself with a lower mind or *animus*. The soul produces or creates this lower mind from its own essence and breathes life into it. That is, the soul forms the *pure intellectory* <term>pure intellectory</term> <note>original: "pure intellectory"; the faculty of pure intelligence that mediates between the soul and the rational mind</note> from its own essences, and the mind of this intellectory is natural. This natural mind exists within the pure intellectory and in each of its most specific parts. The shared essence and life of these parts is called the *animus*, which therefore contains only the natural and...

<summary>Swedenborg describes the rational mind as a battleground between spiritual desires and worldly impulses, where the mind's choice defines the individual. ...the bodily but not the spiritual, although it descends from the spiritual and is created from it. But this desire <note>original: "love"</note> is not yet that of the rational mind, but rather that of the pure or spiritual mind.

(ii.) The spiritual mind, having already associated with the natural mind, now loves and desires nothing except what is common to both. The spiritual mind loves its own natural mind, and the natural mind respects and honors its own spiritual mind, yearning with the greatest delight to depend upon it and be subject to it. From this now flows the first shared desire <note>original: "love"</note> common to both: to form the organs and instruments by which the mind may act and operate. As desire and longing involve a mutual "give and take," these organs are formed in the way most convenient for the nature and the desires of each. Each mind regards only those goals; and because these goals cannot be attained except through physical organs and instrumental means, these tools are formed to serve every end common to both. From this arises that "bodily machine" <note>the physical body</note> which is purely organic, built exactly according to the image of the operations of both minds. Yet, even this is not yet the desire of the rational mind.

(iii.) Once this delicate body is formed and emerges from the mother’s egg or womb, another desire immediately follows—or is born and unfolded from the previous one. This is the desire that the being may become a man, or that it may be equipped with a specific, individual mind which may be called **rational**. A human being derives his quality of "manhood" from his rational mind; as that mind is, so is the man. Then the pure mind or soul does its part, and the mind of the **pure intellectory** <term>pure intellectory</term> <note>original: "intellectory"; in Swedenborg’s system, this is the highest level of the natural mind, acting as a bridge between the spiritual soul and the sensory world</note> does its own—that is, the spiritual mind and the natural mind work together. Because each pursues a common cause and desires to pour its essence, nature, and life into this mind, it is called "rational." For the "rational" represents the spiritual and the natural acting together or mutually participating.

The bronze age <note>original: "brazen age"</note> occurs when the <term>animus</term> <note>the lower, natural mind associated with emotions and sensory desires</note> begins to fight against the higher mind and attempts to cast it down from its throne. If the dominant loves are those of the body, the animus, or the world, it is proof that spiritual loves have been driven from their thrones and extinguished. But when spiritual loves reign, the bodily loves submit and become, as it were, cold; in this state, the lusts of the body are said to be "dead." For to the extent that the things of the body are alive, the things of the spirit fade away, and the reverse is also true <note>original: *vice versa*</note>.

(ix.) A "state of integrity" <note>a state of original spiritual perfection or wholeness</note> would be one in which spiritual loves alone reign. In such a case, there would not be a rational mind as we know it, but only a spiritual mind, because there would be no conflict or "confluence" of opposing loves. Consequently, as physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> beings, we cannot easily exist in that state; it would be superhuman and miraculous. Nevertheless, we achieve a better life when the higher and lower loves are in balance, and the rational mind is raised above the body. In this state, the mind is so naturally informed about what it encounters that it has no need for external science as a teacher. We are always leaning toward lower things; thus, we are drawn away from this equilibrium—which is the essence of rationality itself. If we remained as infants, our rational mind would be nothing, or if it were something, it would be spiritual rather than rational.

(314.) But let us return to the affections or the loves, and inquire whether there are any in the rational mind which may be properly called its own. This love, once excited, is the beginning, the end, the middle, and the entirety of the thought; without love, the thought could never exist. 

This is also known from our desires, from the will, and from the goals <note>original: "ends"</note> of the mind; unless there were love, there would be no desire, for we only desire what we love. Love itself resides in the will, which would become sluggish or non-existent without it. The goal itself is the subject or the object of that love; therefore, love is the first, the middle, and the last thing in our rational mind. However, these loves are innumerable, and the very means we use to reach our goals are also considered loves because they are seen as being united with those goals or leading directly into them.

(316.) The mind is therefore the very soul or life of the intellect. The intellect may be compared to the body of that soul. Their connection is such that if the mind or its loves are withdrawn, the intellect becomes nothing, like a lifeless body. Conversely, love without the intellect can be described as a soul without a body. Therefore, a certain love exists in our rational mind even before the intellect, and the intellect is formed from the mind just as a body is formed from its soul, in which it is the beginning, the end, and the whole.

(317.) But the question arises whether these loves that are understood to be in the rational mind are its own, or whether they come from elsewhere. They certainly appear as if they were its own; however, so that we are not carried away by mere appearance, we ought to examine some of these loves, and afterwards the other affections that appear to be in the mind.

### *The Love of Understanding and of Being Wise*

(318.) In earliest infancy, there does not seem to be any love of being wise in our rational mind. This is because we are still unconscious of that love, and we do not yet know how to reflect upon phenomena <note>observable events or facts</note> to discover the principles within them. Furthermore, at that age, it is a universal love that has not yet been limited or focused toward a particular type of knowledge. 

Nevertheless, we can conclude for certain that this love exists because of its effects; without such a love, we would never be able to educate our minds or develop an intellect. The intellect is kept in constant motion by this active principle or love. Our childhood desires to see, hear, remember, imagine, and think come from an implanted love of understanding and being wise. Even the pleasures found in the senses themselves could not be delightful without this universal internal principle. 

But during this period of life, the love of understanding is quite general and unfocused. It is a pure love of being wise without a specific object—something lovable—that drives our desire for intelligence. In adulthood, however, we direct this universal love toward a single kind of knowledge that we prefer over others, such as military science <note>original: "art of war"</note>, maritime science <note>original: "nautical science"</note>, politics, mathematics, civil law, theology, and so forth. 

As we age further, we focus this love even more on a specific branch or part of a broader science. In this state, we only love the specific types of knowledge that help perfect our chosen field, valuing them only as far as they relate to it. From this, it appears that there is a natural love in our developing rational mind. This love is initially a universal love for all things, which in time becomes a particular love. If this universal love did not exist in infancy, we would be entirely unable to provide the mind with an intellect unless we were specifically driven toward some particular knowledge from the start. ### *The Love of Knowing Hidden Things, and Admiration*

(319.) We can see that there is an innate love of being wise through a desire familiar to everyone: the desire to know hidden things. It is this love that shapes our entire intellect. Everything stored in the memory of an infant or child was previously hidden from them. As soon as something is learned, the child is seized with the desire to discover what still remains hidden within that known object—that is, its qualities and many other details. 

This love draws us into the sciences, where we believe we will gain knowledge of these secrets. The entire world of scholarship is driven toward physical experiments so that through them, we may understand or penetrate the mysteries of nature. The ancient philosophers were all possessed by this love, but for them, it was the desire to penetrate nature's secrets *from the cause* <note>original: "a priori"</note>—that is, through first principles and rational philosophy. In contrast, those of our own day wish to penetrate secrets *from the effect* <note>original: "a posteriori"</note>—that is, through experimentation. Both groups share the same love, for they agree on this ultimate goal.

Admiration <term>admiration</term> <note>In this context, "admiration" means "wonder" or "amazement" at something unexpected or unknown.</note> is the feeling we have toward perfection, relative to the subject being observed. Therefore, as long as we have little or no knowledge of an object, we wonder at its perfection, however small it may be. This is why we marvel at the infinite wonders of nature, its hidden forms, and the like. 

This is also why children wonder at everything: because to them, everything is hidden. Thus, wonder coincides with the love of discovering hidden things; for whatever we wonder at is deeply imprinted on our memory. We wonder that nature is so remarkable in her various kingdoms; but if we truly knew what nature is—that she is most perfect and is only capable of producing such things—our wonder would then cease.

### *The Love of Foreknowing the Future*

(321.) The love of foreknowing the future ranks third alongside the love of knowing hidden things. We love to know the future because it is hidden, and because we love it, we desire it. The only difference is between things that are hidden all at once <note>original: "simultaneously hidden"</note> and those that are hidden by the passage of time <note>original: "successively hidden"</note>; for what is present now will be brought about through the passage of time. Therefore, when we know these things, we think of them as present and existing now, for all past things were once future.

This love also proves that there is something implanted in our minds which serves as the active principle in the formation of our intellect. This love so dominates every human mind that it is present in every goal we desire. When we desire any end and some impossibilities stand in our way, we immediately want to know the final outcome, which is where hope comes from. Therefore, in everyone who has hope, there is a love for the future that we desire to know. 

As a result of this human love, many arts have been invented, such as physiognomy <term>physiognomy</term>, geomancy <term>geomancy</term>, Pythagorean arithmetic <term>Pythagorean arithmetic</term>, and judicial astrology <term>judicial astrology</term>; and in former times, auspices <term>auspices</term>, the consultation of oracles, divinations, the interpretation of dreams, and many other similar things. <note>These terms refer to various historical methods of fortune-telling: physiognomy (face-reading), geomancy (interpreting markings on the ground), Pythagorean arithmetic (number mysticism), judicial astrology (predicting human affairs by stars), and auspices (interpreting the flight of birds).</note> Even the countless events of the past, such as the fates and

The histories of kings and empires do not delight the mind as much as that one new thing which we desire to know. This same love is a sign that such knowledge exists in the soul, and that from this knowledge come the mind's premonitions <term>presages</term> <note>presages: Forewarnings or intuitive feelings about the future.</note> and the fulfillment of dreams.

### *The Love of Truths and Principles*

(322.) The intellect of our rational mind could not be shaped <note>original: "informed"</note> and become a functioning intellect without the love of truths, for it needs as many truths as it has ideas. When these ideas are analytically examined and compared, a new truth arises; from this and other similar ones, even more new truths emerge, until we eventually arrive at those universal truths that belong to the soul and the pure intellectory <term>intellectory</term>. <note>intellectory: Swedenborg's term for the faculty of pure intellect, which acts as a bridge between the soul and the rational mind.</note> The most specific <note>original: "particular"</note> truths, and those introduced first, are the material truths we absorb through the senses. The mind initially accepts all of these just as they appear, treating them as truths; from these, it organizes its rational analysis and forms its intellect. Therefore, the mind assumes as many principles as the conclusions it forms, provided it has faith in the premises and trusts the correctness of its conclusions. These principles are the very truths that exist in the rational mind as if they were its own; however, they cannot be called pure truths but rather probabilities, for they are heavily influenced by hidden qualities. Viewed in themselves, they are opinions and hypotheses, which the mind will perceive if it considers them inwardly and, by comparing them with others, draws any conclusion from them as if they were truths from ex... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

...experiment. These assumed truths are accepted more readily as truths when they are made to seem more probable or likely, or when they are so decorated and hidden that their inner reality is not visible. This is because we often judge internal qualities based on surface appearances, just as we might judge a young woman's virtue by her physical beauty. Therefore, as shown previously, we have an innate love for establishing principles and accepting them as truths—which is the same as the process of forming the intellect. In this section, we will focus primarily on the love of principles, viewed specifically as truths <note>original Latin: *ut veritates spectatorum*</note>.

(323.) The fact that it is natural to love truth can be proven by the order found in the forms and harmonies of nature; truth in intellectual matters corresponds to order in natural things. Just as order and harmony naturally please the physical senses <term>common sensory</term> <note>common sensory: Referring to the *sensorium commune*, a historical anatomical concept of a place in the brain where all the senses meet and are processed.</note> and bring joy to the lower mind <term>animus</term> <note>animus: In Swedenborg’s psychology, this refers to the lower, emotional mind or the seat of the passions, distinct from the higher rational mind.</note>, so too do truths affect the intellectual mind. 

Therefore, just as order assumes a state of harmony, truth assumes the presence of some love or perceived "good" that allows us to determine if something is truly beneficial or harmful. Experience shows that human minds love truths only as far as those truths support their idea of what is "good." There are things that are inherently good by nature, things that only *appear* to be good, and things that are actually bad but are still perceived by the mind as good. 

For example, someone seeking revenge finds delight and "good" in cruelty itself. As long as he is driven by this desire, he loves everything that supports it and hates everything that stands in its way. He might understand the truths that contradict such a mindset <term>animus</term>, but he hates those truths and the people who try to use them to change his mind. Likewise, a greedy person who longs for others' possessions might recognize the truths that prove his greed is against the natural order; however, he hates those truths and instead loves any arguments <note>original: "probabilities"</note> that favor and encourage his own idea of what is "good."

Criminals <note>original: "nals", continuing from "crimi-" on the previous page</note> often talk most wisely; they even give eloquent speeches and use a logical chain of truths to condemn the very crimes they have committed, while in their own minds they still hate the truths they are proclaiming. Thus, there are those who love truths and those who hold them in hatred—or rather, who love things that are contrary to the truth, for hatred is simply the love of the opposite. 

Likewise, the rational mind loves truths through an innate <term>innate: inborn or natural</term> love. Without this love, it would never be able to perfect its intellect or possess sound judgment. However, in place of absolute truths, the mind often substitutes "principles," which are really just probabilities that we have accepted as truths. To love these principles or probabilities is to exercise the same kind of love by which actual truths are embraced. 

This passion exists in the higher mind or the soul, all of whose ideas are truths which the soul either loves or hates. This is evident from the effect of a similar love in the rational mind, and also from the origin of ambition and of anger. These are like "heats and fires" in the soul, roused in defense of these perceived truths. For there are those who are by nature stubborn <note>original: "tenacious of opinion"</note>, even in their childhood resembling old age; this is because the elderly believe their principles to be absolute truths. It is not so with youths, who possess a progressive intellect and are not yet lovers of self.

### *The love of Good and of Evil.*

(324.) Between the love of the true and the love of the good, there is the same difference as between intelligence and wisdom. Truths are the objects of the intellect, but forms of goodness are the objects of wisdom. However, no intellect exists without wisdom, because no intellect exists without the love of some "good." 

Intellect is acquired through the love of understanding truths. Wisdom, on the other hand, is not "acquired" in the same way, because goodness itself is a beloved essence that flows in and introduces itself <note>original: "insinuates itself of itself"</note> of its own accord. The intellect is required, however, so that we may understand whether something is truly good, only apparently good, or not good at all, but only—

...a false good. The truly good is inherently good; the apparently good is good only to the extent that it seems so; the false good is actually evil because it is contrary to what is truly good. Therefore, truth and goodness exist both together and separately, since we are capable of loving evil and hating good, and yet we are gifted with an intellect that allows us to understand the difference between truth and falsehood—or to understand that something is not good even though we pursue <note>original: *adimus*</note> it. This is called intellectual wisdom, which is knowledge-based and external. 

True wisdom cannot exist unless it is joined with love. Because all love is inborn, we cannot become wise on our own; wisdom comes from the influx <term>influx: the flowing in of a spiritual or mental influence</term> of the love for what is truly good. To allow this love to flow in, we are given the freedom to incline our minds toward one side or the other. Therefore, *truths* <note>original: *verities*</note> form the *intellect*. The intellect grows as our principles move closer to actual truths and free themselves from the uncertainty <note>original: "shadow"</note> of mere probabilities. For our rational mind to be as intelligent as possible, it must know universal truths—just as the pure intellect <term>intellectory: the faculty of the soul that perceives truths directly</term> and the soul know them inherently. The rational mind strives to reach the level of perfection found in the soul.

But *goodness* constitutes *wisdom*. To love wisdom is to love the intelligence that reveals the nature of goodness; and to love the truly good itself is to be wise. Consequently, our mind always aspires to the highest good. However, there is much dispute about what that is, since everyone assumes that whatever seems good to them <note>original: "the probable good"</note> is the highest good.

Science is neither intelligence nor wisdom, but is rather the intermediary or tool used to achieve intelligence. Therefore, all science is acquired through our own sensory experience, through the observation and exploration of our own minds, or through the experiences of others. Where there is natural intelligence, science is also present...

(325.) The rational mind never loves the good on its own initiative; instead, it passes judgment on what is evil and what is good. When it chooses <note>original: embraces</note> one in preference to the other, it is said to "love" it, because it lets one in and keeps the other out. The mind allows in whatever is pleasant, delightful, or soothing to the animus <term>animus: the lower mind or seat of passions and emotions, distinct from the higher rational mind</term> and to the senses—essentially, whatever makes up the "loves" of its animus. The mind allows these feelings to flow in; and when it is filled with these ideas and pushes out opposing ones, the mind is then said to "love" because it labels this as "good." Yet, these loves do not truly belong to the mind itself; they flow into it. 

Likewise, when the mind shuts out the emotions <note>original: affections</note> of its animus and admits higher loves, it calls these "goods." It is said to love these because it is completely occupied with their concepts. Thus, the rational mind is possessed by loves that flow into it, for it lacks any love of its own. These loves are called its own only because they enter and take over its thoughts <note>original: ideas</note>.

### *Affirmative and Negative.*

(326.) The fact that the mind is able to affirm and deny clearly shows that it is positioned between two loves that pull it in opposite directions. It is able to choose one and reject the other; this freedom <gloss>original: liberty</gloss> is the only thing truly unique to the mind. Without this property, the mind could not exist, let alone continue to function <note>original: subsist</note>. 

In the entire body, there is nothing else capable of affirming and denying. Our animus cannot do this by itself, because it is influenced by the harmony it finds in an object—a harmony that must agree with its own...

nature. The eye can neither affirm nor deny; instead, it is simply affected by the harmony of an object and the mixture of colors, which follow a natural order just as they do in a rainbow. The pure intellect <term>intellectory: Swedenborg’s term for the faculty of the soul that perceives truths immediately, sitting above the rational mind</term> and the soul itself cannot affirm or deny either. They are pleasantly affected by things that are perfect in themselves and unpleasantly affected by imperfect things, always according to the specific nature of the soul. Thus, the soul can only love one thing and hate another, but the power to affirm and deny is not within its capability; this faculty belongs solely to the rational mind. The truths of the soul are inborn; however, the soul’s current state leads it to either love these truths in themselves or hate them. It is impossible for the soul to love now what it previously hated. Yet, it is possible for the soul to adopt a new state only during this physical life, and only by means of the rational mind, which has the power to affirm, deny, and choose one thing over another.

(327.) Therefore, in order for the rational mind to possess free choice and a will—and thus the faculty of affirming or denying—it is not given any loves that are strictly its own. If it possessed its own natural loves, its ability to say "yes" or "no" would completely disappear. While there seem to be innate loves, such as the love of what is honorable <note>original: honourable</note>—the seeds of which seem to be planted in the mind—and while there are inclinations toward this love, this does not prove that these natural loves belong to the mind itself. Rather, it proves only that the mind possesses a disposition to receive these loves instead of others, or that it can more easily change its state in this direction, or dwell on these ideas more than others. In a word, it is more willing to admit these loves than others. Nevertheless, this is not proof that love is inborn or belongs to the mind itself.

### *Conscience.*

(328.) A good or bad conscience seems to be a specific state <note>original: affection; in this context, a state or inclination of the mind</note> of the rational mind, but whether this is actually the case will become clear by examining its origin. Conscience itself depends primarily on how we define what is truly good. Whenever we believe something to be truly good and yet act in a way that contradicts that belief, it triggers a bad conscience; conversely, acting in alignment with that belief produces a good conscience. Thus, our conscience depends on our personal principles, which we hold to be certain truths. Consequently, the same action could result in a good conscience for one person and a bad conscience for another. The "good" conscience of a criminal would be the bad conscience of an honorable man.

The Devil acts against his conscience if he fails to do evil, because he believes evil to be his "good," even though he knows this is contrary to spiritual truths. Conscience clearly demonstrates that our rational mind is positioned midway between higher and lower loves. A good conscience corresponds to joy in the *animus* <term>animus: the lower, more emotional and sensory part of the mind, as opposed to the higher rational mind</term>, while a bad conscience corresponds to sadness. Therefore, joy and sadness flow through correspondence into the mind and activate the conscience. 

The states of the soul and its loves also contribute significantly to the condition of the conscience within the rational mind. A soul that loves truths, when that love dominates the rational mind, is internally pained by anything that opposes this love; this is a "true" conscience. However, if the soul hates spiritual truths and becomes diabolical, then the mind is distressed by those truly good things themselves when it is guided by them. Therefore, conscience arises from both the *animus* and the higher mind. It is of such a nature that hardly anyone can truly judge its quality in another. In order to judge the truth of someone else’s conscience, one would need to know what the absolute good is, as well as the specific quality of that person's mind and *animus*—knowledge that belongs to God alone. Ultimately, the conscience itself serves as each person's judge.

<summary>Swedenborg defines conscience as the rational mind's reaction to acting for or against one's own held principles of "good." He explains that because conscience is subjective and influenced by the state of the soul, only God can truly judge the integrity of a person's conscience.</summary>

### *The Highest Good and Highest Truth.*

(329.) It is certain that there is a good in itself and a source for this good—that it is essentially goodness itself and love itself. If there is a good in itself, then it follows that all things which flow from that good and which tend toward that good are also good in themselves. However, whatever things deviate from this course—and even more so, whatever things are contrary to this good—are evil in themselves. They are evil precisely to the extent that they are removed from that good. 

From this, it is clear that nothing but God alone can be Goodness itself, for He is the fountain of every good—that is, of every perfect thing. Yet, evil and imperfect things may appear to our minds as good and perfect, thereby persuading us to embrace them. In a more refined and elevated mind, we do not embrace things that we acknowledge to be evil simply because they are evil; rather, evil things are embraced because they are soothing and pleasing to the current state of our mind. In such cases, they are sometimes called "necessary evils."

From this it now appears that every person embraces and labels as the "highest good" whatever agrees with the state of their own mind. Thus, to the vengeful, vengeance is the highest good; to the miser, wealth; and so it is with other desires <note>original: lusts</note>. In short, everyone places the highest good in a good conscience; but we must observe what kind of "good" it is—whether it is truly good or only falsely good. Therefore, we must investigate universal truths and instruct our minds by them.

(330.) The highest good also presupposes a highest truth. Whatever affirms this highest good is itself the highest truth, while other things are false. However, "true" things can also describe evil; therefore, the "highest truth" refers to that which expresses the actual nature of anything—what it is in itself—thus describing the nature of both the good and the evil.

(331.) "Good" in the mind signifies "perfection" in nature; therefore, these two concepts correspond to each other. Perfections...

The highest good of the body is the pleasure which most affects the body. The highest good of the *animus* <term>the "animus" refers to the lower, sensory mind which is the seat of the passions and emotions, as distinguished from the "mens" or rational mind</term> is that love which most affects it. (382.) Every faculty and mind—whether it is superior, inferior, or intermediate—aspires to the highest good because of an implanted love. The highest peak of the lower mind can hardly even be called the lowest level of the higher mind. 

We can see, then, that our rational mind is unable to conceive of what the happiness or the unhappiness of its soul will be; and if it cannot conceive this, neither can it express it. The same is true of the highest truths. Our mind may progress indefinitely and expand its intellect, yet it will never arrive at pure truth such as exists in the soul, unless the rational mind is dissolved and destroyed. Thus, we cannot penetrate into the nature of pure intelligence or the intelligence of the soul. 

A limit is accordingly placed on the advancement of our intellect, beyond which it cannot go. However, a field is still provided in which the intellect may extend itself indefinitely, and the love to extend itself in this way is natural to it. But if the intellect wishes to be elevated above itself or to attain to things...

->*The Love of Virtues and of Vices; the Honorable; the Decorous.*<-

(333.) The honorable <note>original: "the honourable," referring to the quality of being worthy of honor or moral excellence</note> is the common quality of all virtues, for all the virtues taken together constitute what is honorable. Thus, the honorable is the overall form whose essential components are the specific virtues. Each individual virtue is itself a form whose essential components are the specific parts of that virtue.

However, decorum <note>original: "decorum," referring here to outward behavior, etiquette, or the "decorous" appearance of virtue</note> is the external form of the virtues. In order for virtues to be visible, an external expression is required by which we may judge the honorable nature of the virtue and its parts. This is why decorum can be varied in so many ways. Every form may be varied externally in a thousand ways, and the states of the internal form may also change even while the external form remains the same. This is our "political art" <note>the "political art" refers to the social skill of managing one's outward appearance and manners to influence how others perceive one's character</note>: to persuade those minds that judge by external appearances about the nature of our internal thoughts.

(334.) The dishonorable, on the contrary, is a form whose essential components are vices; and every vice is a form whose essential components are the specific parts of that vice. The indecorous is its external form, for every internal form has an external form—which is called the figure—and this corresponds naturally to the internal form.

(335.) There is nothing that is a virtue in itself except the "good in itself." But in order for a virtue to exist and be recognized as such, it must be preceded by an affirmative and...

<meta>This page continues the argument that virtue and vice are not found in outward actions alone, but are determined by the intentions and choices of the rational mind.</meta>

<language>English</language>
<page-num>212</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...negative, a rational intuition that the good is to be chosen; there must be a will and an objective <note>original: "end"</note> which we regard as good. These faculties are formed only within the rational mind; therefore, no moral virtue arises from anywhere else. If an inanimate machine were to give money to a poor person, it could not be called a virtue. Likewise, if someone benefits another without knowing what they are doing, or with an opposite intention, or out of necessity, this is not called a virtue. If an insane person renders service to society, this is not a virtue, but a "good." Therefore, anything that is purely natural or necessary loses the name of virtue. In this way, all virtues belong to the mind alone. The same applies to vices. There is no vice which is a vice in itself; only the underlying evil is evil. It is the mind itself that causes a thing to be morally vicious. Thus, all morality, just like all vice, belongs to the rational mind alone.

(336.) Accordingly, I have already set forth what the virtues and vices are when I treated the affections of the <term>animus</term> <note>The "animus" refers to the lower, more animal-like part of the soul—the seat of emotions, passions, and sensory desires</note>—for instance, ambition, self-love, love of country, revenge, anger, avarice, and other traits. All of these are either goods or evils in themselves; however, they are not called "virtues" or "vices" except in so far as they proceed from the rational mind. Consequently, the more educated the mind is and the greater the intellect, the greater the virtue or the vice that flows from it. Thus, the love of oneself above all others is an evil in itself, and if such a love exists in the mind, it is a vice. On the other hand, the love of the many, or of society above oneself, is a good in itself, but it is not called a "virtue" except when it resides in the rational mind. 

Virtue, accordingly, depends upon the state of the rational mind, specifically how the mind regards what is truly good or what is not truly good (which is evil). When the mind does not know whether a thing is truly good or truly evil, it is held in suspense, and its conscience is said to be in doubt. In this state, it should do nothing, because such an action would be neither good nor bad. It would not be rational, but rather animalistic <note>original: "brutal," meaning characteristic of a "brute" or animal without reason</note> and irrational, or like that of an in-

(337.) Therefore, it is the rational mind that defines <note>original: "qualifies"</note> all those emotions <note>original: "affections"</note> attributed to the <term>animus</term> <note>The "animus" refers to the lower, more animal-like part of the soul—the seat of emotions, passions, and sensory desires</note> and to the body. These are all what they are only because they proceed from the rational mind. For this reason, it is unnecessary to treat them individually here, since they all weave themselves into the loves and "goods" of the rational mind, which then uses its will to put them into action. This is why nothing that flows *into* the rational mind can be called a virtue or a vice—only what flows *from* it. Furthermore, the greater a virtue is, the more that which flows in under the form of "good" persuades the mind that it is indeed such a virtue, even though it may actually be a vice.

(338.) The question now arises: does any love for virtues or vices belong naturally to the rational mind? Experience proves that the "seeds of honor" are sown in the minds of some, or that there are natural inclinations toward what is honorable (and the reverse). However, the mind is nothing without cultivation; it must be formed in order to be rational and possesses nothing of its own except what it acquires. Because of this, it seems that the love of virtues is not a love belonging strictly to the rational mind itself. Instead, it belongs to the superior mind <note>The "superior mind" refers to the spiritual soul or the higher part of the human intellect that receives divine influence</note> which flows in and establishes this as its nature. This occurs if the love of "the good" flows in; this good is called a "virtue" only when the mind rationally observes that it agrees with the nature of good. Thus, we cannot say that the love of virtue is proper to the rational mind, but rather that the soul from which that love flows is good. We might also say that a mind is naturally structured so that it inclines toward receiving these loves rather than others. In this case, its inclination is simply a faculty <note>A natural mental power or capacity</note> for bending itself toward the reception of this or that love.

# XVII.

### CONCLUSION REGARDING THE NATURE OF THE ANIMUS, THE SPIRITUAL MIND, AND THE RATIONAL MIND.

(340.) The animus <term>Latin for the "lower" or "sensory" mind, distinct from the higher rational mind</term> is a form whose defining characteristics are all those emotions <note>original: "affections"</note> that flow in from the body and from the world through the gateway of the senses. In each emotion, there is a specific "animus" whose own defining characteristics are all the smaller emotions that make up that larger feeling, and so on. This animus is our personal temperament or character <note>original: "disposition or genius"</note>; this is why we speak of indulging our temperament or animus. Among the ancients, every character trait or temperament was adored and worshipped as a god, with a universal god presiding over them all. From this came Jupiter, Apollo, Venus, Mars, and the rest, as well as other specific deities belonging to them. In both religious and everyday language, all those emotions of the animus that come from the body are said to come from the heart—as when we say "with the whole heart" or "with the whole soul." We see this also in terms like merciful <note>original: *misericors*, literally "pitying heart"</note>, senseless <note>original: *excors*, literally "without heart" or stupid</note>, and insane <note>original: *vecors*, literally "disturbed heart"</note>. These terms all originally referred to the blood <note>Swedenborg connects the "heart" and "blood" to the lower sensory emotions because of their physical nature</note>.

The spiritual mind is the form whose defining characteristics are all those loves that flow in from above or from God—through His Spirit by means of the Word—and from heaven and the heavenly society of souls.

(341.) This mind is properly called the **spirit**, which resides within the soul. Thus, while the soul is indeed called "spirit," it would be more accurately described as **spiritual**.

But strictly speaking, the rational mind is the form whose essential qualities are all virtues and vices. Within every virtue and vice, a rational mind is present, and its essential qualities are all the individual components of that virtue or vice.

For a universal whole to exist, there must be specific parts from which it is formed and maintained.

### *That the Rational Mind is what is properly called "Man."*

(344.) The external shape is not what makes a human being. An ape has a face like a human and yet remains an ape; wax can be molded into a human form and yet remain wax, even while it looks like a person. Nor is it the external form of the body that defines a human. Brute animals possess similar limbs and organs <note>original: "members and viscera"</note> and a structure similar to even the more imperfect animals like insects. Speech does not make a human, for a parrot talks and yet is not human. The sensory mind <term>animus</term> is not the human, for animals possess a similar sensory mind and are affected just as humans are by the loves of their body and of their world.

They are not recognized as human except for the fact that they still possess some human quality that enables them to think. The greater the intellect, or the more elevated the rational mind, the greater the person is. If it surpasses all others, it is declared to be superhuman and divine—something that is above humanity.

(346.) We also recognize as truly our own only that which we possess mentally, for everything in the entire human system is defined by the mind. Therefore, all loves—both superior and inferior—flow into and converge in the rational mind as if into their center, and from there, they flow out again. Thus, the beginning of all actions and the final destination <note>original: "end"</note> of all sensations—the concentration of the whole—is in the mind. Consequently, everything else outside the mind is regarded as its instruments and organs. The mind neither knows nor cares to know what these things are, provided only that they serve it as its slaves. It even seems as if God held these natural things in contempt and reduced them to mere instruments, since He has not revealed their nature to us, or how the mind acts by means of them. Instead, He has only provided them and surrounded the mind with them so that they may stand ready and obedient for every effect through which the mind wishes to achieve its goals.

(347.) We only love what is pleasing to this same rational mind, as if it were our very self. Every person wishes to appear as they truly are by virtue of their mind; even if they use physical adornments <note>original: "ornaments of the body"</note>, the desire is still that these should reflect the quality of the mind. Thus, we feel hatred and are often carried away by anger toward whatever harms...

(348.) In the rational mind, we find the "face" of the soul, just as the physical face shows the likeness of the <term>animus</term> <note>The lower, emotional, and sensory part of the mind, as opposed to the higher rational mind.</note>. The rational mind may thus be called the "body" of the soul, because it is formed into an image of the soul’s operations.

(349.) This mind indicates the nature of the soul. If the soul were not spiritual and immortal, it would be impossible for such a mind to be formed—one in which the spiritual and the natural are joined together. Therefore, since both the natural and the spiritual exist within the mind, the mind possesses everything a person possesses, serving as a central meeting point <note>original: "centre of confluences"</note>. For this reason, the rational man is what is truly called "man." When this mind is destroyed, the human being perishes. **He then becomes a spirit, because only the soul lives on at that point.**

(350.) This is the reason why a person may be called both "internal" and "external." The spiritual essence that flows into the rational mind is the interior and superior man; but the natural element that flows in from the <term>animus</term> is the external man. The mind is the faculty that perceives within itself the advice or promptings of both the external and internal man. Therefore, the external man is the same as an animal, but the internal man is the same as an angel.

<header>FREE WILL.</header>

# XVIII.

## FREE WILL, OR THE FREE CHOICE OF MORAL GOOD AND EVIL.

(351.) Scholars have been in great disagreement regarding the freedom of the human mind. There are those who argue that in divine and spiritual matters, no mental freedom remains; or if any exists, it is merely a shadow, hardly recognizable as freedom. Some say that full freedom remains in worldly and physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> matters; but others declare that this is slavery rather than liberty, because the rational mind [<term>mens</term> <note>The higher, analytical, and intellectual part of the mind.</note>] is thus kept in chains by the desires belonging to the lower mind [<term>animus</term> <note>The seat of emotions, passions, and sensory drives.</note>]. 

There are others still who assert that there is no freedom at all, even though it may seem like there is. They claim we are drawn away either by our own loves or by other desires that flow into the sphere of our minds, or by some absolute divine direction that carries us along like a current or a ship under full sail. Furthermore, if the rational mind has no desires of its own, but instead all of them flow into it from either above or below, it would follow that the mind does not exercise its own right or free will. Instead, it would belong either to the soul or to the body, appearing to be ignited by their specific desires. 

But let us set aside all these controversies, since adopting arguments just to refute them is a useless <note>original: "barren"</note> task. For if we rely only on arguments derived from effects <note>original: *a posteriori*, a philosophical term meaning reasoning from observed consequences back to their causes</note>, we will surely clash, and our minds will be lost in a dense and dark forest. We would be unable to see beyond the...

<header>THE SOUL.</header>

...the nearest hill or the nearest tree. Let us then rise to higher views—to the principles and origin of things, or to universal truths—and from these let us descend in proper order. We should not turn from our path to refute anyone, but continue straight toward the goal.

(352.) It is acknowledged by everyone that our rational mind can freely judge and decide, or freely think. When impossibilities do not stand in the way, it can also freely will and act out what it thinks. Without the liberty of thinking, or of acting in accordance with what we think, there would be no understanding and no will. Indeed, the very name "will" would be banished from our vocabulary, and we would know nothing about it. Without *free will*, there would be nothing affirmative and nothing negative; there would be no virtue and no vice, and consequently no morality. There would also be no religion and no divine worship, for these require a free mind. 

Thus, there could be no hearing of prayers, and even less any accountability <note>original: "imputation"; the theological or legal concept of attributing actions, guilt, or merit to a person</note> for good or evil, because nothing could be regarded as truly our own. For who holds a machine accountable, or blames someone who acts out of necessity rather than of their own accord? Humans judge actions based on whether they proceed from a will that is not forced; what then should we believe regarding divine justice? In short, without the gift of liberty, we would not be human, but merely animals. For what would our human essence <note>original: "principle"</note> be—or that which is properly our own—unless we could think, will, and act freely? Whoever can think freely can also will freely, for will and action follow thought. Therefore, not only being free, but also having the ability to act freely of one's own self, is truly human. It was also shown above that the only thing that truly belongs to us is this liberty of the will.

(353.) It is also an established truth that without intellectual life or understanding, there is no rational liberty. Furthermore, the nature of one's liberty depends on the nature of their understanding; liberty increases or decreases along with its...

understanding; so that liberty may be called the spouse of the intellect, or the one and only love of the rational mind. For there is no liberty in an infant, but in adults there is liberty. There is none in an insane or delirious mind, and none in the dead <note>original: *nulla quoque in mortuo*</note>, as the intellect is then extinguished. From these points, it follows that there is greater liberty in an intelligent person than in a simple-minded one, and in a learned man than in an ignorant one, and so forth: for this is a direct consequence of what has been stated.

(354.) But because we have formed a mistaken opinion about the essential nature of liberty, we can hardly understand that it increases according to the degree and excellence of the intellect. We usually believe that a man is more free, or enjoys greater liberty, if he is more powerful and wealthy than others, and is thus left to himself—meaning he is less under the restraint of external circumstances. Thus, it is supposed that a commander is more free than a soldier, a king more than his subjects, and every master more than his servant, even if the servant were highly intelligent. Indeed, under certain circumstances, we might even say that a man who is locked in a prison or cast into chains is more free than one who lives according to his own legal rights and free will. But when we speak of the essential nature and perfection of liberty, we do not mean its external form, but its internal one. For a prisoner or a servant may <term>potentially</term> be more free than his master, even if he is not so in practice. A man who is forced to be silent may be more intelligent than a constant talker, and a man whose eyes are bound may have sharper vision than one whose eyes are open—that is, in potential, even if not in action <note>original: "in potency though not in act"; these are philosophical terms describing the capacity for something versus its actual execution</note>.

Rather, because the soul is then free from all connection with the body and its desires, that field of free choice between good and evil—which is offered to us here in our rational mind or intellect—will no longer exist. (See chapter 27.) [*Translator's note.*]

<meta>This page continues the discussion of liberty, arguing that true freedom is an internal quality of the intellect rather than an external status like wealth or power. It distinguishes between genuine liberty and the "license" of acting on animal impulses.</meta>

<page-num>222</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

(355.) We are in the habit of confusing liberty with license—specifically, the impulse to indulge our natural moods and obey the wishes and lusts of the lower mind. We think it is liberty to be able to give free rein to our bodily appetites or to allow the insane cravings <note>original: "cupidities"</note> of the mind to break out into actual deeds. This is not liberty, but license. There is a true liberty, an apparent liberty, and also a false liberty which should really be called slavery. 

True liberty does not consist in being able to think and act according to whatever thoughts we happen to have. Instead, it consists in being able to think and to judge wisely (an ability that increases as the intellect develops) and to act according to right reason—that is, to choose what is good and to refuse and repel what is evil. To give control to our animal or external mind <note>original: *animus*; the seat of lower emotions and physical desires</note> is to rush toward our own destruction in both body and soul, embracing what is actually evil as if it were truly good. Therefore, such a person cannot be said to possess liberty, but rather slavery; for our rational mind is constantly governed by "loves" (motivations), some of which are good and others which are harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note>. Liberty, therefore, is the rational mind's ability to throw off the yoke of the animal mind and to refuse to be governed by harmful loves, choosing instead to be led by loves that are truly good. This is the very purpose and goal for which liberty is given to us.

(356.) If we do not carefully consider the liberty of the will and its power of choice <term>free determination</term>, we cannot avoid forming a false <note>original: "spurious"</note> notion about it. We might imagine that liberty is something separate from the intellectual power of the rational mind; or, if we see them as joined, we might think liberty is something that exists independently <note>original: *per se*; by itself</note>. In reality, liberty is a quality that results from the intellect itself. Because liberty increases and decreases along with the intellect—and because it does not exist in infancy, and its nature matches the state of one's intellect—it follows that liberty exists within the intellect just as a characteristic exists within a subject.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into human liberty by defining the mechanism of the intellect. It transitions from the philosophical definition of freedom to a more technical explanation of how the understanding is formed through "changes of state" in the mind's sensory organs.</meta>

<page-num>223</page-num>
## THE ANIMUS AND ITS AFFECTIONS.

(357.) In order, therefore, that we may acquire a genuine idea of this liberty, it is necessary that we again describe what the intellect (or understanding) is and how it is formed. The intellect, as we have shown in its proper place, consists purely of "intellectual ideas," which are first formed from "material ideas." Thought itself is nothing but the unfolding and revolving of these material ideas in the mind. When these ideas are gathered together into a specific form, the result is a judgment or a mental conclusion. In this conclusion, the various ideas that appeared one after another in our succession of thoughts are now held all at once (simultaneously). 

It has also been confirmed earlier that the ideas found in our memory, imagination, and thought are actually nothing more than changes in the "state" of the internal sensory and the "intellectory" <term>intellectory: Swedenborg’s term for the specific structures in the brain responsible for higher intellectual thought, acting as a bridge between the physical senses and the soul</term>. Such changes can take place within these organs in infinite variety, for their very perfection consists in how easily and variedly they can change their states. 

Consequently, within the sensory organs—and especially within the intellectory—as many changes of state can be produced as there are ratios, analogies, sequences, equations, and varieties of forms in the highest developments of mathematics and geometry. Thus, there are changes of state ranging from the general to the specific, and from the universal to the individual. These states are of manifold variety: some are simultaneous and others successive; some are coordinated with one another while others are layered and subdivided. In fact, these states are as numerous and complex as the equations in the "calculus of infinites" <note>original: "calculus of infinites"; referring to the branch of mathematics dealing with infinite sequences and infinitesimals (calculus), which Swedenborg uses here as a metaphor for the mind's infinite complexity</note>, to which they may be fitly compared. 

We can perceive, therefore, that the mind's ability to change its states is the very same faculty that produces ideas; this is what intellectual power and action truly consist of. However, instead of always saying "the faculty of changing states," let us use more common names like "intellect," "ideas," "thought," "principles," and "judgment." While these common terms do not correspond precisely to the technical reality, they are more familiar to us and do not confuse our understanding.

<summary>Swedenborg defines the intellect as a faculty that produces ideas through complex "changes of state" in the brain's sensory organs. He compares the mind's ability to organize these ideas into judgments to the infinite complexity of mathematical equations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how the mind exercises choice. Having established that the intellect is formed by "changes of state" in the sensory organs, Swedenborg now argues that human liberty lies in the mind's ability to choose which states to adopt and maintain, thereby filtering which ideas are allowed to enter the consciousness.</meta>

<page-num>224</page-num>

# THE SOUL.

(358.) Therefore, liberty itself consists in producing changes of state in the sensory organs, and consequently in the intellectory <term>intellectory: Swedenborg’s term for the specific structures in the brain responsible for higher intellectual thought, acting as a bridge between the physical senses and the soul</term>, or in adopting mental states that harmonize with one purpose or another. We can turn our thoughts in whatever direction we please; and in whatever general state we keep the mind fixed, no other ideas can flow into that state except those that belong to it. Every thought is a form made up of defining characteristics. Into a general form constituted this way, nothing can flow except the specific details that harmonize with it. Similarly, if it is a universal idea, no individual or particular ideas can enter except those that naturally define that universal idea. 

Consequently, the nature of the mind's state determines the ideas that flow into it, the form that arises from them, and the resulting attraction to that form—which is love. Anything that does not harmonize with that form is either not admitted or is reflected back; if such things are already inside, they are cast out and rejected as foreign and destructive to that form. 

We clearly experience this every moment. When we fix our thoughts on any subject, we then repudiate and reject everything that is not similar, as though those things were discordant. For example, when we intentionally and desirously contemplate an object we love to acquire—such as honor or riches—or if we experience sexual desire <note>original: "venereal passion"</note>, the mind then remains fixed in that state. It admits everything that contributes to attaining the object and rejects everything that attempts to destroy that state. In this way, the mind strengthens and fuels itself to such a degree that it cannot be diverted from that state into another. If it should happen to fall from that state, it becomes saddened and attempts to recall and restore it by ruminating on it. If it does not succeed, it becomes dejected and enters a contrary state, which tends to do violence to our rational mind. But let us return to the consideration of liberty.

...to change its states and to pass from one thought to another, but also to become conscious of and to survey—or to have a direct perception <note>original: "intuition"</note> of—all those specific ideas which have entered into the general state. From this, we may clearly see that liberty has the same range and nature as the intellect, and that both are conceived, born, and developed together.

(360.) But the liberty of the human mind itself, which may be called intellectual liberty, can be categorized into certain classes and thus more distinctly understood; for there are as many divisions of liberty as there are of the intellect. The divisions of the intellect are understanding <note>original: "intellection"</note>, thinking, judging, concluding, resolving, and willing—by which what we think (and so on) is determined into action. 

The liberty of understanding is the lowest of all in degree, since we can only with great difficulty prevent sensations from flowing in—that is, material ideas from hearing, sight, and the other senses. Consequently, it is difficult to prevent these sensations from exciting the animal mind <term>animus: the lower, "animal" part of the human soul that deals with physical sensations, emotions, and instincts</term>, and this in turn from exciting the rational mind toward various desires. For there are pleasures and delights which enjoyably excite the rational mind and naturally carry it away into such a state. 

Thus, the cravings <note>original: "cupidities"</note> of the animal mind, which arise from the body, from the world, or from our social interactions, can scarcely be prevented from flowing in unless we were to remove our sensory organs—or indeed, our very selves—from those impressions. Alternatively, when they do flow in, we must turn our minds away from them, which is indeed almost beyond our human nature. The thought immediately takes up the perception derived from the outside; thus, the *liberty of thought* begins, which, like the thought itself, is complete.

(361.) From what has been said, it appears that there is a liberty of thinking and a liberty of acting. (362.) Regarding the liberty of thinking and judging, it is almost absolute; however, the quality of the thought and its resulting liberty depends on the quality of the intellect. This happens when the loves of the lower mind prevail—which is sometimes attributed to human weakness—and by this abuse of our liberty, we cause injury to our conscience.
