However, essential liberty consists in this: the mind can turn itself from one love to another. That is, it can resist and reject a love which is evil or only apparently good, and instead devote itself to a love which is truly good, or which the mind judges to be so. Therefore, liberty does not mean the mind is without any love, desire, or actuating goal, for in that case it would cease to be a mind. Instead, liberty consists in the ability to adopt one principle of love and reject another. Indeed, genuine liberty—that which accompanies a more perfectly developed intellect—consists in adopting the best love as the guiding principle of one's life.

In the natural order of the world, one thing must govern and another must obey. Therefore, that which is superior, prior, and more perfect must give laws and commands to that which is inferior, subsequent, and imperfect. 

Consequently, if the mind subjects itself to this universal law of subordination, it is most free. The mind cannot hold the keys to its own existence alone, since it cannot depend solely on itself. Therefore, to choose and adopt the highest good is to accept it so that the mind may serve what is more perfect and allow itself to be governed by it. For if a servant rises up against his master, or a subject against his sovereign, or a soldier against his commander, this rebellion is not liberty but lawlessness, which destroys a whole society or an entire army.

The superior loves are spiritual, while the inferior are natural and corporeal <note>original: "corporeal," meaning relating to the physical body</note>. Because these are all concentrated in the rational mind, they are prone to struggle against each other.

The former are constant and perpetual, but the latter are inconstant and end altogether in a short time. If, however, the desires of the lower mind were to subject themselves entirely to the desires of the soul, there would be no warfare. Instead, a person would live in a most happy state, as if in a primeval golden age or in early infancy. But in that case, there would be no intellect. As things stand now, the intellect must be formed and instructed by the senses and the emotions of the lower mind. To be truly free, the intellect must know both good and evil, which it would not know if all things proceeded according to their perfect order. Therefore, all the passions are simply intense emotions and excitements of physical life. They are all permissible, provided they are kept in moderation and made to serve the purposes of what is rational and spiritual.

Thus, the rational mind is like a balance scale, and the intellect—with its liberty—holds the beam from which the two scales hang. One scale belongs to the body, while the other belongs to the soul; or, one belongs to the animal mind <term>original: "animus"; the sensory mind driven by instincts and passions</term> and the other to the purely rational mind.

Weights of power constantly flow into the scale belonging to the body, occupying the rational mind. These enter through the doors of the senses from the world, from the body itself, and even from its blood. The mind can never be free from their influence; indeed, the mind is formed by these external things so that it may become a mind, for we must be informed and taught through the path of our senses. 

On the other hand, the loves of the soul—the pure loves—do not enter through any of the senses. Instead, they are introduced <note>original: "insinuated"</note> in a most secret manner from within. They do not reach the conscious awareness of our mind because they are too pure for even our most refined ideas to grasp. Instead, they act like hidden forces that quietly occupy the mind. They have held possession from the very first thread <term>original: "stamen"; the basic structural fiber or beginning of life</term> of its existence until birth, even though no rational mind appears to exist yet. 

From this, one may easily judge that the loves of the body would normally prevail. The mind could not even conceive of the nature of the soul’s loves except by comparing them to things that are obvious to our senses. The soul itself cannot instruct us directly; nothing belonging to it is related to words, nor can it be expressed in speech. Therefore, it cannot flow into our conscious mind in a way we can feel or perceive. 

As a result, the rational mind can only enjoy the gift of its liberty with great difficulty. It is often carried away like a captive by the scale of the body. Therefore, we now ask: what is the nature of liberty in natural and physical things, what is its nature in spiritual and divine things, and how may we be led from natural liberty into spiritual liberty?

(370.) Purely natural liberty does not exist; for liberty without a spiritual principle cannot be called liberty. However, liberty can be attributed to the rational mind because that mind can determine its own path, moving from what is natural to what is spiritual and the other way around <note>original: "vice versa"</note>. Unless there were a scale that could be raised or lowered, there would be no equilibrium and, consequently, no balance. 

There is, in fact, a certain oscillation <term>original: "libration"; the swinging movement of a balance scale</term> between various impulses <note>original: "affections"</note> which are purely natural. In this state, whichever impulse is strongest tips the scale; one desire is cast out while another takes its place. But these are like weights of different materials and sizes placed in the same side of the balance. One kind of natural desire pulls the mind down or turns it away just as much as another, preventing it from being raised to higher things. 

Therefore, liberty in natural things—the power to move from one natural love to another—is not true liberty, but is instead a form of slavery <term>original: "servitude"</term>. This is because the mind, which should choose what is best, is instead drawn toward something that only appears to be good or into outright evil. For example, the freedom to vent savage rage against enemies (even after they are defeated), to cheat friends of their property, to live extravagantly, or to crave power over others is not liberty but slavery. As stated before, true freedom is the ability to conquer oneself. 

In the meantime, the mind has the full liberty to turn away from spiritual and divine things and focus itself on physical <term>original: "corporeal"</term> loves. To prevent this, society provides forms of government, established laws, and punishments for crimes and the abuse of liberty. Another deterrent is the fear of losing one’s earthly pleasures.

(371.) There is also no [purely] spiritual liberty in the rational mind, because the rational mind cannot understand anything about a higher love—that is, things that are above its own level. ### [THE FOUR CONSTITUENTS OF LIBERTY IN NATURAL THINGS.]

(i.) Therefore, liberty regarding natural things consists, first, in the ability to withdraw the mind from bodily concerns and to view them only as tools or instruments that serve spiritual things. Just as the entire physical body is only an organ or instrument for the soul, the lower mind <note>original: "animal mind," referring to the part of the mind focused on sensory perception and biological instinct</note> should be the instrument of the spiritual mind.

(ii.) Second, liberty consists in the mind's ability to be taught—both by the Holy Scripture and by other writings, as well as by one’s own reflection—that there is a superior Spiritual and Divine principle. In this way, the mind can acquire a certain intellectual faith. Once this faith is gained, the mind can stay focused on these higher things and be nourished by them. Because of this capacity to think about spiritual matters, once physical desires <note>original: "corporeal cupidities"</note> are set aside, the mind can be guided toward ideas that harmonize with spiritual loves. Since these loves are always present, they flow in naturally, bringing life <note>original: "vivify"</note> to the intellect and changing its state until, eventually, it is filled with a sense and perception of spiritual realities.

(iii.) Third, liberty consists in the fact that the mind can use established <note>original: "prescribed"</note> sacred methods. That is, it can participate in public worship in churches, observe the sacraments, adore God, and especially pray to Him in private. All these actions are left to the choice of human minds, and they all constitute the liberty that is granted to humanity. When these sacred practices are used correctly, divine grace is never absent; it is always present to instill faith and love. Through its providence, grace governs the individual so that they may become filled <note>original: "warm"</note> with spiritual love and zeal.

<summary>This page defines the first three components of human liberty in natural life: the ability to prioritize the spiritual over the physical, the capacity to acquire intellectual faith through study, and the freedom to engage in religious practices to receive divine grace.</summary>

(iv.) Fourth, a state of liberty arrives where the mind can find delight in spiritual matters whenever it turns away from physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> concerns and yields to the spiritual. When the mind is filled with spiritual passion <note>original: "zeal"</note>, the intellect is reshaped as if anew. This should be called a "spiritual intellect." It involves the most universal and perfect changes of state, which do not belong to the physical senses but to the pure intellectory <note>intellectory: in Swedenborg's philosophy, the "intellectory" is the internal organ of the pure intellect, higher than the sensory mind but lower than the soul itself</note>. In this state, the lower mind <note>original: "animus," referring to the seat of emotions and sensory drives</note> and its feelings surrender. This is because the individual parts of the higher intellect make up the lower mind; if their inner essence is purified, the overall state of the mind is kept in obedience. However, such a state can never be fully realized while living in the physical body. This is the true state of liberty, where the mind delights in the highest good and chooses what is best.

(373.) This is how the human mind reaches perfection. It is most perfect when it is best suited to receive higher forms of love. It is then purified and reshaped—essentially renewed and "re-born" <note>original: "re-generated"</note>. It becomes harmless and innocent, like the mind of an infant, which is guided not by worldly emotions <note>original: "animus"</note> but by the pure mind. Therefore, minds should be brought back to the state they were in before they were developed and shaped through experience <note>original: "*a posteriori*," meaning knowledge gained from sensory observation of the world</note>. Just as the body returns to a state of infancy in old age, the mind should do the same. It should "forget" the physical concerns that stifle spiritual life. This means only being concerned with physical matters enough to live wisely and fulfill one's duties as a citizen. Such minds, which have become almost entirely spiritual even while still in the body, stand as if on the threshold of heaven and its inner happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>. For this reason, they yearn to be set free.

# FREE WILL.

[...such as] Adam was. He enjoyed a most perfect intellect, which was ignited and animated solely by spiritual love. In him, the lower sensory mind <note>original: "animal mind," referring to the *animus*, the seat of emotions and physical drives</note> could not yet rebel or fight against the soul <note>original: *animae*</note> and the spiritual mind. This was because his rational mind was not instructed merely by way of the senses, nor was there any corrupt society in existence that could irritate his mind, nor any knowledge of evil that could infect it. His mind was supremely rational and was entirely subject to his soul, and his soul was subject to God. Thus, his mind was most free because he knew what is supremely good by experiencing it; his mind was not adapted to any other types of love. 

Thus, his entire will was most free because it was led toward the best things. He could also be led toward inferior or evil things—otherwise, no liberty would be possible, as experience has since taught us. This ignorance of evil took nothing away from that state of liberty; for it does not appear to have been a simple ignorance of evil, but rather a natural aversion to it as something contrary to his nature. Therefore, while an evil thought could be suggested or flow into his mind, none could exist in his will. In this way, the image of God—the archetype of all spiritual loves—was manifest in his body. It is from him that we derive the tendency to rebel: just as he desired to rise up against his God and violate the laws of divine order <note>original: "subordination"</note>, so does our lower sensory mind perpetually endeavor to do the same, rising up in rebellion against the spiritual loves of the soul. Therefore, the person who is most free of all is the one who, knowing what evil is and being capable of practicing it, still holds it in total disgust.

(375.) That person who intensely struggles with themselves and who bravely overcomes their physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> desires is more free than one who never engages in such a struggle. The very use and exercise of liberty is to conquer oneself; no one can be a conqueror when they have no enemy to fight. We deduce these things from primary causes—that is, from the very nature of the intellect, which is the seat of liberty. They shun all imperfect states because they offer nothing concordant or harmonious.

For example, through use, the tongue learns its specific movements and positions <note>original: "plications or foldings"</note>, and that same position returns at the first emergence of a similar idea. A muscle also conforms to an action only through use; a mere attempt or effort <note>original: *conatus*, Latin for an internal impulse or drive toward action</note>, however strong, does not teach the method of movement. 

This applies to other things as well. Our intellect—meaning the changes in the state of the sensory and the intellectory—is cultivated and can be taught even into extreme old age. A mere effort or *conatus* <note>original: *conatus*</note> can never bring about a natural change in one's state; instead, it is inclined to relapse into its former state. Yet, just as often, that spiritual love of the soul is ignited with a certain zeal and warmth. It flows in more powerfully, as if acknowledging the intellect as the victor, and so it begins to love its rational mind even more intensely. Thus, the stronger the temptations are, the greater the joy of the soul and the greater the reward after the victory. From these points, it appears that works of charity—although there is no merit in them—are beneficial to the state of the mind because they instill in it the capacity <note>original: "faculty"</note> for receiving spiritual loves.

(377.) Finally, the question remains: Why should human minds be gifted with free will, since it is this very faculty that makes the human race most unhappy and subjects us to infernal punishments? All crimes originate from the abuse of this faculty, while it is thought that without the faculty of free will, we might all be saved. 

To these inquiries, we reply as follows: it is evident that the supreme wisdom of God requires man to have this free will. His providence <term>providence: divine guidance or care</term> is chiefly directed toward guarding and promoting this faculty. This is true to such a degree that He will not allow even the smallest thing to interfere with it; He would rather permit men to rush into the most abominable crimes than deprive them in the least of their free determination <note>original: "free determination," meaning the power to decide or choose for oneself</note>. 

Experience itself clearly shows this. Nevertheless, punishment still awaits every person who is wicked in soul and mind, both in this life and in the future. We are also permitted to think about the causes of this, since this too is granted to our liberty of thought—provided that our conclusions <note>original: "confirmation"</note> are not contrary to divine wisdom and human reason.

(ii.) Without liberty, there could be neither virtue nor vice, and consequently nothing moral; since the ra—

Indeed, there could be no physical association and no diversity. Everyone would be either exactly the same or entirely opposite to one another. There could be no way for people to relate to or adapt to each other. Thus, our human world could not exist, for if all things were identical, nature would perish and become nothing. Nature lives through diversity—specifically, a diversity of such a character that a certain harmony can arise from all the resulting varieties.

(v.) Without liberty, there would be no enjoyment in life, for enjoyment completely perishes under compulsion. Therefore, liberty is essentially the core of human delight.

(vi.) Without liberty, there could be no diversity of souls, and consequently, no heavenly society could exist—a society whose form of government is celestial. In short, without liberty, the goal of creation could not be achieved; that goal is the realization of a society of souls, which is heaven.

## XIX.

### WILL, ITS LIBERTY, AND THE INTELLECT'S RELATION TO IT.

(378.) It is extremely difficult for psychologists to explain what the will is, to distinguish it correctly from the intellect, and to clearly analyze its components. The will is not the same as the intellect, since we are capable of wishing for things that go against our intellect—that is, things contrary to known truths or our better conscience. This is the source of the art of dissembling <note>original: "dissimulating," meaning the act of concealing one's true motives or feelings</note>, which is so common in the world. We are also able to act based on our intellect or our conscience of truth; for the intellect itself searches for truths, but the will is driven to act as if by a specific love, often without knowing whether that love is good or not. This is why it is said, "I see the better path and approve of it, yet I follow the worse." <note>original: "Video meliora, proboque; deteriora sequor" — a famous line from the Roman poet Ovid’s Metamorphoses (7.20-21), describing the conflict between reason and desire.</note>

(379.) However, to understand what the intellect is, we must look at the things below the will that we already know, so that through comparison and a system of correspondence, we may perceive its nature. Below the rational mind [*mens*] <note>original: *mens*, the Latin term for the higher, rational part of the human mind</note> is the lower mind [*animus*] <note>original: *animus*, the Latin term for the lower, more emotional and sensory mind</note>. Similarly, below the intellect are the five senses or the universal sensation called perception. Affections <note>original: "Affections," meaning emotional impulses or states of mind</note> are attributed to the *animus*, as are cravings <note>original: "cupidities," meaning strong physical or emotional desires</note>. In the same way, loves are attributed to the rational mind [*mens*], as are wishes; therefore, the craving of the *animus* corresponds to the will in the rational mind. The intensity of craving in the *animus* is called "desire" in the rational mind, which is directly linked to the will itself. When we truly perceive the relationship that perception has with the *animus*, and also—

<header>WILL AND ITS LIBERTY AND THE INTELLECT.</header>

Once we perceive the relation of the intellect to the rational mind <note>original: *mens*</note>, and understand the relationship of cravings <note>original: "cupidities," meaning strong physical or worldly desires</note> to the emotions <note>original: "affections"</note>, and these in turn to the lower mind <note>original: *animus*</note>, we can see the relationship of specific wishes <note>original: *voluntates*</note> to loves, and how those loves relate to the rational mind.

(380.) Every emotion has its own "spirit" and unique character, and every love has its own specific mind, so that a specific mind is said to exist within it. Just as there are as many emotions or special spirits as there are desires in the lower mind, there are as many loves or special minds as there are specific acts of will in the rational mind. This parallelism occurs in other similar areas, so that by a simple change of terms, we can understand the things that belong specifically to the mind.

(381.) From these parallels, several synonymous terms arise: will, mind, intention, and inclination. For example, people often say, “This is your mind,” “This is your will,” or “This is your intention.” However, no one says, “This is your intellect,” unless they are referring to matters that are directly subject to the operations of the intellect.

(382.) To understand what the will is, we must first separate it from the intellect, or look at the intellect independently from the will. Viewed on its own, the intellect’s goal is truth—discovering its essence, nature, and quality. It even seeks out the connections between different truths, as well as how truth exists within "goods," such as in harmonies, the emotions of the lower mind, or the loves of the rational mind. In short, the intellect reaches out to explore the nature of everything in the universe. Its primary concern is identifying causes based on effects or predicting effects based on causes, which is called the science of Logic <note>original: "Dialectics and also Topics," referring to classical methods of reasoning and categorization</note>. The method of reasoning from causes to effects—starting from established principles—is called the **synthetic** method <note>original: *Synthetics* or *a priori*</note>. The method of reasoning from effects back to causes—starting from observation and experience—is called the **analytic** method <note>original: *Analytics* or *a posteriori*</note>. Indeed, the actual process of investigating causes is **Analysis**. This is similar to the process through which the intellect itself is formed and developed. Once the intellect has been perfected, it becomes possible to proceed in the synthetic way—that is, reasoning downward from universal principles.

Loves are either those of the lower mind <note>original: *animus*; the seat of physical passions and emotions</note> or those of the pure mind. The mind always has a goal <note>original: "end"; from the Latin *finis*, meaning the purpose or ultimate objective</note>. This goal may be its starting principle, it may exist within the methods <note>original: "means"</note> used to achieve it, and it may rule everywhere, so that the same goal remains consistent throughout a whole series of steps. This goal is perceived in the mind as if it were already present, whether it concerns things past or things to come. The mind naturally carries with it all the means that lead to that goal, for nature is structured so that it may serve the mind as a tool while its goals are in progress. 

It is natural that specific steps should be separated by time and space, but not the goal, which remains the same. Because the goal is the same in the beginning, in the middle stages, and at the end, it follows that love is the goal. This is what is desired and promoted through the results <note>original: "effects"</note>, so that we may perceive in the mind the same love, its fulfillment, and the ultimate goal that was there at the beginning. From this arises the pleasure of the body when this love descends into the physical form. 

It is also possible for this process to ascend; accordingly, there are loves of the lower mind or loves of the soul which control our rational mind and are thus regarded as goals. (384.) Let us now consider the nature of the rational mind. Because it is rational, it should not be moved from one goal <note>original: "end"; from the Latin *finis*, meaning the purpose or ultimate objective</note> or purpose to another naturally or spontaneously. Such a natural drive is known as instinct. In an instinctive mind, one cannot speak of "will"—of choosing to want or not want something. Instead, it is simply an involuntary and unconscious drive toward fulfilling its destined purposes. 

Thus, the rational mind—which acts as a kind of internal vision—must join the intellect to itself. It does this not only to recognize the truths of its own desires, or to judge the quality of its goals, but also to see which methods <note>original: "means"</note> to use and how to organize them so that the mind may achieve those goals. To do this, knowledge must be gained from experience <note>original: *a posteriori*; reasoning from observed facts or effects back to causes</note>. When the mind connects the intellect to itself in this way, it is then considered rational and human.

(385.) The reason the mind must join the intellect to itself is that the mind is naturally drawn toward goals that are purely animalistic or part of the lower mind <note>original: *animus*</note>—specifically, bodily and worldly pleasures. To turn away from these and toward higher goals, it is necessary for the mind to attach the intellect to itself. 

The intellect should be the primary master <note>original: "principal"</note> when controlling the cravings <note>original: "cupidities"</note> of the lower mind, but it acts only as a tool <note>original: "instrumental"</note> for the loves and desires of the higher mind. When the mind leans toward bodily desires, the intellect must be at its most active. However, when the mind leans toward spiritual loves, the intellect becomes passive. This is because spiritual loves naturally organize the methods needed to reach their goals from within themselves. In those states, everything flows in a divinely guided <note>original: "provident"</note> order without the effort or occupation of the intellect...

(386.) Thus, the mind regards its goals <note>original: "ends"; from the Latin *finis*, meaning the ultimate purpose or objective</note> as being present in future events. Consequently, it views all the intermediate steps <note>original: "intermediate ends"</note> as forming a single series or chain. In nature, an ultimate goal—or rather, a final result—cannot exist without a sequence of methods <note>original: "means"</note>, nor can it be advanced without a physical nature to support it while the mind focuses on the desired effect. 

The fact that the mind contains these intermediate methods within itself, while nature follows along as a willing tool <note>original: "instrument"</note>, is evident from the various wonderful instincts of irrational animals. For example, the spider constructs its own web with great artistry <note>original: "artificially"</note>; after fastening it under a roof tile, he places himself in the middle of it and seizes his food, winding it in with his threads. Bees crowd their cells, filling them with honey for the winter; they hatch eggs, obey their queen, send out colonies, and kill the drones. Birds build their nests with great skill. All these creatures, as if possessed of a perfect intellect, seem to know all of nature, science, and art—including mathematics, pneumatics <note>the study of the mechanical properties of air and gases</note>, and anatomy. 

In the same way, we humans are governed by many spontaneous activities; these make up our entire "natural economy" <note>the internal biological systems and functions of the body</note>, including our internal chemistry, physics, and mechanics. The mind commands every organ and our entire physical nature. Yet, even after centuries of examination, our conscious intellect is still unable to discover how the mind actually performs these actions. Even the brain itself remains a mystery to our knowledge today. Thus, while our rational mind acts through our will, we remain so ignorant that we do not truly know what the "will" is or how it functions.

(387.) Therefore, the loves of the higher or pure mind do not need our conscious intellect to achieve their goals; instead, the goals naturally follow the mind's love when that love is pure. The only role the intellect plays in this is to ensure that the mind remains steady in directing those goals which are purely bodily desires. If these bodily desires act as the tools <note>original: "instrumental causes"</note> of the higher mind, they then flow in a natural, orderly way. The intellect should also be actively involved in advancing higher goals, but so...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that while the mind sets goals, the complex biological and instinctive methods to achieve them happen spontaneously and unconsciously, far surpassing the conscious intellect's understanding.</summary>

...as long as society is otherwise, being swept away by so many different desires <note>original: "cupidities"</note>, it is enough for the mind to abstain from those things that lead it astray. The rest belongs to Providence, which works secretly through our minds, flowing into our actions. *All things—both through their own nature and by Providence—follow a purely good mind toward its eternal happiness. All things—both through their own nature and by Providence—follow a purely evil mind toward its unhappiness;* however, pure evils are not found within the rational mind itself; if they were, the mind would be completely surrendered to its own body and the lower mind <note>original: *animus*; the seat of passions and instincts</note> which the mind has come to love. But let us return to the will.

(388.) In a general sense, the "will" signifies the mind itself, specifically a particular state of mind or a decided love for something. Because the mind understands all the intermediate steps <note>original: "mediate ends"</note>, it also perceives what helps or hinders it from reaching its goals. Therefore, the rational mind draws its methods <note>original: "means"</note> from its own intellect and organizes them in a natural order; this organization becomes more methodical as the mind becomes more perfect and refined. 

In this organization of methods, there are as many parts to the mind as there are stages of the intellect: namely, thought <note>original: "cogitation"</note>, judgment, and conclusion. The mind thinks while it resolves and considers the methods, keeping the final goal <note>original: "end"</note> in view. It judges when it arranges those methods into their proper order, seeing how the intended results will follow naturally. Finally, it reaches a conclusion or a desire; this conclusion is called the **will**. 

At this stage, all the factors that were previously in the thought are now balanced in the will, like terms in an equation. Thus, the will contains all the essential elements of action, just as physical effort <note>original: Swedenborg likely refers to *conatus*, the internal force or potential that leads to motion</note> contains all the essential elements of movement. 

This conclusion of the will is different from an intellectual conclusion. In an intellectual conclusion, there is no "will" because the goal is not to act, but simply to know what is true. Its purpose is to instruct the mind on what goal it should love, what it should desire, and what it should avoid. In this way, our intellect can suggest goals, but God provides the outcome.

<summary>Swedenborg defines the "will" as the final conclusion of a mental process involving thought and judgment, distinguishing it from a purely intellectual search for truth. He argues that while the intellect proposes goals, Providence governs the ultimate results of our actions.</summary>

(389.) Thus, the mind—with its thinking and its judging of various means—is always present in the will. It views the action itself within the will as if it were already happening. However, because the mind also simultaneously considers obstacles and resistances (arising partly from its own intellect and partly from its natural physical state), the will cannot be channeled into physical action unless those resistances are removed. This is just like a physical force <note>original: "effort"; Swedenborg uses the Latin *conatus*, referring to a latent force or tendency toward motion</note> that is always pushing against a barrier; the moment those obstacles are removed, it rushes forward to satisfy its impulse.

(390.) There are as many "wills" as there are goals <note>original: "ends"</note>. Even the intermediate goals themselves function as wills. Thus, action is simply the will in a state of constant motion, and rational action stops when the will stops. In a human being, the action is shaped by the quality of the will. In animals <note>original: "brutes"</note>, however, the will is shaped by the action, which is the same as the cravings <note>original: "cupidity"</note> of their lower mind <note>original: *animus*; the seat of passions and instincts</note>. This craving is controlled by a type of mind that is purely natural, rather than by a spiritual mind.

(391.) The will always seeks to expand its own internal sensory structures <note>original: "sensories"</note>, just as a physical force always seeks to expand itself. This is similar to how gases in the atmosphere are compressed and held in balance by their surroundings, as if bound by cords. The will is restrained by surrounding factors or by the many intermediate steps in which it is involved, all of which offer resistance. But if they do not resist, the will is immediately translated into open action. Thus, the will is joined to physical force, and action is joined to motion, just as the spiritual realm is joined to the natural realm, or a goal is joined to its result. Therefore, this is not just a similarity <note>original: "correspondence"</note> but a real coupling. In this sense, the will can be called "rational effort," for life added to nature becomes what we call "animal" <note>original: *animal*; in the sense of an "animated" or living being, derived from the Latin *anima* for soul</note>.

(392.) While the mind is focused on its own will, it is limited and specifically directed toward certain fibers of the body that belong to the action it intends to perform. Consequently, it is concentrated within certain internal sensory structures or cortical glands <note>original: *glandulis corticalibus*; Swedenborg’s term for the individual nerve cells or functional units of the brain</note> to which the moving fibers of the body correspond—especially in the brain. From there, the mind views the body’s action as if it were already present. But regarding those resistances...

This results in the exact action that existed within the will. Thus, the mind can move through one fiber after another and one muscle after another with whatever speed it desires, for the muscular system is so articulated and formed that it can correspond to every determination of the rational mind.

(395.) The will also returns immediately with its usual spontaneity because the mind acquires its own changes of state through practice and habit <note>original: "use and culture"</note>; thus, it reverts spontaneously to a similar idea. Through this same repeated use, all the intermediate steps have become so natural that, like "instrumental causes," they serve their primary purpose <note>original: "principal or chief"</note> automatically.

# XX.

### Discourse.

(401.) Speech <note>original: "Discourse"</note>, or the explanation of intellectual ideas through material ideas (which are the specific words that create speech and conversation), does not result through direct flow <note>original: "influx"; Swedenborg distinguishes between "influx" (direct physical influence) and "correspondence" (parallel action between different levels of existence)</note> but through correspondence—much like how the sense of hearing relates to the sense of sight. Thus, many different changes in the state of the sensory organs are formed. To each of these changes, there correspond specific forces or expansions in the cortical cells <note>original: "corticals"; the gray matter of the brain where Swedenborg believed the soul and mind operate</note> which control the muscles of the tongue. This correspondence is developed through use and education; for whether a mental idea is pronounced in one language or another, the correspondence between the idea and the word remains the same.

(402.) However, the action of the tongue cannot be accomplished without the will, because the will is the beginning of action, just as effort <note>original: "conatus" or "striving"</note> is the beginning of motion. Therefore, the idea must be carried from the thought into the will. This is a joint operation of both the intellect and the mind; in this way, the entire thought is brought to a conclusion, which then coincides with the will.

(403.) Nevertheless, it is apparent in speech how distinct the intellect and the mind really are, for speech or conversation is effectively the intellect talking. Through the connection of material ideas (words) and their various arrangements, conjunctions, and verbs—active, passive, simple, and compound, qualities which are partly hidden <note>original: "occult"</note>—a form is produced. This form can be understood by the rational mind and can thus be raised from the sphere of lower <note>original: "inferior"</note> ideas.

<summary>This page describes speech as a process of "correspondence" where intellectual ideas are translated into physical words through the coordination of the will, the intellect, and the muscles of the tongue.</summary>

### Human Prudence.

(405.) Human prudence—sometimes called the providence of the rational mind—consists mainly of finding and arranging the means to reach a good goal <note>original: "end"</note>. This is done so that the goal follows naturally, as it does in nature, or so that the arrangement of these means feels like a natural progression. Prudence does not seem to arise from a prior intellect; rather, it assumes a disciplined and more perfect intellect already exists, along with a mind that agrees with that intellect. Furthermore, the goal itself does not always reveal the original intention. Prudence is considered greater when the goal is better; for whatever prudence allows, it assumes to be good—or at least, the intellect perceives it as true or truly good. For prudence to be of the highest character, it must seek the best possible goals, such as the preservation of society, one's country, religion, the Divine glory, and simi-

His prudence does not need to be active on its own; rather, it is made active by a higher love, and the means appear as if by themselves.

(406.) Prudence is required as long as human minds remain so different—some inclining toward evil, others toward good. Without these various types of minds, there would be no means for advancing a goal. For every person is an instrumental cause and the means to some higher goal; even evil minds can be useful in attaining a good goal. Often a devil can assist in advancing the best goal—as when Judas, inspired [by a devil], betrayed the Messiah. However, this is done not by command but by consent <note>meaning God allows evil choices to happen rather than ordering them</note>, for infinite means are available for a single goal, so that it is not necessary to seek such evil means, but only to allow them through consent.

(407.) Human prudence applies to all actions in civil <note>referring to life in society and the state</note> life, especially in corrupt society or among the wicked. It is used both for self-protection and for advancing things that concern the safety of society. There is both civil and moral prudence, even universal and specific types, including various categories <note>original: "genera and species"</note>.

Concealing the truth is a crime if we fake virtues externally, or if we pretend to have a mind filled with a most perfect love for the purpose of attaining some very flawed goal or selfish desire. For instance, it is a crime if, when our mind desires revenge, we should feign friendship; or when pitiless, feign compassion; or when godless, feign piety. The vice of faking <note>original: "simulation"</note> is always greater when the loves being represented are more noble. Such pretenders are the world's actors, and the true performers <note>original: "comedians"; in Swedenborg's time, this referred to stage actors in general</note> of the theater. 

Acting and concealing become a virtue if we hide our good goals while they are carried out, as if naturally, through the methods of prudence. Indeed, it may even be virtuous to pretend to have bad intentions when among evil people—provided these do not come from our innermost self—so that we might use their own inclinations to work our way into their minds. Once we have become friends and brothers worthy of their confidence, their <term>animus</term> <note>the lower, emotional part of the soul that governs passions and impulses</note> can then be redirected toward what is good.

But this art cannot be described in all its countless features, since its methods are infinite and all unique.

(410.) It should be observed that there is no emotion of the <term>animus</term> that does not show itself in the body—either in the face, the actions, by gesture, or by speech, and even in the very eyes. The art of faking consists chiefly in this: that the facial expression and external appearance differ from the internal state, and we adopt an expression that matches the opposite emotion. Then, we also use the intellect to provide supporting reasons so that the false expression may be believed to be genuine.

(411.) From these principles, it follows that the intellect is granted the power and the right to command the will of the mind, but not the mind itself. For the mind rules universally within the will, while the intellect—supporting the mind—identifies and organizes the means that lead toward the goal <note>original: "end"</note> that the mind is constantly focused on. Consequently, the state of the intellect’s ideas can change independently of the state of the will. They can be so separate that one remains the same after the other has changed; for a change of internal state is one thing, but the focused sensory expression of that state <note>original: "concourse of expansion determined to certain sensories"; Swedenborg is distinguishing between a change in thought and the physical or neurological way that thought is processed by the senses</note> is quite another.

## Cunning and Malice.

(412.) Cunning occurs when evil goals are achieved through craftiness while wearing the mask of goodness—such as under the pretense of honesty, virtue, public safety, religion, or a fake show of love for others. This is done through deceptions by which we flatter the greedy desires <note>original: "cupidities"</note> or wishes of another, and this is done knowingly and with clear intention. The cunning is even greater if the goal itself, even if it is corrupt <note>original: "depraved"</note>, is hidden behind these virtues and made to seem commendable to others. This is achieved through an intellectual "spin" <note>original: "colouring"</note> that makes the matter appear attractive. 

Sometimes this becomes the defining spirit of an entire era, prevailing in republics and kingdoms where officials are praised for how subtly they can deceive others while still maintaining a facade of honesty. For a cunning person never views any goal as final or ultimate, but only as a stepping stone. It would be far too tedious <note>original: "prolix"</note> to list all the different techniques it employs. It is found in small social groups, between individual associates, and even a perfect friendship is often used as its disguise. The truly crafty man is a friend to no one but himself, and he loves himself best of all. Today, this is often called "prudence," while others mistakenly describe it as sincerity or simplicity.

<summary>This page explains that while the intellect can direct the will, the inner mind remains the ultimate ruler of intent. It also defines cunning as the use of intellectual "spin" and virtuous masks to hide selfish or evil goals.</summary>

(413.) Malice, however, exists when no virtue is even faked, but when one does evil from their very nature, without any virtue or honesty. Such a person even pretends that it would be "acting against nature" if they did not act contrary to a better conscience. Thus, such a person is touched by no shame for the crimes they commit and by no fear of punishment. A wicked person is one who understands truths and virtues while simultaneously hating them. The cunning person does not necessarily hate virtues, but simply prefers their own corrupt <note>original: "depraved"</note> desires over virtue. Eventually, the cunning person convinces themselves that their vices are actually virtues; they strengthen their conscience with carefully chosen arguments. In this way, habit and the physical exercise of the brain influence the <term>animus</term> <note>In Swedenborg’s psychology, the "animus" is the lower, emotive mind associated with the body and passions, distinct from the higher rational mind</note> and cause the changes in the rational mind to seem like natural, inherent traits.

*Sincerity.*

(414.) Sincerity is the opposite of simulation <note>original: "simulation"; the act of faking an emotion or intent</note> and pretending, because a sincere person speaks exactly what they think. Sincerity can exist in both the good and the evil. There can even be a praiseworthy sincerity when a person's inclinations are evil, because it is a sign of a truth being misunderstood, or of a mind that does not intend to deceive. Such a person can be a friend to everyone. Sincerity grows out of the principle that pretending is a vice, or from a general principle of honesty, or simply from the habit of not wearing a "false face." However, a sincere person is never accepted as a trusted friend in the company of the wicked <note>because their honesty makes them unpredictable and dangerous to those who rely on deceit</note>.

*Justice and Equity.*

(415.) Our intellect does not only organize, think, and meditate; it also judges and reaches conclusions. In specific instances, it is governed by judgment and decision. Yet, the intellect is still ruled by the mind and its desires, which cause pleasing motives to be introduced into our judgment more readily than those which are distasteful. Since, therefore, there are as many different judgments...

<meta>This page continues Swedenborg’s discussion on justice and equity, following his analysis of sincerity and the inner workings of the mind. <header>DISCOURSE.</header>

Because there are as many individual wills and desires as there are minds, it follows that these minds cannot act effectively when faced with so many conflicting decisions. In order, therefore, that there may be someone or some standard to judge more accurately than individuals, there must be justice. Thus, justice must exist among groups of people when they disagree, and it must apply to everything that ever enters our thoughts.

(416.) Consequently, in all things where form, order, and laws exist—within oneself and one's own mind, in small communities, or in great nations—there are constant debates, lawsuits, and controversies. From these conflicts arise civil and natural laws, legal systems <note>original: "jurisprudence"</note>, judges, kings, magistrates, and other social institutions. Similarly, in the sciences, people spend their time arguing about what is good and what is true. Each person is drawn toward the opinion to which their rational mind and <term>animus</term> <note>The "animus" is the lower, emotive mind associated with the body and passions, distinct from the higher rational soul</note> carry them. If the rational mind were not ruled by the passions of the <term>animus</term> and its selfish desires, a person would instinctively know what is just and fair <note>original: "equal"</note>, and a constant harmony would prevail. Ignorance, persuasion, and arrogance <note>original: "presumption"</note> corrupt our minds, as do political schemes; indeed, if there were no self-love, there would be no need for a code of justice.

(417.) Since truth, goodness, and justice exist as absolute realities in themselves, they are found in perfection in God, who is Truth itself, Goodness itself, and Justice itself. Conscience also commands us toward justice. To prevent anyone from acting against their better conscience and doing what is unjust—and thus destroying both the community <note>original: "commonwealth"</note> and themselves—they are subjected to public punishments affecting their body or property. Alternatively, they may be hindered by misfortunes permitted by Divine Providence, by the stings of conscience, or by fears regarding the fate of their soul and eternity. All these things restrain the mind from rushing recklessly into all types of crimes; for this reason, punishments exist to abolish and root out <note>original: "extirpation"</note> evil.

(418.) Equity truly corresponds to balance <note>original: "equilibrium"</note> in nature. When the natural balance is disturbed, chaotic motion occurs, and nature is, as it were, thrown into confusion,

<summary>Swedenborg argues that justice is a necessary social and psychological standard required to resolve the chaos of competing individual desires. Likewise, in our own bodies and in human society, when conflicts are settled, we call it a state of equity—or, as it were, a state of equilibrium—where each person gives to the other what is rightfully theirs and takes from another only what does not belong to them, and so on.

->*Knowledge; Intelligence; Wisdom.*<-

(419.) We possess *knowledge* [<term>scientia</term> <note>original: "scientia," referring here to the collection of facts and information stored in the memory</note>] of all those things that are in any way introduced into and held by the memory. These are usually introduced directly through the senses, especially through sight and hearing. Knowledge is also acquired through teachers and through books containing all the sciences; it can also be gained by one's own reflection and the discovery of some new truth or principle, which is called the product of ingenuity. Therefore, a "scientific man," a doctor, or a scholar is one who is acquainted with many sciences, experiments, and histories, and can recite all of these. Such a person is often believed to be intelligent, but these two things—knowledge and intelligence—do not always go together. A very small child can be among the most knowledgeable because it can repeat whole books from memory; nevertheless, it does not follow that the child is intelligent. Knowledge must be acquired by humanity; in animals, it is <term>connate</term> <note>meaning innate or present from birth</note>, but it is not recalled in the same way. Not only can material things be retained in the memory, but also purely intellectual concepts, such as those of philosophy and logical conclusions <note>original: "deductions [of logic]"</note>, many of which can be combined into one, and so forth; in this way, the memory can be filled with all things.

(420.) *Intelligence* is the ability to organize the things in the memory into perfect order and into perfect forms, and from there to draw out truths, to examine hidden things, and to draw conclusions about the present from the past, so that...

<summary>Swedenborg defines "knowledge" (scientia) as the accumulation of facts in the memory through the senses and study, distinguishing it from "intelligence," which is the ability to organize and apply those facts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distinction between knowledge and intelligence. It explores how intelligence arises from the interaction between the memory and the higher "intellectory," allowing a person to organize information according to natural laws.</meta>

<page-num>263</page-num>
<header>DISCOURSE.</header>

**...is to be a philosopher, as it were, from birth. There are many aspects of philosophy and physics that a person can penetrate using their own intellect, drawing from the things stored in the memory.** When someone has explored these areas and, through their own reflection, holds many truths in their memory, they are considered intelligent. This is because within the intellect, the <term>pure intellectory</term> <note>original: "intellectory"; in Swedenborg’s psychology, this is the faculty of the pure intellect, acting as an intermediary between the soul and the thought process</note> and a certain higher natural principle work together. This principle directs the specific ideas in the memory to associate correctly—that is, to coordinate and subordinate themselves into their proper forms. Within this principle, all knowledge exists universally and of itself. 

Without this, there would be no intellect—meaning there would be no natural logic, <term>dialectics</term> <note>the art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions</note>, <term>topics</term> <note>original: "topics," referring to the classical study of the "places" or categories of effective argument</note>, grammar, mechanics, acoustics, optics, and so on. For everyone is born with a certain natural law; only the specific ideas are missing, which this law then brings into order. The more capable a person is of making these deductions on their own (and the difference between people in this regard is immense), the more intelligent they are. 

There are many people who only pretend to be intelligent by passing off as their own the various intellectual concepts they have acquired from formal doctrine, as well as the ideas and discoveries of others. There are also those who cannot become intelligent because they lack a knowledge of facts, or due to their ignorance; these people wander, as it were, in darkness, yet they may still show a gift of ingenuity in those things which they do know. The intellect always grows with age and is then called judgment, or the possession of a mature judgment. Many differences occur in its development, for a man can be intelligent in one field of study and not in another. It is rare for a person to be intelligent in all things; however, this may simply be because they lack the necessary application.

<summary>Swedenborg defines intelligence as the ability to organize the memory's data through a higher, inborn natural law, distinguishing true intelligence from the mere imitation of others' ideas.</summary>

<header>THE SOUL.</header>

## *Wisdom.*

(421.) A person is wise who, in all things, looks toward a goal <note>original: "end"; in this context, it refers to the "final cause" or the ultimate purpose of an action</note>, chooses the best path, and rightly exercises their own freedom by embracing what should be accepted and shunning what should be avoided. The wise person is always upright—a lover of everything that is virtuous. They consider themselves a part of a larger whole; they take on obligations out of a sense of duty, and they subdue the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; in Swedenborg's psychology, this refers to the lower or "animal" mind, which is the seat of emotions, passions, and sensory desires</note> to allow the pure mind to act. 

The wise person values bodily and worldly things for the sake of their use as means to an end; in any other respect, or when such things are abused, the wise person disregards them. The wise person values intelligence as a tool, but hates it if it leads the mind into error. Intelligence and wisdom are rarely joined together as long as intelligence is imperfect and misguided—excusing the follies of an irrational mind and justifying obedience to bodily desires—for this destroys wisdom. 

The wisest person is the one who loves their neighbor as themselves, society as many "selves," and God more than themselves, and directs their actions according to this rule, treating those actions as means to those ends. The further someone departs from this rule, the further they depart from wisdom. A wise person is recognized not by their speech, but by the direction of their life. A <term>rustic</term> <note>original: "rustic"; a simple, uneducated country person</note> can be wiser than the greatest philosopher, for wisdom is divine, while the intelligence called philosophy is human. Indeed, it often happens that one retreats and diminishes as the other advances and grows. Only the wise are truly loved by sincere people and by God; to these people, Divine Providence opens a way to ascend. 

Some people are wise by nature, such as those who have an innate sense of honor; some are wise from experience; and some are wise from their intellect—provided that wisdom has inspired their intelligence, and intelligence has, in turn, inspired their wisdom. Wisdom is, therefore, a capacity of the entire mind, and not just of the pure intellect.

<summary>This page defines wisdom as the moral and spiritual application of intelligence, characterized by self-discipline, love for others and God, and the pursuit of virtuous goals. Swedenborg argues that true wisdom is divine and practical, often found more in simple people than in complex but misguided intellectuals.</summary>

<keywords>wisdom, intelligence, animus, ethics, virtue, divine providence, Swedenborgian psychology, altruism</keywords>

### *Causes changing the state of the Intellect and the Rational Mind, or Perverting and Perfecting Causes.*

(422.) There are innate <note>original: "connate"; existing from birth</note> causes which derive their origin from the state of the soul itself, and also from its formation in the mother’s womb. There are acquired causes, such as those resulting from a neglect of education. There are causes originating in the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; the lower, emotional mind or seat of the passions, as distinguished from the higher rational mind</note>, and some, finally, in the body. However, the mind is affected in various ways regarding knowledge, intelligence, or wisdom.

(423.) *Innate causes* are those that arise from the soul itself. This is because the soul of the offspring is derived from the soul of the parent, whose nature is transferred into the child. No two people have exactly the same state of soul. The soul constructs its own organism after its own image; it also forms the nature of the rational mind or its faculties. This is why children are so much like their parents in temperament, and why a grandfather’s traits are frequently reproduced in the grandson. 

The soul of every individual is a spiritual form, and the loves of the mind itself are spiritual. The difference between people consists in this: what one person loves, another hates. A soul of a divine nature loves heavenly society and God, but a soul of a wicked <note>original: "diabolical"</note> nature hates heavenly society and God. Thus, opposite loves exist within the soul itself, and as often as the spiritual mind flows into the sphere of the rational mind, it follows that these contrary loves are introduced. 

Because of this, some are born for wisdom, and some for "insanity" <note>In this context, Swedenborg uses "insanity" not to mean clinical mental illness, but a spiritual state of being oriented toward evil or falsity despite having a functioning intellect</note>. This spiritual insanity does not prevent the mind from being highly intelligent, or from becoming scientific, educated, and learned; such a person might even know better than others what wisdom is, even while they feel a total disgust for it. For all are born for intelligence, but not all are born for wisdom. Those who are born for wisdom are called the elect, or chosen ones.

(424.) *Causes that are innate through formation in the mother’s womb.*—The soul itself is from the parent, or rather—

(425.) Among acquired causes, the main one is that the mind is not improved or is not rightly cultivated. # XXI.

## THE SPIRITUAL LOVES, OR THE LOVES OF THE SOUL.

(429.) To understand the nature of the affections and loves of the rational mind, it is necessary to consider not only the emotions of the <term>animus</term> <note>The lower, emotional mind associated with the physical body and senses</note>, which we have just discussed, but also the loves of the soul's superior <note>original: "supereminent"</note> affections. The latter are called superior and the former inferior; the soul's loves are spiritual, while those of the *animus* are purely natural or corporeal. Because the rational mind does not possess any loves of its own, but is instead ruled and pulled back and forth—either by the spiritual or superior loves of the soul, or by the physical, inferior loves of the *animus*—it is necessary that we understand the nature of the loves of the soul, or rather of our spiritual mind. It is from this source that the virtues and vices flow, which are the essential defining characteristics of the human mind.

(430.) All loves of the soul, which may be called superior or spiritual affections, are universal. They contain within themselves, in potential <note>original: "in potency," meaning as a latent power before it is manifested</note>, every minute detail and every general affection that can exist in a specific or partial form. From a certain universal love—as if from a fountainhead—all special and particular loves flow like streams. These loves cannot manifest themselves anywhere except in the *animus* and the mind, where they are categorized into specific types and forms <note>original: "genera or certain species"</note>. All of these look back toward a certain universal love in the soul. However, as they descend from that source like streams, they are liable to be corrupted by the imperfections attached to physical nature along the way. Consequently, they hardly recognize... <note>The sentence continues on the following page</note>

The <term>animus</term> <note>The lower, sensory mind associated with emotions and physical desires</note> derives its power of desiring or loving from its own soul. However, its ability to love in one specific way and not another comes from its own structure <note>original: "form"</note>, as well as from its connection with the soul through the rational mind. Therefore, the goal of almost all science is to be able to subordinate specific loves under broader ones, and these under general ones—arranging them into their own classes and perceiving how they flow from universal or spiritual loves. This is the true psychological and <term>pneumatic</term> <note>original: "pneumatic science," referring here to the study of spiritual substances or the soul</note> science.

(431.) All souls are purely spiritual forms; consequently, all their minds and loves are purely spiritual, whether they are good or evil. For a spirit, whether it is good or evil, is nonetheless purely a spirit, or purely a mind, and it possesses loves that are purely spiritual—that is, universal—which contain the principles of the lower and purely natural loves. A good angel, just like an evil angel or devil, is purely a spirit, and the loves of both are purely spiritual. The difference is that what the good spirit purely loves is the opposite of what an evil spirit loves, or is what the evil spirit is said to hate; for there exist pure love and pure hate, which are completely opposite loves.

Thus, there are spiritual loves that are good and evil, but they are all universal, superior, and belong to the soul, being most perfectly good or evil. However, because good and evil—like truth and falsehood—are opposites, and because a mixture of good and evil or truth and falsehood may exist within a single person <note>original: "subject"</note>, that which is not purely good is commonly called "impure," and that which is purely evil is called "very impure." 

Therefore, "love" is primarily known as the love of good, even though there is a love of evil which is naturally joined with the hatred of good. To avoid a confusion of ideas in the following sections, we propose to use the expressions *the mind* and *the purely spiritual love*, but not *the pure mind* or *the pure spiritual love*. ### *The love of a Being above Oneself.*

(432.) The first and supreme spiritual love (the love of the soul), and the most universal, is the love of a Being above oneself. From this Being, the soul has derived its essence and continues to derive it perpetually. It is in this Being, through this Being, and because of this Being that the soul exists and lives. This love is the primary love because nothing can exist or sustain itself on its own except God, who exists within Himself and alone "Is Who He Is" <note>This refers to the Divine name in Exodus 3:14, "I Am That I Am."</note>. Because the soul feels this within itself, that supreme love is innate to it; thus, divine love itself resides within us.

(433.) There also exists a completely opposite love, yet it is still spiritual and supreme in its own way: a pure hatred of Divine power or of a Being above oneself. This "love" is called diabolic. From this, we may recognize the quality of good love, and through that good, recognize the quality of evil; for there exist infinitely different intermediate <note>original: "mediate"</note> loves between these two poles. 

This is called the love of evil, or the evil mind itself, which is the state of certain souls. No single soul is exactly like another, nor should it be; this variety allows for a "society of souls," which constitutes the most perfect form of a community. Even the evil spirit or the diabolic mind feels within itself that there is a Being above it, from whom it has derived its own essence. It knows that this Being should be loved above self and that this love should be shown through adoration. But although the evil mind recognizes this, it nevertheless disdains and envies that Being. It rebels against its own consciousness and hates the very truth of its own origin. Thus, it loves itself above that Being, resulting in a perpetual, incurable hatred—a hatred so deep that the spirit would even wish to destroy himself a...

### *The love of a Friend as Oneself.*

(434.) Loving a friend as oneself—or where a love for another exists that is equal to the love for oneself—is a spiritual love. This is because the soul, or the spiritual mind, recognizes another soul and mind as a companion, and as a member of a society or a divine kingdom. This love flows from the very nature of things, as well as from the first and most distinguished <note>original: "eminent"</note> of all loves.

(435.) *From nature:* A single individual, or a part standing alone, is essentially nothing unless it relates to the many things it exists with. From this relationship, a specific form of these things emerges, along with the inclinations <note>original: "affections"; here meaning the qualities or tendencies that arise from a specific structure or arrangement</note> of that form. There is no harmony unless many things are united, and that harmony depends on the way they are joined together. Similarly, there is no happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> for souls unless many are together. No form or connection can exist except through love; and through the love of another as oneself, everything that belongs to the other person is shared with oneself and adopted as one's own. This results in a multiplied happiness for everyone, which is then concentrated within each individual.

(436.) *From Divine love:* Someone who loves a friend as themselves does not do so merely for the friend's sake, but for the reflection of themselves in that friend. (450.) Hatred of one’s own body cannot exist, except in so far as the body is not in connection with its soul and does not obey when the mind commands. For this very love is a connection between body and soul, while hatred is their disjunction. Similarly, an artist does not love an instrument if it is not adapted to his use.

However, when we love anything more than ourselves—whether that love is genuine or not, such as the love of glory, fame, envy, riches, or sexual desire <note>original: "venery"</note>—we then prefer that love over the love of our physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> life; yet, we still do not "hate" the latter. We love the body insofar as it is a means of obtaining what is loved, and insofar as the body is the vessel through which the mind experiences that love. Thus, when death is risked for the sake of love, it is not a hatred of life, but an indication that one desires for that love to live on. 

When, however, someone is cut off from the hope of a higher love, they fall into a hatred of living in the body. This leads to despair and mental instability <note>original: "insanity of the mind"</note>, for without that love, they believe that to live is not truly to live, or that they only live in misery; thus, they desire their own extinction. But such an irrational love or hatred of self is never joined with genuine and truly spiritual love—such as the love of God <note>original: "Deity"</note>, of friends, or of growing society. Therefore, this self-hatred is as contrary to the essence of true love as it is to wisdom, since these two are very closely joined.

### *The Love of Immortality*

(451.) The love of immortality is a spiritual love, and it aligns with the love of God and the love of society. This is because spiritual life consists of being nearer to God, who is Life itself and the source through whom all things live; conversely, spiritual death is being distant from Him. Yet, that spiritual death is not the total destruction of one's essence. Instead, it is the extinction and deprivation of the love that constitutes true life. It is much like a dark surface: darkness is not the extinction of light itself, but rather a suppression <note>original: "suffocation"</note> of it—a state that, paradoxically, cannot exist without the presence of light. 

From this, it appears that the love of immortality is not simply the desire to live for eternity, but rather the desire to live well and happily. The soul already knows it is destined to be immortal; therefore, it does not "love" its own immortality in the sense of a goal to be achieved, because that immortality is already guaranteed. All true love requires the possibility of change or the existence of an opposite; without that choice, it is no longer love. Therefore, love fades when it concerns things that cannot be any other way than they are. 

Instead, the love of immortality belongs to those things that *can* be either mortal or immortal—such as the practice of love, charity, honor, and virtue. We love these things spiritually so that they may become immortal within us. Since the mind (or the soul) is the vessel <note>original: "subject"</note> for these loves, they may or may not exist within it. Furthermore, since these virtues are the means of earning the favor of the Supreme Love <note>The Divine or God</note>, the soul loves them both as a means to an end and as an end in themselves. The soul does this not for the sake of self-promotion or to be superior <note>original: "eminent"</note> to its peers, but out of love for the Divine. It seeks to possess these virtues so it can share them with its fellow beings, making the bond of love between them closer and more permanent. In this way, the soul is better able to connect society to itself and itself to society.

(452.) There is also a hatred of immortality. However, this hatred is never absolute as long as some hope of happiness remains. This is true even for the Devil—at least until after the Last Judgment. At that point, when all hope is gone, the happiness of the blessed souls clearly becomes a source of pain for the wicked.

<summary>Swedenborg defines the love of immortality not as a desire for eternal existence (which is guaranteed for the soul), but as a love for the virtues and spiritual states that make eternal life happy and connected to God. He argues that true love requires the possibility of choice, and thus we love the virtues we must strive to maintain.</summary>

Therefore, a love of immortality is possible even among the wicked and criminal, though it results deeply from self-love. A love for the immortality of one's vices arises when those vices are valued as if they were virtues, or when a vice contains something that suggests a virtue. Furthermore, all true love of immortality fades away within a life of vice; it brings with it a doubt regarding immortality in general, and eventually leads to its denial. These are the results of impiety.

### *Spiritual Zeal.*

(453.) Zeal is the active and passionate force within the loves mentioned above. It is what drives these loves not only toward the act of loving but also toward pursuing the means to achieve their goals. Thus, some form of spiritual zeal is present in every kind of love. For love is not active except to the degree that it is also passive <note>original: "passive"; Swedenborg suggests that love must be moved or affected by an external stimulus or internal need to transition into active zeal</note>; without zeal, there is nothing in love that belongs specifically to the person <note>original: "subject"</note> who feels it. 

Zeal itself is a quality of the spiritual soul. It is born and stirred only by opposites. Therefore, without the actual existence of an opposing force—without the devil or contrary souls—there could be no zeal; it would simply not exist <note>original: "nonentity"</note>. Zeal is stirred in proportion to the strength of the attacking or resisting force, and it stands against its opponent as an enemy. Consequently, the stronger a hellish <note>original: "diabolical"</note> society is, the greater the zeal of the heavenly <note>original: "celestial"</note> society. If the devil were gone, this zeal would also completely fade away. There would be no firing up of minds, no "anger of the <term>animus</term>" <note>In Swedenborg's psychology, the "animus" refers to the lower, natural mind that experiences passions and emotions, as distinct from the higher "soul" or "rational mind."</note>, if there were no actual opponents to provoke them. Zeal is essentially love raised to a higher intensity so that it can match the opposing force it seeks to overcome <note>original: "extinguish"</note>.

(454.) Hatred also possesses its own zeal, which is fierce and deadly—a form of rage and a corrupt, burning fire. In this case, the anger comes not from the zeal itself but from the hatred, which then turns into fury. True zeal, however, never collapses into anger. Instead, it is a mild and gentle fire, inwardly...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that vice leads to a denial of immortality and introduces 'spiritual zeal' as the active force of love that is only triggered when faced with opposition or spiritual conflict.</summary>

...but does not glow outwardly. It shows that one good soul is able to defeat thousands and myriads <note>original: "myriads"; meaning an indefinitely large number</note> of evil souls and devils. Thus, one good angel is sufficient to cast down a thousand devils, for they flee at the first strike, like those who are tormented by an evil conscience. This fear is inborn; while in others, there is no fear, but only the zeal that belongs to courage.

### *The Love of Propagating the Kingdom and City of God.*

(455.) This is a spiritual love. It flows directly from the love of God and of society, but it is stirred and grows in zeal according to the degree of opposition it encounters. The Kingdom of God is the heavenly <note>original: "celestial"</note> society of souls itself, while the "City of God" refers to the earthly society, which is the nursery <note>original: "seminary"</note> for the heavenly. This love of spreading the City of God, or the Church, is the core and spirit of our religion, and all the means of spreading this religion are subordinate to this love.

(456.) In contrast, the love of destroying the Church is devilish, and its kingdom is on this earth. It is the opposite of true religion. This subject is too broad to be discussed here.

### *The Derivation of Physical from Spiritual Loves, and Their Concentration in the Rational Mind.*

(457.) By comparing different loves together—the spiritual and the physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>, for instance—it becomes quite evident that spiritual loves are the sources of all physical loves.

(459.) It can happen, however, that there is a good spiritual love within the soul while a bad love exists in the rational mind or the body. Because the mind is not of the same character as the soul—and the body even less so—it belongs to God alone to judge the soul and its love. All loves, both of the soul and of the lower mind, are concentrated in the rational mind. The rational mind is thus driven not only by its own natural inclinations but also by principles it has acquired or learned intellectually. Likewise, it is pulled apart by the influence <note>original: "authority"</note> of others, by habit, and by the natural temptations of physical pleasures, until a "second nature" is imposed upon it. The most universal source [of both physical and spiritual loves] is the love of God <note>original: "Deity"</note> above all else, and from that, the love of one’s neighbor as oneself.
