### *Pure or Divine Love viewed in itself.*

(460.) God is the very spiritual Being <note>original: *Esse*, a Latin term meaning "to be" or "fundamental essence"</note> in all things. To the extent that this spiritual Being exists within physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> things, God is that very essence within them, so that "in Him we live, move, and have our being." Since God is the fundamental Essence of all things, He is Love itself—a love that necessarily belongs to that Being which originates from itself yet is distinct from itself. For if God were to essentially withdraw from a created spirit, it would no longer be a spirit; its existence is not a property of the spirit itself, but belongs to Him by whom it was created so that it might exist. By way of analogy, we say the body is not the soul, but the soul is the very essence of the body. If the soul departs, the body is no longer a body but falls into decay. Whatever belongs to another in this way—as a derivative belongs to its source <note>original: "as a primitive to its derivative"</note>—must have an unbroken connection with that source in order to exist and continue existing <note>original: "subsistence"</note>. Where there is such a connection, there is love, which in this context is identical to the connection itself. Love allows one’s own image to be seen in another, though the clarity of that image depends on how closely the second is derived from the first, and is therefore often imperfect. Love, then, can be said to belong to the one who reflects the image of another—not because he loves himself, but because he loves in that other person what he wishes to belong to himself or be joined to himself, so that the love may be mutual.

(461.) From this, it appears that God is love itself, and that we are divine to the extent that we mutually love God and, through that love, draw closer to Him. Because God is life itself and wisdom itself, it follows that we truly live and are wise only as we draw near to God. Therefore, love is the actual bond, the life, and the wisdom. Through love and this spiritual connection, all these qualities exist in us more perfectly. To the degree that we distance ourselves from Him, these qualities become imperfect in us—indeed, so imperfect that they can hardly be said to exist in us at all. Therefore, the most absolute and universal source of all types of love is the love of God toward us.

## XXII.

# THE INFLUENCE OF THE LOWER MIND AND ITS EMOTIONS INTO THE BODY, AND OF THE BODY INTO THE LOWER MIND.

(462.) It is well known to everyone that our lower mind <term>animus: in Swedenborg’s psychology, this refers to the lower, sentient soul or the seat of emotions and worldly desires</term> flows into the form of our body in such a way that it finds its own shape reflected there. We may judge from the facial expression <note>original: "countenance"</note> itself what the general state of the mind is, or what its inclination may be. We can also sometimes identify specific emotional states or "affections." When these emotions <note>original: "affections"</note> exist, they show themselves visibly—not only in the face but also in the eyes, in speech, and in individual gestures and actions.

Thus, anger, vengeance, pride, hatred, love, and other emotions are recognized by the "language of nature" alone; for we do not need to learn any formal rules of art to understand the shape that is imposed <note>original: "superinduced"</note> upon the physical structure of the body by these states. Thus, the lower mind—which is the general form whose emotions are so many essential expressions—is actually etched upon us. It is the face itself, in its specific details, which varies according to our inclination toward one particular desire or mood rather than another. It also writes itself there over time, such as when a new personality trait <note>original: "inclination"</note> is acquired through use and habit. 

The lower mind also flows into the blood and the "animal spirit" <term>animal spirit: a historical physiological term for a subtle fluid believed to flow through the nerves to transmit sensation and motion</term> itself, and thus into the specific structures of the internal organs. It makes the bodily fluids <note>original: "bloods"</note> precisely match its own state: for example, anger stimulates the bile and disturbs the specific bodily fluids <term>humours: the fluids—such as blood, phlegm, and bile—that historical medicine believed controlled health and temperament</term>; envy keeps these trapped in the blood, which causes the bluish color that becomes visible in the skin; pride expands the organs and stiffens <note>original: "erects"</note> the nerves and muscles, and

He argues that our emotions and habits are literally "inscribed" upon our physical form over time.</summary>

...it clarifies the blood, while at the same time drawing around it clouds so that it may be easily shaded. The same is true for the other emotions <note>original: "affections"</note> that flow into the specific organic substances of the body as well as into the bodily fluids <term>humours: in pre-modern medicine, the fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine a person's health and temperament</term>.

(463.) It cannot, therefore, be denied that the form of the physical body is the image of the lower mind <term>animus: the seat of emotions and sensory life</term>, and that the lower mind in its initial formation—even in the womb—is itself the form of its own soul. Consequently, the body (in both facial expression and actions) is the image, type, and pattern of the soul or spiritual mind, acting through the lower mind. For the mind first forms its lower mind—or perhaps the soul forms its "pure intellectory" <term>intellectory: in Swedenborg’s system, a theoretical faculty of the brain that governs pure intellectual thought</term>, whose general mind is what we call the *animus*—and then it flows into the body before the body is able to influence its own lower mind.

(464.) How this occurs can also be demonstrated, but the demonstration itself requires an intimate knowledge of the internal sensory organs <note>original: "sensories"</note>, an understanding of "forms" in both general and specific terms, and knowledge of how the spiritual mind influences nature <note>original: "influx of the spiritual mind into nature"</note>. For it is clear that nature is universally subject to a spiritual mind, just as a tool is subject to its master <note>original: "as an instrumental cause to its principal"</note>, or an instrument to a craftsman. Thus, the whole world of nature, out of a certain necessity and therefore spontaneously, yields to the rule of the mind. In this same way, the mind rules the physical body so that the body and its muscles may display every quality, not by their own power, but by the power of the ruling mind. Since all the simple fibers (and those composed of them) originate from the intellectories and internal sensory centers of the brain, and since nothing in the body contributes to its form except the fiber that creates it, it must follow that every emotion affecting those centers of the brain is spread through continuous fibers into the entire body; for there is a continuous connection from their points of origin and first principles.

Even the worst of criminals are sometimes restored to the path of virtue through the sufferings of the body, and so it is in other cases. The lower mind is also changed by individual senses, such as sight and smell, and is transported into joy, love, and other emotions. The reason for this is very evident...

When the blood is infected by some disease, and the purer blood <note>original: "purer blood" — Swedenborg believed a refined, "spirituous" fluid circulated within the nerves, separate from the red blood.</note> is simultaneously affected while flowing through these sensory organs, it induces a change of state in them. Just as a natural effect follows from its causes and principles, and just as the blood is naturally consistent with its lower mind, it cannot remain so if the blood does not agree; when the blood is changed, the effect must become something else entirely.

(467.) But it may be asked whether the intellectory (or the group of intellectories) arising from such a change in the body is changed radically or internally, or only externally and superficially. In other words, after that change has passed and the blood is purified, does the lower mind still remain the same? This is indeed what experience teaches; for after a disease, the lower mind usually returns to the same state as before. This shows that such a change is only superficial and does not alter the internal form. Examples of the lower mind being radically changed by physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> causes are very rare. "Drive out nature with a pitchfork, and she will still come back" <note>original: "Naturam expelles furca, tamen usque recurret" — a quote from the Roman poet Horace, meaning that one's innate nature cannot be permanently suppressed.</note>.

(468.) Thus, diseases and similar causes can only change the external or general form of the lower mind, and not its internal form. This is because only the state of the sensory organs is changed—perhaps because the internal sensories, unable to pass through certain states, are compelled to assume others. The lower mind cannot operate except according to the state assumed by the sensory organs, just as the lower mind adapts the states of those sensories to itself. Hence, that state arising from the internal form of the lower mind...

<header>THE INFLUX OF THE RATIONAL MIND.</header>

## XXIII.

### THE INFLUENCE OF THE RATIONAL MIND ON THE LOWER MIND, AND THROUGH THE LOWER MIND INTO THE BODY; AND THE INFLUENCE OF THE LOWER MIND ON THE RATIONAL MIND.

**(470.)** It is clearly evident from experience that the *lower mind* <term>animus: the seat of emotions, passions, and sensory life</term> flows into the rational mind. Indeed, our rational mind is almost entirely possessed by the emotions of the lower mind, because we desire what the lower mind desires and rush blindly, without understanding, into its strong desires <note>original: "concupiscences"</note>. 

The cause of this is clearly evident through reasoning <note>original: "a priori"</note>, since the internal *intellectual units* <term>intellectories: Swedenborg’s term for the fundamental organic units of the intellect in the brain</term> are what collectively constitute the lower mind; the external form must correspond to the internal form of these units. This external form is the brain, or the *general sensory organ* <term>common sensory: the brain as the collective center for all physical senses</term>. 

Accordingly, whatever the emotional state of the lower mind is, that is also the state of the sensory organ, for the sensory organ adopts the form that agrees with the mind's emotions. As long as this form remains, nothing else—no matter how pleasant or harmonious—can be introduced into the mind unless it aligns with this state. 

The general state includes and contains all specific and individual states. Once this general state is formed, all specific states flow into it harmoniously. The intellectual units are what change the state to agree with the loves of the lower mind. In this way, the lower mind influences the state of the rational mind. The general lower mind is the harmony of all the intellectual units according to the influence from the senses and the blood; these units form and move the general external form, to which the internal form corresponds.

<summary>This page explains how the lower mind (animus) dominates the rational mind by shaping the physical state of the brain's sensory organs to match its emotional desires.</summary>

<keywords>animus, rational mind, influx, intellectories, sensory organ, psychology, brain structure, Swedenborg</keywords>

--- Page 334 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the rational mind can either succumb to or govern the lower mind (animus). It explains the mechanisms of change—influx and correspondence—and the difficult process of reforming one’s basic nature through spiritual and moral discipline.</meta>

<page-num>294</page-num>

<header>THE SOUL.</header>

**(471.)** Therefore, when the rational mind—with the consent of the intellect—remains in the state of the *lower mind* <term>animus: the seat of emotions, passions, and sensory life</term> (which is the state of all the *intellectual units* <term>intellectories: Swedenborg’s term for the fundamental organic units of the intellect</term>), it is blindly overwhelmed by these incoming influences. However, when the rational mind dispels and rejects the emotions <note>original: "affections"</note> of the lower mind, or holds them in check, it is then able to take on more perfect states. 

These changes can be brought upon the more rational mind through illness, and in those cases by **influx** and by **correspondence**. 
*   By **influx**, it may happen because diseases and various external accidents can change the *sense organs* <term>sensory: the brain's processing centers for physical senses</term> so much that they adopt certain states over others; yet these are still states of the intellect. 
*   By **correspondence**, it happens because the mind observes during misfortune and sickness that specific passions of the lower mind—such as vengeance, anger, envy, and hatred—actually destroy the mind; consequently, the mind becomes filled with devotion <note>original: "piety"</note> and virtue. 

In this way, the mind itself, using its own freedom, changes the lower mind as the situation demands through reflection and correspondence. It adopts a state that aligns with more perfect loves; thus, the lower mind—or its internal form—can be changed.

**(472.)** *But to change the lower mind is to change one’s very nature.* This includes changing a good nature into a bad one, which is easily done, or a bad nature into a good one, which is much more difficult. This can only be accomplished by means of the rational mind and its understanding—whether that understanding is truly one's own or one adopted through faith or authority. 

Even then, our nature is not changed unless we shun and hate evils, and never allow our mind to enter that evil state. Whenever the mind does fall into such a state, we must rescue it <note>original: "snatch it forth"</note> using the freedom given to us, and instead adopt a state that aligns with a more perfect love. Indeed, this effort is ineffective unless we remain in this better state for a long time, forcefully resisting the other side. Through frequent virtuous actions and exercises, we must adopt the opposite state and continue until the mind has developed a "new nature" and expelled the old one. This must be done so thoroughly that whenever the old nature attempts to return, we are aware that it must be [resisted]...

## XXIV.

### THE INFLUENCE OF THE SPIRITUAL MIND OR SOUL INTO THE ANIMUS, AND OF THE ANIMUS INTO THE SPIRITUAL MIND.

(473.) The <term>pure intellectory</term> <note>In Swedenborg's psychology, the "pure intellectory" is a subtle organic structure that serves as the immediate organ of the soul, higher than the conscious thought-processes of the rational mind.</note> is where the <term>animus</term> <note>The lower, "animal" part of the mind that contains passions and desires.</note> first resides, for it exists within this as a pure natural mind. Because this belongs to the intellectory—which is formed entirely from the substance of its own soul—it must necessarily also be formed according to the mind or spirit of its soul. Therefore, whatever the soul is like, the animus will be the same in its very formation, even while hidden in the womb and during earliest infancy. 

At that stage, the animus is entirely subject to the <term>spiritual mind</term>. However, later, once the <term>rational mind</term> is formed and the states of the <term>intellectory</term> begin to depend on the state of the <term>sensories</term> <note>the sensory organs or the brain's processing of them</note>, an inversion begins to take place. The animus then depends on an <term>influx</term> <note>original: "influx"; an inward flow or influence</note> of objects and harmonies coming from the world through the external senses, and from the body through the blood.

(474.) From these facts, it follows that the spiritual mind flows into the animus, becoming its very essence and life; for the animus cannot exist or survive without the spiritual mind. This is why the spiritual mind always loves the animus. But when the animus rebels and wishes to make itself superior, it is rejected by the spiritual mind, and a perpetual battle arises, almost as if it were a conflict between God and the Devil. Each desires to occupy the rational mind, but victory can belong to only one. Nor can the animus be expelled suddenly; rather, there must be <term>perseverance</term> until the end of life.

<summary>This page explains that the lower mind (animus) is originally formed by the soul and is initially subject to it. However, as a person develops, the animus begins to be influenced by external senses, leading to a spiritual conflict within the rational mind that lasts throughout life.</summary>

<keywords>pure intellectory, animus, spiritual mind, soul, rational mind, influx, sensory organs, spiritual conflict</keywords>

(475.) When, therefore, a bad <term>animus</term> <note>The lower, "animal" part of the mind that contains passions and desires.</note> has been changed into a good one, or a good one into a bad one—just as an acquired nature tries to expel one's original nature—then the previous animus is changed. Once the animus is changed, the state of the soul is changed as a result. This happens not by direct <term>influx</term> <note>original: "influx"; an inward flow of influence</note>, however, but by <term>correspondence</term> <note>A harmonious relationship where higher and lower levels of existence act in unison without direct physical contact.</note>, with the <term>rational mind</term> acting as the intermediary and Divine grace working alongside it. 

There must be a specific disposition so that the spiritual mind may be able to flow in with its loves; at the very least, there must be a rejection of the base desires of the animus. This ensures the soul is ready to flow in with its spiritual loves, or at least that the mind is prepared for the influx of those loves. In this process, the intellect contributes nothing on its own except for what is learned through revelation. Instead, it is faith springing from God and the calling upon His Divine power that allows His spirit to flow into the soul, changing its state or perfecting it. 

However, long practice is needed for a bad soul to become good, although it does not take as long to restore a good soul through a change of mind. In this sense, there is a certain "election" of souls, for without a miraculous and specific favor from God, a bad soul cannot be made good all at once. There must be self-discipline, most ardent prayer, and a continual zeal for what is truly spiritual and divine. These appear to be the true principles for attaining spiritual perfection. Something spiritual and divine flows down from above into what is below; external things cannot bring any change to what is within except through correspondence, and such correspondence does not exist in the soul except as a gift from the Divine.

### *The Influx of the Spiritual Loves of the Soul into the Rational Mind, and the reverse.*

(476.) The spiritual mind, or that which belongs to the soul, can never flow into the rational mind except through the animus or by its means. Consequently, this only happens while the animus is subject to the spiritual mind. Therefore, in order that—

# XXV.

## INCLINATIONS AND TEMPERAMENTS.

(477.) There are countless human natures or inclinations, since no person is inclined in exactly the same way as another; but all these inclinations, which have infinite variety, may be categorized into three general types: namely, *the inclination toward being wise, or toward honor and virtues; the inclination toward knowing, which is an active and natural principle;* and *the inclination toward understanding, which may be called intellectual.*

(478.) The inclination to be wise, or the spiritual inclination toward what is honorable or virtuous, originates in the soul and signifies a good soul or a spiritual mind, which is guided by genuine loves. But since the body is shaped as a reflection of the soul’s activities, it follows that this inclination must be **connate** <term>existing in a person from birth; innate.</term>. The seeds of honor and virtue appear to be inborn and prevail throughout entire families and their descendants. These virtues themselves are innumerable. One person inclines toward a specific virtue or virtuous quality, while another inclines toward a different one. The reason why this inclination exists is to be found in the spiritual state of the soul itself. This state is inherited at birth from the parents, whose soul the **progeny** <note>original: "progeny"; meaning offspring or descendants.</note> inherits; for the parent, however, this state was achieved through the frequent exercise of virtues and the practice of piety lasting until the end of life. It is also proven that descendants may overcome the crimes of their parents or, conversely, receive rewards on account of their parents’ actions.

<summary>This page categorizes human inclinations into three types—wisdom, knowing, and understanding—and explains how a virtuous disposition is an innate quality inherited from the spiritual state of one's parents.</summary>

(480.) *The inclination toward understanding.*—Some people are born with a prodigious memory, by which they can imitate an intellect; or with a facility for expressing the feelings of their animus; or with a presence of mind, a talent for meditation, or a vivid imagination. Some are born with an inclination toward judging profoundly even regarding wisdom itself, although they may actually lack wisdom; others are drawn toward specific sciences, such as mathematics, philosophy, history, and many other branches. This also is derived from the parent by the same cause: namely, that the senses are more inclined to take on these mutations of state than others. But the inmost cause is found in the intellectory, in the changeability of its animus, and in the love and affection arising from it; for as it was in the parent, so it is in the offspring.

(481.) But all these inclinations can be changed by age, resulting from both external and especially from internal [causes]...

### ***Temperaments.***

(482.) There are four temperaments listed: the sanguine, the choleric, the melancholy, and the phlegmatic. These are merely inclinations of the <term>animus</term> <note>original: "animus"; in Swedenborg’s psychology, this refers to the lower, sensory mind where emotions and passions reside.</note> or the diverse states of the mind into which we are born.

The *sanguine temperament* indicates a state in which the animus is noticeably active in receiving sensations and producing ideas. It is equally prone to various passions and thus not stubborn in its opinions; it is easily pleased and lively. This animus shines through the face, eyes, speech, voice, gestures, and specific actions; a full description of it is provided by the <term>physiologists</term> <note>In this context, authors who write about the relationship between physical traits and character.</note>.

The *choleric temperament* indicates an animus that is not so prone to pleasures and various desires, but is serious—sometimes resentful and gloomy if another person does not favor one’s opinion or love—but otherwise, in a good person, it generally loves what is honorable. The face and outward form belonging to this temperament are also described by these writers.

The *melancholic temperament* indicates a sad mind, lost in fantasies and indulging more in internal rather than external feelings. It is more averse to pleasures and belongs to an internal rather than an external person. Unlike the sanguine temperament, the melancholic person is stubborn in their opinions, believing theories and opinions to be absolute truths, and thinking themselves wiser than—

It is clear that as "diviners" of character, these temperaments are very unreliable, and they change as a person ages. This is because the blood, to which the temperaments are linked, changes in various ways. For instance, we call someone "sanguine" if they have more fluid or refined blood; "choleric" if their blood is sharper, more bilious, more flecked <note>The original translator noted that the editor of the Latin edition was uncertain if "flecked" was the correct reading of the original manuscript.</note>, and drier; "melancholic" if the blood is harder and dry; and "phlegmatic" if it is more sluggish and thick.

# IMMORTALITY.

### XXVI.

### CONCERNING DEATH.

(486.) **We have previously shown what the body is and what its form consists of—namely, that the body is made of forms that are inferior, in an orderly and successive progression, to the soul, which is the spiritual form. Thus, the body is composed of both purer and denser parts. The form of the soul is spiritual; that of the <term>intellectory</term> <note>original: "intellectory"; in Swedenborg’s system, this is the highest organic faculty of the mind, which perceives truths and receives the soul's light.</note> is celestial; that of the internal sensory is <term>vortical</term> <note>original: "vortical"; a complex, high-level form characterized by vortex-like motion, which Swedenborg ranked above the spiral form.</note>; that of the external sensory or the brain is spiral; and that of the physical extension itself, which is strictly called the body, is circular. Its bones, cartilages, and similar parts have an angular form, as do the many elements that enter into and constitute the blood; in every globule of blood, every form is concealed, from the first one to the last.**

(487.) **These forms are so connected that one holds the other very tightly, so that they appear to be a single entity even though they are quite distinct from one another. Consequently, the soul is said to descend from its "heaven" into the world when it enters into these forms and shapes its organs out of itself and its own substance—organs whose forms are ultimately physical and material. The reason for this is so that the soul can participate in the functions of this lowest world and operate in a way that aligns with its own forces. If it did not take on a physical form, it would** <note>This sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>Swedenborg describes the human body as a hierarchy of forms ranging from the spiritual soul down to the angular shapes of bones, explaining that the soul "descends" into these material structures to interact with the physical world.</summary>

All are formed according to their nature, to which the gifts each shall exercise are adapted.

(488.) The destruction of these final <note>original: "ultimate"</note> forms is called dying. The lowest forms are those first destroyed, followed in order by the purer and the higher forms, up to the soul or the spiritual form, which cannot be destroyed. First, the angular form is destroyed—that is, the connection of its parts is severed, and the angular bodies within the blood and the humors <note>original: "humours"; the various fluids of the body</note> are dissipated. This is why such a small portion of the blood is seen remaining in the dead. Afterward, the circular form—or the form of the various internal organs <note>original: "viscera"</note>—is destroyed, as is the outward form of the body, which collapses. Then the brain, or the spiral form, is destroyed, and so on with the remaining ones in their proper order.

(489.) A thing is said to die or to be destroyed when that which is unique to its form perishes or is dissolved. Thus, the arrangement and the connection of the parts, their order, and consequently their state, are the specific properties of a thing; besides these, there is nothing that belongs uniquely to any form. When these are dissolved, then the form perishes or dies, and all that affection <note>original: "affection"; in this context, the capacity of a form to be moved or to respond to stimuli</note> which was adapted to it passes away. Thus, the soul is no longer able to perceive those things that agree with itself—namely, the modifications <note>original: "modifications"; the changes or vibrations in the physical world that produce sensation</note> and influences of the physical <note>original: "ultimate"</note> world and its harmonies, or sensations and similar impressions—nor can it perform other bodily functions, for every muscle is destroyed. Although each motor fiber may remain, the property of the muscle as such perishes, for the arrangement, connection, order, and state of its motor fibers are destroyed. The motor fibers may be dissolved and die, and still the nervous fibers which compose...

The lowest forms are always the first to die because they are changeable, inconsistent, imperfect, and their structures <note>original: "determinations"</note> are less harmonious. The triangular form perishes before the circular, and the circular before the spiral; for as a form ascends, something of the eternal <note>original: "perpetual"</note> is added, or something of the limited and inconsistent is taken away. This is the reason why the dissolution of forms—and therefore of the body, which consists of these forms—takes place in this specific order.

(490.) Hence, it follows that more time is required for the dissolution of a higher form than a lower one, and more for a circular than an angular form. Thus, death proceeds from the external man to the internal man, and the progress becomes slower as it moves toward the interior parts.

(491.) But let us take the blood as an example. A globule of blood consists of all the forms, even up to the first spiritual form. The red blood is dissolved first, and its angular elements are scattered; this effect takes place immediately. Next, the "pure blood" that remains is dissolved, but only after a considerable lapse of time. Then there remains what is properly called the "animal spirit" <term>in historical physiology, the "animal spirit" was a subtle fluid thought to carry sensation and life through the nerves</term> or its individual part. This is not easily dissolved because it is a celestial form. After this, only the soul remains, purified from all that is earthly.

(492.) Thus, through death, that which was taken from the earth is given back to the earth, such as whatever was in the blood and its fluids <term>original: "humours"</term>. What was taken from the air is likewise returned to it, as is what was taken from the ether. What remains is that which is purely *living* <note>original: *animal*; in this context, the word is derived from the Latin *anima* (soul) and refers to the life-force, not a "beast"</note> and the *living* property—namely, the soul <note>original: *anima*</note>—which alone is what truly lives, and lives in the...

Ultimately, the soul is stripped of all earthly components, returning physical elements to the earth, air, and ether.</summary>

(493.) The question arises, therefore: what lives die, or what organic connections are dissolved? For there are as many degrees of life as there are degrees of organs. The life of the tongue is different from that of hearing; that of the ear is different from that of the eye; and that of the eye is different from that of the internal sensory organ, which is called perception. Furthermore, the life of the sensory organ is different from that of the "intellectory" <note>intellectory: Swedenborg’s term for the higher organic structure or faculty through which the intellect functions</note>, and that of the intellectory is different from the life of the soul. The soul is spiritual and is the essential life within all the other degrees of life, in which it resides according to their specific form and through those forms. These forms themselves are called "organic," and they are the actual substances whose changes <note>original: "affections"; the modifications or responses of a physical substance to stimuli</note> are called sensations.

(494.) Therefore, in order to know which forms are dissolved or which lives die, it is quite clear that the general life of the body dies, or that the overall connection <note>original: "nexus"</note> of all its parts is dissolved. Likewise, the external sensory organs—touch, taste, smell, hearing, and sight, along with the physical structures of each—die as well. This also includes the internal sensory organ, the intellect, and the rational mind—specifically, the cortical glands <note>cortical glands: Swedenborg's term for the gray matter or neurons of the brain's cortex, which he believed were the fundamental units of mental activity</note> and the changes in their states. For no such intellect existed in the embryo, and it hardly existed in the infant; it increased with age and reached completion in the adult. It then decreases in old age, is weakened and suffers in disease, and therefore dies along with the body. This intellect has been acquired so that the soul, by means of it, might perceive what happens outside itself (specifically through the senses) and also so that it might perform those functions that must be exercised in this lowest world. When the soul no longer lives in this final world, and no longer wishes to perceive what is happening here in these lowest spheres, nor what...

<summary>Swedenborg distinguishes between the dissolution of the physical organism and the death of the life attached to it, explaining that the intellect and sensory organs are temporary tools developed for life in the physical world.</summary>

Since these tasks are required on earth and within human society, then as the necessity and the use for them disappear, the faculty itself perishes, along with the organ destined for that use.*

Oh, how miserable we would be if, after death, we lived in a rational mind with our imperfect intellect and our inconsistent will—governed by so many shifting states and desires, being ourselves partly spiritual and partly animal! Such a mind could equally change and, after certain intervals, die in the future life just as it does in the present, for it would not have changed its nature. **Therefore, our rational mind with its desires and affections, and our intellect with its principles, opinions, and reasonings, die and do not survive their body.†**

(495.) **As for the pure intellectory <note>intellectory: Swedenborg’s term for the higher organic structure or faculty through which the intellect functions</note>, to which the pure natural mind belongs, this indeed also seems to die or be dissolved,** but only after a very long delay. Because it is a celestial form, there are no forms present that can destroy it; however, it is not within our power to say how long it continues. (496.) But it is asked: why must the body be dissolved, or the physical life extinguished? The reason why this is ordained by Divine Providence is very evident if we consider the goal of creation: namely, that there may be a universal society of souls which shall make up heaven. This would be impossible without a nursery on the earth, and without the death of those dwelling there to allow for a perpetual succession. It is also necessary so that souls may be formed in their bodies and reformed for their eternal state. What is earthly and physical cannot be eternal, because it is inherently changeable, inconsistent, imperfect, and always decaying. Death is therefore inseparable from the physical life, especially since it is subject to the will of the rational mind, which always takes away the physical life <note>original: *quae semper aufert vitam corpoream*</note>.

(497.) Besides this, the soul would never be able to be left to its own authority and free will—according to its living nature—without death; for it is intertwined in—

...writings, namely, that of the Last Judgment as occurring at the end of the world, and as accompanied by a physical fire. In the *True Christian Religion* and in the treatise on *The Last Judgment*, he teaches that the passages of the Scriptures dealing with the end of the world are written according to the law of correspondence (as is all of the Divine Word). They are to be understood according to their spiritual meaning, relating to the end of the first Christian Church or religious era <term>dispensation: a specific period of religious history or a divine system</term>, due to the extinction of its faith and charity. He teaches that the Last Judgment takes place not in our physical world, but in the world of spirits. It consists of the separation of the good from the evil spirits there, and the establishment of "a new heaven and a new earth," in the sense of a new angelic heaven of those who are saved, and a new Church on earth of those who believe in the Lord and obey his commandments. 

In this sense, Swedenborg declares that the "end of the world" has already come, and the Last Judgment has already taken place, and that the former Christian Church has accordingly reached its end. He asserts that a new Christian Church is now being formed of those who receive the Lord in His Second Coming, worshipping Him in His Divine Humanity as the only God of heaven and earth, and endeavoring to keep His commandments through a life of combined faith and charity. This "Second Coming of the Lord" is not in person, but in the Word, which is from Him and is Himself. It is brought about by means of a man before whom He has manifested Himself, and whom He has filled with His Spirit to teach the doctrines of the New Church through the Word, from Him. (See Swedenborg's *True Christian Religion*, no. 776, and following. <note>original: *Tr.*; Translator's note</note>)

<header>IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL.</header>

## XXVII.

### **OF THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL.**

(498.) The nature of the soul has been defined and described earlier: it is immaterial, lacking physical size <note>original: "extension"</note>, motion, or individual parts. Because of this, it contains nothing within it that can decay or die. However, these are really just linguistic descriptions <note>original: "verbal predications"</note> rather than true definitions, because these terms do not quite fit the higher levels of existence—though they do share some similarities in meaning. Without using analogies, it is hard to avoid the idea of "nothingness" when using the definitions above. Therefore, we should instead turn our attention to the *form* <note>In Swedenborg's era, "form" referred to the essential nature or organizational principle of a thing, rather than just its outward shape.</note> of the soul itself. It is said that the form of the soul is spiritual, and within this spiritual form, those qualities that are limited in lower forms become infinite. 

According to this description, all concepts of physical location—such as a center, a surface, "above," or "below"—and thus all concepts of motion and physical space <note>original: "extent"</note>, disappear or are set aside. This follows from the very idea of this form: it contains nothing within it that can perish. For anything to be destroyed, there must be a change in the position and connection of its parts. But in a form that has no concept of place, center, or surface—or rather, a form where the center, the circumference, and the surface are everywhere at once—destruction is impossible to imagine. This form is the very opposite of destruction; it is oriented entirely toward permanence <note>original: "perpetuity"</note>. In fact, the more it is attacked, the more it resists any effort to destroy it.

(499.) If we examine various forms in their natural order, it appears that as a form becomes higher, or ascends to a superior level, it always gains a greater degree of permanence.

<vocab>immortality, soul, immaterial, spiritual form, analogy, permanence, destruction</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the soul is immortal because its "spiritual form" lacks the physical dimensions and parts required for decay or destruction. He posits that higher spiritual forms are inherently resistant to destruction and oriented toward eternal permanence.</summary>
<keywords>immortality, soul, spiritual form, non-extension, permanence, substance, metaphysics</keywords>

Thus, in proceeding from the angular to the circular, the circle becomes perpetual, and all its lines and planes align <note>original: "conspire"</note> toward a certain eternity. However, this circular form—whether by expanding from the center to the circumference or by resisting the impact of other objects on its surface—either returns to its original state or enters into a different one. Therefore, to ensure that the circular form does not perish through expansion, there is a higher level of permanence in the **spiral form**. In a spiral, the coils terminate in and return to a kind of circular surface. By this expansion and return, and by keeping that unbroken surface in view, this figure is more certain to endure. 

But even this spiral figure still relates to a center, and is therefore still liable to destruction. This possibility of perishing is completely removed, however, in even higher forms, such as the **vortical** and **celestial**. The permanence in the **spiritual form** is such that, by virtue of its very nature, the form is secure. In this state, one structural direction <note>term: "determination" (the direction or alignment of the soul's essential forces)</note> so regards another that each renders the other entirely safe from every injury. This is the result of the form itself and the perfection in which it was created.

(500.) Moreover, the spiritual form draws its essence directly <note>original: "immediately"</note> from God by inspiration <note>In this context, "inspiration" refers to the "breathing in" of life from the Divine.</note>, as a child does from its parent. Therefore, in its very creation, the soul acknowledges the Deity—God Himself—as its immediate Father. It recognizes that it exists from the Immortal and Eternal itself, and can neither be destroyed nor become mortal. This is why the soul is immortal: not because of its own power, but because of God, who alone is immortal in Himself. It is through Him that the soul becomes so.

(501.) Since the soul is the most internal and supreme of all forms, the first natural form is beneath it, and the lower forms recede all the way down to the angular, just as the earth recedes from heaven. Consequently, the soul can in no way be touched—and certainly not destroyed—by these lower forms found in nature. Tell me, how can that which is most internal be destroyed by those things which are outside it? Or how can that...

...how can that which is supreme be affected by those things which are below it? Or how can that which is simple be affected by those which are composite <note>original: "compound"</note>, or what is primary by what follows it, or what is most perfect in itself by things which are themselves imperfect? For the imperfect only has the power to exist because of the perfect qualities within it. That which possesses the infinite within itself cannot be touched by the finite, much less destroyed; what is constant in itself cannot be destroyed by what is unstable. These superior forms, especially the spiritual ones, are capable of undergoing infinite changes of state, for their perfection consists in this very ability. 

If we imagine an attack, collision, or something similar occurring (as happens with lower forms), the soul’s state can change in any way and still return to its original condition. This is similar to how the most elastic natural substances can be bent and unbent, expanded and compressed, and yet return to their own shape. Thus, as they are acted upon, they react in kind; therefore, they cannot be forced out of their natural state by any power or shock.

(502.) From this it follows that nothing earthly <note>original: "terrestrial"</note> can touch the soul in any way—whether it be substances moving through the air, ether, or fire, nor anything in the atmosphere, not even the purest natural fire. All of these are far below the soul and have no contact with it. Even if they did, they could not exert the slightest force, for the soul is secure within its own form. 

This is also evident within the body itself, where there is a great deal of turbulence from volatile particles taken in from the earth, the air, and the ether; yet these do not disturb or damage even the smallest organic connection, placement, or order. Millions <note>original: "Myriads"</note> of the substances belonging to the soul could fit within the smallest physical <note>original: "angular form"; Swedenborg often uses "angular" to describe the lowest, least perfect level of geometry/matter</note> form. It would be like saying that a large wooden beam could split a single particle of ether in two, when in reality millions of such ether particles touch that heavy mass and even pass through its pores. Or, it would be as if you said that the posts and beams of a house could destroy the forces of attraction and direction...

For life itself consists of truly spiritual loves. When these are extinguished and replaced by opposite loves or hatreds, then that which truly lived is said to be "dead." To truly live is to love God and to be wise. In this state, the form and essence themselves remain and cannot perish. (505.) However, one might ask why life itself seems to die and be destroyed along with our body—or rather, why what we perceive as life seems to belong to the body more than the soul. We see this in instances like fainting <note>original: "swoonings"</note>, spiritual trances <note>original: "ecstasies"</note>, dreams, near-drownings, or cases where people thought to be dead are revived <note>original: "the buried coming to life"</note>. We see it also in embryonic life and other cases where, after being revived into physical life, the person is completely unaware that they were living in the meantime. No trace remains in their memory of what they thought, or if they even thought at all. From these and similar examples, it appears as though life were merely physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> and not a quality of the soul at all.

(506.) But in these, as in countless other cases, we are misled by appearances. The life of the soul is not like our physical sensation or perception, or even like our conscious thought; it is more perfect and superior, flowing into the thought itself and refining it so that the mind is able to think. Thought itself, however, is something learned through practice; it is a faculty of the rational mind, and it *perishes along with the body*. 

The nature of the soul's pure life and intelligence, and how it flows into our thoughts, can be seen through reflection alone. Specifically, the soul naturally understands all the secrets of any science when it operates within the body, sensations, and thoughts. This knowledge is not learned by the soul but is inborn, flowing from the soul's very life. Does the eye not explore all the secrets of <term>optics</term> <note>The branch of physics that studies the behavior and properties of light.</note>, or the ear those of <term>acoustics</term> <note>The branch of physics concerned with the properties of sound.</note>, in order to know instinctively how to form sounds and how to harmonize them? (507.) Since the life of the soul is of the nature we have described, it cannot leave any impression on our rational mind. It is the soul that hears, sees, perceives, thinks, judges, and wills, though it does so through an organic form <note>the physical structure of the body</note> and not otherwise. For example, sight appears as if it were located in the eye; yet, when the eye is closed, we still see with an internal vision. # XXVIII.

## OF THE STATE OF THE SOUL AFTER THE DEATH OF THE BODY.

(511.) Everyone desires to know what the state of the soul will be after death. There is no one who does not imagine <note>original: "conjecture"</note> that the future state will be similar to our physical life, or the life we experienced in the rational mind. After all, if a person has not mentally grasped the different levels <note>original: "degrees"</note> of life, how could they imagine any life that is superior, more perfect, more universal, or more abstract than what we experience in the rational mind? There are few who deny the continued existence of the life they attribute to the soul and to the *animus* <note>In Swedenborg's terminology, the "animus" refers to the lower or sentient mind—the seat of emotions and sensory perception—as distinct from the higher rational soul.</note>. The wise men of the non-Christian <note>original: "gentile"</note> nations unanimously believed in the survival of the soul, as can be seen in the works of Greek authors, the Sophists, Plato, and Aristotle, as well as in Cicero and all the rest. Furthermore, to place this doctrine beyond all doubt, Pythagoras and Socrates even attempted to describe the soul's state after death. We Christians, being even better informed by the Holy Scriptures, not only believe in the immortal life of the soul, but also that there is a state of happiness, or heaven, and a state of unhappiness, or hell. But let us follow the psychological principles we have proposed in their proper order and explain what these principles dictate.

(512.) It is a common opinion that immediately after the death of the body, the soul is separated, flies away, and leaves its corpse behind. But when we consider that the universal form of the body exists only from the one sub- <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>Swedenborg notes that while most people imagine the afterlife to be similar to physical life, ancient philosophers and Christian scripture agree on the soul's immortality. He begins to examine the soul's separation from the body using his specific psychological principles.</summary>

...substance <note>The word completes the sentence from the previous page.</note>, the soul, or originates from the soul (for nothing exists that does not begin with the simple fibre, and the simple fibre originates from the simple cortex <note>In Swedenborg's anatomy, the "simple cortex" and "simple fibre" are the most fundamental, microscopic building blocks of the nervous system and the body.</note>, and so on). Since the soul is the true essence and substance from which the entire organic form of the body is created—and is therefore the "all in every part," residing deep within the center of everything, even the blood itself (the core essence of which is the soul within it)—it follows that the entire soul does not flee from the body the very moment physical life ends. Instead, it remains as long as there are any parts not yet dissolved in which it can still dwell. 

This is proven by many examples of people who returned to life several days after their funeral rites were performed and lived for many more years among mortals, as historians record. There are also those who have been suffocated by drowning or by strangulation <note>original: "constriction of the throat"</note> and have revived after several days. In such cases, the soul cannot have left the body; once the obstructions are removed and the water is cleared, the soul immediately re-enters its dwelling. There are also those who resemble the dying by undergoing fainting spells, syncope <note>A temporary loss of consciousness caused by a fall in blood pressure.</note>, and similar attacks; nevertheless, the soul does not depart but remains and lives on, even though the body appears as if it were dead <note>original: "extinct"</note>. 

Many examples also exist, even in sacred history, of it being forbidden to disturb the bodies and bones of the dead, so that they may rest in peace and not be scattered. Samuel <note>A reference to the biblical account in 1 Samuel 28, where the spirit of the prophet Samuel is summoned from the dead.</note> was also brought back to life, and many other instances are recorded in both sacred and secular <note>original: "profane"</note> history. We seem to know through an innate sense, as if the soul itself dictates it to us, that if the bones of the dead are disturbed, their spirits <note>original: "shades"</note> will confront those who violate them; many stories are told of such occurrences. Furthermore, it has been part of the religion of some peoples to kiss, revere, and pray to the bones of heroes and saints so that they might provide or obtain help. These practices would be completely pointless <note>original: "the merest vanities"</note> if the soul were to leave the body entirely, leaving behind only that which is earthly...

**Main Content.** Meanwhile, from the course of our arguments, it follows that the soul—which creates the very form of the body and its parts, as well as the blood and the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>In early physiology, "animal spirit" was thought to be a subtle fluid that carried sensory information and motor commands through the nerves.</note>—cannot be released from its bonds until the lower and more unstable physical forms are first dissolved. Although it cannot be denied that much of the soul may be released from these bonds, it is still not separated because of this. It is contrary to the nature of spirits for those substances that are born and made to complete a single system to be separated. What is woven together with other parts may indeed be loosened; yet, even when loosened from those bonds, it appears that an entire separation from all bonds is impossible until a most pure elementary fire intervenes, or until the <term>conflagration of the world</term> <note>original: "conflagration of the world." This refers to the historical belief that the physical world would eventually be destroyed by a great fire.</note>. *

(513.) But it is asked: what kind of life does the soul live while it still remains in the dead body, where the order, arrangement, and connection of the organic parts are completely destroyed? That life must necessarily be a very dim one, or simply life without intelligence. This is clear from the very definition of intelligence. All intelligence requires not only an internal form and a change of state within the individual <term>sensories and intellectories</term> <note>Swedenborg’s terms for the microscopic structures in the brain responsible for sensation and thought.</note>, but also an external form for these parts—one that enables them to maintain a mutual arrangement and order. Once this order among the parts is destroyed, and with it their arrangement and connection, the communication of forces, changes, and emotions <note>original: "affections"</note> immediately stops. In its place, a certain irregularity follows, resulting in a kind of life that is not distinct or determined, but confused and dim; it may be called merely life without intelligence—

Our intellect is immediately disrupted when the position and connection of the sensory or <term>cortical glands</term> <note>Swedenborg used this term to describe the individual functional units of the brain's gray matter, which he correctly identified as the seat of sensation and thought.</note> are disturbed, as we see from medical accounts of brain diseases. (514.) However, when the organism is not yet destroyed and its order is not yet disturbed, a distinct soul-life remains, as seen in the embryo. Here, Swedenborg refers to the soul's transition or rebirth into the next life.</note>.

(515.) Indeed, the substance of the soul, once freed from its physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> bonds, seems to live a distinct life—one that is actually more distinct because it has been liberated from these physical hindrances. These highly individual entities form a society among themselves and establish a very clear order, being left to their own freedom while awaiting companions; for the larger the society, the more perfect the life becomes. For someone who has lived a long life, this society—which forms a unified body—has become that much larger.

(516.) Since the soul is composed of substances with a spiritual form, some might believe that these individual substances will scatter after the body's dissolution and never again unite into the society of a single body. Such an opinion, however, arises from ignorance regarding the world, its purer nature, and the nature of higher beings. For we believe that—

something remains when the body’s small particles are reduced to smoke, vapor, dust, and ashes; but a completely different process follows from this. In that supreme, most pure, and perfect world—or where nature exists in its simplest and most fundamental state—we cannot imagine a separation <note>original: "disjunction"</note> of those entities which, through their mutual harmony and similarity, belong to a single body. Each living and spiritual substance of the soul recognizes its companion in the body as its own; it cannot live in union <note>original: "mutual consort"</note> with any other. 

Nothing prevents them from coming together, for there is no space, place, or time to separate them. These conditions belong entirely to a lower nature and not to the supreme. Place exists only in relation to lower beings, where relationships involve an "up" and a "down," "right" and "left," a center, surface, and diameter—essentially, so that there may be a *where*. But in the supreme world, all consideration of place is based on the relationship between one soul and another, since these are entirely distinct from each other. Nor can these substances of the soul be separated, for one recognizes, feels, and knows the other, even if they were as far apart (relatively speaking) as the sun is from the earth or one star is from another. Indeed, when sensory organs as coarse as the eye can reach from the earth to the sun and stars, what might the sight of the soul—the intelligence—not encompass? This capacity could well be called a spiritual sympathy.

Since nothing prevents these substances of the soul from reuniting, it is only our ignorance of the purer world that deceives us. This ignorance suggests a scattering <note>original: "dissipation"</note> that is impossible in that higher world. This is especially true since the omnipresence of the Divine Spirit, acting upon all souls, cannot allow anything belonging to a specific soul to be separated from it. For there is a Spirit that unites all things under its authority, bringing together what is harmonious <note>original: "concordant"</note>, separating what is clashing <note>original: "discordant"</note>, and thus gathering all souls together. This is a necessary conclusion; if we consider the <term>influx</term> <note>original: "influx." (517.) When similar phenomena occur in the world and in lower, less perfect nature, why would they not also occur in the superior and most perfect realm? For there, nothing exists that is irregular; everything is perfectly harmonious, consistent, and unified. It is well known that shrubs, plants, flowers, and roses, even when burned to dust, can be brought back to life in water; their vegetative lives or spiritual essences <note>Swedenborg refers here to the vital force or formative principle of plants. In the 1700s, this was often associated with "palingenesis," a chemical experiment where the "shadow" of a plant was said to rise from its ashes.</note> are, as it were, reawakened by some means. Once the form itself is reawakened, even if the vessel breaks and it falls back into its ashes, it revives again. Thus, these parts sometimes cannot be so disconnected or separated that they fail to return to their original form. They reunite in their old friendship and habit after these changes—and indeed, they reunite into exactly their original form. Why, then, should human souls not do the same after the destruction of the body?

(518.) I need not speak of those obvious sympathies also recognized in this lower world, which are so numerous that they cannot all be listed. This sympathy and this kind of "magnetism" is so great that it can often be shared among thousands of people. Some consider these phenomena to be mere fairy tales; yet experience itself confirms their truth. I am not even referring to stories of the "shades" <note>shades: spirits or ghosts</note> of certain people becoming visible after the death and funeral rites <note>original: "obsequies"</note> of the body. Even if we admitted such stories were true—which I do not—this could never happen unless the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>The "animal spirit" was historically believed to be a subtle fluid or essence that flowed through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note> were mutually joined and not separated from their shared association. At the very least, such a bond of love exists between the component parts of the body itself that they maintain a mutual relationship and cannot be separated. This is also the reason for the mutual love between people who are physically bonded.

That the soul itself is such a substance is evident from the love of parents toward their offspring. Because a parent knows that the child's soul is taken from their own, they know and love it so inwardly that they wish to be joined to it and to enter into it again—an effort they attempt in vain through kisses and embraces. If this is so, how much more will the various parts of the universal soul of one body desire to be united?

(520.) Meanwhile, it must be admitted that one soul would never be distinct from another if the state of one were absolutely identical to the state of the other. But since it is provided that there shall always be some difference between souls, they cannot be merged; instead, each soul must form its own body and must live its own life. Thus, one soul recognizes the substances that belong to itself and its own system. Drawn by a certain sympathetic love, it is unable to unite itself with any other substance, for that is not its own and cannot be united with it into a single body. A universal Divine providence therefore reigns in distinguishing every individual from every other, so that no single soul shall be precisely like another.

(521.) But it is asked: What is the form of the soul to be in heaven? Will it be similar to the bodily form, or another form which is called "angelic"? And then, is the angelic form like the human form? At this time, I do not believe that we are to take on the human form. <note>original: "put on the human form"</note> *

In heaven, souls are like birds, and they do not interact with any physical earth; they have no need for feet or arms, and therefore no need for muscles—that is, for flesh and bones—because they are spirits. Indeed, they require neither red blood, nor a stomach <note>original: ventricle</note>, nor intestines, nor the supporting abdominal tissues <note>original: mesentery</note>; for these things are only for receiving food, for digestion <note>original: chylifaction; the process of turning food into a milky fluid</note>, and for nutrition.

> *...for I have seen, heard, and conversed with spirits thousands of times, and have even talked with them about the **general disbelief that spirits are human beings**, and have told them that the learned call those people foolish who think so. The spirits were deeply grieved that such ignorance should still continue in the world, and especially that it should prevail within the church. They said that this disbelief originates chiefly with the scholars, who think of the soul according to their physical and sensory perceptions. Thus, these scholars conclude that the soul is mere thought which—when viewed without any physical body in which it exists—is like a fleeting breath of pure ether that must vanish when the body dies. But since the church, on the authority of the Bible <note>original: the Word</note>, believes in the immortality of the soul, they feel forced to credit it with some vital principle like "thought," even though they deny it has any capacity for sensation <note>original: sensitive principle</note> such as a person has, until it is reunited with the body. This is the foundation of the prevailing idea concerning the resurrection, and of the belief that the soul and the body will be joined again at the time of the Last Judgment. Consequently, when anyone thinks about the soul based on this doctrine and hypothesis, they do not imagine it to be a spirit in a human form. Indeed, scarcely anyone today understands what a "spiritual principle" is, and still less that spiritual beings—angels and all spirits—are in the human form. Almost everyone, therefore, who passes out of this world into the other is astonished to find themselves alive, and that they are human beings just as before; that they can see, hear, and speak; that they enjoy the sense of touch as they did before; and that there is no discernible difference whatsoever.*
> 
> *A spirit enjoys every sense, both external and internal, which he enjoyed in the world; he sees as before; he hears and speaks as before; he smells and tastes as before; and when he is touched, he feels as before. He also longs, desires, wishes, thinks, reflects, is moved by emotion, loves, and wills, as before; and he who delighted in studies reads and writes as before. In a word, when a person passes from one life into the other, it is like moving from one place to another, for he carries with him everything which he possessed in himself as a human being. It cannot be said that death deprives a person of anything truly essential to themselves, since death is only the separation of the earthly body. The natural memory also remains, for spirits retain everything which they had heard, seen, read, learned, and thought in the world, from earliest infancy to the end of life. However, since the natural objects which are in the memory cannot be reproduced in the spiritual world, they are dormant <note>original: quiescent</note>, just as they are for a person in this world when he is not thinking of them; nevertheless, they are reproduced whenever the Lord pleases....... Sensual men <note>meaning those who believe only what they can perceive with their physical senses</note> cannot believe that such is the state of man after death, for the sensory-focused person can only think naturally even about spiritual things. Therefore, whatever is not physical to the bodily senses—whatever he does not see with his eyes or feel with his hands—he claims does not exist.*

Regarding the great difference which nevertheless exists between the life of the two worlds and between the senses and their emotions in each, see *Heaven and Hell*, numbers 462, 126, and 235.

See, however, Appendix A, Thesis 12, where the doctrine of the human form of departed spirits seems to be already clearly maintained by our author.

(522.) But it is asked, what form shall we have? This we can no more know than the silkworm can. We are deeply ignorant about the nature of that purest atmosphere <term>aura</term> <note>In Swedenborg's science, "aura" refers to a subtle, invisible fluid or ether through which celestial forces move</note> which is called heavenly, and in which souls are to live. In that state, souls are completely equipped with such a form that—like birds in our own atmosphere—they may travel everywhere and fly through universes and heavens, their limbs and their form being exactly adapted to 그 life. Therefore, until we know what that atmosphere is, and what life we are to live in it, we are wholly unable to say what form we shall take on. ...rather, it is the most perfect of all forms. It is a form into which we shall be changed, just as larvae <note>original: nymphae</note> and chrysalises <note>original: aureliae</note> are changed into more perfect forms. This is a form to which our souls also aspire—and for this reason, they would often accelerate the death of the body. This aspiration is inborn in the soul and is not shared by the body.

(523.) In the meantime, when the soul is left to itself and is no longer connected with the physical <note>original: organic</note> forms necessary for the pursuit of bodily life, it seems to be able to take on any form it may wish. Thus, if it should descend from heaven to earth, it might take on the human form in a moment. For all of nature is formed in such a way that it serves the spiritual life as an instrumental cause <term>instrumental cause</term> <note>A philosophical term meaning a tool or means used by a higher power to achieve an effect</note>. Consequently, nature immediately flows into conformity whenever the soul commands. 

We see this in the body: the soul or spirit commands according to whatever act agrees with its will, and the body immediately submits and hastens to obey. When the soul wishes to view the visible world, the eye is at once shaped for every kind of light and shadow <note>original: modification</note>. If it wishes to hear, the wonderful structure of the ear instantly exists. If it wishes to walk, fly, or swim, the feet, wings, or fins are immediately provided—and so it is with infinite other desires and capacities. 

Indeed, the soul of an infant is often affected by the strong desire or fear of the mother’s soul in such a way that, based on that single impression, the shape of a mouse, a frog, a rose, or another object appears upon the part of the body touched <note>Swedenborg refers here to the historical belief in "maternal impressions," where a mother's experiences were thought to physically mark her unborn child</note>. These are evidences that nature readily hastens to obey when the soul commands. 

Accordingly, after death—when dissolved from these physical <note>original: organic</note> bonds—the soul would seem capable of assuming whatever form it wishes that agrees with its state. Therefore, if it should descend to earth, it would immediately take on the human form. Moreover, if the occasion should require any other animal form, to will this would be all that is necessary; everything else follows of its own accord. Nor would these be miraculous occurrences, for it would be no more contrary to nature than for a specific form to emerge from an egg...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the soul naturally aspires to a more perfect state and, once freed from the body, possesses the power to command nature to take on any form—including the human form—simply through its will.</summary>
<keywords>afterlife, metamorphosis, human form, will and action, maternal impressions, spiritual life, instrumental cause</keywords>

<page-num>329</page-num>

->**STATE OF THE SOUL AFTER DEATH.**<-

...could take on a human form, or might show on its skin the mark of a dormouse <note>original: "mark of the dormouse" refers to a type of birthmark or "maternal impression" thought to be caused by the mother's desires or fears during pregnancy</note>, or similar impressions made during the sensitive period of growth. The soul exists in a state of free will and is no longer restricted as it was on earth. It can also cast off that form and dissolve it in an instant. Indeed, it can present a radiant or "burning" face and similar appearances, like the recorded manifestations of the cherubim, the seraphim, and the angels who appeared to the shepherds. The reason for this is that the entire form originates from the soul; the necessary elements are immediately gathered from the surrounding environment <note>original: atmospheres</note> and arranged into its intellectual centers <term>intellectories</term> <note>Swedenborg's term for the most refined organic structures of the mind where thought occurs</note> and organs.

(524.) For even these essential qualities <note>original: determinations</note> of the form depend on the soul’s own action and internal principles. The soul is not swept away by the impulses <note>original: affections</note> of the lower mind <term>animus</term> <note>The "animus" refers to the lower, more emotional or sensory part of the mind, as opposed to the higher rational soul</note> into various urges, but is moved only toward what is useful and necessary. Loving new things, variety, and curiosities is natural to the lower mind and the rational mind because, to them, everything is initially unknown. This is not the case with the soul, from which nothing is hidden; therefore, it is never driven by curious desires. 

Consequently, the soul creates its own intellectual structures, arranging them in a harmonious order. Without such arrangement and organization <note>original: subordination and coordination</note>, no intellectual activity could take place. Therefore, it also follows that the form of the spirit is purely celestial*—just like the intellectual structure itself. Whether this is a spiral or "vortical" form <term>vortical form</term> <note>A complex, spiraling geometric form that Swedenborg believed was the highest and most perfect movement in nature, superior to the circular or linear</note> is something we can only guess. These are hidden mysteries and, at best, mere conjectures. If anyone "sees" them, it is only because reason has convinced him of them. When we live as souls, perhaps we will laugh at how childishly we tried to guess these things.

(525.) It is not to be believed that in our existence as a soul we shall be wise in the same manner as when we were living in our rational mind or human intellect—in which there is always, however, more ignorance than understanding. This mind, or our thought as it appears to us, passes away entirely, and the life of the soul remains. The soul is ignorant of nothing, but by its very nature knows everything; therefore, it is knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> itself and pure intelligence. This intelligence, however, does not speak or express its meaning through voice or words—since these are merely physical <note>original: "material"</note> ideas—but it encompasses at once everything that pertains to the subject of thought. For the intelligence of the soul is the same in the infant as in the adult and the elderly; it is what flows into our thought and enables us to understand and to connect philosophically all the things we think about. Therefore, after death, such an imperfect <note>original: "impure"</note> intellect no longer exists. When the soul flies away from the body, it is like going from a deep shadow into open sunlight, or coming out of a dark dungeon into the city of Rome—or indeed the whole world—or like a blind man having his sight restored. For the "truths" of our mind are mere hypotheses, deceptive principles, appearances, and opinions; but the truths of the soul are the most genuine truths themselves.

(526.) But the soul, being pure intelligence and a spiritual essence, is above all sciences and doctrines; for these are natural, and either stand still or grope around far below it. The soul knows the hidden mysteries of these sciences which the mind can never penetrate, though it always tries to approach them. For the mind is no more able to express these hidden things than algebra is able to express its series of infinites—those formulated by differential calculus <note>A branch of mathematics dealing with rates of change; Swedenborg uses this to illustrate how the soul's logic operates on a level far beyond ordinary calculation</note> in a long series that cannot be reduced by integral calculus <note>A branch of mathematics dealing with accumulation and finding the whole from the parts</note>. Therefore, regarding its state of pure intelligence, one soul is exactly like another.

(527.) But regarding its state of wisdom, one soul is never exactly the same as the soul of another. For one...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the soul possesses innate, pure intelligence that far surpasses the limited, often-incorrect rational mind of a living person. While all souls share the same level of pure intelligence after death, they differ significantly in their level of wisdom.</summary>

<header>STATE OF THE SOUL AFTER DEATH.</header>

[The soul] has within it more perfect and purer loves; it loves God above itself and its neighbor as itself. Thus, the soul of one person is ruled by Divine love; but the soul of another loves contrary things and hates what the former loves, and thus is more rightly called diabolical. From the study of spiritual loves, it is clear how much souls may differ from one another. Therefore, there are divine souls (those belonging to the divine society <note>In Swedenborg’s philosophy, "societies" refer to the organized communities of spirits in heaven or hell.</note>) and there are those which are diabolical, belonging to the infernal society. All souls, nevertheless, enjoy the most perfect intelligence regarding what is good and true, but they are affected by either the love or the hatred of these things.

(528.) Souls derive this nature during their physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> life, specifically by means of the rational mind. For the soul is then in the process of being formed into a good or evil state, though not into the "intelligence" of the true and the good (as it possesses that inherently). We have already shown how the soul is affected and what divine means must work together to improve and perfect the state of the soul—to make it more complete and restore it to its original divine image. 

But when the body is gone and the rational mind <note>The "rational mind" is the intermediate level of human consciousness that makes choices during life; Swedenborg argues this part of the mind ends at death because it is tied to physical experience.</note> has ceased to exist, the human soul has been fully formed. Whatever its quality is at that point, it remains so forever. Nothing further can be present to improve it. There is no longer any inflow <note>original: "influx"</note> from a changeable mind—the kind of mind that can be perfected or corrupted. Only the rational mind is capable of such change. After death, there is no struggle between the soul and the *animus* <note>The lower, sensory mind driven by passions and instincts.</note>, or between the loves of each; therefore, there is no further hope of victory or change. The soul's intelligence is pure and most perfect; there is, therefore, no changeability in it that could bring about a different state. It is no longer attached to any organic form (the body) which it must obey. In a word: as it is, it remains forever, particularly regarding its loves and spiritual aversions, and consequently regarding its eternal happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> or unhappiness.

(529.) Nor does this prevent the soul from knowing everything that its mind ever experienced in the body, or...
