From the changes of its own state—or from its acquired state itself—it knows all causes, infinite as they are. This is because there is not a single voluntary act ever performed without the will, the desire, and the goal <note>original: "end"</note> of that act affecting the soul and contributing in some way to its state. Therefore, from its own internal state, the soul knows every cause; it knows most perfectly what has been operating as a cause within its own rational mind; and it also clearly foresees what to expect, whether happiness or unhappiness.

(530.) Consequently, the soul enjoys a memory of the past. This is not like the memory and recollection of our physical senses, which is limited to material ideas and images. Instead, it is a pure and most perfect memory, so that not the slightest moment of its past life is hidden from it—not even a word that contributed to the changing of its state. The soul understands all of this not through a faculty of memory, but from its own actual state, since all past things are present to it. Indeed, even in natural things, where there is a connection of causes and possibilities <note>original: "contingencies"</note>, all future things are also present. This follows from the intellect alone, which is pure intelligence.

(531.) The soul cannot change its own state any more than a body can change its own deformed face, distorted mouth, or hunched back—or the muscles that cause the distortion or bring about the change of state. All of this remains as a natural deformity <note>Swedenborg suggests that the "shape" of the soul—its character—becomes as fixed after death as a physical disability is in life.</note> in the body; and the more it wishes to mend itself, the more it becomes deformed; so it is affected by its own self-consciousness.

## STATE OF THE SOUL AFTER DEATH.

...[nature, or any] thing that takes place in the heavens and earths. In the heavens, this occurs through the communication of activities <note>original: "operations"</note> which must be most perfect, especially since even in this life there exists such a communication of minds and a kind of sympathy between friends and relatives. If we acknowledge such a communication between souls, it can be described this way: the soul is occupied with a constant intuition <note>direct, immediate perception without conscious reasoning</note> of both past and present things at the same time. The heavenly aura <note>original: "celestial aura"; in Swedenborg’s philosophy, a subtle, universal atmosphere higher than the air or ether</note> and the universal spirit of all things act as a medium, making it impossible for the activities of one soul not to be shared with another. Without this shared connection <note>original: "communion"</note>, there would be no bond of love between souls.

This may be compared to our physical hearing and sight. There are atmospheres <note>original: "auras and atmospheres"</note> that communicate events occurring at great distances to us; indeed, sight even perceives objects coming from the sun. Why, then, shouldn't the soul—which is pure intelligence—perceive the specific things occurring in other souls, wherever they may be? Such a connection is a logical result of the heavenly aura (once its existence is granted), the Divine Spirit which embraces all things, and the effect of mutual love. However, this communication cannot be compared to that of the physical senses like sight and hearing. Nothing occurring in the universe can be hidden from the soul, for mental sight is limited only by the boundaries of the universe, just as is evident from physical <note>original: "ocular"</note> vision.*

<header>THE SOUL.</header>

### XXIX.

## CONCERNING HEAVEN, OR THE SOCIETY OF HAPPY SOULS.

(533.) There is such a vast difference between souls and minds, and such constant disagreements, conflicts, and controversies—in philosophy and theology as well as in worldly and physical affairs—that one lower mind <note>original: *animus*; in Swedenborg's system, the "animus" refers to the lower or natural mind, which is driven by emotions and the five senses, as opposed to the higher rational mind</note> never agrees with another. For this reason, many divisions <note>original: "schisms"</note>, heresies, and controversies are tolerated as if by God’s special providence. Additionally, great power is granted to the devil at the same time so that he may create division between the lower minds and the intellectual minds of men. This process impresses a unique, individual state upon each specific soul. 

This differentiation also seems to be the reason why Adam was permitted to sin. In the first age of humanity, no soul was distinguished from any other, and because they were all the same, no true "society" could exist. This also seems to be the reason for the strict prohibitions against parents marrying their children or brothers marrying sisters, along with many other circumstances that would otherwise tend to merge souls too closely together. It is also why marriages are declared to be formed and confirmed in God. Nevertheless, evidence of Divine Providence exists in the way marriages are arranged, even down to the smallest details. 

God also grants everyone their own free choice in how they act. He decrees, as it were, that the liberty of any individual shall not suffer the slightest injury. Instead, every person is permitted to rush toward their own destruction or the destruction of others. This is allowed because the very freedom of human souls is the only means of separating the lower minds—and therefore the souls—of those who would otherwise be indistinguishable in their influence on one another.

<vocab>souls, minds, lower mind, providence, Adam, marriage, Divine Providence, free choice, liberty</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg argues that human disagreement, diversity, and even the permission of sin are necessary to create distinct individualities among souls, which is a prerequisite for a complex heavenly society.</summary>
<keywords>individuality, free will, Divine Providence, Adam, marriage laws, animus, spiritual society</keywords>

(534.) Divine Providence works, therefore, specifically to distinguish individuals from one another, because the very purpose of creation is that there should be a most perfect society of human souls. The ultimate goal <note>original: "end"</note> ought to be the very first and last purpose of creation; everything else serves as a means to reach this goal, as will become clear if we examine each thing individually. The progression of these means extends even beyond the natural world. Can anyone argue that an earthly society is the ultimate goal, when the body itself exists for the sake of the soul? Must there not be a further purpose for which the soul, heaven, and the entire universe exist? Can there be any other purpose than for a society and kingdom of God to be formed from all human souls? These conclusions are so clear that it is hard to imagine they could be doubted; they are so obvious that they can be confirmed by everything existing in the world.

(535.) Since, therefore, no soul is exactly like another, but rather some difference or diversity of state exists between them all, this has happened not merely so that souls may be distinguished from one another, but so that the most perfect form of society may arise from that diversity. In a perfect society, there should not only be a variety among all members, but a variety where individuals harmonize so well that they form a society where every need is met by someone. We see this form in the atmospheric world itself, or the macrocosm <term>macrocosm: the great world or the universe as a whole</term>, and we see it in every living body between its constituent parts, whether they are fibers, the cortical glands <term>cortical glands: in Swedenborg's biology, these are the microscopic "hearts" of the brain's cortex where he believed the soul interacts with the body</term>, or other parts. I call this a "harmonic variety." It is a state where all the various parts are naturally related to one another through a certain analogy, and thus form a society that can be *one*. For nothing can come together and form a single unit unless there is a correspondence <note>original: "analogy"</note> between the parts that determine the form and the way they are organized. From this comes conjunction <note>original: *conjunction*; the act of joining or the state of being united</note>, and this is why harmony is pleasing and unites, while disharmony is—

<header>CONCERNING HEAVEN.</header>

...[souls perceive] things as if they were present—as if they could see clearly using the collective experience of everything that has ever existed on earth. There is a manifestation <note>original: "representation"</note> of the entire heaven; in short, there are infinite varieties of joy that fill souls with indescribable <note>original: "ineffable"</note> delights. No impure love exists there; instead, it has been replaced by pure friendship. There is no preoccupation with the future, nor is there desire, hope, or anxiety. Everything exists without worry and without fear of loss; it is completely stable and eternal. This leads to the worship and adoration of God <note>original: "their Deity"</note>, whose praise echoes through the highest heavens <note>original: "heavens of heavens"</note>; this worship raises all other spiritual delights to an even higher level. But these are only a few characteristics of that life, for it would be impossible to describe them all. This appears to be that truly distinct life—the only real life—while physical life is merely a shadow, a dream, or a reflection <note>original: "representation"</note> of it. For to truly live is to understand and to be wise; to live through love in connection with Him who is life itself is the only true way to live.

(542.) From these observations, it follows that by unanimous agreement, the blessed work together for the glory of their Lord and for the love of all citizens in heaven and on earth. Joy increases as more people join the community, and at the same time, the innermost parts of the soul rejoice that the Kingdom of God is expanding, for this is the natural result of both types of love. Eventually, from so many pure minds, a collective spirit <note>original: "common animus"</note> of the society is formed, just as in our own bodies, where a single lower mind <note>original: "animus"</note> is formed by the activity of the intellectories <note>intellectories: Swedenborg's term for the microscopic "organs" of the brain that he believed produced thought.</note>. The same is true for the collective intellect. However, the way this collective spirit <note>original: "animus"</note> flows into our souls will not be described here; the communication between that heavenly society and ourselves occurs only through our souls. Therefore, may Your kingdom come and Your will be done on earth as it is in the heavens!

## XXX.

### CONCERNING HELL, OR THE SOCIETY OF UNHAPPY SOULS.

(543.) The community of those who live in opposing loves—specifically, hatred toward God and their fellow human beings <note>original: "neighbour"</note>—is called hellish <note>original: "infernal"</note>, demonic, and miserable. This society exists so that every possible state between the two extremes can actually exist. In the soul's spiritual perception, nothing can exist unless it is actual; this is because the soul is pure intelligence and is not clouded by any shadows of ignorance. Furthermore, intermediate states cannot exist without their opposites, for the quality of a thing is only understood by knowing its relationship to what it opposes. 

For this reason, the devil actually exists, as does a hellish society—a community burning with the desire to destroy the heavenly society. Without such an evil community, the blessed would not be inspired with passion and intensity, nor would their souls burn with an eager desire to protect the church <note>In this context, "the church" likely refers to the universal body of spiritual believers or the divine order itself.</note>. Thus, the blessed feel their own happiness increase because of the existence of a life so contrary to their own.

(544.) All souls who hate God and their fellow human beings enter into this society. From their core principles—that is, from their distorted love—flow crimes and wickedness of every kind. They are stained by immoral habits <note>original: "vices"</note>. They suffer most deeply from their own consciences when they see clearly the truths that they had tried to dismiss during this life with deceptive arguments <note>original: "specious arguments"</note> and clever but false reasoning <note>original: "sophistic reasonings"</note>. After death, however, there is no more ignorance; souls possess a bare knowledge of truths. ### XXXI.

## CONCERNING THE DIVINE PROVIDENCE.

(549.) I believe no one is so irrational <note>original: "insane"</note> as to deny that there is a certain supreme direction or Divine Providence. For all things are filled with the Divine, and we admire in every single thing the order attributed to nature. This order is not preserved by nature itself—which would be absurd—but by some higher Being from whom nature receives its existence and its continuous survival <note>original: "subsistence"</note>. We see an interwoven multitude of phenomena that prove a regulating providence: everything seems to exist for the sake of a use or a purpose <note>original: "end"</note>. Specifically, one purpose seems to exist for the sake of another, forming a series of goals—from a certain starting point, through intermediate steps, to a final result or a new beginning.

For example: The earth itself exists so that it may be inhabited by living beings; the mineral kingdom exists so that it may produce the vegetable kingdom; the vegetable kingdom exists so that it may nourish and sustain the animal kingdom; the lower species of animals exist to serve the higher; and all of them serve the human race. The atmospheres exist so that we may be contained and held within our bodies, and so that we may breathe and talk. The ether <note>original: "ether"; in the 18th century, this was thought to be a subtle medium filling all space, responsible for the transmission of light and heat.</note> along with the sun exists so that every being may exist, and also so that we may see. But why mention more? There is not a worm, a plant, or a blade of grass without its use—specifically, that it may serve as a means to a certain purpose. Thus, the visible world is a complex of means leading to a purpose beyond the world or beyond its own nature; for there is a progression of purposes through natural effects, and thus through universal nature. That there is such a perpetual

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the intricate order and utility found in the natural world—where every kingdom of nature serves a higher purpose—proves the existence of a directing Divine Providence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Divine Providence, explaining how the interconnectedness of all things in the universe points to a single, purposeful Creator who sustains every detail of existence.</meta>

<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>345</page-num>
<header>DIVINE PROVIDENCE.</header>

The relationship and progression of purposes <note>original: "ends"</note>—specifically, that one purpose always exists for the sake of another—must be attributed to Divine Providence. Indeed, it indicates that God has provided every detail so that they may maintain this order.

(550.) The universe, including every tiny detail within it, is the work of God alone; nothing can originate from itself. What can exist without an origin? If that origin belongs to nature itself, then where did nature come from, unless you worship nature as God? Since these are the works of God, He must necessarily sustain them, because without constant support <note>original: "sustentations"</note>, all things would collapse back into their original chaos. Therefore, He must be truly omnipresent, omniscient, and omnipotent. If He is omnipotent, it follows that He provides for every single thing so that there are intermediate steps leading toward a further purpose. To rule and provide for a universe is the very nature and property of Divinity; this requires neither consultation nor effort. From God’s own essence—which is wisdom and love—all these things flow in their proper connection, order, and natural progression.

(551.) If God’s providence is universal, it must also be specific, for a "universal" concept cannot exist without the specific details <note>original: "particulars"</note> that define it as universal. The quality of a whole can be judged by its parts; thus, by looking at providence in the most minute details, we can judge its nature in the whole. There would be no universal providence unless it concerned itself with every detail. In the case of providence, this ensures that every part works together toward universal goals.

(552.) All providence looks toward a goal and foresees the means to reach it. Therefore, the future is contained within the present, and the present is the sum of the past. In this way, there is a sequence of means leading to a specific goal—a goal that is present from the first step, through the middle steps, and into the final results <note>original: "ultimates"</note>. However, we can understand the nature of Divine Providence much better through examples than through simple statements of principle <note>original: "axioms"</note>.

<vocab>Divine providence, universe, nature, omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, wisdom, love, universal, particulars</vocab>

<summary>This page argues that God’s providence is both universal and incredibly specific, as He must constantly sustain every detail of the universe to prevent it from returning to chaos. Swedenborg emphasizes that the order of the world flows naturally from God's essence of wisdom and love, connecting the past, present, and future through a chain of purposeful means.</summary>

<keywords>Divine Providence, Omnipotence, Sustentation, Universal and Particular, Teleology, Divine Essence, Creation, Order</keywords>

(553.) The purpose <note>original: "end"; Swedenborg uses "end" in the philosophical sense of a final goal or *telos*.</note> of creation—the reason for which the world was brought into being—could be nothing other than the first and the last, or the most universal of all purposes. This purpose is perpetually active in the created universe, which is a network of means working together toward that goal. No other purpose for creation can be identified than the existence of a universal society of souls, or a heaven—that is, the kingdom of God. That this was the goal of creation may be proved by countless arguments. It would be absurd to say that the world was created merely for the sake of the earth and earthly societies, or for this difficult and fleeting life; for all things on earth exist for the sake of man, and all things in man exist for the sake of his soul. The soul cannot exist for no reason. If, then, it exists for a purpose, it must be for a society in which God is present; for His providence focuses on souls, which are spiritual, and His works are designed for men and for their social connection <note>original: "consociation"</note>.

(554.) In order for a celestial society, or a society of souls, to exist, it is necessary that there be a most perfect form of organization. Specifically, this requires souls that are distinct from one another, featuring every possible variety. These varieties may be called harmonies between the souls; and from such harmony, an agreement and accord will arise. This produce the total effect and purpose that is always foreseen and provided by the Divine.

(555.) If we accept this most universal purpose—which is simultaneously the beginning, the essence of all intermediate steps <note>original: "mediates"</note>, and the final result—we shall see at once how Divine providence rules in foreseeing and arranging those intermediate steps. It might be argued that God could have created such a society all at once, without our earth and worldly things; that is, He might have filled heaven with souls without the need for biological birth and the growth of populations on this earth. This, indeed, cannot be denied; all things are possible for God. But there are also countless things which are impossible for Him; for instance, it is impossible for Him to be imperfect, mortal, inconsistent, wicked, or unjust. Such things are contrary to His nature.

...and because such a society [as we have described], which has the most perfect form, cannot exist without every possible variety—ranging from the most perfect to the most imperfect, from purity to impurity, and from love to hatred; or because there must be intermediate stages between opposites (that is, between the highest good, which is God, and the greatest evil, which is the Devil); therefore, based on these premises, it follows that God—since He is perfection, wisdom, goodness, and love itself—could never directly <note>original: "immediately"; in this context, it means without an intervening cause or secondary agent.</note> create any devil, nor any soul in which evil or guilt resides. Consequently, He did not create man with vice, crime, and sin, nor did He directly create the variety required for the society we described. 

Whatever flows directly from God must necessarily be the best and the most perfect. The fact that evil and imperfection exist can be traced not to God as the direct cause, but to the created being <note>original: "subject"</note> in whom it resides as part of its nature. Thus, it was the Devil’s own choice to rise against his God and become a rebel; it was Adam’s own choice to act against the Divine commandment, as he sought a higher and more perfect state of existence for himself. 

It is clear from the *Sacred Scriptures* that Divine providence did not lead Adam directly into this evil, but rather permitted it. Providence permitted the serpent; it forbade the tree to him; it created Adam with free will and did not compel him <note>original: "did not instruct him"; suggesting that God did not dictate Adam's choice in a way that removed his freedom.</note>. At the moment he ate the fruit, he was not stopped or forced to abstain, as Abraham was when he was about to sacrifice his son. These, along with many other examples, clearly demonstrate that there was a providence allowing him the ability to sin, and a foreknowledge that he *would* sin and lose his original <note>original: "pristine"</note> integrity. 

This outcome arose from the very principle of his being: that souls must be distinguished from one another and that every possible variety must exist among them. Only in this way can the goal <note>original: "end"</note> of creation—the kingdom of God—be reached. To achieve this end, it is necessary that humans be granted free will. The variety among individuals <note>original: "subjects"</note> arises solely from the free exercise and liberty of the will. Without this, there would be no intellect, no morality, no virtue, no vice, no crime, no guilt, no mental affection <note>original: "affection of the mind"; referring to emotions, passions, or states of feeling</note>, and no change of state. It is like a bird that a hunter <note>original: "fowler"</note> holds by its foot or ties with a string; the bird can move about only to a certain distance, as it is ensured that it shall not go beyond this limit.

(556.) The means that restrict the free will of men are numerous. There are, for instance, societies and their forms of government, laws, physical punishments, and judges—all established so that men do not abuse their free will. There are also consciences, laws, and rights imprinted on our minds, which are the strongest bonds. There is religion or Divine worship, the fear of eternal punishment and condemnation, and the love and hope for happiness; this, therefore, may be called the bond of society and of all communities. There is a certain fate that follows everyone and stays with them continually, according to their crimes or their virtues. We will discuss this further on. Nature herself hates total equality between one thing and another; for if they were equal, they would be the same, nothing would be distinct, and therefore nothing would be natural.

# XXXII.

## THE UNIVERSAL MATHESIS <term>The term "Mathesis" comes from the Greek word for "learning" or "knowledge"; in this context, it refers to a universal mathematical science or a systematic way of organizing all knowledge.</term>, OR A MATHEMATICAL PHILOSOPHY OF UNIVERSALS.

(562.) The famous John Locke, in his work *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding*, says:

> “The ideas which form the basis of morality are all actual essences <note>original: "real essences"; in philosophy, this refers to the underlying nature of a thing</note>, and are of such a nature that they maintain a mutual connection and fitness <note>original: "adaptation"</note> which may be discovered. It follows that as soon as we discover these relations, we shall, to that extent, possess many real, certain, and general truths. I am certain that by following a good method, one might bring a large part of moral science to such a degree of evidence and certainty that an attentive and sensible man would no longer find any reason to doubt it, any more than he would doubt mathematical propositions which have been proved <note>original: "demonstrated"</note> to him” (Book 4, chapter 12, section 8).

And elsewhere: “Perhaps, if one should consider distinctly and with all possible care the kind of science which proceeds on the basis of ideas and words, this would produce a logic and a critique different from those seen up to this point” (Book 4, chapter 21, section 4).

Again: “I do not doubt that in the current state and makeup <note>original: "constitution"</note> of our nature, human knowledge may be carried far beyond any point reached so far, if men will sincerely and with entire intellectual freedom undertake to perfect the means of discovering the truth with the same focus and the same industry which they employ in disguising <note>original: "colouring"</note> and maintaining a falsehood, or in defending a system—”

...system of which they are declared partisans, or certain interests in which they are engaged" (Book 4, chapter 3, section 6).

Further: "The highest degree of our knowledge is intuition without reasoning; . . . for this is certain knowledge, secure from all doubt, having no need of proof and incapable of receiving it, because it is the highest point of all human certainty <note>original: "certitude"</note>. Such is the knowledge which the angels now possess, and that which the spirits of the righteous <note>original: "the just made perfect"; a biblical reference to Hebrews 12:23</note> will attain in the life to come. It embraces a thousand things which at present escape our understanding entirely; our reason, in its limited range of vision, catches only a few gleams of them, while the rest remains veiled in darkness from our view" (Book 4, chapter 17, section 14).

(563.) There exists a science of sciences, or a universal science, which contains all others within itself. Its parts can be broken down, as it were, into various specific sciences. Such a science is not acquired by learning; rather, it is innate <note>original: "connate"</note>, especially in souls which are pure intelligences. This is the science used by souls released from the body and by angels. If they communicate their thoughts or converse, they do not seem to use words to form connections, because words are merely physical <note>original: "material"</note> ideas and forms which the mind understands as signs based on experience. 

Instead, the soul, using this internal science, perceives all objects immediately as they are in themselves—determining whether they are good or evil—and assents to or turns away from them according to their nature. Unless the soul were equipped with such a science, it would be completely unable to influence <note>original: "flow into"</note> our thoughts or to provide us with the power to understand and express higher things. It would also be unable to adapt all its biological structures <note>original: "organic forms"</note> to the most inward and secret laws of mechanics, physics, chemistry, and many other phenomena. Therefore, there can be no doubt that such a science exists.

I would like to propose another approach as well; I have confirmed that it is possible, but many rules must first be established, data proposed, and truths adjusted before I can attempt it. 

Even then, we ultimately get tangled in a kind of Gordian knot <note>term: an extremely difficult or intricate problem; originally a legendary knot that was impossible to untie</note>—an equation so complex that the effort needed to untangle it is greater than the result is worth. Furthermore, the slightest error in calculation can lead to many false conclusions. For this reason, I will refrain from that attempt. Instead, I wish to propose a certain ***Key to Natural and Spiritual Mysteries through the method of Correspondences and Representations***, which leads us more directly and reliably into hidden truths.* Since this doctrine is still unknown to the world, I should explain it in greater detail.

# APPENDIX I.

---

## TWELVE THESES ON "THE HUMAN SOUL."

->(From the *Economy of the Animal Kingdom*, Part II.)<-

->BY EMANUEL SWEDENBORG.<-

->I.<-

**From the anatomy of the living body <note>original: "animal body"; in this context, "animal" refers to the *anima* or soul, meaning a body endowed with life and soul</note> we clearly see that a certain extremely pure fluid flashes through the finest fibers, far beyond the reach of even our sharpest senses. This fluid rules everywhere throughout the entire body—its own self-contained universe—** and it maintains, waters, nourishes, activates, shapes, forms, and renews everything within it. This fluid is three levels <note>original: "third degree"; Swedenborg’s philosophy uses "degrees" to describe layers of reality, from the most physical to the most spiritual</note> higher than the blood, which it enters as the primary, highest, most internal, most subtle, and most perfect substance and force of the body—acting as the unique and essential life force and the governing principle of all things. Therefore, if we are to study the soul of the body and investigate how the soul and body communicate, we must first examine this fluid and see if it matches the qualities we describe. But because this fluid lies so deep within nature, it cannot be understood except through the "doctrine of series and degrees" <note>term: a philosophical system developed by Swedenborg to understand how different levels of reality (like soul and body) relate to one another</note> combined with observation; nor can it be described without using a mathematical philosophy of universal principles.

->II.<-

Yet this does not stop us from perceiving, through the mind’s intuition alone, that although this fluid is the body's primary substance, it still draws its existence from an even higher source. It comes most directly from those universal elements upon which God has impressed the principles of nature, and which contain the most perfect forms of the natural world. For this reason, it is the "form of all forms" in the body—the formative substance which spins the thread of life from its first moment and continues it until the very end. It connects, preserves, and governs everything, so that all things follow a sequence where later developments relate back to earlier ones. The entire body and its parts—the general along with the specific—relate back to this primary form and substance through a wonderful system of order and coordination.

<meta>catchword: upo (likely "upon")</meta>

<summary>Swedenborg introduces his theory of a "most pure fluid" (often called the spirituous fluid) that serves as the soul's primary instrument within the body, arguing that it is the source of all life, order, and physical formation.</summary>

upon which all things depend, and by which, and for which, each thing exists in its own distinctive manner.

### III.

But as this most pure fluid—or "superior blood"—has acquired its form from the primary substances of the world, it cannot be said to be alive in itself, much less to feel, perceive, understand, or consider goals. Nature, viewed on its own, is lifeless; it only serves life as an instrument. It is entirely subject to the will of an intelligent Being, who uses nature to achieve goals through physical effects. Therefore, we must look higher for the source of life, seeking it from the **First Being** <note>original: "First *Esse*"; from the Latin *esse*, meaning "to be." It refers to God as the fundamental essence of all existence</note> or Deity of the universe, who is essential life and the essential perfection of life or wisdom. Unless this First Being were life and wisdom themselves, nothing in nature could live, much less possess wisdom; nor would anything be capable of motion.

### IV.

This life and intelligence flow with life-giving power only into substances that are prepared both to begin moving and to receive life. Consequently, they flow into the most simple, universal, and perfect substances of the living body—that is, into its purest fluid. Through this medium, life flows into the less simple, universal, and perfect substances (the complex physical parts of the body). All of these manifest the force and lead the life of their primary substance, according to their level of complexity and their form, which makes them what they are. On account of this **influx** <note>term: a central concept in Swedenborg’s philosophy describing how spiritual life and energy flow from a higher level into a lower one</note> of life, which is the primary cause in the living kingdom <note>original: "animate kingdom"; from the Latin *anima* (soul), referring to all beings endowed with life</note>, this purest fluid—the instrumental cause—is to be called the spirit and soul of its body.

### V.

But to know the manner in which this life and wisdom flow in is infinitely above the reach of the human mind. There is no analysis and no abstract thought that can reach so high; for whatever is in God, and whatever law God acts by, is God. The only way we can represent this to ourselves is through a comparison with light. For just as the sun is the fountain of light and all its variations in the physical universe, so the Deity is the sun of life and of all wisdom. As the sun of the world flows in only one way, and without physically merging <note>original: "unition"</note> with the objects of its universe, so also does the sun of life and wisdom. As the sun of the world flows in by mediating atmospheres <note>original: "auras"; in Swedenborg’s physics, these are subtle grades of atmosphere that carry light and gravity</note>, so the sun of life and wisdom flows in by the mediation of His Spirit. But as the sun of the world flows into objects according to the specific nature of each, so also does the sun of life and of wisdom. However, we are not at liberty to go further than this into the details of the comparison, because the physical sun is...

<summary>Swedenborg argues that the soul's "pure fluid" is an instrument that is not alive in itself, but receives life through an "influx" from God, whom he compares to a sun of wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>First Esse, Influx, Animate Kingdom, Supereminent Blood, Divine Wisdom, Instrumental Cause, Correspondence of the Sun</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Swedenborg’s "Twelve Theses on the Human Soul." On the previous page, he established that while the soul's physical vehicle (the "purest fluid") is part of nature, its life and wisdom come from a Divine source. He now explains the boundary between nature and the divine, and the hierarchy of the human mind and body.</meta>

<page-num>357</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX I. 357</header>

One is within nature, the other is above it; the one is physical, the other is purely moral. The first falls under the philosophy of the mind, while the other lies hidden among the sacred mysteries of theology. Between these two there are boundaries that it is impossible for human faculties to cross. Furthermore, through the omnipresence and universal influence <note>original: "influx"</note> of this life into created matter, all things flow constantly in a providential order: from a primary goal, through intermediate goals, to a final goal.

### VI.

There are, then, two distinct principles that determine this spirituous fluid <term>The "spirituous fluid" is Swedenborg’s term for the highest, most refined substance in the body—a "super-blood" that acts as the bridge between the physical and the spiritual.</term> which we assume to be the soul. The first is natural, by which the fluid is able to exist and move in the world. The second is spiritual, by which it is enabled to live and be wise. From these two, a third principle is formed which is properly the soul's own: the power of determining itself into acts suitable to the purposes of the universe. 

But this principle of self-determination concerns the ultimate world—the earth—where these actions take place. Therefore, the soul, endowed with these principles, must descend through as many degrees as there are substances and forces in the world. Consequently, it forms a body adapted to each degree in succession. There are, then, sensory and motor organs, both of which are organized into four degrees:

1.  **The first organ** is the spirituous fluid, or soul. Its office is to represent the universe, to perceive goals <note>original: "have intuition of ends"</note>, to be conscious, and—most importantly—to determine action.
2.  **The next organ** below the soul is the mind, whose office is to understand, to think, and to will.
3.  **The third organ** in order is the *animus* <note>original: *animus*; in this context, the "lower mind" or the seat of emotions, passions, and sensory imagination, as distinguished from the higher rational mind.</note>, whose office is to conceive, to imagine, and to desire.
4.  **The fourth and last degree** consists of the organs of the five external senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. 

The motor organs follow the same pattern, with the muscles being the final degree. These and the sensory organs constitute the body, whose office is to feel, to form expressions and actions, to be disposed, and to do what the higher lives determine, will, and desire. Although there are these various degrees, the living <note>original: "animal"</note> system consists of nothing but the soul and the body; for the intermediate organisms are only specific forms of the soul, and they partake of the nature of both the soul and the body. This is the ladder by which every operation and emotion of the soul and body descends and ascends.

The spirituous fluid is the first of the organs, or the "super-eminent" organ, in the living body. Because it is the soul, it is seated so high above all other faculties that it serves as their order, truth, rule, law, science, and art. Consequently, its office is to represent the universe, to perceive goals, to be conscious of all things, and principally to determine action. It is a faculty distinct from the intellectual mind—prior to it, superior to it, and more universal and perfect. It flows into the intellectual mind much like light. Because of this, it is nearly impossible to fully understand the soul while we are still living in the physical body.

### VII.

The true progression of how things descend from the spiritual to the physical, or ascend from the physical to the spiritual, seems to work in this way: The forms of sounds <note>original: "modulations"</note> in the air perceived by the ear are to the images <note>original: "modifications"</note> of the ether perceived by the eye (or by the lower mind), as those visual images are to the higher activities of the mind. These mental forms are what we call intellectual and rational ideas, which exist insofar as they are lit up by the light of the soul. In the same way, these mental ideas are to even higher forms in the soul—which are too profound for words. We call these "intuitive ideas of ends" <note>The soul’s "intuitive ideas of ends" refers to the ability to see the ultimate purpose or goal behind everything, rather than just the physical appearance.</note>, and they exist insofar as they are lit up by the life of the First Cause <note>original: "first cause," referring to God.</note>.

### VIII.

From the very moment of conception, which begins with the parent, the soul is born ready to initiate movement and receive life. Consequently, it is born ready for all intuition and intelligence. The soul carries this intuition and intelligence with it from its very first structural thread <term>original: "stamen," meaning the fundamental blueprint or beginning of an organism.</term> and earliest infancy through to extreme old age. 

However, the mind is different. Before the mind can be illuminated by the light of the soul, it must be filled with principles learned through experience <note>original: "a posteriori"</note>—that is, through the organs of the external senses, mediated by the lower mind <term>The "animus" or lower mind acts as the bridge between the physical senses and the rational mind.</term>. As the mind is taught and the way is opened, it becomes able to communicate with its soul. The soul has designed and provided that the path leading to it should be opened in this specific order. It follows, then, that there are no innate ideas or "built-in" laws in the human mind itself, but only in the soul. If these ideas and laws were not already present in the soul <note>original: "connate"</note>, we would have no memory of things we perceive through our senses, no understanding, and no animal could exist as a living being.

### IX.

From these points, we can understand the nature of the interaction between the soul and the body. Higher things flow into lower things according to a specific order and through the way the body’s substances are formed and connected to each other. 

We can conclude the following: 
1. If the activity of the spirituous fluid <term>The "spirituous fluid" is Swedenborg’s term for the highest, most refined substance in the body—a "super-blood" that acts as the bridge between the physical and the spiritual.</term> is the soul; 
2. And if the soul’s activity in the brain’s grey matter <note>original: "organic cortical substance"</note> is the mind; 
3. And if the reaction of the entire brain <note>original: "common sensorium"</note> is the lower mind; 
4. And if the ability to feel is in the sensory organs, and the ability to act is in the motor organs of the body...

Then a careful and logical study of anatomy must reveal how this interaction works. It must prove that the soul can communicate with the body only through these mediating organs, and only according to the natural or developed condition of those organs.

<summary>Swedenborg describes a hierarchy of perception moving from physical sound and sight up to the soul’s spiritual intuition. He argues that while the soul is born with innate wisdom, the human mind must be developed through sensory experience to bridge the gap between the body and the soul.</summary>

->X.<-

**The spirituous fluid** <term>original: "spirituous fluid," Swedenborg's term for the most refined and perfect substance in the body, which serves as the immediate vehicle for the soul.</term> is perfectly adapted and ready to take on infinite variety and undergo infinite changes of state. Because of this, it exists in a state of perfect harmonious variety, both within its own system and in relation to other systems. Through this variety, the soul is able to know everything that happens both outside and inside the body, and everything that comes into contact with the body. It can then apply its force to internal events and give its consent to external ones. 

Thus we may understand what free choice is: namely, that the mind has the power to choose whatever it desires when its thoughts are directed toward a specific goal. Therefore, the mind can determine how the body acts, whether it follows what the lower mind <term>original: "animus," referring to the seat of the passions and sensory desires.</term> wishes, or the opposite. However, this only applies to matters where the mind has been instructed through the physical senses, where it views what is honorable, useful, or proper as its goal. But in higher and divine matters, the mind can choose the means, but regarding the ultimate goal <note>original: "end"</note>, it must allow itself to be acted upon by the soul, and the soul by the Spirit of God. Meanwhile, this free power to act or not to act is granted to human minds as a way to reach the ultimate goal of creation, which is the glory of God.

->XI.<-

But this is not the case for brute animals. Their purest fluid receives its form from the "ether of the second order" <note>In Swedenborg’s scientific philosophy, he categorized the atmosphere into different levels of "ethers"; the second order relates to the level of physical instinct rather than spiritual reason.</note>. This fluid is on the same level as—not higher than—their physical organism, which corresponds to our mind. Because of this, animals are born with a fixed connection between their soul and body (all the conditions of their life). They are carried along by the order of nature toward goals <note>original: "ends"</note> that they themselves do not understand.

->XII.<-

**On these premises** it may be demonstrated to the rational mind that the human spirituous fluid is absolutely safe from any harm that happens in this earthly realm <note>original: "sublunary region," meaning the world below the moon or the physical earth.</note>. It is indestructible and remains immortal after the death of the body, although it is not immortal by its own power <note>original: "per se," meaning "in itself." Swedenborg argues the soul's immortality is a gift from God, not an inherent property of the substance.</note>. When it is set free from the bonds and chains of earthly things, it will still take on the exact form of the human body and live a life pure beyond imagination. 

Furthermore, not the smallest deed is done intentionally in this life, and not the least word is spoken by the consent of the will, that will not then appear in the bright light of an inherent wisdom before the court <note>original: "tribunal"</note> of its own conscience. Lastly, there is a society of souls in the heavens, and the *City of God* <note>A reference to the spiritual community of the righteous, both on earth and in heaven.</note> on earth is the nursery for this society, in which, and by which, the ultimate goal of all things is fulfilled.

<vocab>spirituous fluid, soul, animus, free choice, brute animals, ether, sublunary, per se, City of God</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg defines human free will as the ability of the mind to choose its actions, contrasting it with animals who act by blind instinct. He concludes that the human soul survives death in a human form to face the judgment of its own conscience in a heavenly society.</summary>

<keywords>free will, spirituous fluid, animal instinct, immortality, conscience, City of God, Swedenborgian psychology, afterlife</keywords>

# APPENDIX II.

## A SUMMARY* OF THE "EPILOGUE ON THE SENSES OR SENSATION IN GENERAL."

->(*Translated from Part IV of the "Animal Kingdom," as edited in Latin by Dr. J. F. Immanuel Tafel, Tübingen and London, 1848.*)<-

->A.<-

->SENSATION IN GENERAL.<-

**These general principles are to be observed regarding all sensation:**

1. The origin of every sensation comes from an external touch or impulse.
2. This touch or impulse acts upon the fibers or the thin membranes <term>original: "little tunics"</term> surrounding the fibers, and is therefore external.
3. Consequently, the fibers must be organized and formed in such a way that they can clearly receive all the distinct variations belonging to different types of touch.
4. The sensations of touch, taste, and smell arise from the contact or impulse of solid matter <note>original: "heavy bodies"</note>, or from the resistance <note>original: "inertia"</note> of forces—that is, from physical particles.
5. However, the senses of hearing and sight arise from the contact or impulse of substances that are not heavy, but are instead active forces—specifically, components of the atmosphere.
6. In order for a sensation to be perceived and to cause an emotional or physical response <term>original: "affection"</term>, there must be many variations combined in a single touch, creating a "form" made of these differences.
7. The variations within this form will occur either all at once <note>original: "simultaneous"</note> or in a sequence.
8. A form arising from a sequence of variations will take on the same quality as a form where variations occur all at once.
9. Our organic sensory structures <note>original: "organico-sensory forms"</note> are designed to receive the patterns of all these variations in a clear and distinct way.

---

\* Only an outline is provided here, primarily by stating the theories or propositions that the author discusses at length. [*Translator's Note*]

<summary>This page introduces an outline of Swedenborg’s theories on sensation, arguing that all senses—from touch to sight—rely on external impulses and organized fibers to process information.</summary>
<keywords>sensation, physiology, fibers, sensory organs, touch, sight, hearing, Swedenborg, Animal Kingdom</keywords>

--- Page 401 ---
<meta>This page continues the summary of Appendix II, expanding on the physiological mechanics of sensation and how vibrations in the fibers are translated into perceptions by the soul.</meta>

<page-num>361</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX II.</header>

Especially are we to observe that:

10. The organic structures of each sense organ immediately apply these simultaneous and successive variations to the sense itself.
11. These structures communicate these variations to the fibers of which they are composed.
12. These fibers—similar to the way musical strings vibrate—carry these differences up to their origins in the <term>cortical substances</term> <note>the gray matter of the brain</note> by means of a vibration <note>original: "tremulation"</note> or modification.
13. This is carried out perfectly because of the spiritual essence that exists within the fiber.
14. Depending on the nature of this vibration, these differences are carried to every connected fiber and to every part of the cortical substance in the <term>cerebrum</term> <note>the main part of the brain</note> and the <term>cerebellum</term> <note>the "little brain" at the back of the skull</note>, as well as the <term>medulla oblongata</term> <note>the brainstem</note> and <term>medulla spinalis</term> <note>the spinal cord</note>.
15. Through the living essence within the spirit and the fibers, this vibration becomes a sensation. This change of state creates an <term>affection</term> <note>an emotional or physical response, such as pleasure or pain</note> according to the form of the vibration, and so on.
16. The soul itself, which is the only truly living part of the body, provides the ability to feel the qualities of these vibrations.
17. Physical responses <note>original: "affections"</note> give rise to changes of state in the organs.
18. This vibration of the fibers spreads out to the very "beginnings"—the cortical substances—according to every form of variation; for these origins were designed specifically to receive such vibrations.
19. Therefore, just as there are countless variations in and between different types of touch, the brain undergoes just as many different changes of state; for the perfection of these cortical substances lies in this capacity for change.
20. From the form of these differences and the resulting changes of state, responses <note>original: "affections"</note> are produced. These are pleasant if the changes of state agree with the body’s natural state, and unpleasant if they conflict with it.
21. Consequently, every touch or mode perceived as a single unit—whether it contains variations that occur in sequence or all at once—is felt as either pleasant or unpleasant.
22. Likewise, the harmony between these units or modes produces a collective response <note>original: "common affection"</note>.
23. The senses differ in <term>degree</term> <note>Swedenborg's philosophy that reality is organized into distinct, hierarchical levels</note>. Touch is the most complex <note>original: "composite"</note>, while sight is the simplest among the external senses. [The Doctrine of Degrees is illustrated here at some length. —*Translator*]
24. Therefore, the senses differ in the perfection of all their qualities.
25. This difference depends entirely on the objects that touch, impel, strike, and affect the sensory organ.
26. The organic structures of each sense organ are aligned according to these degrees.
27. The fibers that make up these organic structures are themselves composed according to these same degrees.

<vocab>sensory, fibres, tremulation, cortical substances, spiritual essence, cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, medulla spinalis, soul, doctrine of Degrees</vocab>

<summary>Swedenborg describes how physical sensations travel via vibrations through the fibers to the cortical substances of the brain, where the soul interprets them as pleasant or unpleasant. He argues that these processes follow a hierarchical "Doctrine of Degrees," ranging from the complexity of touch to the simplicity of sight.</summary>
<keywords>sensation, fibers, vibration, cortical substance, brain anatomy, soul, affection, Doctrine of Degrees, physiology</keywords>

**28.** According to these same levels <note>original: "degrees"</note>, these physical changes <note>original: "modifications"</note> travel through the nerve fibers.

**29.** According to these same levels, changes are experienced in the common sensory organ, which is the <term>cerebrum</term> <note>the main part of the brain</note>.

**30.** According to these same levels, <term>affections</term> <note>emotional or physical responses, like pleasure or pain</note> are also produced in the brain; that is, they arise according to the changes and whether they are harmonious or discordant.

**31.** This, therefore, is the cause of the variety found among the five senses.

**32.** The physical structures <note>original: "organic forms"</note> determine these qualities within each external sense organ.

**33.** Each sense has its own general sense to which the individual signals <note>original: "modes or units"</note> relate as parts.*

**34.** These general senses differ from one another just as the sequences of parts or signals differ.

**35.** Because of this, individual parts or units are clearly distinguished from one another, and they move toward a clear perfection. Therefore, every sensation has its higher and lower levels—specifically three: the particular, the general, and the most general; *for order and levels of order exist everywhere so that there may be a sequence and <term>correspondences</term> <note>meaningful relationships between different levels of reality, such as the physical and the spiritual</note>.*

**36.** Every sense, regardless of its level, has its maximum and its minimum intensity, and its minimum relates to its greater and maximum points. These levels are to be discussed in their specific doctrine, which will be called the Doctrine of Society and Series.

**37.** All ideas originate from the sensations of sight.

**38.** Hearing, when considered on its own, does not create ideas; instead, it only relates them to visual ideas.

**39.** The patterns <note>original: "modes"</note> of hearing seem to have the ability to influence the imagination.

**40.** All harmony between things that come after <note>original: "posteriors"</note> and things that come before <note>original: "priors"</note>—or between lower and higher things—is not "pre-established" <note>a reference to Leibniz's theory that the soul and body are pre-synchronized clocks</note> but is "co-established" <note>Swedenborg's view that the relationship is dynamic and interactive</note>.

**41.** There is something in the forms of the lower signals, the sensations, and their ideas that naturally influences those levels which are superior.

**42.** These concepts can only be understood through new doctrines—namely, the doctrines of Forms, of Order and Degrees, of <term>Influx</term> <note>the way the higher/spiritual flows into the lower/natural</note>, of Correspondences, and of Modifications.

**43.** It is ideas that form truths, and the form of the truth itself—or rather, the collection of truths—gives the sense of "goodness"; from this, the <term>affections</term> <note>emotions or inclinations</note> arise.

**44.** Because truths are forms, they produce emotional responses, either through simple harmony or because of a love that is set as the ultimate goal <note>original: "the end"</note>.

**45.** Animals recognize the harmonies of things arising from their senses better than humans do, for these things correspond to them in a harmonious way.

---

* Compare Aristotle, *On the Soul* <note>original: *De Anima*</note>, chapter 8, cited in Appendix III, page 377.

## B.

### CONCERNING TRUTHS.

**1.** All sensations are patterns <note>original: "forms"</note> that are either harmonious or discordant.
**2.** The same is true for sensations of the imagination.
**3.** All variations above these levels, or those belonging to the intellect, are not natural; they are acquired through learning or skill <note>original: "art"</note>.
**4.** Nevertheless, there are intellectual truths that produce a natural effect.
**5.** These undeniable truths are merely the components from which higher truths are concluded.
**6.** Therefore, whatever kind of love a person has—and the more powerfully it dominates—the resulting <term>affection</term> <note>an emotional state or disposition of the mind</note> will match it.
**7.** Lower forms of love naturally fight against superior forms.
**8.** Consequently, the more the lower loves step back <note>original: "recede"</note>, the more the higher loves can flow in.
**9.** In short, intellectual truths result either from lower, physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> affections or from spiritual, higher affections. The intellect serves as the center point for both.
**10.** The intellect, viewed on its own, is simply the highest level of sensitivity <note>original: "supremely sensitive organ"</note>.

## C.

### CONCERNING THE AFFECTIONS.

**1.** There is natural affection and spiritual affection.
**2.** There is also a mixed affection that shares qualities of both the natural and the spiritual.
**3.** Natural affection is divided into *sensitive*, *imaginative*, and *intellectual*. Put another way, these are the *physical* <note>original: "corporeal or material"</note>, which belongs to the external senses or the face; the *natural* <note>original: "physical"</note>, which belongs to the imagination or the <term>animus</term> <note>the lower mind, often associated with emotions, moods, and instincts</note>; and the *philosophic*, which belongs to the intellect or the mind.
**4.** Sensitive affection focuses only on the shapes of objects, and therefore on their general and specific qualities.
**5.** The imagination or natural <note>original: "physical"</note> affection, much like sight, focuses on images and ideas, which it organizes into a new order; this creates an affection for harmony.
**6.** The intellectual or philosophic affection focuses on abstract <note>original: "immaterial"</note> or highly elevated ideas.
**7.** Because all these natural affections are harmonious, they assume the existence of certain geometric and analytical elements and principles.
**8.** The philosophic affection is the deepest level of sensation, which is called the intellect.
**9.** The lower affections flow into the higher, and the higher into the

It outlines a hierarchy of the mind, moving from basic sensory input to the abstract reasoning of the "philosophic" mind.</summary>

lower, but with much difference. This is where <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "common sense"; here referring to the internal faculty that coordinates and integrates information from all the external senses</note> comes from.
**10.** This is the faculty of thinking and of judging.
**11.** The faculty immediately below it feels according to the state established by the intellectual faculty.
**12.** Spiritual <term>affection</term> <note>an emotional state or disposition of the mind</note>.

->D.<-

### A GENERAL EXPLANATION REGARDING SENSATION AND AFFECTION*

**1.** Sensation produces affection; affection is either of good or of evil. The affection for good is love, while the affection for evil is hate. The love of good involves harmony, and harmony leads to connection <note>original: "conjunction"</note>. Therefore, good and evil are the starting points of all affections.
**2.** The external senses recognize good and evil through affections. The imagination does so by reproducing and creating new ideas from the memory, and from this innermost memory—that of the intellect—which explores truths and their qualities. It does this through its faculty of summoning ideas and forming them analytically to determine whether a "good" is a true or false good, and whether an "evil" is truly or falsely evil. Within the very knowledge of truth lies hidden the good or the evil that affects the sensation. This is affected according to the natural and the acquired order in which the organic structure of life itself exists.
**3.** What is truly good and what is truly evil is known especially from the love found in the affection of the sensations. The lowest love is the love of the world. The love next higher—and the primary cause of that worldly love—is the love of the body. Still higher is the love of self and ambition. Above this is the love of society, which increases in its degrees according to its quality (its natural, moral, and spiritual bonds) and according to its quantity (its universality). Still superior to this is the love of a heavenly society; and the highest of all is the love of God.
**4.** That loves ascend in this way follows from this reasoning <note>original: "induction"</note>: Our bodies do not exist for the sake of the world; the internal faculties of the body (from which the love of self arises) do not exist for the sake of the body; human societies do not exist for our sake; and heavenly society does not exist for the sake of earthly society—rather, it is exactly the opposite. In the same way, God does not exist for the sake of a heavenly society, but that society exists for the sake of His glory.
**5.** Thus, God is true and pure love and the true and highest good. He is the source from which all love flows, and therefore all affection for good, happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>, harmony, and connection.

---
* Compare Aristotle, *On the Soul* <note>original: "De Anima"</note>, Book 3, chapter 8, as quoted in Appendix III, p. 377.

**6.** Therefore, as is the nature of one's love, so is their understanding of truth; from that love, truth flows as if from its own fountain.
**7.** This is also how all intelligence regarding truth descends. Just as God is goodness itself, so is He truth itself. He is the True Good and the Good Truth, which are one and the same. Higher goodness and truth flow into the lower, but never the reverse. In lower things, there is no goodness or truth that is not received from a higher source. We receive nothing of good and truth from above except as we remove the obstacles and the inferior loves. Then it flows in by Grace, and not by our own merit. For we cannot even remove these lower loves without a higher power—that is, through its balance and consequent presence; then through those circumstances <note>original: "contingencies"</note> that promote or hinder our desires, and thus by Providence. Therefore, everything exists only by Grace.

You will see these things proved—indeed, demonstrated—in my <term>psychological writings</term> <note>Swedenborg refers here to his extensive anatomical and philosophical studies of the soul, which he believed provided empirical proof for spiritual realities</note>; I dare to say *demonstrated*, for I know I can prove them, even to the conviction of those who do not believe.

->E.<-

### **FROM THE "RULES OF HARMONY OR OF MUSIC"***

**1.** The <term>gravity</term> <note>low pitch</note> and <term>acuteness</term> <note>high pitch</note> of sounds proceed from four causes: (i.) The length of the fiber or string; (ii.) its tension or relaxation; (iii.) its thickness or multiplication; and (iv.) its solidity and the specific gravity resulting from it.
**2.** All of these factors are present in the ear and in infinite variety.
**3.** A similar rule applies to simultaneous (consonant) sounds as it does to successive (concordant) sounds.
**4.** Modifications and sounds harmonize <note>original: "have a concordance"</note> across their intervals according to the alignment <note>original: "coincidence"</note> of vibrations, which allows one sound to be applied to another.
**5.** This causes a pleasant variety, because there are oppositions that quickly and truly coincide.
**6.** All <term>modifications</term> <note>vibrations or changes in state</note> of a single sense travel through the nerve fibers at the same time or velocity, regardless of their interval. Thus, general modifications occur in the same timeframe as specific ones.
**7.** Consequently, the sensory fibers and those connected to them become dissonant in the brain if their connection is broken by even the slightest moment of disharmony.

---

\* I have included this portion of the work (merely as an outline) because it provides a striking example of the author's method of reasoning in series from natural to spiritual or mental laws—specifically, from the laws of physical harmony to the laws of mental harmony. [Translator's Note]

**8.** There is also a correspondence or harmony of musical proportions <note>original: "quantities"</note>.

**9.** To understand how sounds, harmonic modes, or chords <note>original: "concords"</note> coincide, we will demonstrate this through drawings. [The author refers here to figures at the end of the work, followed by a demonstration of those figures. —Translator]

**10.** The following general rules result: (i.) The more harmonious <note>original: "consonant"</note> the sounds are, or the more they accord, the more frequently they coincide within the same time and space, according to well-known rules in musical theory, etc. [Many rules follow here. —Translator]

**11.** The proportions of sounds express the soul's emotions <note>original: "affections"</note>.

**12.** Changes of state in the brain, and especially in the <term>cortical substance</term> <note>the grey matter of the brain, which Swedenborg identified as the seat of the soul's activity</note>, take place in a similar way.

**13.** From this it follows that the same rules apply to the cortical substances of the brain as apply to the vibrations <note>original: "modifications"</note> of the corresponding physical environments <note>original: "atmospheres"</note>.

**14.** Furthermore, changes of state in the brain’s substances follow the same harmonic laws as the fibers we have already discussed.

**15.** ...But constant collisions and conflicts will arise, leading to countless other tendencies <note>original: "determinations"</note>, many of them contradictory, even while the common form and action continue. This leads to corrupt <note>original: "perverse"</note> states reaching even the innermost parts, though the battle begins between external and internal changes. If the external forces win, the internal state is corrupted; if the internal forces win, the soul celebrates its triumph, and as it were deadens <note>original: "mortifies"</note> and extinguishes the external states to assert its liberty.

**16.** From these things, it is clear how the inner person struggles against the outer person within the rational mind.

---

**17.** Distinct sounds within the internal sense faculty <note>original: "sensory"</note> are called ideas; these are either sensory, imaginative, or intellectual.

**18.** These same ideas are simply changes of state within the organic or cortical substances.

**19.** These changes of state are recorded in the same way as memories.

**20.** Therefore, the memory is a field formed by both the external and internal senses.

->F.<-

### CONCLUSION REGARDING THE INTELLECT AND ITS OPERATION.

The intellect and its faculties—the rational mind—are granted to the human race so that we may explore truths. We do this by rationally deriving universal principles from individual instances <note>original: "universals from singulars"</note> and general concepts from specific details <note>original: "generals from particulars"</note>. Thus, we move from effects to their causes, or from what follows to what came before <note>original: "priors from posteriors; translating the logic of a priori and a posteriori reasoning"</note>, and from specific types to broad categories...

<summary>This page applies the mathematical rules of musical harmony to the workings of the brain and the struggle between the internal and external man, while defining the intellect as the tool for deriving universal truths from sensory data.</summary>
<keywords>harmony, cortical substance, rational mind, intellect, memory, cause and effect, universals, psychology, Swedenborg</keywords>

--- Page 407 ---
<meta>This page continues a discussion on the operations of the human intellect, specifically how the mind categorizes information and uses logic to ascend from simple observations to spiritual wisdom.</meta>

<page-num>367</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX II.</header>

...groups from their species, and species from individuals; in this way, we also derive varieties from differences, and from these, qualities, accidents <note>original: "accedents"; in philosophy, these are properties or qualities that are not essential to a thing's nature</note>, and modes from essences and the nature of their operations. Then, in a continuous series, we derive the greatest from the lesser, the lesser from the least, and thus determine quantities. We distinguish the simultaneous from the successive, the present from the past, and contingent events from both. These things are considered first in an analytic order <note>moving from effects to causes</note> and afterward in an inverted or synthetic order <note>moving from causes to effects</note>. This follows the method of rational analysis and logic, as well as geometrical or algebraic <term>specious analysis</term> <note>original: "specious analysis"; a historical term for algebra, which uses symbols or "species" rather than specific numbers</note>. The former carries its reasoning toward conclusions, while the latter carries it toward equations; then, in turn, the mind resolves both conclusions and equations and directs them toward their resulting goals.

Thus, truths—into which so many simpler truths enter as essential factors <note>original: "determinations"</note>—are produced like analytic forms. By means of these, our mind leads itself to the knowledge of good and evil, both in a natural and moral sense, and finally in a spiritual sense. These abilities are provided so that we may know how to choose the best path. From there, we are also able to investigate, judge, and select the intermediate <note>original: "mediate"</note> ends which lead to that ultimate or best goal, and to its possession and enjoyment. This is the true work of science and of wisdom.

To the extent that we are moved by the love of what is truly good—and especially of the supreme and best good—we are united to it. To that same extent, the state of our mind and soul is rendered happier and more perfect.

From these points, it follows that the primary purpose of the intellect given to us is that we may rise by degrees from a natural life into a moral life, and from a moral life into a spiritual life. Ultimately, we are to rise into heavenly happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>, which shall be the continuation of the spiritual life.

### APPENDIX III.
---

-> EXTRACTS FROM ARISTOTLE'S TREATISES ON PSYCHOLOGY.* <-

A.

FROM BOOK I., CHAPTER I.

"The soul is the vital principle <note>original: "principle"; here meaning the source, beginning, or animating essence</note> of living beings."
"Living <note>original: "Animated"</note> things possess the power of motion and sensation."
The remainder of Book I is occupied with a discussion of the various

-> ANCIENT DEFINITIONS OF THE SOUL. <-

**Democritus**: "A certain fire and heat."
"Spherical atoms are fire and soul."
"The soul imparts motion."

**Pythagoras**: "The soul is composed of motes <note>original: "motes"; tiny particles of dust visible in a sunbeam</note> in the air."
"The soul is that which moves these."

**Anaxagoras**: "The soul is that which moves."

**Empedocles**: "It is composed of all the elements <note>earth, air, fire, and water</note>, and each of these is soul."

**Plato**, in the *Timaeus* <note>one of Plato’s famous dialogues concerning the nature of the physical world and human beings</note>, describes the soul as being produced by the elements.

**Aristotle**, in the *Philosophy*:—"The living being <note>original: "Animal"</note> comes from the idea of the One."
"The first length and breadth and depth."
"Intellect is unity <note>oneness</note>, Knowledge <note>original: "Science"</note> is the number two, Opinion is a number of surfaces."
"Sensation <note>original: "Sense"</note> is the number of a solid."
"Numbers are said to be the forms of things and the basic principles of all beings, for they consist of elements."

**Xenocrates** <note>original: "Zenocrates"</note>: "The soul is a number that moves itself."

**Anaxagoras**: "The soul and the intellect <note>mind</note> are different. Intellect is specifically the source <note>original: "principle"</note> of all existence—the only thing that is simple, unmixed, and pure."

**Diogenes**: "The soul is air."

**Heraclitus**: "A primary source, a vapor <note>original: "exhalation"</note>, from which all other things are made."

**Alcmaeon**: "An immortal being that is constantly in motion."

**Hippo**: "The soul is water—the reproductive seed."

**Critias**: "The soul is blood. Sensation exists within the soul because of the nature of blood."

"Everyone agrees in defining the soul by three attributes: motion, sensation, and its non-physical nature."

"Those who define the soul by its capacity for knowledge consider it to be an element or made from elements." Thus they argue, "Like is known by like; since the soul knows all things, it must be composed of all primary principles."

### CHAPTER III.

"If the soul moves, it must occupy a space."

"If the soul is moved, it is moved by things perceived through the senses <note>original: "sensibles"</note>."

"The soul appears to move the body through a kind of choice <note>original: "pre-election"</note> and intellect."

"Because of the connection between the body and the soul, the one acts while the other is acted upon <note>original: "suffers"; in this context, it means to be the recipient of an action</note>; one is moved while the other initiates movement."

### CHAPTER IV.

Another opinion is that—

"The soul is a certain harmony."

"Harmony is a specific mixture and composition of opposite qualities."

"But the soul cannot be one of those things that are mixed."

"Harmony does not *move* things, as the soul does."

"The soul cannot be moved from place to place, except *as it exists within subjects that are moved*."

### CHAPTER V.

"To say that the soul is angry is just as if someone should say that the soul weaves or builds."

This is not as if these functions were naturally located inside the soul, but rather that motion sometimes travels toward the soul, and sometimes originates from it. For example, sensation—"

> “Is ‘to know’ the act of being affected by things that are similar, and does the soul ‘know’ things by being similar to them? How does it know the collected whole, or God?”

> “We learn through opposites <note>original: "contrariety"</note>; for by understanding what is straight, we know both the straight and the crooked, since a measuring rule is the judge of both. However, that which is crooked is a judge of neither itself nor of the straight.”

---

# BOOK II., CHAPTER I.

### WHAT IS THE SOUL, AND WHAT IS ITS COMMON DEFINITION?

> “The soul is an essence, or the form of a natural body that possesses the potential for life. This essence is the *actualization* <note>original: "entelecheia"; the state of a thing having reached its full functional purpose</note>. It is the actualization of such a body, and this is described in two ways: partly as knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, and partly as the active use of knowledge <note>original: "contemplation"</note>. The soul exists as knowledge. Because the soul is present, there is both sleep and wakefulness; wakefulness is like the *actual* act of contemplation, while sleep is like having the power <note>potential</note> without the active energy. In the development of a being, however, the potential for knowledge comes first.”

Hence,
The soul is the first actualization <note>original: "entelecheia"</note> of a natural body possessing the potential <note>original: "capacity"</note> for life; but such a body is one that is organic.
*It is therefore:*
> “The first actualization of a natural organic body.”
> “As the eye consists of both the pupil *and* the sight, so the living being <note>original: "animal"</note> consists of both soul *and* body.”
> “The soul cannot be separated from the body, as it is the very actualization <note>original: "entelecheia"</note> of it.”

<vocab>soul, intellect, entelecheia, dianoetically, divinity, contrariety, potentiality, organic body</vocab>

He highlights that the soul provides the body with its form and functional life, making the two inseparable in a living being.</summary>
