### CHAPTER II.

> "Animals are living things which have senses."
> "The intellect appears to be a different kind <note>original: "genus"</note> of soul, and it seems that this alone can be separated, in the same way the eternal is separated from the perishable <note>original: "corruptible"</note>. But regarding the other parts of the soul, it is clear they are *not* separable, as some claim."
> "Essence is defined in three ways: form, matter, and the combination of the two. Matter is potentiality; form is actuality <note>original Greek: *entelecheia*</note>. That which consists of both is alive <note>original: "animated"</note>; however, the body is not the actuality of the soul, but the soul is the actuality of a specific body. Therefore, those who believe the soul is neither without a body nor is a body itself are correct; for it is not a body, but something belonging to a body."
> "*The soul is the actuality <note>original: "entelecheia"</note>, the reason behind that which has the capacity of being a specific thing*" (or the reason why a thing has the potential power <note>original: "potency"</note> of being a specific thing instead of something else. — *Editor's note*).

### CHAPTER III.

->THE POWERS OF THE SOUL.<-

These are:—

Nutritive <note>nourishing</note>, sensitive <note>pertaining to the senses</note>, orectic <note>pertaining to desire or appetite</note>, locomotive <note>moving from place to place</note>, and dianoetic <note>pertaining to logical or discursive reasoning</note>.

*Plants* have nutritive power; some beings have both nutritive and sensitive powers. If a being has senses, it also has desire <note>original: *orexis* or appetite</note>; for desire includes longing, anger, and will.

*Animals:* all have the sense of touch and thus are sensitive beings. Touch is the sense of nourishment <note>original: "aliments"; referring here to taste</note>. Touch is the sense of dry and moist, of hot and cold. Hunger is the desire for the hot and dry; thirst is the desire for the moist and cold. Animals also have powers of movement <note>original: "locomotive powers"</note>.

*Man:* "Humans possess the power of reasoning <note>original: "dianoetic power"</note> and intellect. No sense can exist without touch, but touch can exist without the other senses."
"Animals that possess senses have only a very slight capacity for reasoning and the power of logic <note>original: "dianoetic power"</note>."

## CHAPTER V.

### WHAT IS SENSATION IN GENERAL?

> "Sensation occurs as a result of something being moved and affected <note>original: suffering; in this philosophical context, to 'suffer' means to be acted upon by an external force</note>, for it appears to be a specific change in quality."

> "The power of the senses does not exist in a state of realization <note>original: actuality</note> but in a state of potentiality; it does not perceive itself."

> "Sensation in action <note>original: energy</note> is the perception of specific details <note>original: particulars</note>; scientific knowledge pertains to general principles <note>original: universals</note>, and these are, in a certain way, within the soul. Therefore, we may engage in intellectual thought whenever we wish; but it is not in our power to perceive things through the senses at will, for a physical object must be present to be sensed."

> "The power of the senses is affected <note>original: suffers</note> by something unlike itself; but once affected, it becomes similar to it and takes on the nature of the object being perceived."

But the common sensibles <note>properties perceived by more than one sense, such as sight and touch together</note> are:—**motion, rest, number, shape <note>original: figure</note>, and size <note>original: magnitude</note>.**

## CHAPTER VII.
### THE SENSE OF SIGHT.

> "Light is neither fire, nor a physical body, nor the flowing out <note>original: effluxion</note> of any body; rather, it is the presence of fire or something of this kind in that which is transparent <note>original: diaphanous</note>; for it is impossible for two physical bodies to occupy the same place at the same time."
> "Color moves that which is transparent—for example, the air; and by this medium, which is continuous, the organ of sensation <term>sensorium</term> is moved. It is impossible for the organ to be passively affected by the color itself that is seen; it must, therefore, be affected by an intermediate medium. Hence, there must be a medium; and if there were a vacuum, we would not only fail to see accurately, but nothing would be seen at all. The same is true of sound and color; for neither of these produces sensation by directly touching the sensory organ. Instead, the intermediate medium is moved by odor and sound, and from this medium, each sensory organ is affected. If one places the object that sounds or smells directly upon the sensory organ, he will produce no sensation."
> "The intermediate medium for sound is air; for odor, the medium is unnamed <note>original: anonymous</note>, for there is a certain common quality in both air and water that allows them to be acted upon. Just as the transparent medium relates to color, so does that shared nature in air and water relate to odor; for aquatic animals also appear to have a sense of smell, but humans and those land animals that breathe <note>original: respire</note> are incapable of smelling without breathing."

## CHAPTER VIII.
### SOUND AND HEARING.

> "Not every sound made by an animal is a voice <note>original: word</note>, for it is possible to produce sound with the tongue as one does when coughing; but it is necessary that the thing which strikes should be a living being <note>original: animated</note>, and accompanied by a certain mental image <note>original: phantasy</note>; since a voice <note>original: word</note> is a specific, meaningful sound, and is not simply the sound of breathed air, like a cough."

## CHAPTER IX.
### SMELL.

> "The sense of smell in humans is inferior to its quality in animals. Because odors are not very distinct to us, we borrow names for them from the sense of taste, such as sweet, sharp <note>original: acrid</note>, and so on.

Humans smell only when breathing in <note>original: respiring</note>; when breathing out or holding the breath, they..."

## CHAPTER X.
### TASTE.

> That which can be tasted <term>gustable</term> is something that can be touched; it is not perceived through an intermediate medium <note>unlike sight or sound, which require air or water to travel through</note>. Only moisture produces the sense of flavor <term>sapor</term>, and flavor is what constitutes the tasteable.

## CHAPTER XI.
### THE TOUCH AND THE TANGIBLE.

> The sense located in the sensory organ <term>sensorium</term> does not perceive on its own, but perceives when it is situated in the flesh; therefore, the flesh is the medium for the sense of touch.

## CHAPTER XII.
### THE SENSES GENERALLY.

> A sense is that which receives the forms of things without receiving their physical matter. For example, wax receives the impression of a seal without taking the metal of the seal itself.

The physical organ that perceives has a certain size <term>magnitude</term>; however, neither the essence of the sensory power nor the sense itself is a physical size. Instead, sense is a specific proportion <note>original: reason; here meaning a functional or mathematical ratio</note> and power belonging to that size.

# BOOK III., CHAPTER III.
## THE FIVE SENSES.

> To perceive through the senses is not the same as intellectual perception. Sensory perception is always accurate regarding its specific object and is present in all animals. However, it is possible to perceive falsely through intellectual thought <term>dianoetic energy</term>, and this power belongs only to those animals possessing reason <note>meaning humans</note>. Imagination <term>phantasy</term> is different from both the senses and the power of thought. Imagination does not exist without the senses, and belief <term>hypolepsis</term> <note>original: opinion; from the Greek word for a strong conviction or assumption</note> does not exist without imagination. However, imagination and belief are not the same thing: imagination is within our control; we can imagine objects and create mental images at will. It is not within our control to form beliefs whenever we please, because a belief must necessarily be either false or true. When believing something terrible, we are emotionally affected <term>co-passive</term> <note>original: sympathetic; meaning we suffer along with the thought</note>; in imagination, we are affected only as if we were looking at a frightening painting.

<header>APPENDIX III.</header>

**Judgment <term>hypolepsis</term> includes: science, opinion, wisdom <note>original: prudence</note>, and their opposites.***

## CHAPTER IV.
### IMAGINATION <term>PHANTASY</term> AND JUDGMENT <term>HYPOLEPSIS</term>.

"Intellectual perception, which differs from sensory perception, includes both **imagination** <term>phantasy</term> and **judgment** <term>hypolepsis</term>."

**Imagination** <term>phantasy</term> is not the same as the senses: [it sees its visions as if in sleep, without using the senses]. The senses are always present, but imagination is not. Animals have senses, but they do not have imagination. The senses are always true <note>meaning they accurately report physical stimuli</note>, but imaginations are mostly false. Opinion—which is formed neither with the senses nor through the senses, nor by the conjunction of opinion and sense—is not the same as imagination.

Opinion does not concern some other thing entirely, but rather the very thing that the sense perceives.

The mental connection—formed from both opinion and sensation—of something being white (for example), is what constitutes imagination.

## CHAPTER V.
### HOW INTELLECTUAL PERCEPTION IS PRODUCED.

"The intellect of the soul is only intellect in potentiality; its only nature is that it is possible <note>it is a capacity that can be filled</note>."

"The intellect of the soul (I mean the intellect by which the soul acts **rationally** <term>dianoetically</term> and **judgmentally** <term>hypoleptically</term>) is nothing in the actual reality of beings before it perceives them intellectually. It is not reasonable to think that it is mixed with the body, for if it were, it would take on a certain physical quality—it would be hot or cold and would have a physical organ like the sensory powers. However, it has no physical organ. Those who say the soul is the 'place of forms' speak correctly; though this is not true of the whole soul, but only of the intellective part. Nor are its forms present in **actualization** <term>entelecheia</term> <note>original: entelecheia; a Greek term for the state in which a potential is fully realized</note>, but only in capacity."

"The lack of physical influence <note>original: impassiveness</note> in the sensory and intellective powers is not similar. A sense cannot perceive anything after encountering an intense <note>original: vehement</note> sensory object <note>such as a blinding light or deafening noise</note>; but the intellect, when it understands something highly intelligible <note>abstract or complex</note>, does not understand simpler matters any less. In fact, it understands them even better, because the sensory power cannot exist without the body, but the intellect is separate [from the body]."

"Through the sensory power, the soul distinguishes between hot and cold and those things that make up the physical body <note>original: flesh</note>; but by another power—either separate or existing in a reflective <note>original: inflected</note> relationship to itself—it distinguishes the essence of the body. The very nature of a thing (for instance, if the essence of a 'straight line' is different from a physical 'straight object') it distinguishes by another power. It judges, therefore, by another power, or by a power existing in a different way..."

...manner. In short, just as some things are separate from matter, so too are the things belonging to the intellect.

Someone might wonder:
> "If the intellect is simple and unaffected <note>original: impassive</note> and has nothing in common with anything—as Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who argued that "Mind" (Nous) is the ordering force of the cosmos</note> says—how can it perceive intellectually? If intellectual perception involves being acted upon <note>original: to suffer something</note>, then there must be something common between the intellect and the object; otherwise, one could not act and the other be affected. Again, one might ask whether the intellect itself can be understood <note>original: is intelligible</note>. Either the intellect will be found within other things (assuming it isn’t understood through something else, but is its own distinct kind), or it must contain some mixed element that allows it to be understood in the same way other things are. Or should we say that the ability to be affected depends on having something in common? This is why we previously noted that the intellect is potentially all things that can be understood, but it is none of these in actual reality <term>entelecheia</term> <note>original Greek: entelecheia; the state of being complete or fully realized</note> until it understands or perceives them intellectually."
> "We should think of the intellect like a tablet on which nothing is yet actually <note>original: in entelecheia</note> written. This is the state of the intellect. It can be understood just like other objects of thought. *For in things that lack matter, the intellect and the object of its thought are the same.* Theoretical science and the object of that knowledge are one and the same. We must, however, consider why the intellect does not always perceive things. In things that contain matter, each object of thought <note>original: intelligibles</note> exists only potentially. Therefore, the intellect is not found within them, because the intellect for such things is a capacity without matter. However, the object of thought will be present within the intellect."

### CHAPTER VI.

Since all things must have the "matter" capable of becoming anything within its category <note>original: genus</note>, as well as an active and effective cause that produces these things, these same differences must exist in the soul. One part is the intellect that *becomes* all things, while the other is the intellect that *produces* all things.

For example, light causes potential colors to become actual colors. This [productive] intellect is separate, unmixed, and unaffected <note>original: impassive</note>, because its very essence is activity <note>original: energy</note>. The active force <note>original: the efficient</note> is more noble than the passive one <note>original: the patient</note>, just as the starting principle is superior to matter. Knowledge in action <note>original: science in energy</note> is the same as the thing known, though potential knowledge comes first in time within the individual.

---

* By *objects of thought* <note>original: intelligibles</note> here, Aristotle refers to separate essences or ideas themselves—that is, beings that are truly and essentially able to be understood. Thus, Aristotle indicates that our intellect is immaterial and separate, since it can be understood in the same way as these truly intelligible beings. [Note by Thomas Taylor <note>Thomas Taylor (1758–1835) was a famous English translator of Aristotle and Plato</note>]

It introduces the distinction between the passive intellect (which becomes all things) and the active intellect (which produces thought, much like light produces color).</summary>

<header>APPENDIX III.</header>

...though, in short, neither potentiality <note>original: potency</note> nor actuality <note>original: energy</note> comes first in time. However, the intellect does not think intermittently—perceiving at one time and not at another—but the separate intellect is purely its own essence <note>original: "this *very thing which it is*"</note>,* and this alone is immortal and eternal. However, we do not remember [this eternal state] because this intellect is unaffected by experience <term>impassive</term> <note>original: impassive; meaning it is not changed or influenced by external things</note>. On the other hand, the passive intellect is subject to decay, and without the separate intellect, it understands nothing.

### CHAPTER VII.

> “The intellect understands evil or blackness, in a certain respect, ‘by its opposite.’”

### CHAPTER VIII.

> “When the intellect judges something to be good or evil <note>original: affirms or denies</note>, it either seeks it or avoids it. Therefore, the soul never thinks without a mental image <term>phantasm</term> <note>original: phantasm; a mental representation or image necessary for thought in Aristotle's system</note>. . . . Sometimes the intellectual power looks at the mental images or concepts within the soul to reason and deliberate about future events based on present circumstances. Once it has determined, within the mental image, that a thing is pleasant or painful, it then pursues or avoids it; in short, it acts. Truth and falsehood—even when they do not lead to action—belong to the same category as good and evil.”
> “If the intellect should understand anything in its active state <note>original: in energy</note>—for instance, a cavity—it will understand it separately from the physical flesh in which that cavity exists. In this way, it understands mathematical forms as separate entities, even though they are not actually separate from the objects they form. In short, the intellect, when actively understanding, becomes one with the very things it understands.”
> “Although the external senses are many, the ultimate sense where all sensory information <note>original: sensible energies</note> ends is a single unit, even though it is multifaceted in its nature. Through this ultimate and 'common sense,' the soul distinguishes between the different qualities of objects perceived by the various senses.”
> “Just as there is one sense that judges all physical objects, so too is there one practical intellect that judges all mental images or objects of the imagination.”
> “Just as the common sense observes and judges the physical things <note>original: sensibles</note> known by the individual senses, the practical intellect observes the forms of things represented by mental images and known through the power of imagination. When the common sense distinguishes physical objects, it is prompted to seek or avoid them; similarly, the practical intellect considers mental images—even when the physical objects are not present—and by reasoning that something should be avoided or pursued, it is moved to action.”

---

* Compare Swedenborg’s concept of "being itself" <note>original Latin: *ipsum esse*</note>.

<summary>This page summarizes Aristotle's views on the "common sense" and the "practical intellect," explaining how the soul uses mental images to reason and make moral or practical choices. It also distinguishes between the immortal, active intellect and the perishable, passive intellect.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, De Anima, active intellect, passive intellect, phantasm, common sense, practical intellect, potentiality, actuality, Swedenborg, ipsum esse</keywords>

--- Page 418 ---
<meta>This page continues Swedenborg’s collection of citations from Aristotle’s works, specifically moving from the nature of the intellect and mental images to the mechanics of physical motion, sensory perception, and the biological "heat" required for life.</meta>

<page-num>378</page-num>
<header>THE SOUL.</header>

### CHAPTER IX.

> "A stone is not physically inside the soul, but the *form* of the stone is. The soul is, as it were, a hand; just as the hand is the tool of tools <term>organ of organs</term>, the intellect is the form of forms, and the senses are the forms of things that can be perceived <note>original: sensibles</note>."
> "When the intellect contemplates, it must contemplate a specific mental image <term>phantasm</term> <note>original: phantasm; in Aristotelian philosophy, these are the mental 'pictures' derived from the senses that the mind uses to think</note>; for mental images are like sensory objects, except they lack physical matter. The faculty of imagination <term>phantasy</term> differs from making affirmative or negative statements, because truth or falsehood consists of the *connection of mental concepts*."

### CHAPTER XI.

->THE ORIGIN OF MOTION<-
<note>original: The Genesis of Motion</note>

> "There are three components to motion: first, that which sets something in motion; second, the means by which it moves; and third, the thing that is moved.
> "The source of motion <note>original: what moves</note> is twofold: one part is immovable, and the other part is both a mover and is itself moved.
> "The immovable part is the 'practical good' <note>The desired goal or end-result that motivates an action without moving itself</note>. That which moves others and is itself moved is the *appetitive power* (since a being that desires is moved in proportion to its desire, and appetite is a form of motion since it is an active energy).
> "The thing being moved is the animal; and the organ by which the appetite causes motion is physical <term>corporeal</term>."

### CHAPTER XII.

> "Animals possess the sense of *touch* for the sake of *survival* <note>original: existence</note>; however, they possess all other senses for the sake of *living well*."
> "An animal cannot exist without the sense of touch."
> "Touch perceives by coming into direct contact with objects themselves; all other senses also perceive by contact, but *through other substances acting as mediums* <note>such as air for sound or light for sight</note>."

---

### B.

->ON THE GENERATION OF ANIMALS<-
<note>original: De Generatione Animalium</note>

> "Within the seed of every animal, there is an inherent quality that makes the seed fertile <note>original: prolific</note>, namely, what is called 'heat.' This, however, is not fire, nor a power similar to fire, but a spirit contained within the seed and its foam-like substance. The nature of the spirit is similar to the element that makes up the stars. Therefore, fire does not produce <term>germinate</term> animals... rather, it is the heat of the sun and the heat of animals together that possess this vital heat." — (*On the Generation of Animals*, Book II.)

<vocab>intellect, mental image <note>original: phantasm</note>, imagination <note>original: phantasy</note>, motion, appetitive power, touch, existence, seed, spirit, vital heat, On the Generation of Animals</vocab>

<summary>This page contains citations from Aristotle regarding the relationship between the soul and mental forms, the mechanics of animal motion driven by desire, and the essential nature of the sense of touch. It also explores the concept of "vital heat" in reproduction, comparing it to the substance of the stars rather than ordinary fire.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, intellect, phantasms, appetitive power, sensory perception, touch, vital heat, generation of animals, rational psychology</keywords>

<header>APPENDIX IV.</header>

# APPENDIX IV.

## ERRORS IN THE TEXT OF THE LATIN EDITION, PROPOSED BY THE TRANSLATOR.
<note>These corrections refer to the Latin version of Swedenborg's manuscript edited by Immanuel Tafel, the scholar responsible for publishing many of Swedenborg's works in the 19th century.</note>

Page 113, line 6 from the bottom, for **because/for** <note>original: nam; noted as a doubtful reading (lectio dubia) by Tafel</note> read **not** <note>original: non</note>.
Page 121, line 18, for **we see** <note>original: videmus</note> read **we seem** <note>original: videmur</note>.
Page 128, line 3, for **which** <note>original: quae (feminine/neuter plural)</note> read **who/which** <note>original: qui (masculine singular/plural)</note>.
Page 157, line 10, for **we hate** <note>original: odimus</note> restore the original **we approach** <note>original: adimus</note>, which was changed by Tafel.
Page 160, line 2 from the bottom, for **they are received** <note>original: recipiuntur</note> read **they receive** <note>original: recipiunt</note>.
Page 171, line 3 from the bottom, for **stored away** <note>original: reposta</note> read **stored away** <note>original: repostus (matching masculine gender)</note>.
Page 191, line 14 from the bottom, for **which** <note>original: quae</note> read **who/which** <note>original: qui</note>.
Page 251, line 14 from the bottom, for **and they can be joined together** <note>original: et consociari possunt</note> read **so that they might be joined together** <note>original: ut consociari possint</note>.
